m-fe665ebc.t: SumUp's Cyprus help centre (article 'Bank account compatibility', el-CY, undated, read 6 October 2026) lets a sole trader receive payouts into a personal bank account: under 'I am a sole trader' the account must be held in a euro-area country, and its holder must match the SumUp profile holder 'for personal accounts' or the registered business name 'for business bank accounts'; one account at a time. The same article says that separating personal and business money 'is necessary' for compliance with anti-money-laundering standards, linking Directive (EU) 2018/843, without making a separate account a condition.

m-fbe6472d.t: Whether a new Cyprus business must accept cards for payments by consumers turns on its main activity code. Decree K.D.P. 259/2021 under art. 30A of Law 4/1978 listed 87 codes; K.D.P. 52/2022 added taxis (49.32) and K.D.P. 248/2022 four personal-service codes (96.01, 96.03, 96.04, 96.09). The list takes in most in-store retail codes from 47.11 to 47.78 and restaurants and bars (56.10, 56.30), but not retail via mail order or internet (47.91), computer programming or IT consultancy (62) or management consultancy (70.22). A listed business that starts after the original deadline must comply within one month of starting (para. 3(δ)). cylaw's indexes to K.D.P. 372/2026 show no later amendment.

m-e721de2e.t: JCC's merchant application form (version 2.2, Internet Archive copy of 11 June 2026; the live v2.3 file answered a bot check on 6 October 2026) offers a 'Natural Person' merchant category beside 'Company/Legal Entity', asks for the merchant name 'exactly as it appears on the Bank system', and has fields 'Reg. No', 'TIC' and 'VAT' without saying which a natural person must fill. Its bank block is headed 'current account is mandatory' and does not ask for a business account; the form must be signed, and the 'Merchant Stamp' is marked mandatory. A €17 one-off registration fee is debited to that account.

m-d7020ae5.t: Stripe's 'Acceptable verification documents' page for Cyprus (read 6 October 2026) has no separate rule for a company owned by another company: ownership may be shown by articles, a certificate of corporate status, a partnership agreement, a registration document or the beneficial-owner register, directorship also by annual reports, and director and UBO 'digital attestation' templates are offered; it needs the entity name and, where applicable, all director, shareholder and beneficial-owner names and positions. Identity and entity documents 'must be current and not expired'; if a person's country lists no address documents, a utility bill or bank statement 'issued within the last 6 months'.

m-d363bdbc.t: Some one-person service businesses in Cyprus do fall under the duty to accept cards for consumer payments. The Annex of Decree K.D.P. 259/2021 (read 6 October 2026) lists legal activities (69.10), accounting, bookkeeping, auditing and tax consultancy (69.20), architects (71.11), engineering and related technical consultancy (71.12), photography (74.20), veterinary activities (75.00), education codes such as 85.51, 85.53 and 85.59, medical and dental practice (86.21-86.23) and computer repair (95.11). No amendment after K.D.P. 248/2022 appears in cylaw's indexes to K.D.P. 372/2026.

m-c1debd8c.t: Per providers' texts read 4-6 October 2026 (no sign-up tested), for a Cyprus self-employed person in his own name: JCC has a 'Natural Person' category (paper form, stamp marked mandatory, current account); myPOS admits a sole trader on his home address; SumUp has a sole-trader type; Viva's general guide has 'freelancer accounts'; Revolut's terms cover Pro accounts, Cyprus Pro pages seen only in 2025 copies; Stripe takes Cyprus-resident individuals, Terminal in preview; Shopify Payments takes an unregistered resident; Wise's card acceptance is closed to new customers. JCC has TIC and VAT fields, Viva asks a registry or VAT number, Wise a tax or VAT number; none asks a social insurance number.

m-b025f1fb.t: myPOS's Legal Agreement for the myPOS Service (Cyprus edition on merchant.mypos.com/en-cy, last updated 3 April 2026, read 6 October 2026) admits a sole trader on his personal address: clause 3.1 requires the business to be established 'with an address in a country that is part of the EEA (registered address or personal address, if you apply as a sole trader)', full legal capacity, age 18 or over, any licences required, and use of the service 'solely for your business activity'; clause 3.3 forbids using it for 'personal purposes that are not related to your business'. Card takings are credited to the merchant's myPOS e-money account.

m-ad2a1f87.t: Decree K.D.P. 446/2021 (Official Gazette Annex III(I) No. 5624, 5 November 2021, in force on publication) added to the Annex of Cyprus's card-acceptance decree K.D.P. 259/2021 the codes 85.10.2 private kindergartens, 85.52 cultural education and 74.10 specialised design activities; payees with those main codes had three months from publication to comply, later starters one month from starting. With K.D.P. 52/2022 (taxis) and 248/2022 (four personal-service codes) it is one of three amending decrees; cylaw's K.D.P. indexes 2021-2026 (to K.D.P. 372/2026, read 6 October 2026) show no later one.

m-aca24003.t: myPOS's English help centre says it supports 'Sole traders', 'Self-employed individuals', 'Freelancers', 'Private limited liability companies', 'Public companies' and 'Partnerships (and their local equivalents in Europe)' registered and operating in the EU, the EEA, the UK or Switzerland, which 'can be owned or directed by nationals from other countries as well'; bearer-share companies are among unsupported industries. Read in web-archive snapshots of 14 October 2025 (English) and 5 August 2025 (Cyprus Greek edition, where the partnership item reads 'Συνεταιρισμοί', cooperatives); the live article was behind a Cloudflare challenge on 6 October 2026; its current wording was not seen.

m-8be92df3.t: JCC's own FAQ on the card-acceptance decree (Internet Archive copy of 11 June 2026; live page behind a bot check on 6 October 2026) says JCC lets merchants 'use their existing current accounts, regardless of the local bank they belong' for crediting card takings, credits them 'the next business day', and rents its POS terminals only ('not available for sale'). It offers fixed and wireless POS, a SoftPOS app for NFC Android phones, pay-by-link through JCCsmart and JCCgateway for websites; to become a merchant one downloads the form, signs, stamps and e-mails it with the documents. The page still gives the fine as 'up to €4000', a ceiling raised to €6,000 from 1 January 2026.

m-87f1a104.t: Revolut Bank UAB's Payment Processing Terms (version applying from 28 September 2026, read 6 October 2026) cover card acceptance through a Revolut Business account 'or your Revolut Pro account'. A Pro customer applies with information on his activity as a 'freelancer' or 'sole trader', which 'might include' website, merchant category code, average and highest ticket, monthly volumes, chargeback ratio, 'tax information' and countries of activity; if accepted, the service is switched on in the Pro account itself. Takings are settled 'into the relevant Revolut Business account or Revolut Pro account in your name'; Revolut may suspend or cut settlement for disputes, fraud or sums owed.

m-85af87ac.t: Stripe's support article 'Verify your bank account ownership' (not country-specific, modified 6 October 2026, read the same day) sets whose name the payout bank account must carry by business type: for an 'Individual', the 'Account owner name or DBA name listed on your Stripe account'; for a 'Sole proprietor or single-member LLC', the legal business name, trading (DBA) name or representative name; for a company, partnership or charity, the company's legal or trading name. The test is the name on the account; the article does not say whether a personal or a business account is required.

m-81957881.t: Shopify's Cyprus requirements page (undated, read 6 October 2026) says that from June 2026 brand-new Shopify Payments Cyprus accounts have 90 days from the first order processed to complete verification; after 90 days 'any orders that you processed using Shopify Payments might be automatically refunded'. A missed verification deadline first pauses payouts, then possibly order acceptance; the pauses lift once verification is done. The refund rule applies only to European countries and to accounts created on or after June 2026.

m-7b33a9a8.t: Shopify Payments, which Shopify lists as available in Cyprus, takes a one-person business with no registration at all: its Cyprus requirements page (undated, read 6 October 2026) says to choose 'Individual / Sole Trader' if 'you haven't registered with any government agency, or you have registered but run the business as a sole trader', for one owner 'living in Cyprus', freelancers included. Such a seller gives legal name, date of birth, e-mail, phone and a Cyprus home address; no tax or VAT number is listed for this type, unlike a company. Payouts need a euro SEPA account with an IBAN from listed countries; savings, multi-currency and money-transfer-service accounts are refused.

m-65807939.t: JCC's merchant application form v2.2 (created 23 April 2026; identical files at upload paths 2026/04 and 2026/05, read in web-archive copies) asks, for a company, the 'certificate of registered shareholders' of each company holding directly or indirectly 25% or more of it, a director-signed extract of the beneficial-owner register, and ID and address proof of directors, direct shareholders, signatories and ultimate beneficial owners. Its only age rule: proof of residential address 'must be up to 6 months old'; nothing on apostille, translation or the age of company certificates, and JCC 'reserves the right' to ask for more. The current v2.3 (August 2026) could not be read on 6 October 2026.

m-45a70ae1.t: Revolut's card acquiring for Revolut Pro accounts did not start on 28 September 2026: the Payment Processing Terms version applying from 17 November 2025 (Revolut Bank UAB, PDF eeff7f25 v1.1.0, linked from the current version as the terms that apply until 28 September 2026; read 6 October 2026) already require 'a Revolut Business account or Revolut Pro account' and carry the same paragraph on Pro applicants as 'freelancer' or 'sole trader'. Both versions say Revolut 'will always withhold' a Reserve of each transaction, 'anywhere between 0% and 100%', for a period at its discretion.

m-377082ee.t: Wise's Cyprus page 'Accept card payments' (wise.com/cy, read 6 October 2026) carries the banner 'This feature to accept card payments is currently unavailable to new Wise Business customers'. For businesses registered in the European Economic Area it lists fees of 1% for EEA consumer cards and 2.9% for non-EEA consumer cards and for business cards, no monthly fee, card payments through payment links, invoices and QR codes, and payment into the Wise account. A self-employed person opening Wise now therefore cannot take cards through it, on Wise's own page.

m-35871b5a.t: Viva.com's 'Getting Started: Onboarding & Activation Guide' (not country-specific, updated 2 September 2026, read 6 October 2026) provides for 'freelancer accounts': the Expected Annual Turnover field 'does not appear for freelancer accounts', and for freelancers the signatory to select is 'the business owner', whereas legal entities select their registered legal representatives. Business details are retrieved from 'your country's official registry' (gov.gr for Greece) and the application is reviewed under an Onboarding & Activation Policy that 'may vary slightly depending on your country and business type'. The guide does not say which Cyprus registry or number serves a freelancer.

m-30ef2137.t: Cyprus's card-acceptance rules say nothing about the account into which takings are paid. Art. 30A of Law 4/1978, Decree K.D.P. 259/2021 with amending K.D.P. 446/2021, 52/2022 and 248/2022, and the Tax Department's Implementing Directive 20/2021 (all read 6 October 2026) require no business bank account, registered business name or company. They regulate the means: a contract with a lawfully licensed payment service provider or its agent; four-party scheme cards accepted by POS, mobile or virtual POS (credit transfer, direct debit and e-banking do not count); notices at entrance and till. The directive: the duty applies 'regardless of' amount, turnover and VAT registration.

m-2d82f768.t: SumUp's developer documentation of its Merchant data model ('Last updated: Oct 5, 2026', read 6 October 2026) lists for Cyprus the legal type 'Ατομική επιχείρηση' (sole trader, code cy.sole_trader) beside private and public companies, companies limited by guarantee, general and limited partnerships, a cooperative type ('Συνεταιρισμός', code cy.associations), foundations and 'other'. The only Cyprus company identifiers it defines are the VAT registration number (cy.fpa) and the company registration number (cy.crn); it defines no Cyprus tax identification code, and the Cyprus personal identifier listed is the identity card. This is SumUp's API model, not its sign-up form.

m-1fb779ff.t: Cyprus's duty to accept cards can bind a self-employed person trading in his own name; no text names the self-employed, the reading rests on the definitions. Law 4/1978 (consolidated, read 6 October 2026) defines a 'payee' as 'the natural or legal person' that is the final recipient of the funds (Article 2(13) of Regulation (EU) 2015/751); art. 30A(1) obliges payees, in transactions with consumers, to accept cards as a decree sets by activity code, and K.D.P. 259/2021 (Annex amended by K.D.P. 446/2021, 52/2022 and 248/2022) binds payees whose main activity codes are listed. A 'consumer' acts outside his trade, business or profession, so payments by business clients fall outside the duty.

m-07030962.t: Revolut's Cyprus help centre article 'Who can use Revolut Pro and how do I get started?' (Internet Archive copy of 4 August 2025; the live page answered a security check on 6 October 2026) says Pro is for 'freelancers, side-hustlers, sole traders' and the self-employed, can be used 'if you're not registered in your local business registry (depending on regional requirements)', and 'isn't for legal entities or partnerships'. It is opened inside the personal Revolut app (Accounts, Add new, Pro account); the application asks a business category and description, and Revolut 'may ask for proof of business activity' or a URL (registration proof, website, social-media page, map link).

m-dfa5e875.t: Stripe's Tap to Pay on Android is also only in public preview for Cyprus. The Android tab of Stripe's Tap to Pay page, read 5 October 2026, lists 21 countries under 'Availability' and 18 under 'Availability in Public preview', Cyprus among the latter (with Bulgaria, Croatia, Czech Republic, Estonia, Gibraltar, Hong Kong, Hungary, Latvia, Liechtenstein, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Mexico, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia and Spain). The iPhone tab lists 22 and 17, Cyprus again in preview. So on that date neither phone-as-terminal product of Stripe was generally available to a Cyprus account.

m-d05e553f.t: Article 30B of Cyprus's Assessment and Collection of Taxes Law, inserted by Law 126(I)/2020 together with the card-acceptance duty, provides that transactions paid by card or another electronic payment instrument count towards a programme of public draws (lotteries) with cash or in-kind prizes charged to the state budget; a decree of the Council of Ministers is to set its duration, procedure, criteria and prizes. No such decree was found on 5 October 2026: the Tax Department's own list of decrees under the Law (K.D.P. 281/2015 to K.D.P. 260/2026) has none, and CyLaw's K.D.P. indexes for 2020-2026 show no decree on draws under this Law.

m-cd87e2aa.t: Times stated by card-acceptance providers on their own pages, read 5 Oct 2026. SumUp (Cyprus help centre): verification 'can take a few days'; a merchant who expects to reach the limit for unverified profiles soon may ask to have it speeded up. Stripe (support site): approval of a new account is 'in most cases ... nearly instantaneous', and a review of an uploaded proof-of-entity document 'can take up to 24 hours'. Viva: identification 'can take only a few minutes', after which the application is 'reviewed according to our Onboarding & Activation Policy', with no time given. JCC states none (archive copy of 11 June 2026; the live page answered with a bot check). None is a commitment.

m-a7621f97.t: ECB payment statistics (dataset PTN, compiled by the Central Bank of Cyprus) count POS terminals provided by Cyprus-resident payment service providers: 136,215 for 2022, 142,532 for 2023, 151,399 for 2024 and 181,874 for 2025. Most are located abroad: the cross-border series shows 92,806, 94,080, 104,622 and 132,670 (73% in 2025). The domestic series is suppressed (status Q) for 2019-2025 - last published 24,651 for 2017 and 26,878 for 2018 - but total minus cross-border leaves about 43,400, 48,500, 46,800 and 49,200 terminals in Cyprus. Terminals placed in Cyprus by providers passported from other states are outside this count. Read 5 October 2026.

m-a3f6490c.t: Bank of Cyprus changed its description of JCC Payment Systems Ltd in the subsidiaries tables of its annual reports while the holding stayed at 75%. The reports for 2016, 2017, 2019, 2021 and 2022 give the activity as 'Card processing transaction services'; the report for 2023 as 'Development of inter-banking systems processing of card transactions, other payment services and other activities'; the reports for 2024 and 2025 add the word acquiring: 'Development of inter-banking systems, acquiring and processing of card transactions, other payment services and other activities'. The reports for 2018 and 2020 were not opened.

m-8a3362ee.t: ECB detailed card statistics (dataflow PCP) give the point-of-sale location of payments acquired by Cyprus-resident providers. Of 1,576 million payments worth EUR 63.8 billion in 2025 (second half provisional), 369 million and EUR 20.1 billion were initiated at points of sale in Cyprus and 1,207 million and EUR 43.7 billion abroad - 77% by number, 68% by value; of those abroad, 903 million and EUR 31.0 billion in other EEA countries, 304 million and EUR 12.7 billion outside the EEA. In 2022 the share abroad was 79% by number and 62% by value. Cyprus-licensed acquirers thus work mainly for points of sale outside the island; acquirers passported into Cyprus are not in these figures.

m-89bda1c2.t: Bank of Cyprus disclosed a possible sale of JCC on 12 November 2024. Its results announcement for the nine months to 30 September 2024 says: 'In the context of its wider strategic evaluation, the Group is undertaking a strategic review which may result in a potential disposal of part or all of its holding in JCC, although no decision has been taken at this stage.' The same paragraph calls JCC 'a leading player in the card processing business and payment solutions, 75% owned by the Bank', with net fee and commission income of €21 million for the nine months. This is the earliest dated mention of the review found; the first-half 2024 release of 8 August 2024 was not located.

m-7e544298.t: Archive snapshots of Stripe's country page bracket the date Cyprus became a supported country. On 1 May 2020 stripe.com/global read 'Available for businesses in 37 countries' (35 listed plus 2 under 'Request an invite') and Cyprus appeared only in the drop-down for countries awaiting launch; on 1 June 2020 it read 'Available for businesses in 39 countries' (38 listed plus 1) with Cyprus, Bulgaria and Malta in the list. That agrees with Stripe's own announcement of a launch in Cyprus on 27 May 2020. The earliest archived capture of the Cyprus-locale Stripe Services Agreement (stripe.com/en-cy/ssa) is of 16 November 2020.

m-76f7461a.t: As of 5 October 2026 the Tax Department's Implementing Directives page on gov.cy (published 22 January 2026) lists 18 directives, 01/2020 to 20/2021: the newest is 20/2021 of 4 August 2021 on card acceptance, and none is dated 2022 or later. Its Circulars page lists 29 circulars numbered 2022/01 to 2026/03 (29 May 2026), none on card acceptance. The department's old mof.gov.cy file addresses now redirect to the gov.cy tax home page; the Internet Archive keeps its card-acceptance announcement of 24 September 2021 (PDF) and the page of a second one whose attachment, named '..._03_05_2022.pdf', was not captured.

m-7668d6ff.t: EcommBX Ltd (HE354749, Central Bank of Cyprus e-money licence 115.1.3.20/2018, services 2, 3, 5, 7, 8) calls itself a card acquirer and scheme member. Its business-acquiring page, in an Internet Archive snapshot of 12 June 2026, says 'As proud members of Visa and Mastercard, ECOMMBX is your number one worldwide payment service provider and direct acquirer', and the site footer (snapshots of 12 June and 31 August 2026) adds 'We provide acquiring services using the “ECOMMPAY” trademark under license'. The statement is at brand level and names no membership class; the two pages carry no price, merchant terms or prohibited list. On 4-5 October 2026 the live site failed on a certificate error.

m-672d832c.t: SumUp's Cyprus pages give two different rates for its €19-a-month Payments Plus plan, both read on 5 October 2026: the price page (sumup.com/el-cy/times) says 0.89% for in-person debit and credit card payments, while the help article 'Πόσο κοστίζουν οι συναλλαγές;' says 0.99% for all domestic transactions. The standard rates agree on both pages: 1.95% at terminals, 2.75% for payment links. The price page also promises payouts 'the next business day' at no extra charge, while the help article on payouts says they take 2-3 business days to arrive in a bank account once sent. SumUp reconciles neither pair.

m-60794614.t: As of 5 October 2026 no decree on card acceptance appears after K.D.P. 248/2022 of 24 June 2022 in either list of instruments made under the Assessment and Collection of Taxes Law: CyLaw's yearly indexes (to K.D.P. 372/2026) or the Tax Department's own page of decrees on gov.cy. Sixteen instruments followed - K.D.P. 315 and 373/2022; 183, 184 and 311/2023; 59, 209, 348, 359, 383 and 384/2024; 52, 176, 358 and 359/2025; 260/2026 - and every one extends a filing or payment deadline or exempts persons from filing a return (the Department lists all but 315/2022). Its announcement of 3 May 2023 names the same three amending decrees - K.D.P. 446/2021, 52/2022, 248/2022 - and no other.

m-5c04a67a.t: Article 50ΣΤ of Cyprus's Law 4/1978 sets a short procedure for the card-acceptance fine (consolidated text read 5 October 2026). The officer who finds the breach reports to the Tax Commissioner within five working days, and the decision imposing the fine is issued within fifteen working days of the report. The business may object to the Commissioner within 30 days of notification and the Commissioner decides within 30 days; the decision on the objection can be taken to the Administrative Court, and a fine already paid is returned if the objection or the action succeeds. An unpaid fine is recovered as a civil debt. Implementing Directive 05/2020 (3 November 2020) restates these steps.

m-51996425.t: The Cyprus Tax Department's announcement of 3 May 2023 names the decrees in force - K.D.P. 259/2021 and the amending K.D.P. 446/2021, 52/2022 and 248/2022 - recalls the administrative fine (then up to EUR 4,000) and says the department carries out continuous checks and examines every complaint, imposing the penalties the law requires 'without necessarily publicising the results or its actions'; it asks citizens to report breaches to complaints@tax.mof.gov.cy. No card-specific count of inspections or fines was found by 5 October 2026; press of 29 July 2026 reports 30 coastal businesses inspected in ten days, about half in breach on receipts or card acceptance, not split.

m-473de0f0.t: The Cyprus Tax Department's announcement of 24 September 2021 on the card-acceptance decree K.D.P. 259/2021 (read in an Internet Archive capture of 2 November 2021) gave the working dates: existing businesses had to comply by 18 September 2021; businesses that started in the last 30 days before that deadline, by 18 October 2021; a business that becomes obliged later, within one month of becoming so. The Department said it intended to carry out inspections 'within October 2021', recalled the duty to post a notice at the entrance and at the tills, gave the fine as up to EUR 2,000 and pointed to its Implementing Directive 20.

m-20690f7e.t: The Cyprus Tax Department's Implementing Directive 20/2021 'Acceptance of Card Payment Instruments', issued on 4 August 2021, is a one-page reading of Article 30A of Law 4/1978 and Decree K.D.P. 259/2021. It states that every payee whose economic activity is in the decree's Annex must accept card payments 'regardless of the amount of the payment, the turnover of the business and regardless of whether it is registered or obliged to register in the VAT Register', and that all obliged payees must keep a card-acceptance terminal 'at all tills without exception' and post a notice at the entrance and at the till. It adds no exemption, threshold or technical requirement.

m-14fb4422.t: ECB payments statistics split the POS terminals that Cyprus-resident providers supply abroad. Terminals 'located in other EEA countries' (series PTN.A.CY.G3.2222._T.PN) were 49,741 in 2022, 44,336 in 2023, 57,288 in 2024 and 50,294 in 2025, against cross-border totals of 92,806, 94,080, 104,622 and 132,670. The series for terminals outside the EEA is suppressed; by subtraction it is 43,065, 49,744, 47,334 and 82,376. In 2025 about 62% of the terminals that Cyprus-licensed providers had abroad therefore stood outside the EEA, and the whole 2025 rise in the total (151,399 to 181,874) came from there, while terminals in other EEA countries fell.

m-0cd2eac0.t: Adyen's documentation ('Sales day payout', docs.adyen.com, read 5 October 2026) calls sales day payout 'the default payout model' and gives the payout delay for a typical mix of payment methods: 2 business days where at least 80% of transactions are in AUD, CAD, EUR, GBP, NZD, RON, SEK or USD and are acquired in the country or region of that currency; 3 business days for other accounts; 3, 7 or 12 business days, by industry, for merchants onboarded through a partner. The delay is longer where slow-settling methods dominate (American Express: 7 business days). Merchants based in the EEA may ask for a shorter delay, subject to Adyen's approval.

m-fdf3aa97.t: Two of JCC Payment Systems' minority shareholder banks changed identity in 2025, per GLEIF records read on 4 October 2026: Hellenic Bank Public Company Limited changed its legal name to Eurobank Limited with effect from 2 September 2025 (same entity, LEI CXUHEGU3MADZ2CEV7C11, registration HE 6771), and Astrobank Public Company Limited (LEI 549300VB6UM9TUOCYW67) is retired after a merger effective 31 October 2025, with Alpha Bank Cyprus Ltd (LEI 529900VS0F7BA91P4I60) as successor. A JCC shareholder list naming Eurobank instead of Hellenic Bank would therefore reflect a rename, not a new shareholder.

m-fca13740.t: JCC Payment Systems' governance page, in Internet Archive snapshots of 7 December 2019, 5 December 2022 and 19 March 2025, says JCC 'is fully owned by local commercial banks in Cyprus', that Bank of Cyprus Public Co Ltd 'has a controlling interest', and names the other shareholders as Hellenic Bank Public Company Ltd, Alpha Bank Cyprus Ltd, National Bank of Greece (Cyprus) Ltd and Astrobank (AstroBank Ltd in 2019 and 2022), without percentages. No later snapshot exists, and on 4 October 2026 the live page could not be read as raw text (bot challenge): a tool-model reading that it now names Eurobank Ltd in place of Hellenic Bank is not confirmed in page text.

m-f89abac7.t: Mastercard Rule 5.1.1 (edition 2 June 2026) requires an acquirer, before entering into, extending or renewing a Merchant Agreement, to verify that the merchant is a bona fide business, has safeguards protecting account data, complies with applicable laws and that each POS transaction will reflect bona fide business with a cardholder, and to check whether it is a Government Controlled Merchant. Section 7.1.1 of the Security Rules and Procedures - Merchant Edition (4 August 2026) lists eight screening steps, among them: KYC collection and verification of the entity and each principal owner; sanctions screening; a MATCH Pro inquiry including the website URL; assigning the most accurate MCC.

m-f85da0fa.t: JCC's Customer Acceptance Policy (website version v4.1, posted June 2026) lists customers it does not accept, including online gambling or online casino companies, businesses mainly selling cannabis/CBD products, shell companies, entities with bearer shares, and the industries online pharmacies selling prescription medicine, binary options trading, dating, adult entertainment, fortune telling and crypto-asset service providers. It scores customers on a risk scorecard in which the e-commerce gateway product carries a higher risk score than other products.

m-f83caf22.t: Card-acceptance decree K.D.P. 259/2021 (Cyprus Gazette, 18 June 2021), read 4 October 2026: obliged are payees whose main activity code is in its Annex; three months from publication to comply, one month for later starters. A 'terminal' is any device or application that accepts cards, with the card present or not — POS, mobile POS, virtual POS; credit transfers, direct debits and e-banking do not count. Only cards of four-party schemes must be accepted. Acceptance must be signposted at entrance and till. The Annex lists store retail codes 47.11–47.78 but not 47.91 (mail-order and internet retail); amending decrees K.D.P. 446/2021, 52/2022 and 248/2022 added eight codes, none of them 47.91.

m-f5791329.t: JCC's net fee and commission income, as reported by Bank of Cyprus: €27 million in 2022 (8% of the group's non-interest income, up 22%); €30 million in 2023 (10%, up 11%); €28 million in 2024 (10%, down 4%, on 'higher third-party commissions absorbed internally'); €30 million in 2025 (10%, up 5%). In that passage only the 2024 report calls JCC 'a leading player in the card acquiring and processing business' (2022, 2023, 2025: 'card processing business'), but the segment notes of the 2023, 2024 and 2025 reports all describe JCC as 'acquiring and processing of debit and credit card transactions'. None of the four reports counts JCC merchants, terminals or transactions.

m-f5333eb3.t: Walk-through (ii), café through JCC, part 2 of 2 - contract and money. (4) The pack goes by email to JCC, a Cyprus-licensed EMI 75% owned by Bank of Cyprus. (5) The café signs the individual 'Agreement for the Participation in Card Schemes'; it takes effect when signed by the merchant and accepted by JCC in writing; either side can end it on 15 days' notice. (6) That agreement, not any public page, sets the merchant service charge, payout timing and any rolling reserve or bank guarantee; interchange and scheme-fee changes pass to the merchant. (7) A once-off €17 fee is debited from that account. JCC's not-accepted list does not name cafés.

m-f28428fa.t: The Central Bank of Cyprus's statistical release 'Payment Statistics: second half of 2025' (published 22 July 2026), built on data from 'all Cyprus resident payment service providers', says payment institutions and electronic money institutions 'are the exclusive providers of money remittances and card acquiring services in Cyprus' - which implies that no resident credit institution acquires cards. The release backs this with no figures: footnote 9 says card acquiring 'is not presented separately nor analyzed in this report'. The sentence is absent from the two previous releases, and it does not cover providers serving Cyprus merchants cross-border.

m-f1f3b1a4.t: SumUp's Cyprus price page (sumup.com/el-cy/times, Greek only), as of 2026-10-04, offers two card-present tariffs: pay-as-you-go at €0 a month with 1.95% on all cards including American Express and premium cards, or 'Payments Plus' at €19 a month with 0.89% on debit and credit cards, 1.95% still applying to American Express and premium cards - worded in the page's FAQ as international or corporate cards. The plan is pitched at more than €3,200 of monthly transactions. Online payments by payment link and other digital products cost 2.75%. Next-business-day payouts carry no extra charge. Readers cost €34 (Solo Lite), €139 (Solo with printer) and €169 (Terminal), excluding 19% VAT.

m-f0056b11.t: Card payments acquired by providers resident in Cyprus ('card payments, received', ECB series from 2022): 954 million and EUR 36.8 billion in 2022; 1,178m and 45.1bn in 2023; 1,450m and 56.4bn in 2024; 1,576m and 63.8bn in 2025 (second half provisional). By counterpart most are cross-border, i.e. the card issuer is outside Cyprus: in the second half of 2025, 763 of 848 million payments and EUR 29.0 of 33.0 billion; domestic in 2025: 162 million, EUR 7.8 billion. Acquired payments are about six times the number made with Cyprus-issued cards (251 million in 2025). That split is by issuer, not merchant; by point of sale (a separate series) 77% of the 2025 number and 68% of the value are abroad.

m-eed57b86.t: SumUp publishes a Cyprus-locale list of business categories that 'are not always supported' (help.sumup.com/el-CY, undated, read 4 October 2026); its General Terms forbid use for businesses listed there (section 12). For all payments it lists, among others: delivery more than one year after payment, travel services (airlines, cruise lines, timeshare), debt collection, firearms, sales of motor vehicles, investments including crypto-assets and CFDs, gambling, real-estate sales and commercial leases, political organisations, adult services, cannabis and CBD products, insurance sales and pyramid selling. For remote payments it adds pharmaceuticals and nutrition, tobacco and e-cigarettes.

m-eeb7c9ab.t: Walk-through (i), online shop via Stripe, part 2 of 3 — verification and risk. (4) If Stripe asks for proof, the company uploads documents from Stripe's Cyprus list: certificate of incorporation or articles for the entity, passport or ID card for persons, a utility bill or bank statement for address, and an ownership document such as the UBO-register extract. (5) The shop's line of business must be outside Stripe's prohibited list; restricted categories such as dating, tobacco or online pharmacy trigger extra questions and licence proofs at sign-up. (6) Stripe may hold the first settlement longer and may impose a reserve by notice, with no published percentage.

m-ed5561e4.t: Paycomcy Limited (pay.com) says it acquires. Its site footer, read 4 October 2026, calls PAYCOMCY LIMITED (HE 408974) 'a Cyprus Payment Institution regulated by the Central Bank of Cyprus (licence no. 115.1.2.42), providing payment services and acquiring of payment transactions'; the home page says 'As a licensed acquirer and principal member, we control the full stack', naming no card scheme. The only price shown is 'US based pricing', 2.85% + $0.27 per successful transaction, and the published merchant terms are US-only (a Cross River Bank service agreement, Merchant of Record terms); for the Cyprus entity there are website Terms of Use, no EEA merchant agreement or prohibited list.

m-eb5a333f.t: Mastercard Rule 7.1 (edition 2 June 2026) sorts third parties around an acquirer by 'Program Service': an Independent Sales Organization solicits merchants, processes applications and deploys terminals; a Merchant Payment Gateway sends transaction data from merchant to acquirer; a Payment Facilitator contracts with sponsored merchants as the acquirer's agent and pays them. Rule 7.6.1 requires the Merchant Agreement to be signed by the acquirer, with no separate agreement between Service Provider and merchant; if the Service Provider is a party to it, the agreement must deny it access to funds due to the merchant. Rule 7.6.2: the acquirer, not a Service Provider, collects the discount rate.

m-eb4d1a46.t: Stripe lists Cyprus among its supported countries and publishes a Cyprus price list. As of 2026-10-04 the Cyprus (en-cy) pricing page shows a blended pay-as-you-go tariff for online card payments: 1.5% + €0.25 for standard EEA cards, 2.8% + €0.25 for premium EEA cards, 2.5% + €0.25 for UK cards, 3.15% + €0.25 for international cards, plus 2% when currency conversion is required. The page states there are no setup or monthly fees; custom pricing is offered for large volume.

m-e93794bf.t: Apple Pay: Bank of Cyprus's Terms and Conditions for Apple Pay are 'valid as from 26 June, 2019' - the earliest dated primary trace found for Apple Pay with a Cyprus issuer. Trade press (NFCW, 26 June 2019) reports that Apple Pay went live that day in Cyprus and twelve other European countries, without naming a source or a Cyprus issuer. No launch announcement by Apple or by the bank was found (searched 2026-10-04), so the primary document proves a terms date at one issuer, and the national go-live date rests on press.

m-e92f6272.t: myPOS's Cyprus price page, as of 2026-10-04, shows a blended tariff with no fixed monthly cost for merchants under €10,000 monthly card turnover. Card-present: 1.69% + €0.05 for domestic and EEA consumer cards, 2.49% + €0.05 for American Express, 2.89% + €0.05 for all other consumer and commercial cards. Online: 1.30% + €0.20 for domestic and EEA consumer cards, 2.50% + €0.20 for American Express, 2.90% + €0.20 for all others (UK cards count as non-EEA online); MO/TO adds 0.5%. Above €10,000 a month the rate is quoted individually.

m-e81a2a9a.t: Visa's detailed onboarding standard is public: the Visa Acceptance Risk Standards (VARS), October 2024, marked 'Visa Public', replaced the Global Acquirer Risk Standards and was on usa.visa.com on 4 October 2026 (latest version: Visa's client portal). Its mandatory KYC/KYB controls (AACQ.C6.1-C6.2) make the acquirer collect the merchant's trading and legal name, outlet address, telephone, business registration or tax number; each principal's or director's name, address, government ID number, email and telephone; ownership percentages; a business licence or registration certificate; screen sanctions lists; and, for e-commerce, list the merchant's URLs and verify it owns the domains.

m-e5a562a0.t: Central Bank of Cyprus payment statistics for the second half of 2025 (data from Cyprus-resident providers only): card payments were 75% of the number of non-cash payments, the highest share in the euro area. By number, 70% of card payments were made at a physical point of sale and 30% online, but online payments carried 60% of the value (average about EUR 129 online against EUR 38 in person; euro area EUR 60 and EUR 33). Payment cards outstanding: 2.2 million, 84% of them debit cards. The release states that payment and e-money institutions 'are the exclusive providers of money remittances and card acquiring services' in Cyprus and that no domestic card scheme operates.

m-e4c4aca1.t: Bank of Cyprus has held 75% of JCC Payment Systems Ltd since 29 March 2013 and the figure has not moved. The prospectus of Bank of Cyprus Holdings dated 30 November 2016 records that, following the acquisition of certain operations of Laiki Bank, the holding 'increased from 45% to 75%' and JCC was fully consolidated from 29 March 2013 (before that, proportionally). The subsidiaries tables of the Annual Report 2016 and the Annual Financial Reports 2017, 2019, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025 each show 75%; the reports for 2018 and 2020 were not opened.

m-e3bcbad5.t: Adyen publishes no Cyprus price list: its pricing page has no Cyprus locale. As of 2026-10-04 the page charges a fixed processing fee per transaction - €0.11 on the euro versions (nl_NL, de_DE), £0.11 on en_GB, $0.13 on the default version - plus a payment-method fee, which for Visa and Mastercard is 'Interchange+ + 0.60%'. Adyen states it has no monthly, set-up, integration or closure fees but does have a minimum invoice 'depending on industry or business model', whose amount it does not publish. Adyen N.V. is a credit institution supervised by De Nederlandsche Bank (ECB list of supervised entities, cut-off 1 July 2026) and says its licence covers cross-border acquiring across the EEA.

m-dfdde613.t: Visa's public rules use one umbrella term, 'Third Party Agent': 'an entity, not defined as a VisaNet Processor or Visa Scheme Processor, that provides payment-related services, directly or indirectly, to a Member and/or its Merchants or Sponsored Merchants or their agents' (glossary ID# 0025921, edition 18 April 2026). Section 10.10.1.1 names a Payment Facilitator, Marketplace, Digital Wallet Operator and Independent Sales Organization as Third Party Agents. A member must register the agent with Visa before any services (1.9.8.6; its exemption for agents of affiliated members excludes facilitators and marketplaces); an acquirer must register an agent engaged by its merchant (1.9.8.7).

m-dcaf3b7e.t: JCC's published terms (v2.10) do not state a settlement delay: batches are transmitted daily and 'payments shall be made pursuant to the Agreement'; JCC deposits the sales amount net of the MSC into the merchant's bank account, and a payment date falling on a weekend or bank holiday moves to the next business day. The agreement takes effect when signed by the merchant and accepted by JCC in writing, can be terminated by either party on 15 days' written notice, and can be amended by JCC with at least two months' notice.

m-d80df257.t: TFI Ecommpay Ltd does not yet present itself as an acquirer. Its announcement of 22 March 2026 on the change of name from TFI Markets Ltd calls it 'the next step in our strategy to expand our regulated services to include acquiring of payment transactions and the issuing of payment instruments, pending the regulatory approval from the Central Bank of Cyprus'. The Central Bank register (file of 28 September 2026) records the extension of its licence to service 5 on 14 July 2026, but on 4 October 2026 its site (home, pricing, fees and legal pages) still offered only currency conversion, payments and hedging to corporate clients, with no card-acceptance product, merchant terms or card price.

m-d5e7b79e.t: Providers serving Cyprus that state wallet acceptance, pages read 4 October 2026: myPOS (Cyprus page) - 'Accept all card types, Google Pay and Apple Pay using our diverse range of card machines'; payabl. (POS page) - Google Pay, Apple Pay and Samsung Pay; SumUp's Cyprus page shows Apple Pay and Google Pay among payment methods; DECTA's acquiring page lists Apple Pay; Unlimit EU publishes Apple Pay and Google Pay terms, but those are cardholder terms for its own cards. Stripe's Apple Pay guide says 'Stripe handles Apple merchant validation for you, including creating an Apple Merchant ID', that use on the web is subject to Apple's terms, and that 'you pay only the Stripe processing fees'.

m-d489510c.t: Eurobank moved its merchant acquiring in Greece into a venture with a card processor, and Alpha Bank's partner presents itself as a Greek business too. Worldline's release of 4 July 2022 says that, 'Effective as of 30 June', it formed a joint venture with Eurobank in which it holds 80% 'of the new company in Greece', serving 123,000 merchants; Cyprus is not mentioned. Nexi's Greek site, read 4 October 2026, says 'Teaming up with Alpha Bank, Nexi Payments provides unparalleled physical and online payment acceptance solutions' and names NEXI GREECE PAYMENTS INSTITUTION SOCIETE ANONYME; it does not mention Cyprus either. National Bank of Greece's venture, NBG Pay, could not be read.

m-d29d1e22.t: JCC's 'Terms for the Participation in Card Schemes', Version 2.10 (file path 2026/08, downloaded from jcc.com.cy on 4 October 2026), define the card schemes as Visa, Mastercard, UnionPay, JCB and Diners Club International including Discover, 'to which JCC is a member' (clause 1.12). The agreement runs one year with automatic yearly renewal (24), either party may terminate on fifteen days' prior written notice (15.1), JCC may terminate without further notice on listed grounds including fraud, illegal activity, breach of card-scheme rules and PCI DSS non-compliance (15.2), and the laws and courts of Cyprus govern (25.1). Version 2.9 (2024) has the same clauses without the scheme-rules ground.

m-cf2dba8f.t: Under paragraph 4 of Decree K.D.P. 259/2021 a Cyprus business meets the card-acceptance obligation with any acceptance device or method - wired or wireless POS, mobile POS, virtual POS, card-present or distance sales - but not with credit transfer, direct debit or e-banking, which the decree says are not a card-acceptance terminal. It must accept cards of four-party schemes 'such as VISA, MASTER CARD, MAESTRO, UNION PAY', acceptance of three-party scheme cards is not obligatory, and it must contract only with lawfully licensed payment service providers under Law 31(I)/2018 or their agents; paragraph 6 requires clear notice of card acceptance at the shop entrance and at the till.

m-cb238775.t: As of 4 October 2026 PCI DSS v4.0.1 (June 2024) is still the current version, and a successor is in preparation but not published: from 3 June to 20 July 2026 the PCI Security Standards Council ran a six-week request for comments on 'the currently published' v4.0.1, stating that it 'is beginning the next iteration of PCI DSS by soliciting industry feedback on the current version PCI DSS v4.0.1'. The Council's Document Library page still links only PCI-DSS-v4_0_1.pdf as the standard.

m-cafd37c8.t: The fine for breaching Cyprus's card-acceptance decree is an administrative fine imposed by the Tax Commissioner under Article 50ΣΤ of the Assessment and Collection of Taxes Law 4/1978; its ceiling has risen twice: up to EUR 2,000 as inserted by Law 126(I)/2020 (in force 20 February 2021, six months after the Law of 20 August 2020); up to EUR 4,000 from 4 March 2022 (Law 15(I)/2022, Gazette No. 4876); up to EUR 6,000 from 1 January 2026 (Law 243(I)/2025, Article 32, Gazette No. 5070, 31 December 2025). It is halved if paid within 30 days of notification and before any objection, or if a terminal purchase invoice is filed within 30 days of the complaint or inspection (Article 50ΣΤ(7)).

m-c90c7522.t: Cyprus Development Bank sends merchants to JCC rather than acquiring itself: its 'Merchant Services' page, read 4 October 2026, is headed 'Connect Your POS With Your Account with cdbbank Through JCC' and offers to link POS devices to a cdbbank current or overdraft account; it has no merchant terms, prices or card-scheme statement. Ancoria Bank's business-banking page lists no card-acceptance product. National Bank of Greece (Cyprus) carries 'Αποδοχή καρτών (POS)' (card acceptance) in its site menu, but that link and its parent menu page returned 'Page not found' (HTTP 404) on 5 October 2026: no product page exists, and whom the bank refers merchants to is not established.

m-c598b7e4.t: JCC's merchant application (form v2.3, read 2026-10-04) is a paper-style process: the merchant downloads the form, signs and stamps it, and emails it with the KYC documents to customerservice@jcc.com.cy. The form asks for registration, TIC and VAT numbers, expected annual card turnover, average transaction value, years in business, and for e-commerce the transaction URL; it states that a current bank account is mandatory and authorises JCC to credit and debit it. New merchant registrations carry a once-off registration fee of €17, charged automatically to that account.

m-c1f73f5e.t: Stripe announced its official launch in Cyprus on 27 May 2020, together with the Czech Republic, Romania, Bulgaria and Malta; the release says Stripe had 'been available for beta testers in these countries for a while'. Press reports dated 28 May 2020 are a day later than the company's own release.

m-bf752478.t: myPOS settles card takings instantly into the merchant's myPOS e-money account rather than to a bank: its Cyprus pages, as of 2026-10-04, state that opening the account with IBAN is free with no monthly or annual fee, and that moving money out by SEPA or SEPA Instant transfer costs €4.00 per transfer. The public fee page also lists exceptional fees — €75 'no-cooperation' fee when required documents are not supplied, €15 inactivity fee and €30 'no acquiring' fee after 10 months without transactions. A merchant-side chargeback fee is not on the public page; acquiring fees are 'listed in the myPOS account'.

m-bf4a1b61.t: Google Pay: Bank of Cyprus's Terms and Conditions for Google Pay apply from 15 November 2022 — the earliest dated primary trace found for Google Pay with a Cyprus issuer, about three years and five months after the same bank's Apple Pay terms (26 June 2019).

m-bdc1a470.t: Adyen publishes one global list of 'Prohibited and Restricted Products and Services' (updated 13 November 2025, read 4 October 2026), with separate columns for merchants and for platforms. Prohibited for a merchant: adult content and entertainment, binary options, bearer-share entities, shell banks, credit repair, payday loans, counterfeit goods, pawn shops, detective agencies, illegal drugs and hazardous materials sold to consumers. Restricted (extra documents before onboarding): legal gambling, airlines, travel agents, ticket agencies, drop shipping, alcohol, tobacco, pharmaceuticals, crowdfunding, non-profits, money transfer, insurance and jewellery. The list has no country section.

m-bd9be488.t: The Ecommpay brand's public merchant documents belong to its UK company, not to the Cyprus one. The 'Regulatory notice' on ecommpay.com (archive snapshot of 7 February 2026) names only Ecommpay Limited, London, authorised by the UK Financial Conduct Authority (reference 607597), with a branch in Riga, and says 'Ecommpay is a fully licensed principal member of Mastercard and Visa'. The merchant 'Terms and conditions' Version 2.1 (marked effective 30 May 2025 to 15 January 2026; snapshot of 22 March 2026) are made with Ecommpay Limited, company number 08580802. On 4 October 2026 the live site returned only a bot-protection script, so later versions were not read.

m-b8dd4ea6.t: Xryma PLC, formerly ISX Financial EU Plc (Cyprus e-money licence 115.1.3.17, service 5 only), trades as ISXPay and is, besides JCC, the one Cyprus-licensed firm found that posts merchant documents: its 'Merchant Documents' page, read 4 October 2026, links a merchant acquiring agreement, standard terms, a website declaration letter and a Restricted/Prohibited list. The card-acquiring page says ISXPay combines 'acquirer, processor and fraud protection services' and accepts 'Mastercard, UnionPay, and Discover' - Visa is not named. The agreement (V7.0, February 2026) is stamped 'DRAFT' and 'COMMERCIAL IN CONFIDENCE', the standard terms (2021) 'Commercial in Confidence'; neither was used.

m-b83a9721.t: Mastercard Rule 5.1 (Mastercard Rules, edition 2 June 2026) obliges each acquirer to directly enter into a written Merchant Agreement with every seller from which it acquires, except for transactions acquired from its registered Payment Facilitator under a Sponsored Merchant Agreement; acquiring without an agreement in effect may be assessed up to USD 2,500 per day per entity, retroactive to the first day of the practice. Rule 5.1.2 requires each Merchant Agreement to contain the substance of Rules 5.5 through 5.15.

m-b773bd4e.t: No card-acceptance product of their own was found on the websites of the three large Cyprus banks on 2026-10-04. Checked: Bank of Cyprus's business and wholesale pages and its sitemap (3,148 URLs); Eurobank Limited's business page with all 20 business-section links and its cash-management page; Alpha Bank Cyprus's business page and sitemap (1,011 URLs); and the three fee tables. None has a POS-terminal, merchant-acquiring or payment-gateway page or fee line. JCC appears only as a bill-payment service (Bank of Cyprus 'JCC Smart bill payments', Alpha 'JCC Payments'). Acquiring sold through branches would not show on a website; whom Eurobank and Alpha refer merchants to is not established.

m-b62b3b8c.t: Visa requires an e-commerce merchant's website or app to show a customer service contact (email or telephone), the address for cardholder correspondence, the multiple-shipment delivery policy and the country of the merchant outlet - on the checkout screen or within the checkout sequence, not via a link to another page. In the Europe Region it must also show the outlet address and, if it delivers abroad, a local and an international telephone number; a link is allowed only if it forms part of the 'click to accept' acknowledgement and refers to the cancellation policy. Gambling, marketplace and non-fiat-currency merchants carry extra statements (section 5.8.4.1, ID# 0008635, 18 April 2026).

m-b4ad5277.t: JCC publishes the card scheme fees it passes on to merchants: its 'General FAQs for merchants' page links one-page schedules titled 'CARD SCHEME FEES VISA' and 'CARD SCHEME FEES MASTERCARD', the latest both dated 16/07/2026 (read 2026-10-04), and refers to the Visa and Mastercard websites for interchange. The Visa schedule lists, for example, an acquirer authorisation fee of €0.0032 / €0.0068 / €0.0425 per transaction and a clearing and settlement fee of €0.005 / €0.010 / €0.065 in its 'Domestic / Intra / Inter' columns. Earlier schedules on the same page date from June 2025 onwards.

m-afee625a.t: The European Central Bank's current payment statistics (data from 2022) carry series for a Cyprus retail payment system named 'JCC Cards' but publish no values in them: the number and value of domestic transactions processed, annual 2022-2025 and half-yearly 2022-S1 to 2025-S2, are blank with status Q (suppressed), as are participants for 2013-2025 (shown for 2000-2012: 21, of them 20 direct, in 2011 and 2012). The ECB's earlier dataset does publish card volumes for the same system, labelled 'retail system 2', for 2000-2012 and 2014-2021. So what is missing as of 4 October 2026 is an official count of JCC transaction volumes for 2013 and for 2022 onwards, not for all years.

m-aeee4e0c.t: JCC's governance page updated one shareholder's name between March 2025 and October 2026; no shareholder changed. The archive snapshot of 19 March 2025 lists the other shareholders as Hellenic Bank Public Company Ltd, Alpha Bank Cyprus Ltd, National Bank of Greece (Cyprus) Ltd and Astrobank Public Company Ltd. The live page, as returned by a fetch tool on 4 October 2026 (three concordant reads; raw text is behind a bot challenge), has 'Eurobank Ltd' in place of Hellenic Bank - the same company, renamed Eurobank Limited from 2 September 2025 - and still lists Astrobank Public Company Ltd, which merged into Alpha Bank Cyprus on 31 October 2025. No percentages are given.

m-ae027d92.t: In the Central Bank of Cyprus registers, 20 of the 32 rows of locally licensed e-money institutions (file of 28 September 2026) and 6 of the 10 rows of locally licensed payment institutions (file of 17 September 2026) list Annex I service 5, 'issuing of payment instruments and/or acquiring of payment transactions', with no issuing-only marker; 3 more EMI rows read '5(iss.)'. Payabl. CY and Paycomcy are in both, so the 26 rows are 24 legal entities. Service-5 holders include JCC Payment Systems (115.1.3.55), Nuvei Limited (115.1.3.9/2018), Unlimit EU (115.1.3.7/2018), Decta (115.1.3.54) and TFI Ecommpay (115.1.3.52). The register does not show which of them acquire rather than issue.

m-a9593505.t: Mastercard's Site Data Protection programme (Security Rules and Procedures - Merchant Edition, 4 August 2026, section 2.2.2) sets how a merchant validates PCI DSS compliance: Level 1 (more than six million combined Mastercard and Maestro transactions a year, or designated by Mastercard) - annual assessment with a Report on Compliance; Level 2 (more than one million up to six million) - annual SAQ, with a QSA or ISA for SAQ A, A-EP or D; Level 3 (more than 20,000 up to one million e-commerce transactions) - annual SAQ; all other merchants are Level 4 - compliance required, SAQ optional. Only Levels 1 and 2 must validate their compliance to Mastercard; for Levels 3 and 4 that is not required.

m-a67e734b.t: Stripe defines the two domestic card tiers of its EEA and UK price lists in a support article (read 2026-10-04): 'standard' cards are consumer cards issued by Visa, Mastercard and Cartes Bancaires, plus all cards issued by American Express, Discover, Diners Club, Maestro and UnionPay; 'premium' cards are commercial, corporate or business cards issued by Visa, Mastercard and Cartes Bancaires. On the Cyprus price list, as of 2026-10-04, that is the difference between 1.5% + €0.25 and 2.8% + €0.25 per online card payment, and Stripe classifies the card from card-network information at the point of capture.

m-a5f596f8.t: Six Greek-home institutions are notified into Cyprus in the Central Bank of Cyprus passport registers (files dated 23 September 2026). Four are marked '5(acq)': Worldline Greece Payment Institution S.A. (19 November 2021, acquiring only), Delivery Hero Payments (10 February 2025), Everypay Payment Services (18 October 2018) and Tora Wallet (30 October 2023); the other two are a remitter and an account-information firm. No row contains 'Nexi Payments Greece', 'NBG Pay' or 'Cardlink'. The Nexi rows are Nexi Payments SpA (Italy, 16 April 2020, services 3,4,5) and Nexi Germany GmbH (5 October 2023, service 5).

m-a56c1ae9.t: American Express's acquiring entity is notified for Cyprus with Bank of Cyprus as its agent: the Central Bank passport register (file of 23 September 2026) lists the bank as agent, by right of establishment, of American Express Payments Europe S.L. (Spain) for service '5(acq)', notified 10 December 2018. The bank's reports record that the competition authority alleged that its 'exclusive arrangements' with American Express broke competition law and in May 2017 fined it €18 million for that and for card-payment conduct with JCC and other banks; a court annulled the decision in June 2018, and in July 2024 the bank was told the case would not be reopened - 'the matter is now considered closed'.

m-9f867b90.t: Self-description of the 24 Cyprus-licensed holders of payment service 5 (registers of 17 and 28 September 2026), from their sites on 4 October 2026 (EcommBX, Ecredo: archive snapshots of June-August 2026). Eleven offer card acquiring now: JCC, Paycomcy, Intraclear, Decta, Nuvei, Unlimit, payabl., Xryma (ISX), Solid Processing, AEON, EcommBX. Two announce it as planned: TFI Ecommpay, Zolvat. Eight name no acquirer: Oro Pay and Appla advertise a merchant gateway for Visa and Mastercard, CSC Europe merchant solutions; EPMAP, Revsto, Hapic, Altery, Ecredo show accounts and cards. Three were unreadable: Onevault, Payz, Griner. Only Intraclear names its own legal entity as principal member.

m-9a0bde5e.t: Mastercard's Specialty Merchant Registration Program (Security Rules and Procedures - Merchant Edition, 4 August 2026, s. 9.1) has the acquirer register: non-face-to-face adult content (MCC 5967, 7841), gambling (7801, 7802, 7995), pharmaceutical (5122, 5912) and tobacco (5993) merchants; government-owned lotteries (9406; 7800 in the US); skill games (7994); high-risk cyberlockers (4816) and securities (6211); crypto (6051); negative-option billing of physical goods (5968); cannabis in Canada. Section 9.1.1 requires Mastercard's prior written consent from 1 May 2026 (1 October 2026 in most of Europe, incl. Cyprus); acquirers with merchants registered before 1 May 2026 are deemed to have it.

m-9830b291.t: Walk-through (ii), the same café using an online-onboarded provider instead of JCC, part 1 of 2 - onboarding. (1) It signs up on the web with myPOS Ltd, an Irish EMI, Viva, a Greek bank, or SumUp, a Lithuanian EMI - none Cyprus-licensed. (2) myPOS emails a document list - proofs of registered and operating address, of the activity, of directors and of owners above 25% - and says verification usually completes within 72 business hours; Viva says it mostly retrieves company data from the business registry and asks for a valid ID, more if needed. (3) myPOS's agreement is accepted by click under Irish law; Viva's is with the Greek bank.

m-9645ec91.t: DECTA says it acquires and is a scheme member, at brand level. Its acquiring page, read 4 October 2026, says 'DECTA is a Mastercard and Visa Principal Member', gives its credentials as 'EMI licensed by the FCA (UK), The Central Bank of Cyprus & by The Central Bank of Ireland', offers online, POS and mPOS acquiring to merchants and payment service providers, and fixed or IC++ pricing without rates. Onboarding documents named: proof of business ownership, passport or ID of directors and owners, an industry licence if required, six months of processing history when migrating, a signed application form. No merchant agreement or prohibited list is published; the site's terms are website terms.

m-948f0138.t: The ECB's pre-2022 payment statistics (dataset PSS) publish card volumes for the Cyprus system it labels 'retail system 2', which is JCC Cards: its participant counts for 2000-2012 are identical, year by year, to the series now titled 'Participants in JCC Cards'. Card payments processed (cards issued by resident providers): 36.5 million in 2012, 39.4 million worth €2.82 billion in 2014, 42.7 million in 2015, 48.3 in 2016, 56.5 in 2017, 66.7 in 2018, 78.2 in 2019, 83.1 in 2020 and 106.8 million worth €6.08 billion in 2021. 2013 is suppressed (status Q) and the series end in 2021; as read from the ECB data API on 4 October 2026.

m-93bd14a0.t: Cyprus's card-acceptance decree K.D.P. 259/2021 makes the Tax Department the authority that inspects and fines; neither the decree nor its three amending decrees (K.D.P. 446/2021, 52/2022, 248/2022) contains a requirement to connect the card terminal to the tax administration's systems (texts read 2026-10-04).

m-91af71d8.t: Walk-through (ii), café in Limassol taking cards via JCC, part 1 of 2 - application. (1) The café's company holds a current account - mandatory on JCC's form; a bank may ask for corporate certificates, articles, a board resolution, IDs and address proofs. (2) It fills in JCC's form - registration, TIC and VAT numbers, expected card turnover, average ticket - and signs and stamps it. (3) It attaches 13 company items: Registrar certificates, memorandum and articles, a board resolution, IDs and address proofs of directors, shareholders and UBOs, the Beneficial Owners Register extract, proof of outlet address, IBAN certificate. A sole trader attaches 5.

m-8faea685.t: Three rows of the Central Bank of Cyprus passport registers (files dated 23 September 2026) carry the home-country code in Greek capital letters that look like Latin ones: payment institutions Foris DAX MT Limited ('ΜΤ', notified 2 March 2026, services 1,2,3) and CCBill IE Limited ('ΙΕ', 23 June 2026, 3(a,c),5(acq)), and e-money institution Rippling Payments Ireland Limited ('ΙΕ', 23 March 2026, 3(a,c)). Only CCBill affects a '5(acq)' count. Four 2026 rows of Dutch B.V. companies, among them eMerchantPay Netherlands B.V. (8 April 2026, services 3 and 5), carry the code 'NV', not 'NL'; none is marked '5(acq)'.

m-89e46946.t: The Central Bank of Cyprus registers of EU institutions that notified a passport into Cyprus (files of 23 September 2026) hold 244 e-money-institution rows and 346 payment-institution rows (344 distinct names). Service 5, issuing and/or acquiring, appears in 202 EMI rows (22 marked '5(acq)', 21 '5(iss)') and 189 PI rows (70 '5(acq)', 12 '5(iss)'). '5(acq)' rows include Worldline Greece Payment Institution S.A. (notified 19 November 2021) and American Express Payments Europe S.L. (10 December 2018), the latter with Bank of Cyprus Public Company Limited as its agent in Cyprus for 5(acq). A notification is not evidence of merchants in Cyprus; credit institutions are outside these registers. Three rows carry the country code in Greek letters and one services cell is a float (4.6 stored as 4.5999…): a Latin-only filter gives 243 and 344 rows, a substring search gives 190.

m-82f2cec1.t: A Cyprus business obliged to accept cards escapes the fine where it objectively cannot obtain a terminal (Article 50ΣΤ(8) of the Assessment and Collection of Taxes Law 4/1978, consolidated text read 4 October 2026): the fine is not imposed if at the inspection it shows a document certifying that a licensed payment service provider rejected its application for a terminal, or if it applied before the deadline and the terminal was not supplied for reasons attributable to the credit institution, certified in writing. Under Decree K.D.P. 259/2021, paragraph 3(δ), a business that starts a listed activity after the initial deadline has one month from the start or the change to comply.

m-827fd9a1.t: Beyond transaction rates, Viva.com's Cyprus price list (effective 16 September 2026) charges €20 per lost dispute, €0.03 per 3-D Secure attempt online, and a refund cost of the acceptance fee plus €0.30. Payment plans are monthly subscriptions: 'Zero' at €0.00 with a minimum monthly charge of €4.99, 'Default' €4.99, 'Standard' €12.99, 'Premium' €19.99, all listing real-time settlement. Outgoing SEPA transfers cost €0.80, and the account with a GR IBAN costs €10 a month with unlimited free incoming transfers or no monthly fee with a charge per incoming transfer from €0.50.

m-8272cc46.t: Nuvei's 'Licences and Certifications' page, read 4 October 2026, lists Nuvei Limited as 'an Electronic Money Institution authorized and regulated by the Central Bank of Cyprus with license number 115.1.3.9/2018' (HE129880, head office in Strovolos, Nicosia) and, under 'European Licenses', states 'Principal membership from Mastercard and Visa for currency processing and settlement in the Europe area' - without saying which entity holds it; Nuvei Global Services B.V. (Netherlands) and Nuvei UAB (Lithuania) are listed beside it. The legal menu has a privacy notice, cookies policy, terms of use and this page: no merchant agreement, price list, onboarding checklist or prohibited-business list.

m-82185abe.t: POS terminals located in Cyprus: the ECB publishes the domestic series (PTN.A.CY.W2.2222._T.PN) only for 2017 (24,651) and 2018 (26,878); 2014-2016 and 2019-2025 are suppressed. Subtracting the published cross-border series from the published total gives 33,612 (2019), 36,535 (2020), 39,712 (2021), 43,409 (2022), 48,452 (2023), 46,777 (2024) and 49,204 (2025) terminals of Cyprus-resident providers inside Cyprus. By the series definition, terminals supplied in Cyprus by providers licensed in other member states (passported acquirers) are in none of these figures.

m-7efd8a3f.t: In the Central Bank of Cyprus register of EU payment institutions notified into Cyprus (file dated 23 September 2026), the 70 rows marked '5(acq)' - service 5 limited to acquiring - come from 21 home states: France 17, Spain 9, Luxembourg 6, Lithuania 5, Netherlands 5, Germany 4, Croatia 3, Ireland 3, Malta 3, Greece 2, Italy 2, Slovakia 2, and one each from Austria, Denmark, Finland, Hungary, Latvia, Norway, Poland, Romania and Sweden. One Irish row, CCBill IE Limited (notified 23 June 2026), has its country code typed in Greek letters, so a Latin-only filter returns Ireland 2 and a total of 69.

m-7e8cd43c.t: Before submitting transactions of High-Integrity Risk merchants, payment facilitators, sponsored merchants or ramp providers, a Visa acquirer must have a High-Integrity Risk Acquiring Registration Application approved by Visa, undergo a financial review and register each such merchant, facilitator, ramp provider and soliciting agent with Visa (section 1.9.5.1, ID# 0026383, edition 18 April 2026). Which MCCs count is set in the Visa Integrity Risk Program Guide, which Visa makes available only through its client portal, Visa Access. The term 'Global Brand Protection Program' occurs 16 times in the edition of 23 April 2022 and not at all in the 2026 edition.

m-7aa29f1e.t: ECB payments statistics, POS terminals provided by payment service providers resident in Cyprus (series PTN.A.CY.W0.2222._T.PN, end of year): 2011 - 24,319; 2012 - 26,109; 2013 - 21,493; 2014-2016 - suppressed; 2017 - 24,651; 2018 - 26,956; 2019 - 99,515; 2020 - 108,168; 2021 - 117,574 (2019-2021 flagged as estimates); 2022 - 136,215; 2023 - 142,532; 2024 - 151,399; 2025 - 181,874. The series counts terminals by the provider's residence, not by location: terminals placed outside Cyprus were 78 in 2018, 65,903 in 2019 and 132,670 in 2025, so about nine tenths of the 2019 jump (65,825 of 72,559) is terminals abroad of Cyprus-licensed providers, not terminals in Cyprus.

m-7841a484.t: Viva.com's Cyprus price list, effective 16 September 2026, is blended for domestic and EEA consumer cards — 1.69% in person (minimum €0.03 per transaction) and 2.19% + €0.24 online — and interchange-plus-plus for everything else: for commercial, UK and international Visa/Mastercard the merchant pays interchange and scheme fees plus a Viva acquiring fee of 1.16% in person or 2.06% + €0.24 online. American Express is 2.75% in person and 2.95% + €0.24 online, with 0.40% extra for cards issued outside the EEA.

m-76dd5fdf.t: Unlimit markets acquiring but publishes nothing for merchants. On 4 October 2026 its site offered 'Global card acquiring for international expansion' and 'direct acquiring', and its partner page listed 'Principal members' and 'principal card scheme memberships' - naming neither a scheme nor the member entity. The documents page of Unlimit EU Ltd holds account, card and wallet terms and fee lists (General Terms in force from 1 July 2024) and no merchant acquiring agreement, acquiring price list or prohibited-business list. The Europe coverage page lists Visa and Mastercard for the 'European Union' without member states and names Cyprus only under 'Direct banking', for five banks.

m-73ba5904.t: Visa replaced its Global Brand Protection Program with the Visa Integrity Risk Program (VIRP) with effect from 1 May 2023, and from 1 October 2023 in Brazil. Visa's own public rulebook says so: the Summary of Changes of the Visa Core Rules edition of 15 April 2023 lists 'Visa Integrity Risk Program to replace Global Brand Protection Program - Effective 1 May 2023 / Effective 1 October 2023', and its glossary marks the old programme 'Effective through 30 April 2023' and the new one 'Effective 1 May 2023', with the Brazil dates in footnotes. In the same change 'High-Brand Risk Merchant' became 'High-Integrity Risk Merchant'.

m-6fed27a2.t: Stripe's 'Prohibited and Restricted Businesses' list (last updated 22 September 2026) is one global list: the text at the Cyprus path equals the Irish one and its jurisdiction-specific section has no Cyprus entry (checked 2026-10-04). Both its lists are representative, not exhaustive. Prohibited examples: gambling and games of chance, adult content and services, cannabis products, debt collection agencies. Restricted examples, for which Stripe asks for extra information such as proof of licences at account creation and may still refuse: cryptocurrency exchanges and wallets, dating, crowdfunding platforms, tobacco, online pharmacies, travel reservation services.

m-6e016c2c.t: Three more Cyprus holders of payment service 5 describe acquiring in three different ways (sites read 4 October 2026). Solid Processing Ltd (Solidgate, e-money licence 115.1.3.58) sells orchestration: 'access to card acquiring through 100+ global and local acquirers - routed through one orchestration layer, under a single contract', naming JP Morgan, Adyen and Worldpay, and claims no scheme membership. AEON Payment Technologies Ltd (payment institution 115.1.2.39/2023) offers 'merchant acquiring services' for shops and e-commerce on its processing platform. Zolvat Ltd (115.1.3.59) says of acquiring: 'This service is currently in development and will be available soon'.

m-6d48007c.t: Cyprus obliges listed consumer-facing businesses to accept card payments under Article 30A of the Assessment and Collection of Taxes Law (No. 4/1978), inserted by Law 126(I)/2020 (Official Gazette No. 4774, 20 August 2020), and the Council of Ministers' Decree K.D.P. 259/2021 (Official Gazette No. 5548, 18 June 2021), which gave payees whose main activity code is listed three months from publication to comply. The decree's annex lists 87 activity codes - among them retail trades, vehicle sale and repair, hotels, restaurants and bars, telecoms, legal and accounting services, schools, medical and dental practices, gambling, gyms and hairdressers - and the duty covers payments by consumers.

m-6bdc2d65.t: Cyprus tax law says with whom a merchant may contract for card acceptance. Art. 30A(2) of Law 4/1978 (in force since 20 August 2020): to accept card payment instruments, payees contract with lawfully licensed payment service providers within the meaning of the Payment Services Law 31(I)/2018; the proviso forbids payees, for card acceptance and for collection on behalf of a third party generally, to contract with entities that are not lawfully licensed payment service providers or their agents, unless legislation expressly provides otherwise. Decree K.D.P. 259/2021 repeats the rule, and breaches of the decree are finable under art. 50ΣΤ. The text does not mention payment facilitators.

m-678f76bc.t: Walk-through (i), online shop via Stripe, part 3 of 3 - published Cyprus tariffs as of 2026-10-04, restated, nothing computed. A standard EEA card costs 1.5% + €0.25 (premium 2.8% + €0.25), a UK card 2.5% + €0.25, other cards 3.15% + €0.25, plus 2% if converted. Settlement timing: 7 calendar days for the first payout, then 3 business days. A dispute costs €20, and €20 more if contested and lost. Other online rates for an EEA consumer card: Revolut 1% + €0.20, myPOS 1.30% + €0.20, Viva 2.19% + €0.24, PayPal 1.9% + €0.35 without a PayPal account, 3.4% + €0.35 via one; Adyen €0.11 + interchange + 0.60%; JCC's merchant service charge is unpublished - its stated model is interchange plus scheme fees plus an acquirer fee.

m-6580acf4.t: JCC's merchant menu, read as raw text in the Internet Archive snapshot of 11 April 2026 and through a fetch tool on 4 October 2026: online - JCC Gateway, JCCSmart.com, JCCSmart Checkout; in the shop - Flexible POS Solutions, DCC, Gift, Instalments, Cashback, Contactless, Tips, Pre-Authorisation, Multi-Merchant, myLOYALTY, and an item named 'JCC SoftPOS' in April and 'JCC Tap to Pay on Android' in October; for partners - Mobile Payments, Business Continuity, SEPA Direct Debits, ATM Management, Card Services. Footer logos: Visa, Mastercard, American Express, Diners, Union Pay, JCB. The 'about' page counts no merchants or terminals ('first credit card 35+ years ago', 'thousands of people').

m-5eb6c772.t: Visa classifies as a Marketplace only an entity that: brings cardholders and retailers together on a website or app; shows its brand more prominently than the retailers' and in the app name or URL; handles payments and receives settlement for the retailers; is financially liable for disputes and resolves them by a binding decision or a money-back guarantee it funds; and lets no retailer outside its jurisdiction exceed both USD 10 million in annual Visa volume through it and 10% of its annual Visa volume (5.3.4.1, ID# 0030069, edition 18 April 2026). Franchisees lacking franchisor permission, travel agents, High-Integrity Risk Merchants and charity or crowd-funding merchants are ineligible.

m-5ce2339d.t: For users in Cyprus the Stripe Services Agreement (General Terms last modified 28 September 2026) names Stripe Payments Europe, Limited as contracting entity and Stripe Technology Europe, Limited as an additional party providing the regulated financial services and acting 'as a Payment Method Acquirer' (Stripe Financial Services Terms, EEA regional terms, 5.1). The Central Bank of Ireland register lists Stripe Technology Europe, Limited (C187865) as an e-money institution authorised on 22 March 2019 and passported to Cyprus under freedom of services; the Central Bank of Cyprus incoming register (file of 23.09.2026) shows it notified on 25 March 2019 for payment services 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8.

m-5b32cd89.t: In the Europe Region (also CEMEA and most of Asia-Pacific) a Visa acquirer must participate in the Visa Merchant Screening Service 'unless prohibited by or otherwise specified in applicable laws and regulations': query VMSS before signing a Merchant Agreement, without refusing solely on VMSS information; warn the merchant in writing at the start that termination for cause may lead to a VMSS listing; and list each merchant terminated for cause by the end of the business day after written notification was sent (section 10.17.1.1, ID# 0030572, edition 18 April 2026). VMSS is 'a database of Merchants and Third Party Agents whose contracts with their Acquirers have been terminated for cause'.

m-5aca5f19.t: Surcharging by merchants in Cyprus, Payment Services Law 31(I)/2018 (consolidated text read 4 October 2026): art. 62(5) — a payee may not request charges for the use of a specific payment instrument; art. 62(4) — a charge is never allowed for instruments whose interchange fees are capped under Chapter II of Regulation (EU) 2015/751 or for payments under Regulation (EU) No 260/2012; art. 60(1) — where a payee charges or offers a discount for a given instrument it must tell the payer before the payment is initiated. Under art. 99(1A) the Consumer Protection Service, not the Central Bank, is the competent authority for payees' compliance with arts 60 and 62.

m-598243c3.t: Visa defines a 'Tap to Phone Solution' as a merchant-owned or controlled multi-functional NFC mobile device that uses an application to act as an acceptance device, excluding devices primarily made or used as acceptance devices (glossary ID# 0031003), and requires the acquirer to register the solution with Visa and obtain approval before launch (section 5.6.3.1, ID# 0031002; edition 18 April 2026). In Cyprus, JCC's Terms v2.9 (as archived 19 March 2025) cover 'JCC SoftPOS', an Android application, making the merchant responsible for the security of the mobile device (clause 9.2(c)), and Decree K.D.P. 259/2021 counts mobile POS and virtual POS as card-acceptance terminals.

m-5802933b.t: The myPOS Acceptance Policy (last amended 6 July 2026), part of the merchant's contract with myPOS Ltd (Ireland), prohibits among others: gambling and games of skill, adult entertainment, virtual currency and NFTs, banking or money-transfer services, dropshipping, SaaS providers, payment facilitators and marketplaces, and 'future services' merchants such as airlines, car rental and travel agencies. The Legal Agreement defines a 'Reserve' — an amount, usually a percentage of acquired volume, withheld against chargebacks — without publishing the percentage or holding period.

m-566965a9.t: Walk-through (i), online shop run by a Cyprus Ltd through Stripe, part 1 of 3 - contract and data. (1) The company needs an account with an IBAN for payouts; a Cyprus bank may ask for Registrar certificates, memorandum and articles, and IDs of signatories, shareholders and UBOs. (2) It accepts the Stripe Services Agreement online - nothing is signed on paper; the counterparty is Stripe Payments Europe, Limited, with Stripe Technology Europe, Limited, an Irish EMI passported into Cyprus, as acquirer.
