Law 242(I)/2025 (in force 1 January 2026, art. 9) raised an individual's lifetime exemptions in art. 5 - general from 10,000 Cyprus pounds to €30,000, agricultural land sold by a person whose main occupation is farming from 15,000 pounds to €50,000, main residence from 50,000 pounds to €150,000 - and lowered from 50% to 20% the share of value that must derive from Cyprus immovable property for a disposal of shares in a company holding such property indirectly to be taxed.

m-a61424bb.t: Deemed dividend distribution in Cyprus is abolished for profits of tax year 2026 onwards (Law 245(I)/2025, in force 1 January 2026). It survives as a transitional rule in new art. 3Γ of SDC Law 117(I)/2002: a Cyprus-resident company is deemed to have distributed 70% of its after-tax accounting profits of tax years 2024 and 2025 at the end of two years from the end of the year of the profits, and 17% SDC is charged on the deemed dividend — only for profits attributable to individuals resident in Cyprus (for SDC purposes: resident and domiciled) at the deemed-distribution date.

m-a56eb79c.t: Outline, a list not a computation — a café run by a sole trader in Cyprus, as of 4 October 2026: profit taxed on the personal scale (0% to €22,000, 35% above €72,000); social insurance 16.6% between the category's notional minimum and €1,325 a week; Human Resource Development levy 0.5% from 6 April 2026; GeSY 4% (income capped at €180,000); VAT, card-acceptance, receipt and rent-payment rules as for a company; no accounts under art. 30(1)(β) up to €120,000 turnover, review up to €200,000 with assets up to €500,000, audit otherwise; provisional tax estimate before 31 July; return by 31 July, or 31 January of the second year if accounts are audited or reviewed, subject to extension decrees.

m-a309d45b.t: Cyprus income tax return for tax year 2025: Decree K.D.P. 260/2026 (Gazette of 12 June 2026, made on 4 June 2026 under arts 5(1A) and 13(1) of Law 4/1978) extends to 31 October 2026, 23:59, the deadline for filing the 2025 return and paying the tax due under it for a natural person other than a self-employed person obliged to prepare audited or reviewed accounts. The statutory dates in art. 5(1A) are 31 July of the year after the tax year, or 31 January of the second year for persons whose accounts must be audited or reviewed; the Council of Ministers may set later dates by decree. On 4 October 2026 the extended deadline had not yet passed.

m-97e393dc.t: From 1 January 2026 a company is tax resident in Cyprus if (i) its control and management are exercised in Cyprus, or (ii) it was incorporated in Cyprus under the Companies Law, unless a double tax treaty provides otherwise; a company that moved its registered office or seat to Cyprus counts as incorporated there (art. 2 of Law 118(I)/2002 as replaced by art. 2 of Law 244(I)/2025). The Tax Department notes that the earlier condition — that the company not be resident in another state — was deleted.

m-8f4d8d43.t: The CRS decree in force in Cyprus on 4 October 2026 is K.D.P. 434/2020, issued under art. 6(16) of the Assessment and Collection of Taxes Laws (Official Gazette no. 5360, 18 September 2020). Its para 44 repeals the Decree of 2017 (K.D.P. 379/2017, 17 November 2017), which had repealed K.D.P. 161/2016, which had repealed the first decree, K.D.P. 477/2015 (31 December 2015). The CyLaw K.D.P. lists for 2021-2026 contain no later CRS decree. The Tax Department's CRS page (published 28 January 2026) lists K.D.P. 434/2020 first among the decrees, after Law 205(I)/2012, which it names as the law governing CRS in Cyprus.

m-8dfd908e.t: The 35% top band of Cyprus personal income tax dates from tax year 2011, not 2008: Law 116(I)/2011 (Official Gazette, Annex I(I), No. 4291 of 31 August 2011) replaced '30% on every euro over €36,300' in para 1(β) of the Second Schedule to Income Tax Law 118(I)/2002 with '30% on €36,300-60,000' and '35% over €60,000', with effect from tax year 2011. The consolidated text on cylaw.org shows the amended table under the heading 'from tax year 2008 onwards', which hides the date of the change.

m-8cdf6021.t: Interest paid from Cyprus to non-residents after the 2026 reform: special defence contribution names one class of recipient abroad. Under art. 3B(γ) of Law 117(I)/2002 a company resident or registered in an EU-listed non-cooperative jurisdiction (or a permanent establishment kept there) bears 17% on interest from Cyprus sources received or credited, 'whether or not paid', if linked by more than 50% with the paying Cyprus company; excluded are interest paid by an individual and interest on listed securities if the payer cannot reasonably know. The charge dates from Law 195(I)/2021 (in force 31 December 2022), was recast with the 50% link by Law 48(I)/2025 and renumbered by Law 245(I)/2025.

m-8a71008a.t: Provisional tax in Cyprus: a person with income other than emoluments submits its own estimate of the year's chargeable income before 31 July of the tax year (art. 24 of Law 4/1978) and pays in two instalments — the Tax Department's deadline calendar for 2026 lists 31 July and 31 December. The estimate can be revised until 31 December. If the provisional chargeable income is below three quarters of the final figure, an additional tax of one tenth of the difference between final tax and provisional tax is due (art. 26(1)). A company formed after 30 June files its estimate by 31 December (proviso added by Law 243(I)/2025).

m-89db0a8b.t: Special defence contribution (SDC) on dividends received by an individual who is tax resident and domiciled in Cyprus is 5% from 1 January 2026 (art. 3(1)(α) of SDC Law 117(I)/2002 as replaced by art. 3 of Law 245(I)/2025); the Tax Department describes this as a reduction from 17%. Transitional proviso (ii): dividends received from a Cyprus-resident company within six years of 1 January 2026 (the Tax Department writes 'until 31/12/2031') and paid out of profits of tax years up to and including 2025 still bear 17%. The 17% proviso is limited to dividends from Cyprus-resident companies; other dividends bear 5% from 1 January 2026.

m-83a12b44.t: Cyprus's low-tax jurisdictions for tax year 2026, per Tax Department Circular 1/2026 (9 April 2026): Anguilla, Vanuatu, Bermuda, British Virgin Islands, Guernsey, Cayman Islands, Turks and Caicos Islands, Isle of Man, Bahamas, Bahrain, Jersey - eleven. The definition (art. 2 of Income Tax Law 118(I)/2002 and of SDC Law 117(I)/2002) is a third-country jurisdiction whose corporate tax rate is below 50% of the Cyprus corporate rate, that is below 7.5% with the rate at 15%. The Department's page (28 May 2026) notes that Anguilla and Vanuatu were also on the EU list of non-cooperative jurisdictions of October 2025, so the non-cooperative rules apply to them while they remain listed.

m-80f97559.t: Two definitions decide what a Cyprus shareholder-director pays on dividends. SDC Law 117(I)/2002, art. 2(1): for an individual, 'resident of the Republic' means a person who is resident under the Income Tax Law and in addition has a domicile in Cyprus — so a non-domiciled resident is outside SDC. General Healthcare System Law 89(I)/2001, art. 2: 'income' on which the 2.65% GeSY contribution of an income earner is charged includes dividends as defined in the SDC Law, with no domicile test. Both read in the consolidated texts on 4 October 2026.

m-7c601025.t: Cyprus's IP box is still in place on 4 October 2026: art. 9(1)(κ) of Income Tax Law 118(I)/2002 allows a deduction of 80% of the qualifying profits generated by a qualifying intangible asset, and Law 244(I)/2025 did not amend that paragraph. With the corporate rate at 15% from 1 January 2026 the effective rate on qualifying profits is 3% (it was 2.5% at the 12.5% rate). If the computation produces a loss, only 20% of it can be set off or carried forward.

m-7713e523.t: Non-dom regime: Law 119(I)/2015 amending the Special Contribution for the Defence of the Republic Laws was published in the Official Gazette No. 4523 on 16 July 2015 and entered into force on publication; it made liability depend on the person additionally having domicile ('κατοικία (domicile)') in the Republic.

m-766c23a6.t: DAC7 (Council Directive (EU) 2021/514, applied from 1 January 2023) requires platform operators to collect and report data on sellers using their platforms, annually by 31 January for the previous calendar year. Excluded is, among others, a seller for whom the platform facilitated fewer than 30 sales of goods with total consideration not exceeding EUR 2,000 in the period. Cyprus transposed it after the 31 December 2022 deadline, by Law 105(I)/2023 (Gazette No. 4963 of 3 November 2023), which amended the Administrative Cooperation in the Field of Taxation Law 205(I)/2012; reports are filed with the Tax Department. Status on 4 October 2026: in force.

m-7371915b.t: Cyprus's Tax Department stated on 1 December 2023 what a CRS self-certification at account opening must contain: the account holder's name, residence address, jurisdiction(s) of tax residence, tax identification number for each reportable jurisdiction and date of birth. It 'may be provided in any form'. The institution must confirm that it is reasonably consistent with the other information collected at opening, obtain and validate it within 90 days at the latest and, if the holder does not respond, close or freeze the account after the 90 days; copies go to the Tax Department on request. The notice rests on paras 34 and 50 of the CRS Guidance Notes (K.D.P. 408/2017).

m-706de75f.t: The 17% Cyprus contribution on dividends to companies in low-tax jurisdictions never took effect. Law 48(I)/2025 (Gazette No. 5035, 16 April 2025) rewrote art. 3(2)(α1) of the SDC Law - the 17% charge on dividends to connected companies in EU-listed non-cooperative jurisdictions, in force since 31 December 2022 under Law 195(I)/2021 - and extended it to companies resident or registered in low-tax jurisdictions; the Law took effect on publication, its low-tax-jurisdiction part only on 1 January 2026 (art. 4(2)). On that same day Law 245(I)/2025 replaced art. 3 and set the low-tax-jurisdiction rate at 5%, keeping 17% for non-cooperative jurisdictions.

m-6dcd9b9b.t: Books and audit for a sole trader in Cyprus (art. 30 of Law 4/1978 as amended by Law 243(I)/2025; threshold change applies from tax year 2026): a person with income from business, rents, royalties and certain other sources issues invoices and receipts and keeps books. An individual in business whose annual turnover and other gross income do not exceed €120,000 (before: €70,000) is exempt from preparing the accounts required by art. 30(1)(β), which must be audited or reviewed; above €120,000 and up to €200,000, with total assets up to €500,000 for two consecutive years, the accounts may be reviewed; otherwise audited. Books are kept at least six years from the return deadline or filing date.

m-6d265b3d.t: DAC8 in Cyprus: Directive (EU) 2023/2226 was transposed by the Administrative Cooperation in the Field of Taxation (Amendment) Law 38(I)/2026, published in Gazette No. 5081 on 27 March 2026 and deemed in force from 1 January 2026 (art. 20(1)). Reporting crypto-asset service providers apply due diligence and report users to the Tax Department by 30 June of the following year; the first report, for 2026, is due by 30 June 2027 per the law and the Department's announcement of 2 April 2026 (its DAC8 page says 30 September 2027). The reporting-standard definition of depository institution now covers entities holding e-money or central bank digital currencies for customers.

m-68156bd1.t: Cyprus's Income Tax Law has no special withholding rate for a non-resident director's fee. Art. 5(2)(β) of Law 118(I)/2002, as replaced by Law 244(I)/2025 (in force 1 January 2026), taxes a non-resident on income or benefits granted 'in respect of any office or employment exercised in the Republic' to the person holding the office; art. 25 and the Second Schedule give one personal scale (0% up to €22,000 from 2026) without distinguishing residents, and the 10% gross withholding of art. 23 is worded for professions, vocations and entertainers, not offices. Neither the Law nor the Tax Department's withholding page says where a director's office is exercised when the director acts from abroad.

m-678540b9.t: Outline, a list not a computation — café run as a Cyprus Ltd with a POS terminal, as of 4 October 2026: VAT 9% on food and drink supplied with service for immediate consumption, the goods' own rate on take-away without it; registration above €15,600; quarterly returns; card acceptance compulsory for activity codes 56.10 and 56.30 (art. 30A of Law 4/1978, K.D.P. 259/2021), four-party scheme cards, contracted with a licensed payment service provider or its agent; receipts under art. 30(1)(α); since 1 July 2026 rent only by bank transfer, card or other electronic means (art. 48A); corporate tax 15%, provisional tax; payroll contributions; card-processing services 'in relation to credit cards' fall outside the VAT exemption.

m-63f89304.t: Income tax reliefs for a founder who moves to Cyprus and takes employment there (Income Tax Law 118(I)/2002, art. 8, read on 4 October 2026): (23Α) 50% of remuneration from employment in Cyprus is exempt for a person not resident in Cyprus for at least 15 consecutive years before first employment starting on or after 1 January 2022, for 17 tax years, in any year remuneration exceeds €55,000; (21Α) 20% of remuneration or €8,550, whichever is lower, for seven tax years, for first employment starting up to 2027 after three years' employment abroad by a non-resident employer. The two cannot be combined.

m-63a69186.t: Cyprus's 2026 tax reform was published in the Official Gazette, Annex I(I), No. 5070 of 31 December 2025, as six tax laws: 239(I)/2025 (repeal of the Stamp Duty Laws), 241(I)/2025 (Collection of Taxes), 242(I)/2025 (Capital Gains Tax), 243(I)/2025 (Assessment and Collection of Taxes), 244(I)/2025 (Income Tax) and 245(I)/2025 (Special Defence Contribution); the same issue also carries Law 240(I)/2025 (International Trusts), not counted here. The Ministry of Finance announced their passing on 22 December 2025, the plenary date an employers' federation circular also gives. They took effect on 1 January 2026; a few provisions apply from tax year 2026, from 1 July 2026 or from 1 January 2031.

m-60852614.t: How Cyprus withholding on payments to non-residents is paid, per the Tax Department's page read on 4 October 2026: the payer of royalties (art. 21, 10%), film rentals (art. 22, 5%) or fees of non-resident professionals, entertainers and athletes for activity in Cyprus (art. 23, 10% of gross) withholds the tax and files the 'DAS - Deducted At Source' return and pays through the Tax For All portal by the end of the month after the month of payment (a payment in March: by 30 April). The rates are those of domestic law; a double tax treaty prevails where more favourable, on production of a tax residence certificate. The page lists no withholding on dividends, interest or directors' fees.

m-5ec93183.t: History of Cyprus's special defence contribution rate on dividends (art. 3(2)(α) of Law 117(I)/2002): 15% from 1 January 2003 (original law); 17% for dividends arising from 31 August 2011 (Law 114(I)/2011, Gazette No. 4291); 20% under Law 190(I)/2011, in force 1 January 2012 and applying only to income arising from 1 January 2012 to 31 December 2013; 17% again afterwards - the archived consolidated texts of 4 April 2016 and 7 November 2025 read 17%; 5% from 1 January 2026 under Law 245(I)/2025, with 17% kept for dividends paid by 31 December 2031 out of pre-2026 profits of Cyprus-resident companies.

m-5c7c4ee5.t: Tax losses in Cyprus can be carried forward for seven years instead of five: art. 8(α) of Law 244(I)/2025 replaced 'five' with 'seven' in the first proviso to art. 13(1) of Income Tax Law 118(I)/2002, in force 1 January 2026. The time limit in that proviso is written for persons obliged to keep books, prepare audited accounts and file a return. The Tax Department's presentation explains that a loss of tax year 2019 can therefore be set off against profits of tax year 2026 (but not 2025), while a loss of 2018 could be carried only to 2023.

m-57e61bff.t: IP box reform: Law 110(I)/2016 (Income Tax (Amendment) Law of 2016) was published in the Official Gazette No. 4579 on 27 October 2016 and is deemed to have entered into force on 1 July 2016, except its section 4, which took effect on publication. The date usually cited (1 July 2016) is therefore a retroactive commencement set by a law published almost four months later.

m-5730fa3d.t: Since 1 January 2026 the Cyprus Tax Commissioner can shut a business for not issuing receipts. Art. 32A of Law 4/1978 (added by art. 18 of Law 243(I)/2025) lets him suspend a business and seal its premises for up to ten days where its operator did not issue the invoices or receipts the Law requires or issued inaccurate ones, owes over €20,000 of declared or finally assessed tax including charges, obstructs a tax audit, or - for omissions from 1 January 2027 - failed to file at least two tax returns, twelve monthly withholding returns or three VAT returns. Three notices come first: two giving at least ten days each to comply, a third five days for written views. A further 20 days may follow.

m-54ee419e.t: The two DAC8 dates in Cyprus belong to two different duties, both in Law 38(I)/2026 (Gazette No. 5081, 27 March 2026; deemed in force from 1 January 2026). Reporting crypto-asset service providers submit to the Tax Department by 30 June of the year after the calendar year reported (new Annex VI, Section II, para Δ): for 2026, by 30 June 2027. The Tax Department passes the data to other Member States within nine months of the end of that year (new art. 7ΣΤ(5)): by 30 September 2027. The Department's announcement of 2 April 2026 gives 30/6/2027; its Greek DAC8 page, which cites the Law and links that announcement, still gave 30 September 2027 as the providers' first deadline on 4 October 2026.

m-514a9607.t: Pillar Two in Cyprus is Law 151(I)/2024 (Gazette No. 5019 of 18 December 2024), transposing Directive (EU) 2022/2523 and deemed in force for fiscal years starting from 31 December 2023. It applies the 15% minimum effective tax only to constituent entities of multinational or large domestic groups with consolidated annual revenue of at least €750,000,000 in at least two of the four preceding fiscal years (art. 4(1)), so a stand-alone small trading company is outside it. On 15 June 2026 the Tax Department published two announcements on the Law, one of them on deadlines for the first fiscal year (beginning between 31/12/2023 and 30/12/2024).

m-50573154.t: Income tax return duties in Cyprus from tax year 2026 (art. 5 of the Assessment and Collection of Taxes Law 4/1978 as amended by art. 4 of Law 243(I)/2025): every company incorporated or resident in Cyprus files a return each year whether or not it has income; so does every resident individual aged 25 to 70 at year-end, and one with gross income files at any age. The return is due by 31 July of the year after the tax year; a person obliged to keep books and prepare audited or reviewed accounts may file by 31 January of the second year after it. The Council of Ministers may by decree exempt categories of persons or set later deadlines. Supporting documents are kept six years.

m-4e1f2eea.t: Cyprus's notional interest deduction was left untouched by the 2026 reform (Law 244(I)/2025 does not amend art. 9B of Income Tax Law 118(I)/2002). A company gets a deduction equal to the reference rate multiplied by new equity used in the business; the reference rate is the 10-year government bond yield of the state where the new equity is invested, on 31 December of the preceding year, plus five percentage points; the deduction cannot exceed 80% of the taxable income generated by the new equity and is not given where that income is a loss.

m-4c4d60eb.t: History of Cyprus's special defence contribution rate on interest (art. 3(2)(β) of Law 117(I)/2002): 10% from 1 January 2003 (original law); 15% for interest arising from 31 August 2011 (Law 114(I)/2011, Gazette No. 4291); 30% for interest received or credited from 29 April 2013 (Law 29(I)/2013, Gazette No. 4385); 17% from 1 January 2024 (Law 157(I)/2023, Gazette No. 4975 of 20 December 2023); since 1 January 2026 17% under new art. 3B (Law 245(I)/2025). Archived consolidated texts read 30% on 4 April 2016 and 1 April 2023 and 17% on 26 February 2024. Interest on government savings certificates and similar paper bore 3% throughout.

m-433d6361.t: An incorporation test was added to Cyprus corporate tax residency with effect from 31 December 2022: Law 193(I)/2021 (Gazette No. 4867 of 21 December 2021) added a proviso to the definition of 'resident of the Republic' in art. 2 of Income Tax Law 118(I)/2002 under which a company incorporated or registered under any law in force in Cyprus whose management and control are exercised outside Cyprus is treated as resident unless it is tax resident in any other state. Before that date the only test was management and control exercised in Cyprus.

m-28d07470.t: Cyprus Law 123(I)/2026, the Administrative Cooperation in the Field of Taxation (Amendment) (No. 2) Law of 2026, was published in Gazette No. 5093 on 17 July 2026 to transpose Council Directive (EU) 2025/872 of 14 April 2025 amending Directive 2011/16/EU; it is deemed in force from 1 January 2026 (art. 12(1)), its art. 9 from 1 January 2028. It is the latest amendment of Law 205(I)/2012 in cylaw.org's numbered index on 4 October 2026, after Law 38(I)/2026 (DAC8, Gazette of 27 March 2026) and Law 105(I)/2023 (DAC7, Gazette of 3 November 2023). Any statement about Law 205(I)/2012 'as amended' made after 17 July 2026 has to count this law.

m-28b69ad6.t: Section 29 of Cyprus's Assessment and Collection of Taxes Law (Law 4/1978), as replaced by art. 16 of Law 243(I)/2025, is in force from 1 January 2026, not tied to a tax year: art. 35 excepts only arts. 4(α)-(β), 8, 9, 14 and 17(α) ('in respect of tax year 2026 and later') and art. 29 of the amending Law (rent payments, 1 July 2026 - not s. 29 of the basic law). Tax computations produced to the Commissioner or filed with returns 'may, at his discretion, be disregarded' unless prepared and certified by a holder of an ICPAC practising certificate or one from another recognised body of auditors; accounts, unless by a statutory auditor or audit firm. A power to disregard, not a filing condition.

m-24d0db00.t: Under s. 50A(α) of the Assessment and Collection of Taxes Law (Law 4/1978), as amended by art. 31 of Law 243(I)/2025 with effect from 1 January 2026, a person who fails to give a notice or perform a duty within the period the Law prescribes is charged €250 if a legal person, €500 if a legal person whose turnover or assets exceed €1,000,000, and €150 if a natural person; until 2025 the charge was €100. By its terms this covers a company's notice for registration in the Tax Register within 60 days of incorporation (s. 5A(2)). Section 50B separately allows an administrative fine of up to €20,000 for breaches of the Law.

m-24ac9d24.t: Dividends paid by a Cyprus company to non-residents after the 2026 reform bear no general withholding. Among recipients abroad, art. 3(1)(δ) of SDC Law 117(I)/2002 (as replaced by Law 245(I)/2025, in force 1 January 2026) reaches only a non-resident company, or a permanent establishment kept there, resident or registered in a low-tax jurisdiction (5%) or in an EU-listed non-cooperative jurisdiction (17%; 17% if both), and only where payer and recipient are linked by more than 50% of votes, capital or profit rights; listed securities are excepted if the payer cannot reasonably know. The 17% charge dates from Law 195(I)/2021 (in force 31 December 2022), the low-tax limb from Law 48(I)/2025.

m-1e073d82.t: For tax years from 2026, section 5(1A) of the Assessment and Collection of Taxes Law (as replaced by Law 243(I)/2025, Official Gazette No. 5070, 31.12.2025) sets the income tax return deadline at 31 July of the year after the tax year, or 31 January of the second year after the tax year for persons whose accounts must be audited or reviewed - which covers companies. For tax years 2020-2025 the company deadline was 31 March of the second year; on 4 Oct 2026 the Tax Department's calendar shows the company return (T.D.4) for 2024 as due 31.3.2026 with an extension to 30.11.2026.

m-1ae0a9a6.t: Outline, not a computation: paying a Cyprus director a salary versus a dividend after 1 January 2026. Salary: deductible against the 15% corporate tax; taxed in the director's hands on the 0-35% scale (first €22,000 at 0%); social insurance 8.8% employee plus 8.8% employer up to the insurable ceiling; GeSY 2.65% plus 2.90%; employer-only funds 1.2%, 0.5% and 2% (the 2% Social Cohesion Fund has no earnings ceiling). Dividend: paid out of profit after 15% corporate tax; SDC 5% - or 17% if paid by 31/12/2031 by a Cyprus-resident company out of profits of years up to 2025 - and only if the recipient is resident and domiciled; GeSY 2.65% on the dividend, with all GeSY-liable income capped at €180,000 a year; no social insurance.

m-15afe111.t: Royalties paid from Cyprus to non-residents (Law 118(I)/2002, read 4 October 2026): under art. 21 gross royalties or technical-assistance fees earned from Cyprus sources by a non-resident not carrying on business there are taxed at 10%, withheld by the payer (art. 24); a right granted for use outside Cyprus is not Cyprus-source; payments to an associated EU company (25% direct holding) are exempt. Art. 22 taxes film rentals at 5%. Art. 21A taxes at 10% royalties earned by a connected company in an EU-listed non-cooperative jurisdiction, unless paid by an individual; that charge dates from Law 193(I)/2021 (in force 31 December 2022) and was recast, with a 50% link, by Law 47(I)/2025.

m-148dc6dd.t: Cyprus personal income tax bands. Tax years 2011-2025 (Second Schedule para 1(β) of Law 118(I)/2002 as amended by Law 116(I)/2011): 0% up to €19,500; 20% on €19,500-28,000; 25% on €28,000-36,300; 30% on €36,300-60,000; 35% above €60,000. In tax years 2008-2010 the top rate was 30% on everything above €36,300. From tax year 2026 (new para 1(γ), Law 244(I)/2025 art. 24(a)): 0% up to €22,000; 20% on €22,000-32,000; 25% on €32,000-42,000; 30% on €42,000-72,000; 35% above €72,000. The tax-free amount rose from €19,500 to €22,000. In force on 4 October 2026.

m-12c75029.t: Individual tax residence in Cyprus from 1 January 2026 (art. 2 of Law 118(I)/2002 as replaced by Law 244(I)/2025): more than 183 days in Cyprus in the tax year; or the '60-day rule' — the person does not stay more than 183 days in any other single state and, cumulatively, stays at least 60 days in Cyprus, carries on a business or is employed in Cyprus or holds an office in a Cyprus tax-resident person at any time in the year (not terminated during it), and keeps a permanent home in Cyprus that is owned or rented. The Tax Department states the 60-day rule now applies whether or not the person is tax resident of another state.

m-0f9a9166.t: On payments to low-tax jurisdictions Cyprus denies the deduction instead of withholding. Under art. 11(17) of Income Tax Law 118(I)/2002 (inserted by Law 47(I)/2025, Gazette No. 5035 of 16 April 2025; in force from 1 January 2026) a Cyprus company may not deduct royalties, or interest, 'whether or not paid', payable to a company resident or registered in a low-tax jurisdiction with which it is linked by more than 50% of votes, capital or profit rights. Tax Department Circular 1/2026 of 9 April 2026 confirms that for 2026 this rule and the 5% contribution on dividends apply to the jurisdictions it lists, except Anguilla and Vanuatu while they stay on the EU non-cooperative list.

m-06635813.t: Until abolished on 1 January 2026, Cyprus's special defence contribution on rent was 3% of gross rents reduced by 25%, in effect 2.25% of gross rent, payable by a person resident in Cyprus (art. 3(2)(δ) of Law 117(I)/2002, in force 1 January 2003). The rate clause reads the same in the 2002 Gazette text and in archived consolidations of 4 April 2016, 1 April 2023, 26 February 2024 and 7 November 2025; provisos present from 2023 exclude finance-lease instalments and exempt certain rents. Under art. 4 (7 November 2025 snapshot) a tenant that was a company, partnership, the State or a local authority withheld it and paid by 30 June and 31 December; otherwise the landlord paid on the same dates.

m-ea576ed4.t: Two Migration Department notices on immigration-permit holders, read 6 Oct 2026. Per a notice of 7 July 2025 (modified 12 March 2026), the residence card of an immigration-permit holder and dependants is renewed from three months before expiry on form MIP2 with a passport copy, the old card and a €50 fee. Per a notice of 19 March 2026, a dependent student's Regulation 6(2) application is examined on the 4th revision's criteria even where the parent got the permit under the 2013-2023 revisions; such a parent must file a sale agreement for property worth at least €300,000 plus VAT, proof of payment of at least €300,000 plus VAT and proof of a matching transfer from abroad.

m-df4b839b.t: Cyprus's Aliens and Immigration Regulations 1972 to 2013 (made by the Council of Ministers under Cap. 105, s. 20(1)) define the 'Τμηματάρχης' (Regulation 2, amendment of 27.12.1986) as 'the Immigration Officer in the Immigration Service of the Ministry of the Interior', and 'Minister' as the Minister of the Interior in his capacity under the Law as chief immigration officer, including any duly authorised Ministry officer. Under Regulation 2A immigration officers and the Τμηματάρχης exercise the powers the Regulations give them, subject to the Minister's instructions; immigration permits are granted by the Minister on the Immigration Control Committee's report (Regulation 6(1)).

m-db6b03a6.t: In April 2026 AKEL MPs (G. Loukaides, A. Damianou, M. Nikolaou, V. Fakontis) proposed amending Cyprus's Aliens and Immigration Law so the investor permit scheme continues only if the government issues House-approved regulations - within three months of enactment, per Cyprus Mail; Loukaides said the criteria rest on the Interior Minister's 'absolute discretion'. Cyprus Mail (14 Apr 2026) wrote that the Migration Department cautions a say for parliament risks 'constraining' the scheme's 'flexibility'. The House interior committee closed its discussion on 15 April; the bill was expected at the last plenary, 23 April. No outcome found as of 6 Oct 2026; cylaw shows no 2026 amendment of that Law.

m-daa940b6.t: For a company, Regulation 12(6)(γ) of Cyprus's Aliens and Immigration Regulations limits the independent-profession permit to alien partners with active participation whose presence is necessary to carry out the company's objects and manage it. Under 12(6)(δ), where such a partner does not hold the majority or a significant part of the company's shares, the Τμηματάρχης may reserve the option of admitting him as an employee by granting him an employment permit under Regulation 11.

m-d8ca0d42.t: Money rules of Cyprus's investor-permit policy (4th revision, read 6 Oct 2026): funds must be proved transferred to Cyprus from abroad, from the applicant's account or the spouse's if the spouse is a dependant on the application, or - per the clarification of 17 May 2023 - from a company solely owned by applicant and/or spouse, if that shareholder is on the application; payment goes to the seller's account at a Cyprus financial institution. For real estate, the money must be shown to come from abroad, not domestic borrowing, with receipts of at least €300,000 excluding VAT. A purchase through a legal person counts if applicant and/or spouse are its sole shareholders or beneficial owners.

m-d81930b9.t: In Greek, the Cyprus Registrar's review criteria for business-name form EE1 (page published 25 April 2019, read 6 October 2026) word the nationality check as 'in case it is outside the EU, a permit from the Immigration Officer (Λειτουργός Μετανάστευσης) is required'; the English page says 'permission is required by the Immigration Officer'. Neither page names the law, the document or how it is shown. The same page's 'most common reasons for rejection' open with 'failure to fill-in/submit the above details', which covers this item; a missing permit is not named separately. A web-archive copy of the English page of 2 August 2022 carries the same wording.

m-d52402bb.t: The current Cyprus entry in the Commission's list of residence permits under Article 2(16) of the Schengen Borders Code is C/2025/3595 (Official Journal C series, 1 July 2025), which replaces the list of OJ C 126, 12.4.2021. It keeps the same 17 'Type of Permit' categories on the ID-1 residence permit card, none for self-employment, and adds that the Registration Certificate (MEU1) and Certificate of Permanent Residence (MEU3) of Union citizens stay on paper until mid-2026, when ID-1 cards start. Of the 37 updates of the list from 6.10.2020 to 1.9.2026, only these two carry a Cyprus entry.

m-ccf969d9.t: Cyprus's residence permit for third-country nationals is an ID-1 card in the EU uniform format of Regulation (EC) No 1030/2002 whose 'Type of Permit' field shows one of 17 categories, per Cyprus's entry in the Commission's list of residence permits (OJ C 126, 12.4.2021, replaced with the same categories by C/2025/3595 of 1.7.2025): Temporary Permit BCS, GEN, CY, DW, VIS, NSP ('employment outside of single permit'), EDU, ESW, ICT, SUP ('startup scheme'); Long-Term Resident LT; Family Reunification FR; Immigration Permit IP; Special Permit SPE and IPA; ICTM and EDUM. None is labelled self-employment or independent profession.

m-cc7cc364.t: Cyprus's Aliens and Immigration Regulations 1972-2013 use two officer titles. A lower-case 'λειτουργός μεταναστεύσεως' (immigration officer) issues transit and visitor permits (regs 10(1), 14(1)) and, on the Τμηματάρχης's written approval, employment permits (11(1)). The 'Τμηματάρχης', defined in reg. 2 as the Immigration Officer in the Immigration Service, decides independent-profession permits (12(6)) and pupil's permits (13(1)), extends permitted stays (9(6)), grants re-entry permits (9(7)) and gives a visitor prior written permission to work or do business (14(3)); without it, taking a job ends the visitor's permit and doing business may get it revoked (14(4)).

m-c3f4391c.t: Per the Cyprus Migration Department's 'Appointments' page (updated 15 September 2026, read 6 October 2026), its headquarters at 90 Archiepiskopou Makariou III Avenue, 1077 Nicosia, need an appointment only for immigration permits, long-term residence, permanent-permit card renewal and the student point (plus weekly slots for providers filing for foreign-interest companies); other applications are received without one, first come first served, Monday-Friday 08:00-14:30, last entry 14:00. The page does not name MEU1. Residents of other districts go to the police Aliens and Immigration unit of their district, or to headquarters only through an authorised representative with a Nicosia office.

m-bee91e29.t: Who decides a Cyprus investor-permit application and how long it takes, per the policy page read 6 Oct 2026: the Migration Department handles it 'under an expedited procedure' and sends it through the Permanent Secretary of the Deputy Ministry; if all criteria are met and there are no criminal-record, public-order or public-security concerns, it is presented for examination and decision to the Deputy Minister of Migration and International Protection. The 'estimated examination period' is 'approximately two (2) months' from submission of the completed application - an estimate, not a legal time limit; no actual processing times were found on the Department's policy, forms or news pages.

m-b6b5bd39.t: Cyprus intends to tighten its 'golden visa' programme, Deputy Migration Minister Nicholas Ioannides told the House Audit Committee on 24 September 2026 (Cyprus Mail and the Cyprus News Agency): decisions on tightening are expected, he has already submitted proposals to the other ministers involved, and one question is whether investments could also go to education, defence and innovation; he linked it to Schengen entry making Cyprus more attractive. He said about 1,500 golden visas were issued in the past two years and that about 12,000 issued since 2013 are being checked; the English report calls them permits, and neither report says what is counted. No proposal text, Cabinet decision or date was found on gov.cy or in the press as of 6 October 2026.

m-b255a5b1.t: Until Law 4(I)/2025, s. 2 of Cyprus's Aliens and Immigration Law (Cap. 105) defined the Chief Immigration Officer as the Minister of the Interior, who could delegate in writing any power under the Law or Regulations (s. 4(1)(α)); CyLaw still shows it on 6 October 2026. Law 4(I)/2025 (Gazette No. 5026, 14.2.2025) deletes the term, defines the Department as the Migration Department of Law 23(I)/2024 (s. 2) and lets the Council of Ministers or Deputy Minister delegate powers to the Director or staff (s. 3). Where the title stood, deportation (art. 14) and enforcing and postponing removal (18Π(1), 18ΠΑ(1)-(2)) pass to the Council of Ministers, other return powers (18ΟΗ-18ΠΕ) to the Director.

m-ae1bc352.t: Per status (texts read 5-6 Oct 2026), a third-country national may run his own business in Cyprus as: a long-term resident; a family member of an EU citizen, of a Cypriot (once holding a residence and work permit) or of a Blue Card holder; a beneficiary of international or temporary protection (Refugee Law 6(I)/2000 arts 21Α(1), 20Η(1)(α)); a Startup Visa founder in his own company (scheme stated valid to Dec 2026); an immigration permit holder in a self-employment category; a Regulation 12 permit holder (applied for abroad). A master's graduate may stay 12 months to set up a business. Not on a visitor's or another employer's permit, a Blue Card, or a Digital Nomad permit for Cyprus clients.

m-aa420bf8.t: Quality criteria of Cyprus's investor-permit policy (4th revision, read 6 Oct 2026): applicant and spouse file clean criminal record certificates from their country of origin and their country of residence if different, and must not threaten public order or security; applicant and dependants file a health insurance certificate covering inpatient and outpatient care. For categories B-D, or where the new home has too few bedrooms for the family, evidence of accommodation in Cyprus is required (title, sale contract with proof of payment, or a lease). Applicant and spouse also sign a statement that they will take no employment except as directors of the company they invested in.

m-a56f40c3.t: The four €300,000 investments of Cyprus's investor-permit policy (4th revision, in force 2 May 2023; read 6 Oct 2026): (A) a house or flat bought new from a development company, €300,000 plus VAT, up to two units, resales only if the contract was filed with the Land Registry before 7 May 2013; (B) other real estate - offices, shops, hotels - which may be a resale; (C) €300,000 into the share capital of a new or existing Cyprus company based and operating in Cyprus, with proven physical presence and at least five employees (proved by Social Insurance records); (D) €300,000 in units of a Cyprus AIF, AIFLNP or RAIF whose investments are held in Cyprus, with CySEC's confirmation of the fund.

m-a519fff4.t: Besides the €300,000 investment, Cyprus's investor-permit policy (4th revision, read 6 Oct 2026) requires a secure annual income of at least €50,000, plus €15,000 for a spouse and €10,000 for each dependent minor child; the spouse's income may be counted. For a new-home investment (category A) the income must come from abroad (salaries, pensions, dividends, deposit interest, rents); for categories B, C and D it may come wholly or partly from activities in Cyprus. Per the clarification of 17 May 2023, it is proved by the tax return of the country of tax residence or by official certificates of an independent certified accountant.

m-a1589ddf.t: Cyprus's Ministry of Interior announced on 28 April 2023 that revised investor-permit criteria, approved by the Council of Ministers on 21 April 2023, apply from 2 May 2023, 'with the aim of shielding the Scheme's procedure and eliminating weaknesses that were observed and might have left room for its exploitation'. Its example: under the previous scheme one €300,000 property could also secure permits for the investor's parents and parents-in-law; now no permanent residence goes to other adults who have not themselves invested. It added a control mechanism of yearly proof that investment and income are kept, on pain of cancellation for the holder and family.

m-950a5298.t: What Cyprus's 4th revision of the investor-permit criteria (in force 2 May 2023) changed against the 3rd (24 March 2021), reading the two texts side by side: minimum income €30,000 to €50,000; per spouse €5,000 to €15,000; per minor child €5,000 to €10,000; per student child aged 18-25 €5,000 to €10,000; real-estate payments proved at application €200,000 to €300,000; criminal record from the country of residence (or Cyprus) to both country of origin and of residence; health insurance and a yearly monitoring duty added; permits for the investor's parents and parents-in-law dropped. The four €300,000 investment categories and the director exception stayed.

m-8a9fa0a7.t: How an EU citizen going self-employed in Cyprus meets the Migration Department, read together (6 October 2026): the registration certificate may not be made a condition for exercising a right that can be proved by other means (Law 7(I)/2007 art. 23(1)), yet he must apply for it within four months of arrival (art. 10(1)); Social Insurance registration is due at the latest on the day the work starts, with an ID card or passport; the Department's MEU1 list then asks for four months of paid contributions (or, if insured in another EU state, form A1 and health insurance), while the Law asks only 'proof of self-employment' (art. 10(4)(α)). No text read reconciles the two four-month periods.

m-8994cdba.t: How many Cyprus investor permits exist is known only from press figures that do not match, as of 6 Oct 2026. Cyprus Mail (14 Apr 2026) reports 'data given to MPs' that 7,088 'golden visas' were issued since 2013, all still valid. On 24 Sep 2026 Cyprus Mail reports the Deputy Migration Minister saying about 1,500 were issued in the past two years and about 12,000 permits issued since 2013 are being scrutinised; the Cyprus News Agency's Greek text of the same hearing says holders of 'about 12,000 such passports'. None says what is counted (main applicants or each family member, grants or cards); no official table was found on the Migration Department's site.

m-84ec4ab1.t: Two groups of third-country nationals in Cyprus may be self-employed by statute: under the Refugee Law 6(I)/2000 (cylaw text read 6 October 2026), every beneficiary of international protection may pursue employed or self-employed activity 'immediately after the grant' of protection (art. 21Α(1)), and persons under temporary protection may, for the period of protection, pursue employed or independent activity, subject to the law on the profession and to the Aliens and Immigration Law, Cap. 105, with priority for EU citizens and for applicants on unemployment benefit (art. 20Η(1)(α)).

m-828f7a50.t: For the company-shares route of Cyprus's investor permit, the 4th-revision policy (read 6 Oct 2026) describes €300,000 put into the share capital of a newly registered company or a €300,000 increase of an existing company's share capital, proved by Registrar certificates, a business profile, payment proof and Social Insurance staff records. The Department's required-documents list for the same category instead opens with a 'Share Purchase Agreement of a minimum value of €300.000' - wording that also fits buying existing shares from another holder, carried over from the 3rd revision of 2021 ('Συμφωνία αγοράς μετοχών'). No text reconciling the two was found.

m-81dc788c.t: Reading the texts together (6 October 2026): no text says what the Registrar accepts as a non-EU business-name owner's 'permission by the Immigration Officer'. Candidates: a Regulation 12 independent-profession permit, decided by the Regulations' Τμηματάρχης and covering activity exercised individually; for a visitor, the Τμηματάρχης's prior written permission (Regulation 14(3)). Rights to self-employment by law or scheme - long-term resident, international protection, family member of an EU citizen, of a Blue Card holder or (on his terms) of a sponsor, a self-employment immigration permit from the Minister - are no officer's permission; whether the Registrar accepts them is not stated.

m-7e07f59a.t: Cyprus's investment citizenship programme and the Regulation 6(2) investor permit were different instruments that met at one point. The programme naturalised investors 'by exception' under s. 111A(2) of the Civil Registry Laws. Per Ministry of Interior guidelines of 20 October 2016, a Council of Ministers decision of 13 September 2016 required investor and adult family to hold a Cyprus residence permit first; those without one could apply for a Regulation 6(2) permit alongside naturalisation 'solely' for that purpose, on 'no other conditions than those stated in the Scheme', and it was cancelled on naturalisation or refusal. The 6(2) permit alone gives residence, not citizenship.

m-798b949f.t: The 3rd revision of Cyprus's investor-permit criteria (Ministry of Interior, in force 24 March 2021) widened the 2016 scheme, which took only new real estate (up to two dwellings, or a dwelling with a shop or office): it allowed four €300,000 investments - a new home, other real estate including resales, share capital of a Cyprus company with five staff, or Cyprus fund units. It dropped the €30,000 three-year deposit, kept income at €30,000 plus €5,000 per dependant and €8,000 per dependent parent, parents' permits and the €200,000 paid on property. Applicant and spouse could now be directors of the company invested in or, if not investing in shares, unpaid directors.

m-77b43b72.t: Under Regulation 9(1) of Cyprus's Aliens and Immigration Regulations, a temporary entry permit is one of: transit, airport transit, employment, 'exercise of an independent profession' (since 31.12.2001), pupil, temporary student, student, visitor or special permit. Regulation 9(2)(β), subject to the Minister's instructions and the Regulations' other provisions, leaves the issue of each kind except the airport-transit and independent-profession permits to the discretion of the immigration officer at the port of entry; but an employment permit needs the Τμηματάρχης's written approval (11(1)) and a pupil's permit is his (13(1)). The Τμηματάρχης decides the independent-profession permit (12(6)).

m-74d6d8d1.t: Regulation 12(1) of Cyprus's Aliens and Immigration Regulations (text of 31.12.2001) defines 'exercise of an independent profession' as any activity, artistic activity included, exercised individually or in the form of a company within the meaning of the Companies Law (Cap. 113), the Partnerships and Business Names Law (Cap. 116, whose 'company' is a partnership) or the Cooperative Societies Law (Cap. 114), without dependence on an employer in either case. Cap. 116 is also the law under which a business name is registered on form EE1; a sole owner trading under a business name is covered as activity exercised individually.

m-6517ad6a.t: The Cyprus Migration Department's current texts disagree on whether VAT counts toward the €300,000 an investor must have paid for real estate, as read 6 Oct 2026. The 4th-revision policy (para 4.1, English and Greek pages) asks for official payment receipts of 'at least €300,000 (excluding VAT)'; its own required-documents list for Regulation 6(2) asks for 'proof of payment for at least €300.000 (plus VAT)' for categories A and B, and a notice of 19 March 2026 on dependent students also asks for payment of 'at least €300,000 plus VAT'. No text reconciling them was found on the Department's policy, forms or news pages.

m-62cbc341.t: Under Cyprus's Aliens and Immigration Regulations, an alien who wants to enter for an independent profession applies to the Cypriot consulate where he lives or, if none, to the Τμηματάρχης (reg. 12(2)), in an official language of the Republic or English (12(4)), giving his identity and the kind, extent, duration, seat, staff and premises of the business, a clean criminal record, a passport copy and, where applicable, foreign chamber registration, a certified declaration of the sum to be invested, a licence the profession needs, and a company's constitution, registration and officers (12(3)). On arrival he registers (regs 33-36) with a Central Bank certificate of currency imported (12(8)).

m-5cb555dd.t: Adult children who are not financially dependent can get a Cyprus investor permit on the same investment only if it is larger: the 4th revision (read 6 Oct 2026) says the €300,000 is 'multiplied by the number of adult children', but its examples - €600,000 with one adult child, €900,000 with two - mean €300,000 for the applicant plus €300,000 per adult child. For real estate (categories A or B), proof of payment of at least 66% of market value is filed with the application. Each such child shows a secure income of at least €50,000, plus €15,000 for a spouse and €10,000 per dependent minor; the investment may be in the joint names of applicant and child or the applicant's alone.

m-57b84ebf.t: The online service for renewing third-country nationals' residence permits, launched by the Deputy Ministry of Migration and the Migration Department on 6 July 2026, covers at this stage only temporary permits for remunerated employment, domestic employment, employees of companies of foreign interests, family reunification for family of long-term residents and of such employees, and long-term residents' permits - not immigration-permit cards. As of 6 Oct 2026 those cards are still renewed on form MIP2 under the Department's notice of 7 July 2025 (passport copy, old card, €50 fee, from three months before expiry).

m-57635aed.t: Where an application for a Cyprus immigration permit includes minor children as dependants without the participation of both parents, the Migration Department accepts only consent declarations signed before a consular officer of the Republic of Cyprus, which must state explicitly that the parent consents to the child residing permanently in Cyprus - per a clarification printed under the investor-permit policy (4th revision) on the Department's page, read 6 Oct 2026. The page gives no date for this clarification.

m-569a0a2a.t: How the Cyprus investor permit is applied for, as read 6 Oct 2026: form MIP2 (file of 9 March 2026, box 'Regulation 6(2) - Investment Criteria') is filed at the Migration Department's head offices in Nicosia (90 Makarios III Avenue), in person or by an authorised representative, 'after arranging an appointment or any other way decided'; the policy page sets the fee at €500 plus €70 per person for an Alien Registration Certificate where none exists. An applicant in Cyprus attends for photograph, fingerprints and signature; one abroad gives them before the card is issued. Foreign documents are apostilled and in Greek or English or officially translated.

m-54a2fc05.t: Reading the Cyprus texts together (6 Oct 2026), the Regulation 6(2) investor permit is a status of a person - permanent residence for investor and family for €300,000 invested and €50,000 income, with no employment except as director of the company invested in (or, if not investing in shares, unpaid director of Cyprus companies). A 'company of foreign interests' is a status of a company - registered by the Business Facilitation Unit on a €200,000 initial investment - that may employ third-country nationals on temporary residence and employment permits, directors among the staff categories. Neither is a condition of the other; none of these texts says whether the owner may hold such a permit.

m-52461022.t: Since 17 June 2024 (notice K.D.P. 203/2024) Cyprus's Civil Registry and Migration Department, renamed the Migration Department, belongs to the Deputy Ministry of Migration and International Protection (Law 23(I)/2024, Gazette No. 4986 of 15 March 2024, art. 5(4)(α)). Until the immigration laws are amended, art. 18(1) reads references to the Ministry of the Interior as the Deputy Ministry, to the Minister of the Interior as the Deputy Minister (except powers to issue decrees or regulatory acts), to the old Department and its director as the Migration Department and its director, and to the Chief Immigration Officer as the Deputy Minister.

m-5244b3fd.t: Outside Nicosia district, Cyprus's Police Aliens and Immigration district units receive applications by appointment requested by e-mail - limetiseis@police.gov.cy (Limassol), larnacaetiseis@police.gov.cy (Larnaca), pafosetiseis@police.gov.cy (Paphos) - with the applicant's particulars in capitals; the Migration Department's notice (PDF of 15 September 2026, read 6 October 2026) says the answer comes within five working days. Addresses: Limassol, 223 Franklin Roosevelt Avenue, 3046; Larnaca, Piale Pasha, 6027; Paphos, corner of Eleftheriou Venizelou Avenue and Kaniggos Street, 2nd floor, 22 Eleftheriou Venizelou, 8021. Hours Monday-Friday 7:30-14:30 (last entry 13:30).

m-4316a254.t: Under the 2nd revision of Cyprus's investor-permit criteria (Ministry of Interior, 22 February 2016, replaced 24 March 2021) the only investment was real estate: property worth at least €300,000 excluding VAT, with at least €200,000 paid, bought new from a developer (resales after 7 May 2013 refused). The applicant also had to pledge a €30,000 deposit with a Cyprus bank for at least three years and show a secure annual income from abroad of €30,000, plus €5,000 per dependant and €8,000 per dependent parent; parents and parents-in-law could get permits. Applicant and spouse confirmed they would take no employment in Cyprus at all; holding shares and receiving dividends was allowed.

m-4227a833.t: The European Commission's EU Immigration Portal page 'Self-employed worker in Cyprus' (dated 1 April 2025, read 6 October 2026) tells non-EU citizens that self-employment needs an 'immigration permit, which is a type of permanent residence permit', applied for at the 'Civil Registry and Migration Department' (renamed the Migration Department on 17 June 2024), and lists categories A-D with capital of €427,000, €342,000 and €256,000. It does not mention the one-year independent-profession permit of Regulation 12, whose criteria (effect on the economy, jobs, imported currency) it attaches to the immigration permit. It is the Commission's summary, not a Cypriot text.

m-3ef37792.t: As of 6 October 2026 no decision on the Cyprus Startup Visa after December 2026 had been published. The gov.cy page 'Apply for a Cyprus Startup Visa' (read 6 October 2026) takes applications by e-mail to the Deputy Ministry of Research, Innovation and Digital Policy and links the Practical Guide dated December 2024 as a PDF (created 17 July 2025) and as a Word file named for 2026 (last modified 18 August 2026, new contact officer); both say 'The Scheme is valid until December 2026 and up to 150 visas can be issued'. The Deputy Ministry's news list, read 6 October 2026, has no item on the scheme from 11 to 30 September 2026 and none after.

m-3c74e360.t: Read together on 6 October 2026, Cyprus's texts put CY Login on only part of path 1: the Tax Register can be reached with a separate Tax For All account opened with an e-mail, while the Registrar's online name approval and e-filing, and by September 2026 the payment of Social Insurance contributions through SISnet, run through CY Login. A profile identified in person needs a Cypriot identity card, a residence permit showing the alien registration number, or an EU registration certificate, so an EU citizen without online banking identifies in person only after his MEU1 certificate; the published alternatives are a commercial bank's e-banking and, for EU citizens, eIDAS sign-in.

m-3bebe21e.t: After a Cyprus investor permit is granted, the policy (4th revision, read 6 Oct 2026) requires the holder to prove to the Migration Department every year that the investment is kept and, for those no longer covered by GeSY, that health insurance is held; holder and adult family file clean criminal record certificates from country of origin and residence every three years. Disposing of the investment without at once replacing it with one of the same or greater value meeting the criteria leads to cancellation under Regulation 6, as does failing these proofs, for holder and family. The clarification of 17 May 2023 dropped the yearly proof of income and made the record check three-yearly.

m-2a2f9000.t: Law 4(I)/2025 (Official Gazette No. 5026, 14 February 2025) replaced the words 'Λειτουργός Μετανάστευσης' (Immigration Officer) - the Greek words of the Registrar's business-name criterion - with 'Διευθυντής', the Director of the Migration Department, in two articles of Cyprus's Aliens and Immigration Law, Cap. 105: art. 9A(2), where that officer may still allow a border visa for humanitarian or national-interest reasons (s. 7), and art. 7A(4)(γ) (s. 5). CyLaw's consolidated Cap. 105 (amendments to 149(I)/2024, read 6 October 2026) still shows 'ο Λειτουργός Μετανάστευσης' in art. 9A(2). The Aliens and Immigration Regulations, unamended since 2013, keep 'Τμηματάρχης'.

m-22190c57.t: Family under Cyprus's investor-permit policy (4th revision, read 6 Oct 2026): the permit covers the spouse and children under 18 as dependants; each spouse may hold a separate permit on a separate application and fee without the other meeting the criteria, but cancellation of the investor's permit cancels the spouse's. Unmarried children aged 18-25 who are tertiary students abroad and financially dependent may file their own application with a fee if the parents show €10,000 more income per such child; that permit stays valid after 25, but cannot include the child's own spouse or children. The 4th revision has no provision for the investor's parents.

m-159a5817.t: The transitional window into Cyprus's old investor criteria came in two versions. The Civil Registry and Migration Department's notice of 27 April 2023 let applicants who had filed sale contracts with the Land Registry between 2 January 2023 and 28 April 2023 apply on the 3rd-revision criteria (24 March 2021). A notice of 29 August 2023, 'after a decision of the Minister of Interior', amended it to contracts filed from 2 January 2022 to 28 April 2023, and said the old criteria cover dependants (parents, students, spouses, minor children) only if their applications are filed together with the main applicant's. The window had no closing date until it was ended on 3 March 2026.

m-13afa89c.t: The Cyprus investor immigration permit under Regulation 6(2) gives a permanent residence right, per the Migration Department's page read 6 Oct 2026 (which speaks of residence only and says nothing about citizenship): the residence right is 'of unlimited validity' for the holder and adult dependants, but the residence card expires ten years after issue and must be replaced; the residence permit of minor dependants is valid until age 18. The permit ceases to be valid if holder and dependants residing outside Cyprus fail to acquire residence in Cyprus within one year of approval, or if they acquire permanent residence abroad or are absent from Cyprus for a period of two years.

m-11900f13.t: Family members admitted to Cyprus under the family-reunification articles of the Aliens and Immigration Law (Cap. 105, arts 18ΚΘ-18ΛΗ; the sponsor must hold a permit valid at least one year with reasonable prospects of permanent residence, art. 18ΚΙ(1)) have access to employment and self-employed activity 'on the same terms and conditions as the sponsor' (art. 18ΛΔ(1)(β)), subject to the conditions in force for employing third-country nationals and national policies (18ΛΔ(2)). That access is restricted for a period of up to twelve months for a labour-market examination, after which it is allowed on application (18ΛΔ(3)). Law 4(I)/2025 does not amend art. 18ΛΔ.

m-039f8977.t: Cyprus's Deputy Minister of Migration and International Protection, Nicholas Ioannides, stated after the House Audit Committee session of 24 September 2026 that 'in the coming months' more categories of residence permits will be renewable online, that 'our fellow citizens' will be able to pay online the fees of submitted applications, and that 'in the next period' citizens will be able to follow an application online and be told by SMS or e-mail when its examination ends. He framed this as serving citizens who employ foreigners and gave no dates or list of new categories. Online renewal already exists for some permits (five categories since 6 July 2026).

m-fdf91697.t: For third-country family members of a Cypriot citizen the rule on work is a policy stated on the Migration Department's page; no provision on it was found in Cap. 105 or Law 4(I)/2025: entry and residence fall under Cap. 105 and 'a policy is applied for facilitating them'. Per the page (read 5 Oct 2026), spouses or partners and parents of minor Cypriot citizens 'have free access to the labour market including self-employment', a right that 'can be exercised after obtaining a residence and employment permit'. Fees: €80 for a residence and work permit with paid employment (decree K.D.P. 284/2022, in force 18 July 2022), €50 without, plus €70 first registration; examination within four months.

m-f9450372.t: The Cyprus Migration Department revised all its application forms in March 2026: its notice of 11 March 2026 says that 'as of 2 April 2026, only the revised and updated versions of the forms will be accepted'. The files on its site read on 5 Oct 2026 carry the date in their names - MEU1B_20260309 (EU citizens), MBCS4_20260309 (companies of foreign interests), MVIS8_20260309 (visitors and digital nomads), MIP2_20260309 (immigration permits), MSUP2_20260309 (Startup Visa). A form copy saved before March 2026 is not accepted.

m-f6c1dd74.t: The Alien Registration Certificate (ARC) rests on Regulations 31-36 of the Cyprus Aliens and Immigration Regulations: an Aliens' Register is kept for each district, and every alien must on registration obtain a certificate; the fee is €70 (Fourth Schedule, as amended 1.2.2013). The Migration Department's glossary (read 5 Oct 2026) says 'ARC' is also used for the alien registration number. In practice first registration is made with the first residence application: the Department's fee lists carry 'Registration in the Aliens' Register (only in cases of first registration): €70'. The EU citizens' form MEU1 has an 'ARC' field for official use, so EU citizens receive the number too.

m-ee7ced0f.t: Regulation 6(2) of Cyprus's Aliens and Immigration Regulations lets the Minister grant an immigration permit outside the Regulation 5 categories if not harmful to the Republic's inhabitants. The investor route rests on this power and a published policy, not a law: the 'Criteria for granting an Immigration Permit within the scope of the expedited procedure', 4th revision, in force 2 May 2023, issued by the Minister of Interior 'having notified the Council of Ministers'. It requires €300,000 invested (new dwelling, other real estate, shares of a Cyprus company with five staff, or fund units) and €50,000 annual income. From 3 March 2026 the 3rd revision (24 March 2021) is closed to new filings.

m-ecf8726d.t: Cyprus immigration fees by instrument, as read on 5 Oct 2026. Law 7(I)/2007: €20 each for an EU citizen's registration certificate (art. 10(4)) and permanent residence certificate (art. 17(1)). Schedules of the Aliens and Immigration Regulations (amended 1.2.2013): €70 alien registration certificate, €70 visitor's residence permit, €500 immigration permit application. K.D.P. 284/2022 (in force 18 July 2022): €70 and €80 for permits in a company of foreign interests, €120 and €130 for other single permits. K.D.P. 200/2025 (in force 7 July 2025): €110, €95, €40 for the EU Blue Card. Long-term resident status: the biometric identity-card fee (Cap. 105 art. 18Ι(1)); €30 per the Department page.

m-e95aa050.t: Immigration applications in Cyprus are handled by the Migration Department of the Deputy Ministry of Migration and International Protection. Law 23(I)/2024 moved the Civil Registry and Migration Department out of the Ministry of Interior and renamed it Migration Department (art. 5(4)(α)), leaving civil registry, marriage and citizenship matters with that Ministry; the Deputy Ministry 'was established on 17/6/24'. Until the sector laws are amended, references to the Minister of Interior are read as the Deputy Minister, except powers to issue decrees (art. 18(1)(β)) - hence the 2025 Blue Card fees decree is signed by the Minister of Interior. The Department's site is now gov.cy/mip-md.

m-e7057606.t: Visitor's temporary residence permit for a third-country national, per the Migration Department, 5 Oct 2026: form MVIS8 filed before the entry visa expires; fee €70 for issue or renewal plus €70 for first registration in the Aliens' Register (fixed in the Fifth and Fourth Schedules of the Aliens and Immigration Regulations as amended 1.2.2013); first permit one year, renewable; examination 'usually before the completion of four (4) months'. The list requires foreign remittances of at least €2,000 a month or €24,000 a year for one person (plus 20% for a spouse, 15% per child), a ten-year bank guarantee, health insurance and, for a first permit, a criminal record certificate and medical tests.

m-e48ed338.t: What the Cyprus Migration Department asks of a Startup Visa founder, per its supporting-documents list (file uploaded 29 December 2025, read 5 Oct 2026): the Registrar's certificates of incorporation, registered office, directors and shareholders, proof of levy payment and a tax clearance certificate for the company (each 'Not necessary in case of self-employment'); the Notification of Initial Approval; for paid employment a contract with a gross monthly salary of at least €850; for self-employment proof of at least €10,000 a year for living expenses and a ten-year bank guarantee for repatriation costs. A founder changing status inside Cyprus adds a 'Letter of approval for change of status'.

m-df4a731e.t: A third-country national works in a Cyprus company of foreign interests on a temporary residence and employment permit issued by the Migration Department under the strategy approved by the Council of Ministers on 15 October 2021 (in force 2 January 2022), per the Department's page read 5 Oct 2026. 'Highly paid' staff need a minimum gross monthly salary of €2,500, relevant academic qualifications or two years' relevant experience, and an employment contract of at least two years; there is no quota and no labour-market test. Below €2,500 the post is 'supportive level', needing a labour-market test and a contract sealed by the Department of Labour. 'Director' is one of the staff categories.

m-da66deae.t: For a citizen of another EU or EEA state the registration certificate is a duty backed by a fine, not a legal precondition for economic activity in Cyprus. Art. 23(1) of Law 7(I)/2007 provides that possession of the registration certificate or permanent residence certificate may 'in no case' be imposed as a precondition for exercising a right or completing an administrative formality where entitlement can be attested by any other means of proof; being employed or self-employed is itself a ground of residence (art. 9(1)(α)). The Migration Department's MEU1 page (read 5 Oct 2026) says Union citizens 'enjoy free access to employment, including employed or self-employed activity'.

m-d7880868.t: Capital thresholds for the self-employment categories of the Cyprus immigration permit, in two texts. The consolidated Aliens and Immigration Regulations (to 2013; euro amounts by notice K.D.P. 312/2007) require freely disposable capital of €341,720 for Category A (agriculture) and B (mining) and €256,290 for C (trade or business), 'or such lesser sum as the Committee may decide'. The Migration Department's page (5 Oct 2026) gives 'approximately' €430,000 (CY£250,000) for A, €350,000 (CY£200,000) for B and €260,000 (CY£150,000) for C. At CY£0.585274 per euro the Regulation's sums equal CY£200,000 and CY£150,000, so the texts differ only for A. C also requires any licence the business needs.

m-cfc1822d.t: As of 5 Oct 2026 the Migration Department publishes no page and no document list for the Regulation 12 permit to exercise an independent profession. Its general employment form MNSP3 (file MNSP3_20260309) has a 'Self-employment' box, but the only list published for it asks for the identity card for persons of Greek origin or the approved list of Syrians of Cretan origin and Kurds; the page 'Employment - other cases' says these groups 'have the right to self-employment in the Republic'. The site's other routes for founders: employment in a company of foreign interests, the Start-up Visa, the investor immigration permit, and a 12-month stay to set up a business after a master's degree.

m-cfb67515.t: For a third-country national the Cyprus Aliens and Immigration Regulations treat running one's own business as 'exercise of an independent profession', needing a permit (regs 9(1)(γ), 12): any activity exercised individually or as a company under the Companies Law or the partnerships law, without dependence on an employer (12(1)). The Immigration Officer (the Regulations' 'Τμηματάρχης') decides after hearing the labour and commerce ministries, weighing benefit to the economy, jobs and imported foreign exchange (12(6)); in a company only alien partners with active participation whose presence is necessary for its management may get it (12(6)(γ)). The permit lasts one year, renewed if the activity is profitable and beneficial (12(9)).

m-ce8da959.t: The Cyprus Startup Visa expressly lets a third-country founder be self-employed or employed in his own company. Its Practical Guide (Deputy Ministry of Research, Innovation and Digital Policy, dated December 2024, read 5 Oct 2026) says the scheme 'is valid until December 2026 and up to 150 visas can be issued', covers a sole founder or a team of up to five, requires at least 25% of the shares to be held by the applicants, and gives founders the 'Right to self-employment or paid employment in their registered company within the Republic'. The company must be an 'innovative startup' (early-stage ones are scored on a business plan); the Deputy Ministry decides within five weeks.

m-cc5c7ebc.t: Swiss citizens' free movement in Cyprus rests on a treaty, not on the text of Law 7(I)/2007: by Article 1 of the Protocol to the EC-Switzerland Agreement on the free movement of persons (OJ L 89, 28.3.2006, p. 30) the ten states that joined the EU in 2004, Cyprus among them, 'become Contracting Parties to the Agreement'. Both acts resolve in CELLAR on 5 Oct 2026 (the brackets of the CELEX number must be percent-encoded). No Cyprus law or decision applying the Law's registration procedure to Swiss citizens was found in the Law or on the Migration Department's pages; only the Department's MEU1 page says the procedure covers them.

m-ba6fb56d.t: The Cyprus Digital Nomad Visa is a residence permit, not a work permit, under Council of Ministers decisions of 15 October 2021 (ceiling 100) and 3 March 2022 (ceiling 500). It is for non-EU, non-EEA nationals working remotely for an employer registered abroad or, self-employed, for clients abroad, with net income of at least €3,500 a month; the applicant affirms that neither he nor his family will provide work or services 'to an employer or clients established in Cyprus'. The ceiling was exhausted by early 2024; on 26 March 2025 applications were announced as accepted, and the page (read 5 Oct 2026) says the maximum 'remains at 500'. Fee €70 plus €70 registration; examination 5-7 weeks.

m-b6e93b94.t: A third-country national who finished studies in Cyprus at master's level or above may stay to found a business: art. 25 of Law 7(I)/2019 (CyLaw text as amended by Law 110(I)/2024, read 5 Oct 2026) entitles researchers and students who held a permit under that Law to remain for twelve months 'to seek employment or set up a business' at the level of the research or studies completed; for students the minimum is level 7 of the European Qualifications Framework. The application is filed at least 30 days before the study permit expires; after three months the authority may ask for proof of a genuine chance of being hired or of setting up the business. The Migration Department has a page on it.

m-b330f776.t: The entry test for a Cyprus 'company of foreign interests' changed in 2022-2026. The government's Q&A (file updated 19/7/22) asked only for majority third-country ownership (or a foreign stake of at least €200,000 in nominal capital) and independent offices, applications going to the Business Facilitation Unit by e-mail or letter. A Council of Ministers decision of 30 November 2022, in force 12 December 2022, brought back the duty to prove an initial investment of at least €200,000 (Unit's page, archived 6 December 2022); an electronic system opened in December 2023; since 30 June 2026 applications go only through the company's CY Login profile, and the criterion applies 'in all the cases'.

m-b2898630.t: Registration as a company of foreign interests in Cyprus requires proof of an initial investment of €200,000 'in all the cases', per the Business Facilitation Unit's page as of 5 Oct 2026. The investment must have been made up to six months before the application and still be present: a deposit by the shareholders into the company's account at a credit institution licensed by the Central Bank (electronic money and payment institutions are not accepted), or the purchase of an office or equipment for business use. Proof is a bank SWIFT or equivalent showing the transfer from abroad to the company's account in Cyprus with the balance on the application date, or invoices in the company's name.

m-b1010dee.t: Regulation 12(10) of the Cyprus Aliens and Immigration Regulations bars the in-country route to the independent-profession permit: the holder of a pupil's, student's, visitor's or employment permit or of any other special permit may not, during its validity or after its expiry while remaining in the Republic, apply for it. Under 12(2) an alien 'who wishes to enter the Republic' applies through the consular authority of his country of residence or, where there is none, to the Immigration Officer (the Regulations' 'Τμηματάρχης'); under 12(11) a holder of that permit may not seek an employment permit unless he has an immigration permit. Long-term residents and EU citizens' family members have self-employment by Law, outside this permit.

m-b0774442.t: As of 5 Oct 2026 the Cyprus Migration Department's pages and document lists still call for stamped contracts although stamp duty was abolished from 1 January 2026: the procedure page for companies of foreign interests says 'employment contracts should be stamped', their document list (dated 21.3.2024) asks for an employment contract 'dully signed and stamped', and the MEU1 list asks for a rental document 'duly stamped by the Superintendent of Stamping'. The Department addressed the point in a Greek-only notice of 29 January 2026: a document drawn up and signed, even by one party, after 01/01/2026 is not subject to stamp duty; documents signed up to 31/12/2025 are stamped as before.

m-aefb85c0.t: Reading the Cyprus texts together for a third-country founder (5 Oct 2026): no approval to hold shares or to be entered as a director was found in the Companies Law or the immigration texts read. What is regulated is activity. Employment needs a permit naming the employer. Running a business needs a status with free access to work (long-term resident, family member of a Cypriot or EU citizen), a Startup Visa, an immigration permit in a self-employment category, or a Regulation 12 permit, which holders of visitor, student or employment permits may not apply for while in Cyprus. A company of foreign interests may employ third-country staff; no text read says whether its owner may be one.

m-aeaf8a50.t: Whether a third-country national on a visitor's permit may hold shares in a Cyprus company is not stated in the Regulations, but the Migration Department's document list (read 5 Oct 2026) accepts as income, 'by exception', dividends from a company in the Republic, on the company accountant's certificate that the applicant 'does not receive any salary from his position'; the same list still requires remittances from abroad of at least €24,000 a year. It thus assumes a visitor who is a shareholder with an unpaid position. No published text was found on whether an unpaid directorship is 'carrying on business' under Regulation 14(3), or on how the prior written permission of the Immigration Officer (the Regulations' 'Τμηματάρχης') is sought.

m-ad7ea716.t: Which company may register as a 'company of foreign interests' in Cyprus, per the Business Facilitation Unit's page as of 5 Oct 2026: a business (e.g. a local company, HE, or an overseas company's branch, AE) meeting one of nine criteria, the first being majority ownership by third-country nationals ('50% plus'). Where a third-country national owns 50% or less, that share must be worth at least €200,000 - 'additional to the initial investment of €200.000'. The others: listed public companies, former offshore companies, Cypriot shipping, high-tech or innovation, pharmaceutical or biotech companies, companies of persons naturalised on economic criteria, private tertiary-education institutes.

m-9d192074.t: The Migration Department's own FAQ (read 5 Oct 2026) draws the line for third-country nationals who want to work in Cyprus: 'I have a visitor residence permit. Can I work? No, a visitor's residence permit does not allow employment'; a permit naming an employer allows work only at that employer. It sorts cases into four groups: posts needing a Department of Labour permit; persons with 'free access to the labor market', for example family members of a Cypriot or EU citizen and long-term residents; cases checked by the Migration Department itself; and cases needing another authority's approval, such as companies of foreign interest, which 'need approval from the Business Facilitation Unit'.

m-9c9475f1.t: A third-country national who is a family member of a citizen of another EU or EEA state residing in Cyprus - spouse, descendant under 21 or dependent, dependent ascendant (Law 7(I)/2007, art. 2) - may work without a work permit: under art. 21 family members of a Union citizen, irrespective of nationality, with a right of residence or permanent residence may take up employed or self-employed activity, and art. 22(1) gives them equal treatment with Cypriot citizens. The residence card is sought on form MEU2 within four months of entry, at the district office, with the Union citizen present; fee €20; decision within six months; card valid up to five years (Migration Department, 5 Oct 2026).
