On 5 October 2026 the cylaw.org consolidation printed 15.600 once and £9.000 four times, all four in Part I, para 1.

m-6e84fbeb.t: The first VAT return of a Cyprus company registered in late 2026 falls due by the quarter given at registration, normally by NACE activity code. Reg. 17(1) of the VAT Regulations K.D.P. 314/2001 requires each return by the tenth day after the end of the month following the period; proviso (β): the first return covers the scheduled period in which the person was registered, starting that day. The Tax Department's 2026 calendar shows three staggered sets of quarters and moves a weekend or holiday due date to the next working day. A period ending 30 November 2026 falls due on 11 January 2027 (the 10th is a Sunday), one ending 31 December on 10 February, one ending 31 January on 10 March.

m-5e579547.t: Cyprus's VAT 'legal receipt' duty dates from 16 January 2012. Interpretative Circular 161 of 13 January 2012 (VAT Service, then part of the Customs Department) announced that, under para 1A of the Tenth Schedule to the VAT Law and reg. 13A of K.D.P. 314/2001 (inserted by K.D.P. 536/2011, Gazette No. 4539 of 30 December 2011), from that date every taxable person making a taxable supply to a non-taxable person in Cyprus issues and delivers a VAT receipt at the time of supply. The circular already states both sanctions that stand in the VAT Law on 4 October 2026: a charge equal to 20% of the transaction value and, on conviction, a fine of up to €1,700, up to three years' imprisonment, or both.

m-4fa8b074.t: How a supplier addresses an e-invoice to the Cyprus central government, per the Treasury's 'Instructions to parties contracting with the State' (PDF on its e-invoicing page, read 5 October 2026): get access to PEPPOL by connecting its system to an access point bought from a licensed provider, or buy a provider's integrated e-invoicing service; enter the Republic's PEPPOL ID 90007641D, which covers all central government; and name the ministry, department or service invoiced with its VAT number or assigned code in the fields BuyerReference and CompanyID, from the list annexed. The government's announcement of 27 March 2025 adds that an invoice sent as a PDF is not an e-invoice.

m-35930d2f.t: Treasury of Cyprus Circular No. 8 of 7 April 2025, on Law 89(I)/2019 (read 5 October 2026): the Republic 'has the obligation and accepts' e-invoices since 18 April 2019; they travel over PEPPOL, following Council of Ministers decision 82.077 of 15 February 2017, and are received on a platform run by the Treasury, so central government authorities need take no further step. Suppliers 'who wish' to issue e-invoices follow the steps on the Treasury's site. Received e-invoices are to be prioritised and paid in no more than 20 days from receipt of the invoice or acceptance of the works, goods or services, whichever is later, against the 30 days of existing legislation.

m-13ddb734.t: A new Cyprus company can register for VAT on intention, before any sale: para. 9(b) of Part I of the First Schedule to VAT Law 95(I)/2000 has the Commissioner register, on written request, a person who satisfies him that it carries on business and intends to make taxable supplies, from the day of the request or an earlier agreed date. Form T.F. 1101 (2024) has the matching box - 'I intend on ../../.... to start making taxable supplies and have the right to register' - and requires an attached document proving the right or duty, the expected supplies of the next 12 months by rate and a signature (company: representative, director, secretary or authorised officer); it asks for no bank account.

m-0c87b843.t: Two Tax Department texts differ on whether a VAT application may go in before the tax identification number exists. Form T.F. 1101 (edition 2024, PDF of 26 January 2024), Part A point 3, says an applicant without a number 'must FIRST' apply for the Tax Register through Tax For All and send the VAT application after receiving the number. The Department's VAT registration page (read 5 Oct 2026) and the government business portal (page modified 15 September 2026) say that where the request has been filed but no number issued, the form may be submitted with the request's reference number (REGXXX) written on it. The web pages are the later texts; neither says which the district offices follow.

m-f7fd5dd9.t: Cyprus VAT Interpretative Circular 139 of 3 March 2010 (on the place-of-supply rules applying from 1 January 2010, Directive 2008/8/EC) states that taxable persons belonging in Cyprus who receive from abroad, for other than private purposes, services whose place of supply is where the recipient belongs must account for VAT by reverse charge, and that persons not registered 'must register in the VAT Register' if they receive such services. No reverse charge is due on received services that are exempt under the Seventh Schedule. The circular names no threshold; it was still listed among the Department's circulars on 4 October 2026.

m-f31b7ae5.t: VAT penalties in Cyprus for not issuing a legal receipt (VAT Law 95(I)/2000, read 4 October 2026): under art. 45(9) a person who fails to comply with the regulations requiring a legal receipt is liable to a charge equal to 20% of the value of the transaction the receipt relates to; under art. 46(11A) failing to issue and deliver a legal receipt at the time of the transaction is a criminal offence punishable on conviction by a fine of up to €1,700, imprisonment of up to three years, or both. The Tax Department's page on rights and obligations describes the administrative charge as 'up to' 20%.

m-f2aa5ebc.t: The VAT exemption for payments and transfers (art. 135(1)(d) of Directive 2006/112/EC, ex art. 13B(d)(3) of the Sixth Directive) is read narrowly by the Court of Justice. Under the Sixth Directive, SDC (C-2/95, 5 June 1997) - an outsourced service is exempt only if, viewed broadly, it forms a distinct whole fulfilling the specific, essential functions of a transfer, not a mere physical or technical supply; Nordea (C-350/10, 28 July 2011) - SWIFT messaging not exempt. Under art. 135(1)(d): Bookit (C-607/14, 26 May 2016) - a 'card handling' fee on a cinema ticket paid by card is not exempt; DPAS (C-5/17, 25 July 2018) - asking banks to run direct debits and onward transfers is not exempt.

m-ebf7a92b.t: Two Court of Justice judgments of 2010 on payment handling. AXA UK (C-175/09, 28 October 2010): a service that consists, in essence, in asking a third party's bank to transfer by direct debit a sum due to the supplier's client, reporting receipts, chasing non-payers and passing on the money less a fee is not covered by the exemption of art. 13B(d)(3) of the Sixth Directive (it is debt collection). Everything Everywhere (C-276/09, 2 December 2010): extra charges a telecoms provider invoices to customers who pay by credit card, debit card, cheque or cash rather than direct debit are not consideration for a separate supply; they share the VAT treatment of the principal supply.

m-eb2888fc.t: For a shop, the commission kept by the card company does not reduce the VAT base. In Chaussures Bally (C-18/92, judgment of 25 May 1993) the Court of Justice held, on art. 11A(1)(a) of the Sixth VAT Directive (now art. 73 of Directive 2006/112/EC), that where the purchaser pays by credit card and the card-issuing organisation pays the supplier the price after deducting a percentage as commission for the service it renders to the supplier, the sum so deducted must be included in the taxable amount on which the supplier pays VAT. A merchant therefore accounts for output VAT on the full price charged to the customer, not on the amount settled after the merchant service charge.

m-eaccadd8.t: Cyprus applied a zero VAT rate to fresh, chilled or frozen meat (beef, pork, sheep and goat meat, edible offal, poultry, rabbit and hare) and to fish, cuttlefish, squid and octopus from 6 April 2026 to 30 September 2026 under Decree K.D.P. 168/2026 (Official Gazette, Annex III(I), No. 6012 of 27 March 2026), which amended the Fifth and Sixth Schedules of VAT Law 95(I)/2000. K.D.P. 354/2026, as described by the Tax Department on 2 October 2026, carries the same goods at zero rate from 1 October 2026 to 31 May 2027, so there is no gap.

m-ea667d94.t: A VAT-registered shop or café in Cyprus must hand every consumer a 'legal receipt' at the time of sale. Reg. 13A of the VAT (General) Regulations K.D.P. 314/2001 (inserted by K.D.P. 536/2011, applied from 16 January 2012) requires a taxable person making a taxable supply to a non-taxable person in Cyprus to issue and deliver at that time a receipt showing at least: date of issue; identifying number; supplier's name, address and VAT number; description of the goods or services; the total payable including VAT; for each VAT rate the total including VAT and the rate; and whether the sale is for cash, an advance or part payment. A cash invoice under the income-tax rules takes its place.

m-de217c70.t: Cyprus VAT Interpretative Circular 230 of 20 February 2019, signed by the Tax Commissioner: transactions of buying and selling prepaid electronic means of payment (the example given is paysafecards) fall within the exemption of para 3(δ) of Table B of the Seventh Schedule to VAT Law 95(I)/2000 (transactions concerning currency, banknotes and coins used as legal tender); both the purchase and sale and the commission arising from that trade are exempt from VAT. The circular does not deal with card acceptance or merchant fees. Listed among the Department's circulars on 4 October 2026.

m-d4658631.t: Cyprus VAT Interpretative Circular 127 of 28 May 2009 applies the Court of Justice judgment Ecotrade (joined cases C-95/07 and C-96/07, 8 May 2008): where an audit finds output VAT not accounted for because the reverse charge was not applied, the right to deduct the corresponding input tax is granted in parallel, to the extent the taxable person has that right. A person who missed the entry may correct the books under reg. 24 of the VAT (General) Regulations K.D.P. 314/2001 or, if the correction exceeds €1,710 or is older than three years, under reg. 25 as the Commissioner requires. The same treatment applies to intra-EU acquisitions of goods.

m-d3c1056d.t: The European Commission's country sheet 'eInvoicing in Cyprus' (updated 6 March 2026, read 4 October 2026) records no e-invoicing mandate for suppliers to the State, none between businesses, none towards consumers, no VAT real-time reporting and no monitoring mechanism. Public contracting authorities must accept e-invoices compliant with EN 16931 for contracts above the EU procurement thresholds; a central platform exists, suppliers may submit voluntarily through Peppol access points and the government gateway, and Cyprus follows Peppol BIS Billing 3.0 with no national specification. It names the Ministry of Finance as responsible and says discussions on a mandate for suppliers are ongoing.

m-cf6f0fe3.t: Price pages of providers serving Cyprus state VAT for hardware, not plainly for transaction fees (read 4 October 2026). myPOS (en-cy): the terminal price is marked 'excl. VAT'; the 1.69% + €0.05 fee has no VAT wording, and its Legal Agreement (3 April 2026, cl. 19.7) leaves 'any applicable taxes arising from use of the Service' to the merchant. SumUp (el-cy): terminals are shown net and 'with VAT' (169 € / 201,11 €, i.e. 19%); the 1.95% fee has no VAT wording, but the 0.89% fee of its paid plan carries an asterisk to a footnote 'Price without VAT', whose object is ambiguous. JCC's merchant terms v2.9 (archived 19 March 2025) define the Merchant Service Charge without mentioning VAT on it.

m-c897562f.t: Cross-border B2C sales inside the EU: under art. 59c of Directive 2006/112/EC, inserted by art. 2(7) of Directive (EU) 2017/2455 and applied from 1 July 2021 (Council Decision (EU) 2020/1109), a supplier established in only one Member State keeps taxing intra-EU distance sales of goods and telecom, broadcasting and electronic services to consumers at home while their total value does not exceed EUR 10,000 (net of VAT) in the current and the preceding calendar year; once exceeded, VAT of the customer's Member State is due. Cyprus lists Law 181(I)/2021 and K.D.P. 499-503/2021 as its OSS legislation; OSS returns are quarterly, due by the end of the month after the quarter (2026 calendar).

m-c2f60a05.t: As of 4 Oct 2026 the Cyprus Tax Department requires a VAT registration request on form T.F. 1101 (T.D. 1101), filed on paper at a District Office together with the company's registration certificates from the Registrar of Companies and evidence of economic activity or of the obligation or right to register (issued invoices, agreements or correspondence). The applicant must first be registered in the Tax Register and hold a TIN, or quote the reference number (REGXXX) of a pending TFA registration request.

m-bed110dc.t: The EU SME VAT scheme of Directive (EU) 2020/285 applies from 1 January 2025: a Member State's exemption threshold may not exceed EUR 85,000, and a small enterprise established in another Member State gets the same exemption if its Union annual turnover does not exceed EUR 100,000. Cyprus transposed it by Law 104(I)/2025 (Gazette No. 5043 of 25 June 2025), deemed in force from 1 January 2025: an EU business not established in Cyprus is exempt from registering there if its Cyprus turnover does not exceed €15,600 and its EU turnover €100,000; a Cyprus business using the exemption elsewhere is identified by a number with the suffix 'EX' and reports quarterly within one month.

m-bb22d2f0.t: The card carve-out in Cyprus's VAT exemption for financial services dates from 2006. Law 64(I)/2006 (Official Gazette, Annex I(I), No. 4082, 14 April 2006; in force on publication) added sub-paragraph (iii), 'services of processing, clearing and authorisation for the movement of money in relation to credit cards', to para 3(γ) of Table B of the Seventh Schedule to VAT Law 95(I)/2000, next to (i) collection of third-party debts and (ii) factoring, which were in the 2000 text. The wording is unchanged in the consolidated text read on 4 October 2026: it says 'credit cards' and no provision of the paragraph names debit cards.

m-b9f04773.t: No domestic business-to-business or business-to-consumer e-invoicing mandate, and no announcement of one, was found for Cyprus on 4 October 2026. Looked in: the Tax Department's VAT invoice page and list of VAT circulars (latest No. 2026/04 of 26 August 2026); the Treasury's e-invoicing page; the government announcement of 27 March 2025, which concerns invoices to the State; and the Commission's country sheet of 6 March 2026. Under reg. 11A of K.D.P. 314/2001 an invoice may be sent on paper or electronically, and 'the use of an electronic invoice is subject to acceptance' by the customer. The first binding date remains 1 July 2030, for intra-EU supplies, under Directive (EU) 2025/516.

m-b1a0522b.t: Time of supply for reverse-charged services in Cyprus: reg. 41 of the VAT (General) Regulations K.D.P. 314/2001, as replaced by reg. 2 of K.D.P. 94/2010 with effect from 1 January 2010, treats services deemed supplied by the recipient under art. 11(1) as supplied when they are performed; services supplied over a period for consideration fixed or payable periodically are treated as supplied at the end of each period paid for; a payment made earlier brings the time of supply forward to the payment date. Before 2010 the rule was payment-based (when payment was made). Read in the Tax Department's consolidated text (last update K.D.P. 71/2025) on 4 October 2026.

m-afd04f84.t: VAT returns in Cyprus are filed electronically through the Tax For All (TFA) portal, normally for quarterly periods assigned at registration by the business's NACE activity code; the Tax Commissioner may set monthly or annual periods. In the Tax Department's 2026 calendar each return and payment falls due on the 10th day of the second month after the period ends (for example the quarter April–June 2026: 10 August 2026, extended that time to 20 August 2026). Monthly VIES and Intrastat statements and quarterly OSS returns have their own deadlines.

m-aa65b58d.t: How reverse-charged services appear in the Cyprus VAT return, per the Tax Department's completion guide (dated 31/08/2020, linked from its returns page on 4 October 2026): the VAT due on services received from abroad goes in box 1 (output tax); the same amount may go in box 4 as input tax under the conditions of art. 21; the net value is entered in box 6 (outputs) and in box 7 (inputs); services received from taxable persons in other Member States are also totalled in box 11B. For a fully taxable business the entry is cash-neutral; a business with exempt outputs recovers only part.

m-a940612b.t: Reverse charge on services bought abroad is art. 11 of Cyprus VAT Law 95(I)/2000. Paras (1)-(2) come from art. 4 of Law 13(I)/2010 (Gazette No. 4233, 5 March 2010; in force 1 January 2010): where a person belonging outside Cyprus supplies services whose place of supply is Cyprus to a 'relevant taxable person', the Law applies as if the recipient had supplied them, 'and the supply is a taxable supply'; for services of Parts I-II of the Thirteenth Schedule only if the recipient is registered. Art. 11(5), as replaced by Law 4(I)/2011, excludes Sixth and Seventh Schedule services (zero-rated, exempt): an exempt financial service bought abroad bears no reverse charge. In force 4 October 2026.

m-a7ac4853.t: Tax invoices for a Cyprus shop or café: a retailer need not give a VAT invoice unless a customer who is a taxable person asks; if the consideration does not exceed €85 and the customer is not in another Member State, a simplified invoice suffices, showing the retailer's name, address and VAT number, the date of issue, a description, the total including VAT and, per rate, that total and the rate (reg. 14 of K.D.P. 314/2001); otherwise a full invoice under regs 11-12 is due. An invoice may be on paper or electronic, the latter only if the customer accepts it (reg. 11A). Under art. 30(6) of Law 4/1978 invoices are issued within 30 days of the transaction, unless the Commissioner allows longer.

m-9b764f66.t: Cyprus VAT Circular 228 of 20 December 2018 (follow-up to Circular 161 of 13 January 2012) is for businesses that find reg. 13A hard to apply, such as canteens at sports grounds and schools and mobile units selling for cash only: the Commissioner suggests pre-printed receipts of fixed value (€1, €1.50, €2 etc.) from numbered blocks, one per value, given to the customer or stuck on the goods, pre-printed at least with a serial number, the seller's name, address and VAT number, a description of the goods or services, and the total including VAT with the rate. The business must also record, daily or per event, the serial numbers used, takings and VAT, or the receipts are not accepted.

m-90401a4f.t: Temporary zero VAT on basic goods in Cyprus, announced by the Tax Department on 2 October 2026: by Decree K.D.P. 354/2026 (Official Gazette, Annex III(I), No. 6050 of 30 September 2026) the zero rate applies from 1 October 2026 to 31 May 2027 to fresh, chilled or frozen meat and fish, and from 12 October 2026 to 31 May 2027 to bread, milk, coffee (beans, ground, instant), sugar and baby food. Prepared meat and fish products stay at 5%, and ready-made drinks based on coffee are expressly excluded — so a café's purchases of coffee are affected, not its drinks sold.

m-84ab0867.t: Cyprus's law on e-invoicing in public procurement, Law 89(I)/2019 (Gazette No. 4714, 26 June 2019), transposes Directive 2014/55/EU and puts the duty on the buyer: under art. 4, contracting authorities and contracting entities 'receive and process' electronic invoices that comply with the European standard. It entered into force on publication; for central government authorities 18 months, and for non-central contracting authorities 30 months, after the reference of the standard was published in the EU Official Journal (art. 8). Nothing in it obliges a supplier to issue an e-invoice. On 4 October 2026 cylaw.org lists no amendment to it.

m-730990da.t: Two further Court of Justice judgments reading the payments exemption (art. 13B(d)(3) of the Sixth Directive, now art. 135(1)(d) of Directive 2006/112/EC) narrowly. National Exhibition Centre (C-130/15, 26 May 2016, same day as Bookit): a service described as 'processing of payment by debit or credit card', supplied by a ticket agent when a customer buys a ticket by card, is not exempt. Cardpoint (C-42/18, 3 October 2019): operating and maintaining cashpoints for a bank, replenishing them, installing the hardware and software that reads card data, sending the authorisation request to the issuing bank, dispensing cash and registering withdrawals is not an exempt payment transaction.

m-71c753a0.t: How long a Cyprus business keeps its records. For VAT: six years, unless the Commissioner provides otherwise (reg. 22(1)(β) of K.D.P. 314/2001; seven years until K.D.P. 360/2012 changed it from 12 October 2012). For income tax: at least six years from the return deadline or the date the return or revised return was filed, whichever is later, extended if an audit starts in the last year (art. 30(2) of Law 4/1978 as replaced by art. 17 of Law 243(I)/2025); the text archived on 7 November 2025 counted the six years from the end of the tax year. Books are updated by the end of the fourth month after the month of the transactions (art. 30(5)).

m-70c881f9.t: For Cyprus VAT the 9% rate on 'restaurant and catering services' (VAT Law 95(I)/2000, Twelfth Schedule, para 2) covers the supply of prepared or unprepared food or drink for human consumption accompanied by sufficient support services allowing immediate consumption, on the supplier's premises (restaurant) or off them (catering). A supply of food or drink, with or without transport, not accompanied by other support services is not such a service; the Fifth Schedule, Table A, para 7 counts it as foodstuffs at 5%, except alcoholic drinks, beer, wine and soft drinks, which are left to the standard 19%. This is the line a café draws between table service and take-away. Read on 4 October 2026.

m-6beb305f.t: Cyprus VAT Circular 156 of 11 October 2011 follows the Court of Justice in Nordea (C-350/10): SWIFT services are electronic messaging, cause no legal or financial change between the parties, and are not exempt. A person established in Cyprus that receives them accounts for output VAT at the standard rate (then 15%) by reverse charge. Where a financial institution uses them for a money-movement service exempt under para 3(γ) of Table B of the Seventh Schedule, they are an inseparable part of that single supply and cannot be invoiced separately. It adds that Member States are in principle bound to apply the reading retroactively; in Cyprus the provision dates from 1 February 2002.

m-6602caae.t: Decree K.D.P. 337/2025 (Official Gazette, Annex III(I), No. 5981 of 21 November 2025) zero-rates in Cyprus, from 1 January 2026 to 31 December 2026, baby milk, baby and adult diapers, feminine hygiene products and listed fresh vegetables and fruit, by amending the Fifth and Sixth Schedules of VAT Law 95(I)/2000. On 4 October 2026 the Tax Department's 'VAT rates' page still summarised the temporary zero rate on basic goods as running 'until 30/9/2026', which does not match this decree's end date - the page is a summary, not the rule.

m-659629de.t: Cyprus's Tax Department states that issuing invoices and receipts electronically requires an approved fiscal device. Its leaflet 'Issue of lawful invoices and receipts' (June 2017, linked from its VAT invoice page on 4 October 2026) says this needs an approved fiscal electronic device (ΦΗΜ) or fiscal marking device (ΦΗΜΣ), approved models being listed by the Electromechanical Services Department; K.D.P. 29/1997 governs handwritten invoices and receipts, and Notifications K.D.P. 179/1997, 108/2005 and 224/2010 set the specifications of devices with fiscal memory. Reg. 13A(3) of K.D.P. 314/2001 makes a taxable person who uses such devices for VAT receipts comply with the notification in force.

m-56c794cf.t: One announced route for sending an e-invoice to the Cyprus State (voluntary on 4 October 2026): the Treasury of the Republic announced on 11 April 2025 that it accepts e-invoices addressed to the government submitted through the Jinius platform via the central government's existing PEPPOL Access Point, which it says is provided by AC Goldman Solutions and Services Ltd; e-invoices are expected to be paid within 20 days of receipt or acceptance. The Treasury's own instructions to suppliers describe the general route: any PEPPOL access point bought from a licensed provider. Its e-invoicing page links Circular No. 8 on Law 89(I)/2019, those instructions and a manual for handling e-invoices.

m-4d6b97dc.t: A Cyprus business that only receives services from abroad has no separate VAT registration trigger in the statute. The First Schedule of VAT Law 95(I)/2000, read 4 October 2026, has Part I (taxable supplies), Part IA (non-established persons), Part III (acquisitions from other Member States), Part IV (electronic notifications) and Part V (services to taxable persons in other Member States); Part II is deleted; none covers services received. That they count toward the Part I threshold (€15,600 in 12 months per the Tax Department; Part I still prints £9,000) is a construction of art. 11(1), which deems them the recipient's taxable supply; the Department's registration page is silent on it.

m-4b92c21f.t: No Cyprus Tax Department circular on the VAT treatment of a merchant service charge was found on 4 October 2026. Its index of VAT interpretative circulars (254 PDF links; EE 001 of 23 September 1996 to No. 2026/04 of 26 August 2026) has no title on cards, acquiring or merchant fees; the two on payment services are Circular 156 (SWIFT, 2011) and Circular 230 (prepaid payment instruments, 2019). Its page on exempt transactions only restates the statute: processing, clearing and authorisation 'in relation to credit cards' bears the standard rate. Whether a blended charge is one supply or must be split, and whether that carve-out covers debit cards, no published text of the authority says.

m-4a97c5b4.t: A reading, not a ruling (4 October 2026): for a Cyprus merchant the VAT on a foreign provider's card fee turns on one classification. If the fee is 'processing, clearing and authorisation' in relation to credit cards (Seventh Schedule, Table B, para 3(γ)(iii)), it is standard-rated and the merchant self-accounts at 19% under art. 11 (return boxes 1 and 4); if it is an exempt payment service, art. 11(5) switches the reverse charge off. Stripe (Ireland) says it charges no VAT and leaves self-accounting to the user; PayPal, myPOS and Viva say only that fees exclude or include applicable taxes. The Tax Department's page only restates the statute. On debit cards the statute is silent.

m-4a35df94.t: Cyprus VAT rates on 4 October 2026 (VAT Law 95(I)/2000): standard rate 19% since 13 January 2014 (art. 17); reduced rates of 9% (art. 18A, Twelfth Schedule — restaurant and catering services, hotel accommodation, taxis and tourist buses), 5% (art. 18, Fifth Schedule — among others food and drinks other than alcoholic and soft drinks, water, medicines, hairdressing) and 3% (art. 18B, Fifteenth Schedule, added by Law 75(I)/2023 — books, newspapers, certain aids for disabled persons, waste services); zero rate for exports and for temporarily listed basic goods.

m-41aa524d.t: Stripe on VAT on its fees, read 4 October 2026: 'For European account holders, Stripe supplies payment processing and other services (such as Billing, Radar and Tax) from our establishment in Ireland and does not charge VAT on Stripe fees, except to those account holders in the following jurisdictions' - Ireland, Norway, Switzerland or Liechtenstein, United Arab Emirates. Cyprus is not listed. Stripe adds that a user who may need to self-account ('reverse charge') for local VAT should consult a tax adviser. Its Services Agreement for Cyprus says fees exclude all taxes unless the pricing page or other documents state otherwise; the pricing page prints 'Excl. VAT' only next to card readers.

m-3ab92c70.t: What two providers serving Cyprus say about tax on their fees (read 4 October 2026). PayPal's User Agreement for Cyprus (last updated 7 September 2026): consumer and merchant fees 'are exclusive of any taxes', including value-added tax; a user paying for a PayPal service agrees to pay PayPal any legally applicable taxes on the amount due. Viva (Vivabank Banking S.A., terms effective 30 September 2026, clause 10.1): 'the transaction costs due to VIVA BANK including applicable taxes' are deducted automatically from collected amounts. Neither text, nor either provider's Cyprus price page, says whether VAT is in fact charged on the merchant fee or at what rate.

m-337208b2.t: ViDA, Council Directive (EU) 2025/516 of 11 March 2025, was published on 25 March 2025 and entered into force on 14 April 2025. Application is staged (art. 6): Article 2 from 1 January 2027; Article 3 from 1 July 2028, except that its deemed-supplier rule for platforms in short-term accommodation and passenger transport may apply as late as 1 January 2030; Article 4 from 1 July 2029; Article 5 — structured e-invoices and digital reporting for intra-EU business-to-business supplies — from 1 July 2030. Since 14 April 2025 Member States may mandate domestic e-invoicing (Article 1). The Directive itself imposes no e-invoicing duty on 4 October 2026; a Cyprus domestic mandate was not checked.

m-2f0e6d47.t: Cyprus has announced, but on 4 October 2026 not enacted, a move to mandatory e-invoicing towards the State. At a press conference of 27 March 2025 the Deputy Minister for Research, Innovation and Digital Policy and the Accountant General set out four measures: priority handling of e-invoices, with payment expected within 20 days; a mandatory e-invoicing clause in new IT framework agreements and tenders, to be widened gradually; a bill, then in public consultation, amending Law 89(I)/2019 so that decrees of the Minister of Finance can make e-invoicing compulsory for existing contracts above set values; and cooperation with private platforms. No date for an obligation was given.

m-281d84b2.t: Why the Cyprus VAT registration threshold reads £9,000 in the consolidated law and €15,600 in practice: VAT Interpretative Circular 122 of 9 January 2008 attaches a table of the pound amounts in the VAT legislation with the corresponding euro amounts, applied from 1 January 2008 - registration threshold £9,000 = €15,600; threshold for acquisitions from other Member States £6,000 = €10,251.61; maximum value of a retailer's simplified invoice (reg. 14(1) of K.D.P. 314/2001) £50 = €85. On 4 October 2026 the cylaw.org consolidation of the First Schedule, Part I, para 1 still printed £9,000, while the Tax Department's registration page gave €15,600.

m-26f38749.t: VAT registration in Cyprus (Tax Department page read on 4 October 2026): a person established in Cyprus must register when taxable supplies in the 12 months ending at any month-end exceeded €15,600, or when there are reasonable grounds to believe they will exceed €15,600 in the next 30 days; capital assets are not counted. Separate triggers: intra-EU acquisitions above €10,251.61 in a calendar year; supplying services to taxable persons in another Member State where the recipient accounts for the VAT there — no threshold, registration from the first transaction plus VIES recapitulative statements; persons not established in Cyprus — no threshold. Late notification costs €85 per month. Voluntary registration is allowed below the threshold.

m-23ba1526.t: The Cyprus Tax Department's VAT Leaflet 3 'Registration in the VAT Register' (edition of November 2001, still the copy linked from its registration page on 4 October 2026) tells a business that receives certain services from abroad - it lists advertising, data processing, supply of information, consultants', lawyers' and accountants' services - to treat them for tax as if it supplied them itself and to include them in the value of its taxable turnover. The leaflet predates the 2010 place-of-supply rules and refers to the 'Third Schedule' list of that time; it gives no separate threshold for services received.

m-1b6a920e.t: CESOP: Directive (EU) 2020/284 (applied by Member States from 1 January 2024) obliges payment service providers to keep quarterly records of payees and cross-border payments once they provide more than 25 cross-border payments to the same payee in a calendar quarter. Cyprus transposed it by VAT (Amendment) Law 10(I)/2024 and Regulations K.D.P. 52/2024, both published 23 February 2024; the Regulations are deemed in force from 1 January 2024 (reg. 7) and require the records to be submitted to the Tax Commissioner by the end of the month after each quarter. Failure to submit carries a €15,000 charge (VAT Law art. 45(7Γ)). Filing is through the Tax Department's CESOP portal.

m-0e341665.t: Cyprus writes a card carve-out into its VAT exemption. Seventh Schedule, Table B, para 3(γ) of VAT Law 95(I)/2000 exempts transactions concerning deposits, current accounts, money transfers and the issue and management of payment instruments (including credit cards), but excludes (i) collection of third-party debts, (ii) factoring and (iii) 'services of processing, clearing and authorisation for the movement of money in relation to credit cards'. The Tax Department's page on exempt transactions lists those card services among supplies subject to the standard rate (19%). Read on 4 October 2026.

m-0a487e8b.t: Outline (VAT and data; a list, not a computation) — Cyprus Ltd selling online to EU consumers through a payment facilitator, as of 4 October 2026: VAT registration above €15,600 of taxable supplies in 12 months; sales to consumers in other Member States taxed in Cyprus up to EUR 10,000 a year EU-wide, above that at the customer's Member State rate, optionally via the One Stop Shop; quarterly VAT returns via Tax For All; services of processing, clearing and authorisation 'in relation to credit cards' are outside the VAT exemption (the statute does not name debit cards); the merchant's payment service provider reports it to CESOP above 25 cross-border payments a quarter; platforms report sellers under DAC7. Fees of a provider outside Cyprus: reverse charge under art. 11 of the VAT Law where the service is taxable, none where it is exempt.

m-028f8422.t: The Cyprus Tax Department's only VAT leaflet on financial services, Leaflet 16 (March 1998, written under the earlier VAT Law 246/90 and still linked from its leaflets page on 4 October 2026), has a section on 'credit and debit cards': charges by card-issuing companies to cardholders for issuing the card or for the annual subscription are exempt, as is interest charged to the cardholder. For a shop that accepts credit or debit cards it says only that this does not affect the VAT the shop charges: tax is due on the full selling price. It says nothing about the commission the shop pays for card acceptance.

m-effc8f3d.t: The Social Insurance Services' contributions payment portal (SISnet, read 6 October 2026) tells users that they can link their existing account in the payment system to their CY Login account, and that a new user can create an account that will be linked to his CY Login account; the page still shows user-name and password fields and gives no date for the change.

m-ee245f67.t: Cyprus social insurance bases differ by rung. Under s. 2 of the Social Insurance Law 59(I)/2010 (consolidated text, 6 October 2026) an employed person's 'earnings' are his money pay and money-valued gains from it (less extraordinary commissions and ex-gratia payments); a self-employed person's are 'every profit and gain' from his work, computed as Regulations set (s. 78) - from a category minimum unless lower income is proved. Both count only up to the insurable-earnings ceiling; neither names dividends. A pension-reform draft bill (consulted 2-16 September 2026; not tabled by 6 October 2026) would add 'every dividend' a shareholder employed by his own private company receives from it.

m-db33ceb3.t: Cyprus's Social Insurance Services now link electronic payment of contributions in SISnet to a CY Login profile: step-by-step linking guides, including one for 'a self-employed person who is not an employer', are on the Services' site under 26 August 2026 and were announced on gov.cy on 7 September 2026. A Services notice dated 25 September 2026 says that, for users having difficulty registering on CY Login, contributions may be paid at the cashiers of the District Social Insurance Offices until Friday 30 October 2026, without extending the normal payment deadline, and that district officers will help users with identification on CY Login.

m-d6850f22.t: The gov.cy page for self-employed insurance (updated 20 April 2026, read 6 October 2026) names as the contact the Social Insurance Services' call centre: 1450 free from Cyprus, +357 22008020 from abroad, telephone hours 08:00-17:00, e-mail infocentre@mlsi.gov.cy; its 'Address' field is empty. A July 2026 notice of the Services adds district e-mail addresses for certificates and for complaints, not for registrations.

m-d3753bf5.t: The Cyprus Social Insurance Services' page 'Where you will be served' (as served 6 October 2026, site stamp 30 September 2026) lists the district offices: Nicosia, 56 Athalassas Avenue, 1466 Strovolos, with a branch at the Agios Dometios Multi-purpose Centre, 22 Laertou, 2365 Nicosia; Limassol, 80 Franklin Roosevelt Avenue, 3012; Larnaca, 1 Filiou Tsigaridi, 6023; Paphos, 1 Filikis Etaireias, 8047; Famagusta, 82 Eleftherias, 5380 Deryneia. Neither this page nor the Services' contact page states opening hours or an appointment requirement; the contact page gives the head office at 26 Spyrou Kyprianou Avenue, 1075 Nicosia, and links a notice giving the 1450 helpline.

m-bb3b9c26.t: Cyprus's Labour Ministry said on 28 September 2026 that the social partners are expected to submit their proposals on the pension reform on 8 October 2026 at the Labour Advisory Body, which meets twice a week in October, and that the dialogue continues regardless of the bill's tabling. For the second pillar (provident funds) a technical committee meets every Tuesday from 6 October to the end of October, aiming, if agreement is reached, at a framework agreement rather than a law; the Government will state its position on that pillar after the dialogue.

m-b85b90c3.t: The Human Resource Development levy on Cyprus's self-employed (0.5% of insurable earnings, collected by the Social Insurance Services) started on Monday 6 April 2026: the Ministry of Labour and Social Insurance announced that from that day the self-employed join the Human Resource Development Authority's schemes and pay the levy (CNA report carried by SigmaLive, 7 April 2026), matching the commencement clauses of Law 15(I)/2026 (art. 11) and K.D.P. 128/2026 (reg. 11). Registration with Social Insurance counts as registration for the levy (reg. 4(3)). As served on 6 October 2026, the Services' 2026 Table II still dates the duty 'from 5.1.2026'.

m-b2fac71f.t: A self-employed person in Cyprus must apply for registration at the nearest District Social Insurance Office 'at the latest by the day his employment starts', on the approved form. This is reg. 4(3) of the Social Insurance (Contributions) Regulations as replaced by reg. 3 of the amending Regulations K.D.P. 167/2017 (Official Gazette No. 5017, 2 June 2017), which took effect on 13 September 2021 by notification K.D.P. 378/2021. The rule names every self-employed person and sets no nationality or residence condition. Read 6 October 2026.

m-aae3a6a4.t: Cyprus's pension-reform bill (first pillar, the Social Insurance Fund) had not reached the House by 6 October 2026: Nomoplatform lists no such bill, and on 1 October the Labour Minister said it was complete and expected to be approved by the Council of Ministers and put before the House 'in the coming days' (Alphanews). It missed the Cabinet of 30 September for pending legal vetting (Alphanews, 29 September); on 21 September he had expected tabling by end-September and debate from around 13 October (KYPE). The Government aims to start the first pillar on 1 January 2027 (Cyprus Mail, 21 and 28 September).

m-9cecb54e.t: Cyprus sets a self-employed person's minimum insurable income by occupation in the Social Insurance Services' Table I for 5.1.2026-3.1.2027 (EUR 220.76 a week times a coefficient): EUR 331.14 for farmers and for a group that includes 'persons responsible for providing services and sellers'; EUR 364.25 butchers, bakers, confectioners; EUR 452.56 shopkeepers (kiosks, hairdressers, beauticians); EUR 474.63 drivers, clerks, craftsmen; EUR 485.67 liberal professionals (doctors, lawyers, accountants) in their first ten years, designers, computer operators and anyone not classed elsewhere; EUR 982.38 those professionals after ten years and 'directors (businessmen)', estate agents, wholesalers.

m-765f5e25.t: The Social Insurance Services' forms section for employees and the self-employed (read 6 October 2026) carries two registration forms: YKA 1-008 'Application for registration of an employee / self-employed person', filled in 'for insuring an employee/self-employed person', and YKA 1-013 'Application for registration of a self-employed person' (edition 5/2024). The government business portal links instead a 2011 Greek-English YKA 1-008, which says 'This is a guidance Form. You should fill and submit the application which is in Greek'. No text read says whether a newcomer files one form or both.

m-72ac6b26.t: Self-employed insurance in Cyprus does not count towards unemployment benefit: under s. 24(2)(α) of the Social Insurance Law 59(I)/2010 (consolidated text read 6 October 2026) self-employed periods 'are not taken into account for the purposes of unemployment benefit'. A founder working for his own private company is insured as employed (First Schedule, Part I, para. 5). A day counts as unemployment only if the claimant proves he is unemployed, capable of and available for work (or in approved training); a day of gainful occupation does not count unless he could normally do it besides his usual work, outside its hours, and earns no more than a prescribed amount that day (s. 31(4)(β), (ε)).

m-601eb143.t: Two rules of Cyprus's Social Insurance Law 59(I)/2010 (First Schedule, consolidated text read 6 October 2026) separate the rungs. Employment 'in the service of the spouse' of the person employed is an excepted, non-insurable employment (Part II, para. 3), so a sole trader's husband or wife working for him or her is not insured as an employee. Employment of a person 'under any circumstances' in a private company in which he is a shareholder is insurable employment as an employed person (Part I, para. 5); the paragraph names private companies within the Companies Law only, not partnerships.

m-49b8c03e.t: The Cyprus Social Insurance Services list five forms for a self-employed person (read 6 October 2026), besides the joint registration form YKA 1-008: YKA 1-013, the registration application (edition 5/2024) - identity card, alien registration or passport number, addresses, start date, occupation, a line for EU and EEA citizens and an authorisation to verify the data, with no list of attachments; YKA 1-017, to pay contributions on actual income; YKA 1-016, non-employment 'for a specific period'; YKA 1-015, termination; YKA 1-014, change of occupation or place of work. Per the Services' Insured Person Guide (June 2025) unemployment benefit goes to employed persons, not the self-employed.

m-2a0172b2.t: The list of services offered at Cyprus's Citizen Service Centres (KEP), dated 1 December 2025 and linked from the Public Administration and Personnel Department's KEP page on 6 October 2026, gives 30 Social Insurance items (4.01-4.30): certificates, change of personal details, pensions and benefits, IBAN, refunds, 'submission of additional supporting documents' and information. None is the registration of a self-employed or employed person, or of an employer. The Services' Employer Guide (June 2025) nevertheless says the employer form YKA 1-001 may be handed in at a Citizen Service Centre; neither text addresses the other.

m-22b7be78.t: As of 6 October 2026 the gov.cy service page 'Self-employed insurance' (Greek, updated 20 April 2026) offers one electronic route for the self-employed registration form YKA 1-013: a Word version marked as signable with the eID, which, once signed electronically, may be e-mailed with any supporting documents to the district address - applicationsnic@sid.mlsi.gov.cy (Nicosia), applicationslim@ (Limassol), applicationslca@ (Larnaca), applicationspaphos@ (Paphos), all @sid.mlsi.gov.cy. The linked guide says signing is done with the eID through JCC's Signing Portal, one e-mail per application, at most 10 MB. The English page says only 'Available in greek'.

m-20f82a0f.t: A Government bill tabled in Cyprus's House on 17 June 2026 (file 23.01.067.114-2026; Cabinet approval 27 May 2026) would cap the €50-a-day increase on late-paid fines for undeclared work (Social Insurance Law s. 85A(6), applied to the self-employed by s. 85D(3)) at twice the fine, retroactively from 2 June 2017. The Labour Ministry's report of 12 June says many employers and self-employed have owed 'very large amounts' since 2017 and that the cap matches Law 88(I)/2020. Its Annex I: to 31 March 2026, 827 fined persons (722 employers, 105 self-employed) owed €65,606,770 on €2,515,500 of fines, €7,907,870 under the bill; €6,198,680 collected. Pending in the Labour Committee on 6 October 2026.

m-17980a66.t: Officers of a Cyprus company can answer personally for its social insurance offences. Under s. 85(9) of the Social Insurance Law 59(I)/2010 (consolidated text read 6 October 2026), where an offence under the Law or its Regulations is committed by a legal person and is shown to have been committed with the consent, connivance or negligence of a director, manager, secretary or similar officer, both that person and the legal person are guilty of it. Failing or neglecting to pay any contribution is itself an offence (up to one year's imprisonment, a €3,400 fine or both, s. 85(1)); on conviction the employer must also pay the unpaid contributions plus up to 25% as the Court orders (s. 85(2)).

m-02c985f1.t: What standing still costs a registered self-employed person in Cyprus in 2026, from the Social Insurance Services' Tables I and II. On the lowest notional minimum, EUR 331.14 a week (category 6, farmers, and category 13, which includes 'persons responsible for providing services and sellers'), social insurance at 16.6% is EUR 2,858.40 a year whatever the real income; GeSY at 4% adds EUR 688.77 and the 0.5% training levy, from the second quarter, EUR 64.57 - about EUR 3,612. Higher minima apply by occupation: shopkeepers (category 11) EUR 452.56 a week, EUR 3,906.48 social insurance a year; liberal professionals in their first ten years and computer operators EUR 485.67, EUR 4,192.32.

m-01b8d96b.t: Read together on 6 October 2026, the Cyprus texts leave a self-employed person who is not a Cypriot citizen no published fully online way to register with Social Insurance: the only electronic route on the Services' gov.cy page is a form signed with the eID and e-mailed, and the eID is issued only to Cypriot citizens aged 18 or over with a valid biometric identity card (Civil Registry Law 141(I)/2002, art. 65A(4)). What remains is paper at a District Social Insurance Office; posting is offered only by the business portal, for the form it links (YKA 1-008). This is an inference: no Social Insurance page says that non-citizens must attend, or whether another qualified e-signature is accepted.

m-f0c9b3f0.t: The 'Τελευταία Ενημέρωση' (last updated) line on pages of Cyprus's Social Insurance Services site (mlsi.gov.cy/mlsi/sid) is a site-wide stamp, not a page date: on 5 October 2026 five different pages - the form YKA 1-008 page, the Employer Guide, the Insured Person Guide and the two 2026 tables for the self-employed - all showed '30/09/2026 03:08:36 PM', identical to the second. A form or guide on that site is dated by its own edition mark or file metadata (YKA 1-008: edition 5/2019; Employer Guide: PDF created 2 June 2025), not by that line.

m-bd816ee8.t: For third-country nationals the Health Insurance Organisation's FAQ (undated; read 5 October 2026) gives five cases of GeSY entitlement: resident in the government-controlled areas and (a) employed, (b) with permanent residence, (c) refugee or 'supplementary' protection, (d) family member of a beneficiary, or (e) insured in another EU Member State; for EU citizens the same without (c). Its 'Beneficiary Categories' page words the non-EU case as a permanent residence permit or 'the right of equal treatment in the social insurance sectors' and adds that it 'may, at its discretion, include, on a voluntary basis' excluded persons. Neither page names the temporary residence (visitor) permit.

m-b33c1fb0.t: How a fine for undeclared work runs in Cyprus (Social Insurance Law 59(I)/2010, read 5 Oct 2026): the inspector serves a notice of the finding on the spot and the employer has five days for representations (s. 85Α(4)); the fine is payable within 30 days of service of the fining act (s. 85Ζ), is cut by 30% if paid in time and grows by €50 per day of delay (s. 85Α(6)). An objection goes to an Objections Committee within 15 days and does not suspend the decision (s. 85Θ). After a second fine within two years a committee may, with the Minister's consent, suspend all or part of the business for up to 48 hours (s. 85Γ(1)). Households employing domestic workers or carers are exempt (s. 85Α(7)).

m-b00a9998.t: An employer in Cyprus pays social insurance and the other payroll-fund contributions by the end of the calendar month after the month for which they are due - on the next working day if that day is a Saturday, Sunday or holiday (Social Insurance Services' Employer Guide, PDF of 2 June 2025; their web page of 23 March 2021 has the month-end rule). Late payment bears an additional charge on social insurance, social cohesion and health-system contributions: 3% for up to a month, 3 points more per further month or part of one, at most 27%. A first payroll for November 2026 is thus payable by 31 December 2026; the Tax Department's calendar puts the GeSY contribution for November on the same day.

m-aa7dedee.t: GeSY beneficiaries are fixed by art. 16(1) of Cyprus's Law 89(I)/2001: a person ordinarily resident in the government-controlled areas who is (α) a Cypriot citizen; (β) a Union citizen who is an employed or self-employed worker in Cyprus, retains that status or has acquired permanent residence; (γ) a third-country national with a lawful right of permanent residence; (δ) one with a lawful right to equal treatment in the branches of social security under the Aliens and Immigration Law; (ε) a refugee or person with subsidiary protection; (στ) a family member of persons under (α), (β) or (δ); (η) a family member of a (γ) person who himself holds permanent residence. Read 5 October 2026.

m-a292cae9.t: Cyprus's Health Insurance Organisation re-checks beneficiaries against art. 16 of Law 89(I)/2001 and may end the right to care. The procedure rests on Decisions 21-27 of K.D.P. 164/2019 (Gazette 17 May 2019, made under art. 16(5)): renewal is examined automatically when a residence or work permit expires or changes, or after the Organisation's checks; a refusal may be objected to in writing to the Board within 30 days. The Organisation's page (read 5 October 2026) adds that for third-country nationals it 'may proceed automatically', without the notification procedure, to end the right where other departments' data show the Law's requirements are not met and no valid residence permit is held.

m-7f7ab9d6.t: Cyprus's Social Insurance Law 59(I)/2010 has no rule for third-country nationals as such (text read 5 October 2026): insurable employment turns on work in Cyprus (First Schedule, Part I, para 1). Part II, para 4 excludes by residence, not nationality: a person not ordinarily resident in Cyprus or another Member State employed by an employer with no residence, seat or place of business in Cyprus. Only the Services' Employer Guide (PDF of 2 June 2025) names them: 'international activities companies' owe contributions for all employees, but third-country employees who prove to the Director, on application, that they are not ordinarily resident in Cyprus are exempted. It cites no legal basis.

m-7ed65a6d.t: The duty to enter terms of employment in Cyprus's Ergani system rests on a ministerial decree, not on the social insurance regulations: the Transparent and Predictable Working Conditions (Essential Terms of Employment for Entry in an Electronic System) Decree 2024 (K.D.P. 455/2024, Gazette No. 5915, 20.12.2024, in force on publication), made by the Minister of Labour under s. 11(6) of Law 25(I)/2023 as amended, obliges every employer to enter the essential terms of employment of all its employees in the information system 'ERGANI'. The entry period was 2 January to 28 February 2025, extended to 31 May 2025 by K.D.P. 58/2025. The decree sets no period for employees hired later.

m-692cb564.t: Cyprus law fixes no minimum insurable earnings for a shareholder employed by his own company. Section 4 of Law 59(I)/2010 makes contributions due for each period in which a person was employed as an employed person 'except where the earnings of the employed person are negligible'; reg. 7 of the Contributions Regulations (K.D.P. 289/2010) puts negligible below €2 a week or €7 a month. Deemed earnings exist only for apprentices and prisoners (s. 5(3)-(4)). Notional minimums by occupational category apply to the self-employed alone (reg. 16). Read on 5 October 2026 in the Law, K.D.P. 289/2010 and its amendments K.D.P. 398/2013 and 167/2017; the Services' June 2025 guides add nothing.

m-62f5c232.t: Under Cyprus's Social Insurance Law 59(I)/2010 a person who works for a private company in which he holds shares is an employed person, not a self-employed one: paragraph 5 of Part I of the First Schedule lists as insurable employment of an employed person the 'employment of a person under any circumstances in a private company in which he is a shareholder', 'private company' having the Companies Law meaning. The self-employed are defined by exclusion (Second Schedule, Part I): work for gain in Cyprus that is not insurable under Part I of the First Schedule. The rule does not depend on nationality or on the size of the shareholding. Read in the consolidated text on 5 October 2026.

m-5f3f10e3.t: For a GeSY beneficiary whose status rests on a document of the Civil Registry and Migration Department, the right to care follows that document under K.D.P. 164/2019 (decisions under art. 16(5) of Law 89(I)/2001, Gazette 17 May 2019). Decision 22: the IT system starts renewal automatically when an identity card or a 'residence and/or work or other permit' is about to expire, or when the Government Data Warehouse reports a change in employment dates or in the permit; re-evaluation starts three months before expiry, with notice by e-mail. Decision 24: the system may approve or reject automatically. Decision 25(2): objection to the Board within 30 days. Decision 27: rejection ends the right.

m-5de8e182.t: Between 2012 and 13 September 2021 Cyprus employers had a separate pre-start duty: reg. 4A of the Social Insurance (Contributions) Regulations, inserted by K.D.P. 52/2012 (Gazette No. 4551, 24.2.2012, no commencement clause), required the employer to secure for every employee, before the employment began, and hand over at once a 'certificate of commencement of employment' in the Director's form, to keep a copy for inspection and to notify the nearest District Social Insurance Office of its issue no later than the end of the month from the start date; failure was an offence settled out of court. K.D.P. 167/2017 repealed reg. 4A with effect from 13 September 2021.

m-5ca8a65a.t: One of the few durations the Cyprus government publishes for a founder's own registrations concerns the self-employed route: the government business portal ('Start your business', page modified 15 September 2026) says the application to register as self-employed (form YKA 1-008) is handed in or posted to the District Social Insurance Office with a copy of the identity card, passport or alien registration certificate (ARC), and that 'the social insurance number is usually given within 1-2 weeks of submission'. The same portal gives no duration for a company's employer registration, tax number or VAT number.

m-51a82ce1.t: The Cyprus Ministry of Labour's own announcement of the September 2021 change is public on the announcements page of the Ergani system (dated 26 August 2021): on 13 September 2021, by decision of the Council of Ministers, K.D.P. 167/2017 takes effect; an employer applies for registration no later than one day before it expects to become an employer and notifies each hiring no later than one day before the hiring; notification of new hires is made 'only electronically' through the information system 'ERGANI' at ergani.mlsi.gov.cy; and from that date the issue and use of the 'certificate of commencement of employment' is abolished. Read 5 Oct 2026.

m-2da02b7c.t: A person without a Cyprus social insurance number is registered on form YKA 1-008, the registration application of an employed or self-employed person (edition 5/2019, served by the Social Insurance Services on 5 October 2026). Part I has fields for identity card number, alien registration number and passport number; a line 'to be completed only by citizens of EU and EEA member states' asks nationality and an 'insurance no. / registration no.'; Part III, for an employee, asks the employer's name and registration number. The form lists no attachments. An employee's employer files it within seven days of the hiring (reg. 4(2) of the Contributions Regulations, as replaced by K.D.P. 167/2017).

m-2845cca6.t: Enrolment in GeSY has two steps (Health Insurance Organisation Decisions, K.D.P. 164/2019, Decisions 5-8 and 20; its page read 5 October 2026). First, enrolment in the Beneficiary Registry: open to a person within art. 16 of Law 89(I)/2001 registered with the Civil Registry and Migration Department and/or the Social Insurance Services, through the Beneficiary Portal or a personal doctor; the page adds that non-Cypriots must 'possess a valid residence permit'. Requests not approved automatically are examined 'within reasonable time', with provisional care meanwhile. Second, registration in a personal doctor's list. A beneficiary over 2 may change doctor after six months.

m-18416e84.t: The Cyprus Social Insurance (Contributions) Regulations, K.D.P. 289/2010, are not in their 2010 state. K.D.P. 308/2020 (Gazette No. 5316, 17 July 2020) cites earlier amendments of 24 February 2012, 15 November 2013 and 2 June 2017 and itself added a proviso to reg. 17(5): for a self-employed person's application to pay on actual earnings filed within twelve months of its commencement, the Director's decision 'may take effect also before the start of the quarterly period in which the application was filed', with no surcharge if filed within six months. That window is spent; on 4 October 2026 the base rule (effect from the quarter of filing) applies. The earlier amendments were not opened.

m-1536e358.t: Joining Cyprus's GeSY is governed by the Health Insurance Organisation's Decisions K.D.P. 164/2019 (Gazette No. 5161, 17 May 2019, under art. 16(5) of Law 89(I)/2001); cylaw's indexes to K.D.P. 372/2026 list no amendment. A non-Cypriot is identified by 'the relevant number issued by the Migration Department' (Annex I). A request meeting Decision 5 is approved automatically; three groups must also send a signed paper request with documents: S1 holders, EU citizens who retain worker or self-employed status (alien registration certificate, proof of ordinary residence and e.g. Labour Department form R 210 (ES19)), and family members. A refusal can be contested before the Board within 30 days.

m-fd5cf607.t: What the choice of category costs a small Cyprus sole trader in 2026 (Social Insurance Services, Table II, quarters of 13 weeks at 16.6%): on the minimum of category 13 (coefficient 1.50, €331.14 a week) the quarterly contribution is €714.60; category 12 (1.65, €364.25) €786.05; category 11 'shopkeepers' (2.05, €452.56) €976.62; categories 15-16 (2.20, €485.67) €1,048.08; category 3 'directors (businessmen), wholesalers' (4.45, €982.38) €2,119.98; at the ceiling of €1,325 a week €2,859.35. GeSY at 4% and, from the second quarter of 2026, the 0.5% Human Resource Development levy come on top. The coefficients are those of Table I of K.D.P. 289/2010, unchanged since 2010.

m-f4f41a41.t: Under reg. 4 of the Cyprus Social Insurance (Contributions) Regulations, as replaced by K.D.P. 167/2017 (in force 13 September 2021), an employee gives the employer his identity number and social insurance number at least one day before being hired; if the employee is not yet in the insured persons' register, the employer supplies the registration application and files it at the nearest District Social Insurance Office within seven days of the hiring. A self-employed person applies for registration no later than the day he starts work. Regulation 4A was repealed by the same regulations.

m-f151c31f.t: The Human Resource Development levy on the self-employed in Cyprus starts with the second contribution quarter of 2026. Law 15(I)/2026 (art. 11) and Regulations K.D.P. 128/2026 (reg. 11) both enter into force on 6 April 2026; for the self-employed the levy period is the quarter (reg. 2) and the levy is 0.5% of insurable earnings (reg. 5(3)), payable by the 10th day of the second month after the period (reg. 7(2)). In the Social Insurance Services' own 2026 table the second quarter runs 6.4.2026-5.7.2026, so the commencement date is its first day. The note under that table, dating the duty 'from 5.1.2026', has no basis in either text; no correcting notice was found.

m-e3a8f9ea.t: A self-employed person in Cyprus registers with the Social Insurance Services and the Tax Department. The Services' forms list (read 4 Oct 2026) carries YKA 1-008 (registration of an employed or self-employed insured person) and YKA 1-013 (registration of a self-employed person); the government business portal names only YKA 1-008, filed at a district office with ID, passport or ARC. The contribution rate is 21.8% of insurable income, 16.6% paid by the self-employed and 5.2% by the State, in force since 1 January 2024 (Services' announcement of 27.11.2023; no later change found on 4 Oct 2026). The portal puts the VAT registration threshold at €15,600 of turnover in 12 months.

m-e2e47c72.t: GeSY (General Healthcare System) contributions under art. 19(1) of Law 89(I)/2001, read 4 October 2026: employee 2.65% and employer 2.90% of earnings; self-employed 4.00%; pensioner 2.65% of pension; office-holder 2.65% plus 2.90% from the payer; 'income earner' (any individual with income other than earnings or pension, such as rent, interest or dividends) 2.65%; the State adds 4.70% of the earnings and pensions of the first four groups. The €180,000 cap is in the law itself (art. 19(4)): above that sum of earnings, pensions and income, contribution is due only on €180,000, counted in that order; excess paid for contribution years from 2025 is refunded by the Tax Commissioner.

m-e0563b6b.t: The Cyprus Social Insurance Services' Insured Person Guide (PDF created 2 June 2025, read 4 October 2026) restates the rule for the self-employed: each pays on the minimum insurable earnings of the category in which he was classified; if actual income is lower he 'is entitled to submit an application accompanied by evidence of his income, so as to pay contributions on his actual income'. A person with two or more self-employed occupations is insured only for the one with the highest insurable earnings; a person who is both employee and self-employed is insured for both. Registration is due from the first day of the activity.

m-d9a00504.t: Actuarial valuation of Cyprus's General Social Insurance Scheme as of 31 December 2020 (ILO report ILO/TF/Cyprus/R.27, copyright 2024, on the Social Insurance Services' site): Table A1.2 gives the legislated contribution rates for employed persons as 8.8% employee + 8.8% employer + 5.2% State = 22.8% for 2024–2028; 9.3% + 9.3% + 5.5% = 24.1% for 2029–2033; 9.8% + 9.8% + 5.8% = 25.4% for 2034–2038; 10.3% + 10.3% + 6.1% = 26.7% from 2039. The report concludes that this schedule, following the 2009 and 2012 reforms, is sufficient for the long-term benefits branch over 2021–2080. These are the future steps quoted in the Services' Employer Guide, not the higher ones printed in Law 59(I)/2010.

m-d042eb68.t: Cyprus social insurance from 2029: both published figures come from law. Art. 5(1)(ζ) and art. 12(η) of Law 59(I)/2010, as replaced by Law 126(I)/2019 (Gazette No. 4725, 5 August 2019), print 9.5% each for employee and employer and 18% for the self-employed, but two provisos say (1) if an actuarial study before a step shows that no increase, or a smaller one, is needed, the rates it indicates apply, and (2) the increases may not be lower than the rates in force just before the 2019 Law. The Services treat the schedule of Law 193(I)/2012 (Gazette No. 4372, 21 December 2012) as that floor, as they did for 2024: 9.3% + 9.3% and 17.6% from 2029. On 4 October 2026 no 2029 decision was published.

m-ca7d597e.t: Every employer who employs staff in Cyprus must register with the Employers' Register of the Social Insurance Services (SIS). The SIS page (last updated 23.03.2021) names form YKA 1-001, to which a legal entity attaches the Registrar's certificates of incorporation, of directors and secretary and of shareholders. The government business portal (modified 12.08.2024) adds that registration precedes recruiting and that each hire is notified electronically through the ERGANI system no later than one day before the employee starts, on 13 September 2021 the 'certificate of commencement of employment' was abolished and the hiring declaration became electronic-only (the portal's English calls the certificate 'Declaration for the recruitment'); the SIS pages still describe the paper declaration. Read 4 Oct 2026.

m-bd6644a3.t: Employer-only payroll funds in Cyprus, per the Social Insurance Services' Employer Guide (PDF created 2 June 2025, read 4 October 2026): Redundancy Fund 1.2%; Human Resource Development levy 0.5% (restated by Regulations K.D.P. 128/2026, in force 6 April 2026); Social Cohesion Fund 2%; Central Holiday Fund by leave entitlement (8% for 20 days in the guide's example). Earnings count up to the insurable-earnings ceiling for every fund except the Social Cohesion Fund, which is charged on total earnings without ceiling. The holiday contribution is itself treated as earnings for the other funds. The duty arises from earnings of €2 a week or €7 a month.

m-61ae1a0f.t: Failure to notify a hire in Cyprus is 'undeclared work': s. 2 of the Social Insurance Law 59(I)/2010 defines it as insurable employment not declared to the Director under reg. 5(1) (employees) or reg. 4(3) (self-employed) of the Contributions Regulations. Under s. 85Α(1) an inspector fines the employer €1,000 per undeclared employee for the month of detection (€500 until Law 127(I)/2024, 15 November 2024) plus €500 per earlier calendar month or part of it; s. 85Β presumes six earlier months unless the employer proves less. Repeats within two years: €2,000, then €3,000 (s. 85Α(1Α)). Up to ten insured persons: cap €10,000 per finding (s. 85Α(3)). Introduced by Law 52(I)/2017. Read 4 Oct 2026.

m-5c81c461.t: Social insurance contributions for employees in Cyprus, as applied on 4 October 2026: 8.8% of insurable earnings from the employee and 8.8% from the employer (plus 5.2% from the State), in force since 1 January 2024. Art. 5(1)(στ) of Social Insurance Law 59(I)/2010, as replaced by Law 126(I)/2019, prints 8.9% + 8.9%, but its provisos apply the lower rates shown by an actuarial study, floored at the pre-2019 schedule; the Social Insurance Services announced on 27 November 2023 that the study required no extra increase. Next step: 1 January 2029 (9.5% in the statute, 9.3% in the Services' Employer Guide). Contributions are due by the end of the following month.

m-53854105.t: Procedure for a self-employed person in Cyprus paying social insurance on actual income (reg. 17(4)-(5) of K.D.P. 289/2010; form YKA 1-017, edition 5/2024): until the Director decides, the applicant pays on the weekly amount declared; the decision takes effect from the start of the quarter of filing (K.D.P. 308/2020 allowed earlier effect only for applications within 12 months of 17 July 2020). It asks for the previous year's turnover, cost of sales, operating expenses and net income, with a yearly list of invoices and receipts or till Z-reports, a purchases list, the lease, utility statements, and trial balance and accounts if any; an incomplete application is treated as not received.

m-4d967e63.t: Self-employed persons in Cyprus pay 16.6% social insurance in each quarter of 2026 (Social Insurance Services, Table II) on insurable income between a notional weekly minimum per occupational category — €220.76 times a coefficient; for 'shopkeepers' (category 11) 2.05, i.e. €452.56 a week, a contribution of €976.62 per 13-week quarter — and €1,325 a week. Art. 12(ζ) of Law 59(I)/2010 prints 16.8% from 2024; the lower rate applies under its actuarial proviso. They also pay GeSY 4% and a 0.5% Human Resource Development levy: the Services' table dates the levy from 5 January 2026, but Law 15(I)/2026 and Regulations K.D.P. 128/2026 entered into force on 6 April 2026.

m-4a31101f.t: A new employer in Cyprus must apply to register with the Social Insurance Services no later than one day before the day on which it expects to become an employer: reg. 3(2) of the Social Insurance (Contributions) Regulations, as replaced by reg. 2 of the amending regulations K.D.P. 167/2017 (Official Gazette No. 5017, 2.6.2017), which the Council of Ministers brought into force on 13 September 2021 by notification K.D.P. 378/2021 (Gazette No. 5592, 3.9.2021). From 2010 (K.D.P. 289/2010, Gazette No. 4437, 9.7.2010) until then reg. 3(2) allowed one month from the day the applicant became an employer. The deadline sits in the Regulations, made under s. 78(η) of Law 59(I)/2010, not in the Law.

m-4250bb3a.t: Since 13 September 2021 every employer in Cyprus must notify the competent District Social Insurance Office of each hiring no later than one day before the hiring, by a declaration submitted only electronically (reg. 5(1)-(2) of the Social Insurance (Contributions) Regulations, as replaced by K.D.P. 167/2017). Before that the declaration was due within one month after the end of the calendar month following the contribution month of the hiring (2010 text), and from 2012 the employer also had to issue a 'certificate of commencement of employment' before the employee started (reg. 4A, K.D.P. 52/2012, repealed in 2021). The employer must also keep a register of hirings (reg. 6(2)).

m-3f0c2de0.t: On 27 November 2023 the Cyprus Social Insurance Services announced the contribution rates applying from 1 January 2024 'under the schedule set in 2012': employees 22.8% (8.8% employee, 8.8% employer, 5.2% State); self-employed 21.8% (16.6% + 5.2%); employees in non-contributory occupational schemes 4.45% + 13.15% employer. It added that an actuarial study showed no additional increase was needed to fund widowers' pensions. This explains why the applied rates sit below those printed in arts 5 and 12 of Law 59(I)/2010 as replaced by Law 126(I)/2019 (8.9% + 8.9%; 16.8%): provisos added in 2019 apply the study's lower rates, with the earlier schedule as floor. Still applied on 4 October 2026.

m-399d690c.t: No text read on 4 October 2026 assigns a café or restaurant owner or an online retailer to a Cyprus social insurance occupational category (read: Table I of K.D.P. 289/2010, the Services' 2026 Table I and Insured Person Guide, forms YKA 1-013 and 1-017). Reg. 16 classifies the self-employed 'according to their occupation' into 16 categories; none names catering or distance sales. Nearest: 11 'Shopkeepers' (coefficient 2.05; the 2026 table adds 'including kiosks, hairdressers, beauticians'), 12 (butchers, bakers, confectioners, food preparers; 1.65), 13 (ends 'persons responsible for provision of services, and sellers'; 1.50), 3 (directors (businessmen), wholesalers; 4.45), 16 (others; 2.20).

m-30275f6b.t: The electronic channel for hire notifications in Cyprus is the Ministry of Labour's 'Ergani' information system (ergani.mlsi.gov.cy), whose login page, read 4 Oct 2026, says every employer is obliged to notify through it the hiring, the termination and the statement of terms of employment of its employees. The Contributions Regulations do not name the system: reg. 5(2), as replaced by K.D.P. 167/2017, only requires the hiring declaration to be submitted 'only electronically'. The Ministry's announcement of 26 August 2021 on the system's announcements page names Ergani as the only channel from 13 September 2021; the entry of employment terms rests on a ministerial decree, K.D.P. 455/2024.

m-25653987.t: Ceiling of insurable earnings in Cyprus for 2026, from the Social Insurance Services' table of basic insurable earnings: €1,325 per week, €5,742 per month, €68,904 per year for the monthly-paid (€68,900 for the weekly-paid); the basic weekly insurable earnings are €220.76; the contribution year starts 5 January 2026 and the amounts are valid until the end of 2026. For 2025 the ceiling was €1,281 per week, €5,551 per month and €66,612 per year. Social insurance contributions are charged on earnings up to this ceiling.

m-0c0ddac2.t: RSM Cyprus (13 September 2021) reproduces an announcement that, from 13 September 2021 under the Social Insurance (Contributions) (Amendment) Regulations 2017, every self-employed person must apply for registration at a District Social Insurance Office no later than the day he starts work, an employer must apply for registration at least one day before becoming an employer and must notify each hiring at least one day in advance through the 'Ergani' system. The regulations are K.D.P. 167/2017, brought into force by notification K.D.P. 378/2021; the announcement, dated 26 August 2021, is the Ministry of Labour's and stands on the Ergani announcements page (read 5 October 2026).

m-09dd7dd9.t: A self-employed person in Cyprus may pay social insurance on actual income below the category minimum under reg. 17 of the Social Insurance (Contributions) Regulations, K.D.P. 289/2010 (Gazette No. 4437, 9 July 2010): on an application in the Director's form, with evidence of income, he must satisfy the Director that his earnings are lower than the minimum insurable earnings of his occupational category. Weekly earnings are the weekly average of actual earnings in the calendar year before the contribution year, or the amount reasonably expected if he did not work that year. If earnings prove higher than the minimum, contributions are due on actual earnings up to the ceiling.

m-04884377.t: Cyprus extended the Human Resource Development levy to the self-employed in 2026. Law 15(I)/2026 (Gazette No. 5076, 6 March 2026) added art. 20(1A) to the Human Resource Development Law: every self-employed person pays a levy of not more than 1% of income from work; the Law entered into force on 6 April 2026. Regulations K.D.P. 128/2026 (Gazette of 11 March 2026), also in force from 6 April 2026, fix the levy at 0.5% of insurable earnings for both employers and the self-employed, with nothing due above the insurable-earnings ceiling; the self-employed pay per quarter. The Social Insurance Services' 2026 contribution table nevertheless dates the duty from 5 January 2026.

m-fe485e03.t: Founder's own account, not verified: Nikolay Valiotti, founder of Valiotti Analytics LTD (data-analytics consulting), wrote on vc.ru on 10 June 2022 that he moved his business to Cyprus in 2022 and that lawyers formed the company, with advocates taking the papers to the Registrar. He says that, per his colleagues, the filing was quick and took under a month 'by formal deadlines', but with holidays at least a month passed from filing to receiving the documents, expedited filing included. He paid EUR 3,100 for this, expedited filing included, with no split. A bank account 'in the end took 2 months'. The post gives durations, not step dates.

m-fbc53061.t: Shrine's own terms of service (shown as 'Last Update: 28/01/2025', read 6 October 2026) identify the seller as 'Shrine Solutions Ltd, a company incorporated in the Republic of Cyprus with registration number HE 453354' and cover its Shopify themes, used under a licence key, with updates and support. The store runs on Shopify (shop handle shrinetheme.myshopify.com, prices in euro); its cart and footer show Visa, Mastercard, American Express, Apple Pay, Google Pay, Discover and PayPal icons and its header says 'We now accept Crypto!'; the checkout itself was not opened. The site claims '2000+ Happy Customers' - the firm's own figure, method not given.

m-fbb3b671.t: As of 6 October 2026 the Minabocks website (minabocks.com) presents the business as 'Built for Owensboro businesses', with prices in dollars ('Starter $99 /month') and no mention of Cyprus on its home page; in its archived capture of 6 September 2022 the same domain called it 'An American Advertising Agency in Cyprus' and 'Based in Nicosia'. The Cyprus business name MINABOCKS, ΕΕ 56582, is still shown as registered on 6 October 2026. No source read says whether the business still trades in Cyprus.

m-f67e1a91.t: Wolt venue pages (read 6 October 2026) carry in their page data an object named 'digital_services_act_information' with the trader's name, register number, address and self-certification; DSA art. 30(7) requires a platform where consumers conclude distance contracts with traders to show the art. 30(1)(a), (d) and (e) data (name and contacts, trade register and number, self-certification). 'Sunday in Lisboa Concept Store' - Levasco Concept Ltd, HE452057; Furen - KFB HOSPITALITY CONCEPTS LTD, ΗΕ453980; True Heart Cafe - A. K TODOS TACOS LTD, ΗΕ467363; all as in the Registrar. For Sunday in Lisboa it is, besides the Registrar's business-name entry, the only document seen that names the company.

m-e23a3259.t: Dated public steps of Sunday in Lisboa (Limassol): owner company Levasco Concept Ltd registered 4 October 2023; business name registered 13 days later, 17 October 2023; the earliest archived page of the shop's website with content, of 27 March 2024, already presents a 'Fashion Store' and 'Portuguese Café Corner' at 203 Makariou III Av. with opening hours (café 7:30 am-9:00 pm, store 8:30 am-8:30 pm) - 175 days after the company; Cyprus Business News on 8 February 2025, writing from the store's website, said 'Having recently opened in Limassol'. On 6 October 2026 the register lists annual-return (HE32) applications of 14 October 2025 and 16 July 2026, both still pending.
