m-dae40ea6.t: No public record seen dates a licence for etxetera, the Nicosia café and shop of Etxetera Ltd (ΗΕ 486922, registered 25 January 2026, launched in March 2026): the Deputy Ministry of Tourism's Nicosia lists dated 16/02/2026, 08/04/2026, 13/05/2026, 19/06/2026 and 11/08/2026 contain no entry named etxetera (searched ETX, ETC and Greek spellings), and Wolt has no venue page under that name. No source read gives the café's street address, so an entry under another trade name could not be looked for. On 6 October 2026 a Registrar name search for ETXETERA returns only the company, which has no pending service; business names held under other names cannot be searched by owner.

m-d87cedaf.t: Dated steps of the True Heart Café (Nicosia): owner company A. K Todos Tacos Ltd registered 8 November 2024; on 6 December 2025 Cyprus Business News reported that the café, then Blue Heart Café, 'will open in Nicosia early 2026'; business names BLUE HEART CAFE registered 4 February 2026 and TRUE HEART CAFE 15 days later, 19 February 2026; company entered in the Register of Social Enterprises 21 April 2026; inaugurated by the Deputy Minister of Social Welfare on Thursday 14 May 2026 (Cyprus Mail, same day). Company to inauguration: 552 days; TRUE HEART CAFE name to it: 84; social-enterprise entry to it: 23. No public source found dates the licences, bank account or card terminal.

m-d2854e19.t: Dated public steps of Cyber Shop Cyprus: company N.N. Cyber Digital Products Ltd registered 26 October 2023; first archived capture of the live store 29 February 2024 (Shopify, prices in euro, 'Shipping Worldwide') - 126 days later; first annual return (HE32) made up to 27 April 2025, the first reference date of Companies Law s. 120(1A)(a), applied for on 4 December 2025 (221 days after that date); second HE32 made up to 27 April 2026, applied for on 13 July 2026 (77 days). On 6 October 2026 both are listed under 'pending services' and no HE32 is shown as registered.

m-cfdfc346.t: The Valiotti account thanks a named person 'from the company I.A. Practical Ties Ltd' for help, 'without whom everything would have been much harder', and says experienced lawyers helped open the company. That firm is a Cyprus private company, HE 414301, registered 22 October 2020, with the person thanked as an officer. On 6 October 2026 its register status is 'reminder letter sent', dated 9 February 2026; an objection to strike-off of 11 April 2025 and its only annual return (accounts to 31 December 2021) are pending. It is not on the Bar's ASP register, ICPAC's ASP firms or CySEC's approved ASPs as read 6 October 2026.

m-cdff0633.t: Case, premises with a founder from abroad - Furen, a Lebanese wood-oven bakery-restaurant at the top of Ledra Street, Nicosia. The Registrar of Companies' free search (read 6 October 2026) shows the business name FUREN, no. ΕΕ 59030, registered on 29 March 2024 with KFB HOSPITALITY CONCEPTS LTD as owner; the owner is a private company, no. ΗΕ 453980, registered on 23 November 2023, with one director, Fayez Hwalla, and a corporate secretary, Emikal Secretarial Limited. The Cyprus Mail (12 October 2024) presents Hwalla, who is Lebanese, as co-owner with a partner and calls the outlet 'a sizeable investment', without figures.

m-af28a484.t: The True Heart Café's premises, 10B Yianni Kranidioti Street, Nicosia, were on the Deputy Ministry of Tourism's Nicosia lists before it opened, as the cafeteria IHEART at that address and telephone, in every list seen from 22/11/2023 to the English edition dated 08/04/2026. The English list dated 13/05/2026 and the lists of 19/06/2026 and 11/08/2026 carry TRUE HEART CAFE, cafeteria, at the same address and telephone, and no IHEART; no expiry is printed for either name. The renamed entry came between the lists of 8 April and 13 May 2026; the café was inaugurated on 14 May 2026. The lists do not say whether a licence was issued, transferred or amended.

m-abd2430f.t: Dated public steps of the Shrine theme store (Shrine Solutions Ltd, ΗΕ 453354), per web-archive captures and the register: the store, Shopify shop 'shrinetheme.myshopify.com', was live at shrinetheme.com by 6 April 2023, its terms then saying the site 'is operated by ShrineTheme' under 'the laws of Greece'; the company was registered on 3 November 2023, 211 days later; by 18 November 2024 the same shop ran at shrinesolutions.com with terms naming 'Shrine Solutions LTD, a company incorporated in Cyprus'; shrine.io carried it from 15 May 2025 (earlier captures: a domain-sale listing); first prize at the Stelios Awards on 7 October 2025. The store was on sale before the company existed.

m-a9b6bbe4.t: Case, online shop of physical goods - Cyber Shop Cyprus (cybershopcyprus.com), which calls itself 'a Nicosia-based technology e-commerce brand' selling electronics, gaming and computer goods. Its contact page gives 'Legal Name: N.N. Cyber Digital Products LTD' and 'Company Registration: HE 453013'. The Registrar's free search (6 October 2026) shows N.N. CYBER DIGITAL PRODUCTS LTD, private company ΗΕ 453013, registered 26 October 2023, with one director, whose name matches the founder and CEO the shop's own page names (Nearchos Nearchou), and a different person as secretary. Wolt's trader panel names the same company and number, product line electronics, home delivery only.

m-a212d2a5.t: The Registrar gives 28 March 2022 as the registration date of Valiotti Analytics Ltd. That is the very day the founder's post gives for his Estonian e-residency application, which, he says, was refused about two weeks later before he turned to Cyprus. The post's date is doubtful: its disclaimer says it is current 'as of mid-March 2022', and the refusal it describes (all Russian passport holders, pending applications included) matches Estonia's stop on such applications reported on 8-9 March 2022. Either the post's '28 March' is a slip, or the Cyprus filing ran before or alongside the Estonian attempt. The register alone does not settle the order.

m-9a4ca128.t: For the VAT number CY01375414L that Rare Skinstore prints, the EU's VIES service returned on 6 October 2026 'valid' and, as holder, the name of the natural person who owns the business name RARE SKINSTORE (ΕΕ 56521) in the Registrar's free search, not the business name: in this case the VAT registration is the sole trader's own.

m-9820dc21.t: The Shrine theme business dates its own start: its 'About us' page says 'Established in March 2023' in every web-archive capture of shrinetheme.com/pages/about-us, the earliest of 22 July 2023, and on shrine.io as read on 6 October 2026. Its Cyprus company, Shrine Solutions Ltd (HE 453354), was registered on 3 November 2023. So by the business's own account, published 104 days before incorporation, it started between seven and eight months before the company existed (a day in March 2023 to 3 November 2023), which fits its store archived live on 6 April 2023, 211 days before.

m-945f97b9.t: The True Heart Café's Head of Operations, Alexandros Karpis, told the Cyprus Mail (6 June 2026): 'Usually starting out in hospitality takes anywhere between six months to two, three years to start first operations. We went very quickly. We've got help from government, we've got help from private investors.' It is one practitioner's general statement about hospitality start-ups, not a measured time for this café; it does not say which steps, permits or licences the range covers, and 'first operations' is not defined.

m-916d4fbc.t: At 203B Makariou III Avenue, Limassol, the Deputy Ministry of Tourism's lists replace one snack bar with another: the list dated 27/06/2023 carries LA CROISSANTERIE GRAND 6; the list dated 22/11/2023 - 49 days after Levasco Concept Ltd was registered (4 October 2023), 36 after its business name (17 October 2023) - carries SUNDAY IN LISBOA, snack bar, with the same two telephone numbers, one of which (70088888) the lists print for every LA CROISSANTERIE outlet. From the list of 06/11/2025 the entry has another telephone and a licence expiry of 14/10/2028 (also in the lists of 16/02/2026 and 19/06/2026). No list gives an issue date or holder, or says whether the licence was transferred.

m-7ca58bbe.t: Case, shop with premises that also sells online - Sunday in Lisboa Concept Store, Limassol: a fashion boutique with a Portuguese café corner and delicatessen at 203 Makariou III Avenue whose website sells with worldwide shipping. The Registrar's free search (6 October 2026) shows the business name SUNDAY IN LISBOA CONCEPT STORE, ΕΕ 58259, registered 17 October 2023 with LEVASCO CONCEPT LTD as owner - a private company, ΗΕ 452057, registered 4 October 2023, with one director and a different person as secretary. The website signs as 'Sunday in Lisboa - Le Vasco Concept' but, on the pages read, gives no company name, registration number or VAT number.

m-79fbd88b.t: Case, barest (sole trader, business name) - Minabocks, a Google Ads agency. The Registrar's free search (6 October 2026) shows the business name MINABOCKS, ΕΕ 56582, registered on 30 November 2022 and still registered, owned by a natural person whose name matches the founder's as the Cyprus Mail prints it. The agency's own site was live on 6 September 2022, 85 days earlier, as 'An American Advertising Agency in Cyprus', 'Based in Nicosia' with 'over 4 years of experience' - so the register dates the name, not the start of the business. The Cyprus Mail of 30 December 2022 called Kevin Brown 'the founder of digital marketing agency Minabocks'. No source says what registration took or cost.

m-75bb4ea3.t: Across the premises cases found, the time from the company's registration to the first public sign of trading, as dates show it: etxetera, Nicosia, 35-53 days (company 25 Jan 2026; launched 'earlier this month' per an article of 19 Mar 2026); Sunday in Lisboa, Limassol, at most 175 days (company 4 Oct 2023; website with hours 27 Mar 2024); Furen, Nicosia, 160-190 days (company 23 Nov 2023; opened 'in May' 2024; reported 3 Jun 2024); True Heart Café, Nicosia, 552 days to inauguration (company 8 Nov 2024; 14 May 2026), a social enterprise. In every case the business name, where there is one, was registered after the company: 13, 127 and 453 days later.

m-6e294ed7.t: The Registrar of Companies' free search (read 6 October 2026) shows VALIOTTI ANALYTICS LTD, private company HE 432566, registered 28 March 2022, status registered, one director whose name in Latin script matches the author of the vc.ru account; the firm's own privacy policy names 'Valiotti Analytics Ltd (Reg. HE 432566)' as data controller. The register lists four annual-return (HE32) applications, of 10 October 2023, 26 August 2024, 18 August 2025 and 26 June 2026, with accounts made up to 31 December 2022 to 2025, all under pending services on 6 October 2026.

m-6d7a5a0e.t: Case, premises - True Heart Café, 10B Yiannis Kranidiotis Street, Nicosia, a café of the NGO Voice for Autism employing young people with autism. The Registrar's free search (6 October 2026) shows two business names owned by A. K TODOS TACOS LTD (private company ΗΕ 467363, registered 8 November 2024, two directors, one also secretary) at Yianni Kranidioti 10: BLUE HEART CAFE, ΕΕ 62478, registered 4 February 2026 - the name under which the café was announced on 6 December 2025 - and TRUE HEART CAFE, ΕΕ 62543, registered 19 February 2026. The Register of Social Enterprises states that the company's main purpose is employing people with autism at the True Heart Café.

m-61abcd13.t: Case, a one-person business moving up a rung - Kuns Studio, 'a ceramics and sculpture space in the centre of Nicosia' (Cyprus Mail, 23 January 2026, naming Elpida Fragkeskidou Khenkin, an artist who designs and delivers art programmes, as founder). The Registrar's free search (6 October 2026) shows the business name KUNS STUDIO, ΕΕ 54458, registered 20 October 2021 with a natural person as owner and struck off ('Διαγραμμένη') with status date 31 December 2023, and a private company KUNS STUDIO LTD, ΗΕ 455099, registered that same day (a Sunday), whose sole director is also its secretary. From the name to the company: 802 days. No source shows the business passing to the company.

m-61543104.t: Case, café with a shop opened in 2026 - etxetera, a 'collective space' in Nicosia that 'blends a small café with analog photography, artwear, dog goods and community events' (Cyprus Mail, 19 March 2026, naming Aila Mroué El-Bacha as founder and saying it 'launched earlier this month'). The Registrar's free search (6 October 2026) shows ETXETERA LTD, private company ΗΕ 486922, registered on Sunday 25 January 2026, with three directors, one of whom is also secretary. Between registration and a launch in the first 19 days of March 2026 lie 35 to 53 days; the launch day itself is not given.

m-60f3eb91.t: Ellen Georgiou Pontikis, founder of Voice for Autism, the NGO behind the True Heart Café (Nicosia, opened 2026), per the Cyprus Mail of 6 June 2026: 'There were huge challenges in the Cyprus context, number one, navigating the complex legal issues because the EU doesn't have a template, it's given to the member states. The legal costs was another issue'; and 'It's more expensive to set up than a traditional business model. You need a lot of training. You may need an adaptive workspace. You need an in-house support team.' She gave no amounts. Cyprus Business News (6 December 2025) calls the help of the Office of the Commissioner for Cooperative Societies and Social Enterprises 'instrumental'.

m-53aaea8e.t: In the Deputy Ministry of Tourism's lists, two of the three café entries keep the telephone numbers of the establishment they replaced at the same address: SUNDAY IN LISBOA (203B Makariou III Avenue, Limassol) carries on 22/11/2023 and 18/06/2024 both numbers of the earlier LA CROISSANTERIE GRAND 6 entry, 25773773 and 70088888 - the second printed for every La Croissanterie entry in Limassol - and the number its own website gives only from 16/02/2026; TRUE HEART CAFE keeps IHEART's 22432280 on 19/06/2026. FUREN's number differs from ΤΡΙΓΥΡΟ's. The lists do not say whether an entry was renamed, transferred or newly issued.

m-5305343f.t: First annual returns of two new Cyprus companies, per the Registrar's free search on 6 October 2026: KFB Hospitality Concepts Ltd (ΗΕ 453980, Furen's owner, incorporated 23 November 2023) has an HE32 made up to 24 May 2025, statements dated 31 December 2024, applied for on 24 July 2025; Kuns Studio Ltd (ΗΕ 455099, incorporated 31 December 2023) one made up to 1 July 2025, same statements date, applied for on 20 April 2026. Each made-up date is the first reference date of Companies Law s. 120(1A)(a), the day after 18 months from incorporation; the applications came 61 and 293 days later (s. 120(1): 28 days). Both are listed as pending; neither file shows an HE32 as registered.

m-4830fa2c.t: Furen's premises at 272 Ledra Street, Nicosia, as the Deputy Ministry of Tourism's Nicosia lists of recreation centres show them: the list dated 22/11/2023 - one day before Furen's company, KFB Hospitality Concepts Ltd, was registered - carries a different snack bar, ΤΡΙΓΥΡΟ, at that address; the list dated 18/06/2024 carries FUREN, category 'ΣΝΑΚ ΜΠΑΡ' (snack bar), and no ΤΡΙΓΥΡΟ. The change came between those two lists, 209 days apart (the business name FUREN was registered on 29 March 2024). The lists dated 16/02/2026 and 19/06/2026 give Furen's licence expiry as 08/08/2027. No list gives an issue date.

m-45747fb7.t: Case, barest (one-person software business selling online) - Shrine Solutions Ltd, which sells Shopify themes at shrine.io. The store's terms (last update 28/01/2025, read 6 October 2026) name the operator as Shrine Solutions Ltd, 'a company incorporated in the Republic of Cyprus with registration number HE 453354'. The Registrar's free search (6 October 2026) shows that private company registered on Friday 3 November 2023, one officer being director and secretary, which Companies Law s. 171(1) permits only in a single-member private company. The Stelios Awards press release of 8 October 2025 names George Chrysostomides first-prize winner for 'the Shopify website development company Shrine'.

m-401af3d2.t: The True Heart Café's company is a registered social enterprise. The Registrar of Cooperative Societies and Social Enterprises announced on 4 May 2026 that on 21 April 2026 it made the first three entries in the Register of Social Enterprises, among them A. K TODOS TACOS LTD (ΗΕ 467363) as an integration enterprise (entry KE E1) whose main purpose is employing persons with autism at the True Heart Café. The register gives 7 members/shareholders and, in the column for financial statements filed, 'newly established'. The entry came 529 days after incorporation, 61 days after the TRUE HEART CAFE business name and 23 days before the café's inauguration on 14 May 2026.

m-31047e86.t: Anonymous-company account in a formation platform's own marketing: YouReg (Youreg.Tech) published on Medium on 13 April 2022 a 'personal experience' piece quoting a client, described as CEO of an IT start-up (mobile app), who formed a Cyprus company without visiting. He sent an English CV for the bank and a utility bill as proof of address, met a courier once to sign and on a second occasion received the original constituent documents. He says 'the whole process from the date of my application to registration took 1.5–2 weeks'. He took a Cypriot director and a secretary through the platform, paying EUR 99 a month for each as of April 2022. The company is not named.

m-2e5a92c9.t: Dated steps of Furen (Nicosia) as public sources show them: company KFB Hospitality Concepts Ltd registered 23 November 2023; an application dated 9 February 2024 for a certified copy of its memorandum and articles, still listed among the register's 'pending services' on 6 October 2026; business name FUREN registered 29 March 2024; opened 'in May' 2024 per the Cyprus Mail (12 October 2024); reported as newly opened by Cyprus Business News on 3 June 2024. From company registration to the business name: 127 days; to the report of 3 June 2024: 193 days. No public source found gives the opening day or the dates of the municipal licences, the bank account or the card terminal.

m-2d31f78c.t: Founder's own account, not verified: Miriam Alonso, founder of the Cyprus Tax Life site, who moved from Spain, writes (post of 17 June 2026) that she decided in January 2024 and was in Larnaca in June 2024. 'In my case, the entire process from signing the rental contract to having the TIN and the company incorporated took approximately 6 weeks.' A second post says she set up Synaptum Digital LTD in Larnaca on arriving in 2024. No step is dated. The order she gives, written for EU citizens, is her advice, not a document's: rental contract, Yellow Slip, tax number, company bank account, with incorporation in parallel.

m-2cc82cd1.t: In the same 10 June 2022 account the founder says a company used to need at least EUR 200,000 and 'from 1 January this year' no longer did, which let him open his Cyprus company; and that it could employ him only after getting permission for simplified hiring of foreign staff, which 'will take another week'. Both concern registration as a company of foreign interests, needed to employ third-country staff, not forming a company. The Business Facilitation Unit's page of May 2022 set no investment test for a majority third-country-owned company; a Council of Ministers decision of 30 November 2022, in force 12 December 2022, added proof of an initial investment of at least EUR 200,000.

m-2383437f.t: Where named recent Cyprus businesses surface by their founders' choice: the Stelios Awards for Young Entrepreneurs in Cyprus, run since 2023 by the Stelios Philanthropic Foundation. For 2026 it announces €200,000 in three prizes, applications 1 September-15 October 2026 and the ceremony on 10 November 2026. Entry, per the Foundation's 2025 call and the Cyprus Mail for 2026: under 34, a company founded in the Republic of Cyprus within the past five years, annual turnover of €40,000 ('at least' in the Cyprus Mail), any nationality; the 2024 call (Cyprus Mail, 27 May 2024) said under 35 with no turnover test. Past winners include a restaurant and a café (2023) and Shrine Solutions Ltd (2025).

m-1d584e76.t: The Registrar's free search (read 6 October 2026) shows SYNAPTUM DIGITAL LTD, private company HE 470910, registered 5 February 2025, status registered. One person is both its director and its secretary, and one annual-return (HE32) application, of 13 August 2026, is pending. The company named by the Cyprus Tax Life founder was therefore registered in 2025, not in 2024 as her author note says, and seven to eight months after the June 2024 arrival she gives. Her name is not among its two officers; shareholders are not shown on the free search.

m-0324374b.t: The establishments the three cafés replaced had stood at the same addresses for years, per the Deputy Ministry of Tourism's lists: the snack bar ΤΡΙΓΥΡΟ (TRIGIRO) at 272 Ledra Street, Nicosia, and the cafeteria IHEART at 10B Giannou Kranidioti Street, Nicosia, are both on the Nicosia list of 09/12/2020 and every later edition read until 22/11/2023 and 16/02/2026 respectively; the snack bar LA CROISSANTERIE GRAND 6 at 203B Makariou III Avenue, Limassol, is on the Limassol lists of 09/12/2020, 05/01/2022, 21/09/2022 and 27/06/2023. In each case the café's name replaced an entry listed at that address for at least two and a half years.

m-c214a648.t: Dated public steps of Rare Skinstore: business name RARE SKINSTORE registered 17 November 2022; the web archive's capture of www.rareskinstore.com of 3 March 2023 leads to a snapshot of 4 March 2023 that already shows the live store ('Rare skinstore', Shopify, 'Free shipping Cyprus €50+│Greece €7') - 107 days after the name; the store is captured under its own domain from 22 July 2024. The register shows no pending service and no annual-return (HE32) entry for the business name on 6 October 2026.

m-892a5022.t: From registration to the first archived sign of a live business, as dates show it: Rare Skinstore 107 days (business name 17 November 2022, live store archived 4 March 2023); Cyber Shop Cyprus 126 days (company 26 October 2023, store archived 29 February 2024). Mojo's site was first archived 41 days after its company (20 July and 30 August 2022) but already showed client work, and its privacy policy is dated February 2021, so it does not time a start. Shrine's store was live at another domain 211 days before its company (6 April and 3 November 2023), and Minabocks' site 85 days before its business name (6 September and 30 November 2022).

m-796d800b.t: Case, online shop on the cheapest rung - Rare Skinstore (rareskinstore.com), an online shop of Korean cosmetics in Cyprus. The Registrar's free search (6 October 2026) shows RARE SKINSTORE as a business name, ΕΕ 56521, registered 17 November 2022 and still registered, owned by a natural person - a sole trader, not a company, although the shop's legal notice calls it 'a company registered in Cyprus' and prints the number as 'EE56521A'. The notice also gives VAT number CY01375414L, which the EU's VIES service reported valid on 6 October 2026. Wolt's trader panel names RARE SKINSTORE, 'ΕΕ56521', product line health and beauty.

m-6c0c5593.t: What the four case businesses selling online print about their legal identity (pages read on 6 Oct 2026): Shrine Solutions Ltd gives its HE number in its terms; Cyber Shop Cyprus its company name and HE number on its contact page; Rare Skinstore gives its register number with a stray letter ('EE56521A') and a VAT number in a legal notice calling the sole trader 'a company'; Sunday in Lisboa's footer names 'Le Vasco Concept', with no 'Ltd', registration or VAT number, though its terms say prices include Cypriot VAT. Only Rare Skinstore prints a VAT number. Electronic Commerce Law s. 8(1) lists name, register number and, where VAT applies, VAT number among what a provider must make accessible.

m-5d79db3f.t: On 6 October 2026 the Registrar's free search lists each annual return (HE32) lodged by a case company both among 'pending services' and in the file's HE32 archive with its made-up date, with the field 'date of last HE32 registration' empty: KFB Hospitality Concepts Ltd (applied 24 July 2025), Levasco Concept Ltd (14 October 2025; 16 July 2026), Kuns Studio Ltd (20 April 2026), N.N. Cyber Digital Products Ltd (4 December 2025; 13 July 2026), J.P Mojo Design Limited (17 November 2023; 5 November 2024; 22 December 2025) - nine applications, the oldest 1,054 days old. Four other case companies lodged none. Unrelated companies show the same state.

m-17445526.t: Case, barest company rung (services to businesses) - Mojo, a web design and branding agency in Cyprus. The Registrar's free search (6 October 2026) shows J.P MOJO DESIGN LIMITED, private company ΗΕ 436646, registered 20 July 2022, one director whose name matches the founder's as the Cyprus Mail prints it (Jacob Papageorgiou), another person as secretary. The agency's privacy policy names 'J.PMojo Design Limited' as data controller yet is headed 'Updated 18th February 2021'. Its site was first archived on 30 August 2022, 41 days after the company, already showing client projects and testimonials: the agency likely worked before it incorporated (not established). The site lists a team of five.

m-0448a559.t: In the three café cases on the Deputy Ministry of Tourism's lists, the café's name appears at an address where an earlier list showed another establishment of the same category: FUREN (snack bar, 272 Ledra St, Nicosia) on the list of 18/06/2024, where the snack bar ΤΡΙΓΥΡΟ stood on 22/11/2023; SUNDAY IN LISBOA (snack bar, 203B Makariou III Ave, Limassol) by the list of 22/11/2023, 49 days after its company, where the snack bar La Croissanterie Grand 6 stood on 27/06/2023; TRUE HEART CAFE (cafeteria, 10B Giannou Kranidioti St, Nicosia) on 19/06/2026, where the cafeteria IHEART stood on 16/02/2026. List dates bound each change, not date it. etxetera and Rincon Latino are on no list by name.

m-03807f1b.t: Case, premises - Rincon Latino café, which the Cyprus Mail of 3 April 2025 says offers 'authentic, homemade Latin sweet and savoury flavours' and whose owner it names as Roberto Nicolás Aquino. Wolt's trader panel names EL RINCON LATINO CAFE LTD, 'ΗΕ466145', with the venue at Andrea Michalakopoulou 7, Nicosia. The Registrar's free search (6 October 2026) shows that private company, ΗΕ 466145, registered 9 October 2024 (176 days before the column), one person as both director and secretary, and no annual return lodged. No entry named Rincon or Latino, and none at that address, is in the Deputy Ministry of Tourism's Nicosia lists dated 22/11/2023 to 19/06/2026.

m-f1aed4a7.t: PayPal's contracting entity for Cyprus has not changed since at least 2018, but the governing law has. Archive snapshots of the Cyprus user agreement dated 28 February 2018, 16 June 2020 and 30 April 2021 name PayPal (Europe) S.à r.l. et Cie, S.C.A. and apply 'the laws of England and Wales' with non-exclusive jurisdiction of the English courts. By PayPal's notice of 11 February 2022 the agreement moved to Luxembourg law and courts from 6 May 2022; the version effective 1 August 2022 and the text of 7 September 2026 apply 'the laws of the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg' and the courts of Luxembourg City. The 2020 version still listed the United Kingdom with Cyprus; the 2021 version no longer did.

m-ee6c2240.t: Adyen's documentation ('Deposit', docs.adyen.com, read 5 October 2026) gives mechanics its terms leave out. The deposit requirement is recalculated daily before payout as estimated exposure - orders paid but unfulfilled plus chargebacks and refunds predicted from the past 180 days - against coverage: pending and payable balances, any bank guarantee, the existing deposit and an 'accepted risk' set case by case. Funds are withheld from the next payout only when exposure exceeds coverage by more than EUR 10,000. A bank guarantee or standby letter of credit may replace the deposit in part or in full. The deposit is 'exclusively owned by you' and returned about six months after processing stops.

m-e71539f4.t: SumUp's Cyprus help article on chargebacks - the page its Payment Terms (section 16) point to for chargeback charges - says 'payment providers charge a non-refundable fee of €10 for chargebacks' (undated, read 5 October 2026). SumUp first covers the chargeback and takes the amount out of the merchant's next scheduled payout; the merchant must send evidence within the deadline set by the acquiring bank; if the issuing bank decides for the merchant, SumUp keeps the money for 60 days, until the cardholder's objection period ends, and then returns it.

m-db06a9d6.t: Viva served Cyprus through an e-money institution with a Cyprus branch before the business passed to a bank. Its Cyprus terms archived on 16 December 2019 and its 'Terms and Conditions CY' of 16 January to 22 May 2024 are with Viva Payment Services S.A., a Greek e-money institution with 'an established branch registered under no. AE3222, notified to Central Bank of Cyprus'. The version effective 1 July 2024 drops the branch and cites freedom of services across 31 EEA countries. The 1 February 2025 version says Viva Payments was absorbed by Vivabank, a bank, and that 'from 3.4.2025 you will become a depositor of VIVA BANK'. GLEIF records the branch (ΑΕ 3222) as dissolved from 31 January 2025.

m-be97de1b.t: Eight versions of JCC's 'Terms for the Participation in Card Schemes' can be dated from the Internet Archive and JCC's site. An unnumbered text was archived on 17 April 2012; 'JAN2013' on 27 June 2013; 'v1.3 260115' (26 January 2015) was the file linked from JCC's download page in captures from 2015 (seen: 23 April 2015) to 2 November 2017. The page linked 'Version 2-1' on 4 March 2018 and 'Version 2.3 08062018 FINAL' from 5 July to 4 November 2018; neither file was archived. 'V2.8' sits under upload path 2023/05 (archived 7 December 2023), '2.9' under 2024/03 (archived 19 March 2025), and 'V2.10' under 2026/08 is the live text. Versions 2.2 and 2.4 to 2.7 were not found.

m-bb5f7747.t: Four of the changes between JCC's Terms Version 1.3 (January 2015) and 2.8 (2023). Data protection: from JCC being 'responsible for the safekeeping and processing of personal data' under Cyprus Law 138(I)/2001 to the merchant as data controller and JCC as data processor (JCC staying controller for risk and compliance), with Regulation (EU) 2016/679 cited. PCI DSS: from a questionnaire JCC 'may ask' for yearly to an undertaking to complete questionnaires annually, with termination without notice for non-compliance. Card schemes: UnionPay and JCB added to Visa, Mastercard and Diners/Discover. New definitions: 'JCC SoftPOS', an Android application acting as a point of sale, and 'Marketplace'.

m-b9e14c9d.t: Stripe's European agreement shows its regulated entity changing with its Irish e-money licence. In the Ireland version archived on 13 November 2018 ('Last Updated: April 4, 2017') the contract is with Stripe Payments Europe, Ltd. and regulated payment services 'will be provided by Stripe Payments UK, Ltd.'. The version 'Last updated: April 5, 2019' (snapshot of 20 July 2019) says they may be provided by Stripe Payments UK or by Stripe Technology Europe, Limited. The earliest archived Cyprus-locale version ('Last updated: October 28, 2020', snapshot of 16 November 2020) names Stripe Technology Europe alone. All three apply Irish law and JAMS arbitration in Dublin; today's text uses the ICC.

m-b9e08fb1.t: For a Cyprus user the Stripe Services Agreement (General Terms last modified 28 September 2026) is governed by the laws of Ireland. Disputes go to binding arbitration by a single arbitrator in Dublin, administered by the ICC International Court of Arbitration; the arbitrator must be a member of the Law Society of Ireland or the Bar of Ireland unless the parties agree otherwise. Claims that may not be arbitrated, including intellectual-property claims, go to the courts of Ireland, and Stripe may still bring insolvency proceedings 'in an appropriate court under insolvency laws in the User's jurisdiction'. The class-action waiver of the preamble does not apply in the EEA. Cyprus is not named.

m-b8845873.t: PayPal's own notice dates the change of governing law for Cyprus users. Its 'Past Policy Updates' page for 13 countries including Cyprus (last updated 28 September 2026) carries a notice issued on 11 February 2022: effective 6 May 2022 the user agreement was amended by 'Changing the governing law from English law to Luxembourg law, and jurisdiction from English courts to Luxembourg courts to align with the seat of PayPal (Europe) S.à r.l. et Cie, S.C.A., a registered Luxembourg bank'. A later notice, effective 1 August 2022, only clarified the clause, restating that consumers may sue in local courts; one effective 28 May 2024 separated consumer and non-consumer provisions.

m-b75cc80d.t: Between 2019 and 2022 each of the four foreign providers read whose Cyprus contract ran through the United Kingdom moved it into the EU: Stripe's regulated services from Stripe Payments UK to the Irish Stripe Technology Europe (2019-2020); SumUp from SumUp Payments Limited to SumUp EU Payments UAB and Lithuanian law (May-June 2020); Revolut from Revolut Ltd to Revolut Payments UAB (by January 2021), then Revolut Bank UAB (2022); PayPal, a Luxembourg entity throughout, from English to Luxembourg law on 6 May 2022. myPOS (Bulgarian institution, UK agent) moved to an Irish one in 2023; Viva from e-money institution to bank in 2025. JCC kept its entity; Adyen's terms before 2023 were not read.

m-a8fcaa11.t: Revolut's en-CY page data list four versions of the Payment Processing Services Agreement that covers Cyprus (one document for Bulgaria, Belgium, Cyprus, Denmark and Malta, entity Revolut Bank UAB): applying from 22 April 2025, 17 November 2025, 28 September 2026 (in force on 4 October 2026) and 30 November 2026 (dated 28 September 2026). The November 2025 version added a duty to display Revolut's logos, an 'Arbitration Loss Fee' and the option of the courts of the merchant's country; the September 2026 version added SEPA Direct Debit terms; the November 2026 version adds customer-contact duties and a USD 5,000 monthly penalty for submitting American Express charges after being told to stop.

m-a87f1b44.t: Revolut's Payment Processing Services Agreement for Cyprus (version applying from 28 September 2026, in force on 4 October 2026) says Revolut 'will always withhold a percentage of each Transaction value' as a 'Reserve': the percentage 'may be anywhere between 0% and 100%' and the holding period is at its discretion, both changeable on notice. Settlement timing is not in the terms: funds go to a 'Payout account' under a 'Payout Schedule' that Revolut may change; it may suspend settlement or withdrawals, including after the terms end. The same reserve sentence stands in the versions archived on 29 January 2021, 30 September 2022 and 14 January 2025 and in each version since 22 April 2025.

m-a0f504d6.t: For about four months in 2024 the general terms of Viva's Cyprus agreement pointed to the user's own country. Dated versions on Viva's Cyprus terms-history page: 16 January 2024 - laws of Greece, courts of Athens (only the terminal-app terms already applied the law of an EU user's country of residence); 14 February, 21 March, 3 April and 22 May 2024 - 'the laws of the country of User's residence' and its courts, for a Cyprus merchant Cyprus; 1 July, 12 July (printed as effective 11 July) and 1 August 2024 - Greece and Athens again; 1 February and 18 March 2025 - Greece, with Athens in the payment terms and Amarousio in the new account-opening terms; 30 September 2026 - Greece and Amarousio.

m-906032e8.t: None of the eight providers read (JCC, Stripe, myPOS, Viva, SumUp, Adyen, Revolut, PayPal) publishes a reserve rate (terms read 4-5 October 2026). Numbers that do appear: Revolut - reserve 'anywhere between 0% and 100%'; PayPal - an example of 10% held 90 days, holds beyond 180 days after restricted activity; SumUp - reserve kept at most 13 months after termination, bank transfers 3-5 business days; Adyen - reserve released 'generally' about six months after processing ends, payout 'e.g. T+2'; JCC - collateral kept one year after the last transaction, longer after material breach; Stripe - first payout after 7 days, then 3 business days. Viva, myPOS: none. Rates come by agreement or notice.

m-5cfdfb48.t: PayPal's user agreement for Cyprus (last updated 7 September 2026) makes the seller liable for a reversed payment by default: 'If you receive a payment in your account, you owe us the full amount of the payment and our losses arising from processing the payment (including any Chargeback fee or Dispute fee)'. PayPal sets these amounts off against the balance, converting other balances if needed. The stated exception is PayPal's Seller Protection programme, under which an eligible seller may keep the full purchase amount. For a card-funded payment the card issuer, not PayPal, decides the chargeback, and PayPal may hold money until the chargeback risk under card-scheme rules has passed.

m-5205cb70.t: Adyen keeps two sets of merchant terms online (read 5 October 2026). The set 'Effective from: March 7th, 2023', for agreements made before 1 November 2023, defines Adyen as Adyen N.V. and sends disputes to 'the exclusive jurisdiction of the competent courts of Amsterdam'. The set for agreements from 1 November 2023 defines Adyen as Adyen N.V. 'and/or where relevant, one or more of its local affiliates' and replaces the courts with ICC arbitration in Amsterdam; the 'Deposit' is now the 'MPL Reserve'. Both apply Dutch law, two months' termination notice and a 0.5% chargeback tolerance, and release the security as a rule about six months after processing stops unless liabilities remain.

m-494cfd08.t: Revolut's merchant contract for Cyprus is the 'Payment Processing Services Agreement' on its en-CY site. The version in force on 4 October 2026 (applying from 28 September 2026; one applying from 30 November 2026 is posted) is between the account holder and Revolut Bank UAB, on top of the Revolut Business or Revolut Pro terms: the user must hold such an account, apply and be accepted, and then gets a 'Merchant Account'. It is under Lithuanian law; the Vilnius courts have exclusive jurisdiction unless the merchant's place of business is outside Lithuania, when jurisdiction 'may be extended' to the courts of its own country - a carve-out added in the version applying from 17 November 2025.

m-408aca3d.t: Revolut's Payment Processing Services Agreement for Cyprus says: 'Depending on the nature of your business, you may need to enter into a direct contractual relationship with the card scheme or another third party'. Its example: a merchant processing 'at least USD$1m worth of American Express, Mastercard or Visa transactions annually' may need a direct contract 'with a Payment Method Acquirer and us'. Failing agreement within a reasonable time, Revolut may suspend or terminate the services or refuse payments above that amount. The clause is in the version in force on 5 October 2026 (applying from 28 September 2026) and in that of 22 April 2025; the 2023 version names Mastercard and Visa only.

m-354116b7.t: Under Revolut's Payment Processing Services Agreement for Cyprus (version applying from 28 September 2026, in force on 4 October 2026) the merchant answers to Revolut for any transaction later disputed, refunded, charged back or reversed; a challenge is possible, not guaranteed. Since the version applying from 17 November 2025 a merchant losing a chargeback at arbitration pays a flat fee set in the fees pages. A Business customer may end the agreement on one month's notice; Revolut on two months' notice, or without notice on listed grounds, e.g. unremedied material breach, breach of law, sanctions listing, insolvency, or a chargeback ratio that 'exceeds our requirements' (not stated).

m-24e2c792.t: myPOS's regulated entity for EEA clients was Bulgarian before it was Irish, by its own English, all-EEA terms pages. On 13 March 2017 the page offered two legal agreements; the one displayed was between the client and myPOS Europe Ltd, London, as agent of Intercard Finance AD, a Bulgarian e-money institution, under Bulgarian law with the courts of Sofia; the institution depends 'on the country of residence of the Client', and the second agreement is not archived. On 16 January 2021 and 6 February 2023 the page footers name iCard AD, a Bulgarian e-money institution for all EEA countries. The Cyprus page archived on 9 February 2026 offers the agreement 'by myPOS Limited', an Irish institution.

m-1fb93574.t: Under PayPal's user agreement for Cyprus (last updated 7 September 2026) PayPal may close an account for convenience on two months' notice ('but no less than 60 days'), or at any time for breach, three years without access, or suspected unauthorised access. On closure the agreement ends at once, pending transactions may be cancelled, and PayPal 'may retain your electronic money after closure to the extent and for the time we reasonably require' against reversals, fees and fines; then undisputed funds can be withdrawn. No maximum retention period is stated. A limited account is 'normally' released once the requested information is given, but PayPal may act further if it thinks risk remains.

m-1bf4c3a6.t: The only substantive changes between JCC's Terms Version 2.8 (upload path 2023/05) and 2.9 (2024/03) concern anti-money-laundering duties, by a word-level comparison of the two archived PDFs (14 changed passages). Clause 2.5, which already required adherence to Central Bank of Cyprus money-laundering directives, now adds anti-terrorist financing, card-scheme rules and local law. Clause 2.14 now requires 'KYC documents' - verified identification of the merchant and related persons, including ultimate beneficial owners - and immediate notice of changes in legal structure, ownership, activities or financial condition; failure may lead to suspension or termination.

m-1b518f25.t: JCC's security for merchant risk grew from a bank guarantee to a reserve by 2013. The text archived in April 2012 gives JCC only a bank guarantee as security (clause 7.4). The file named 'JAN2013' (archived 27 June 2013, undated) adds a clause 6 'Reserves': an 'Initial Reserve' made of a rolling reserve - a percentage of each day's gross sales kept for a period - and/or a bank guarantee, percentages and period set in the individual agreement, kept one year after the last transaction or indefinitely after material breach. Version 1.3 (2015) extends its use from a bankrupt merchant to one in liquidation; Version 2.8 (2023) renames it 'Collateral'. None of the versions read states a percentage.

m-09e61c54.t: Viva's terms for a Cyprus user (effective 30 September 2026, read 5 October 2026) are governed by the laws of Greece, and disputes not settled amicably or by alternative dispute resolution go to the exclusive jurisdiction of 'the courts of Amarousio, Attica, Greece' (general terms 8.1 and 8.3); the card terms in the same document name the courts of Athens. The agreement has an indefinite term and either side may end it 'for convenience and with immediate effect' by written notice (9.2); the user may then withdraw the available balance (9.4.1). Cyprus is not named; only the software licence in the same document sends its disputes to 'the non-exclusive jurisdiction where you are a resident'.

m-f9a35af2.t: Revolut's card-acquiring contract for Cyprus changed party between 2021 and 2022. The en-CY 'Payment Processing Services Agreement' archived on 29 January 2021 ('These terms apply from 27th December', year not printed) is with Revolut Payments UAB; the version archived on 30 September 2022 ('These terms apply from 18 April 2022') is with Revolut Bank UAB and adds Revolut Pro accounts. Both are under Lithuanian law with the Vilnius courts, both carry the 0%-100% reserve clause and the same notice periods (one month by the merchant, two months by Revolut). The Bank of Lithuania register dates Revolut Bank UAB's acquiring service in Cyprus from 1 June 2022.

m-e7d172a9.t: JCC's own notice period for ending a merchant agreement fell from two months to fifteen days between 2015 and 2023. In the texts archived in 2012, 2013 and Version 1.3 of January 2015, 'JCC may terminate this Agreement upon two months written notice' while the merchant may terminate on 15 days' written notice (clauses 13.1-13.2, later 14.1-14.2). In Version 2.8 (upload path 2023/05) and in 2.9 and 2.10 the agreement runs 'unless terminated by either party upon fifteen (15) days prior written notice to the other' (clause 15.1). The two-month notice for amendments is unchanged. Which version between 2.1 and 2.7 made the change is not known: those files were not archived.

m-e73965e9.t: SumUp settles card takings into an e-money wallet and from there to the merchant's bank account. Its Payment Terms for Cyprus (effective 07/02/2022) say transfers to bank accounts 'may take 3 to 5 business days depending on the provider' (section 10); its Cyprus help article on payouts, as served on 4 October 2026, says payouts take 2-3 business days to arrive once sent, on a daily, weekly (every Monday) or monthly schedule the merchant chooses, or arrive the next day, weekends and bank holidays included, when paid to the SumUp Business card. Payments by international cards 'need more processing time' and may go into a later payout.

m-d665ae60.t: SumUp's reserve clause for Cyprus merchants did not change between the UK-entity terms of 30 March 2017 (archive snapshot of 15 November 2017) and the terms in force on 4 October 2026: in both the reserve is at SumUp's discretion with no published percentage or period, and may be kept after termination for at most thirteen months. Termination changed less than it seems: the 2017 text let SumUp close the account 'for any or no reason at any time' on notice (clause 15.1), wording still there on 17 February 2022; the present Payment Terms, first archived on 23 March 2022, set two months' notice (section 20), but the General Terms still allow closure 'at its discretion' on notice (section 13).

m-cd4671e7.t: SumUp's Payment Terms for Cyprus (effective 07/02/2022, read 4 October 2026) publish no reserve percentage or holding period: SumUp may 'at any time and at its absolute discretion' temporarily withhold payouts and build a 'Reserve' as security, set off any debt against it without notice, and demand any excess debt within three business days (section 15). With excessive chargebacks it may delay payouts or set the reserve at an amount it reasonably determines (section 16). After termination it may keep the reserve until all amounts, including potential chargebacks, are settled, but not longer than thirteen months from the effective date of termination (section 20).

m-c95aed95.t: JCC's surcharge clause changed from a contractual ban to a statutory one in 2018. The 2012, January 2013 and January 2015 (v1.3) terms say the merchant 'shall not increase the price or impose any other fee or surcharge upon any customer who uses a Card' and may not set minimum or maximum amounts (clause 2.1). A letter to merchants dated 30 June 2018 says the terms were amended because PSD2 and 'local legislation as of April 2018' prohibit surcharging consumer debit and credit cards in shops and online, and that paragraph 2.2 now records this. Version 2.8 (2023) and later read: 'in accordance with applicable law, the application of any Surcharge is prohibited'.

m-c71e1ff0.t: Under the Stripe Services Agreement (General Terms last modified 28 September 2026), the contracting entity for users in EEA countries including Cyprus is Stripe Payments Europe, Limited; Stripe Technology Europe, Limited ('Stripe PSP') is an additional party solely for providing regulated financial services and acting as payment method acquirer. The agreement is not signed on paper: it becomes effective when the user first accesses or uses the services, and for a sole proprietor both the user and the representative are bound.

m-b35ee2ec.t: SumUp's Cyprus terms name two different courts. The General Terms (effective 07/02/2022 as printed, read 4 October 2026) apply the law of Lithuania to themselves and any additional terms and give 'the courts of Ireland' exclusive jurisdiction over disputes under either (section 20). The Payment Terms of the same date, themselves additional terms, apply the law of the Republic of Lithuania, say unresolved claims may be taken to the Bank of Lithuania, and otherwise give the courts of the Republic of Lithuania exclusive jurisdiction (section 21). The Irish-courts wording is already in the copy archived on 23 March 2022. Neither text names Cyprus law or Cyprus courts.

m-a121d946.t: JCC's Terms for the Participation in Card Schemes (Version 2.10, downloaded from jcc.com.cy on 4 October 2026; same wording in Version 2.9) record that 'in accordance with applicable law, the application of any Surcharge is prohibited' (clause 2.2), require the merchant to comply with PCI DSS and to complete PCI DSS questionnaires annually (clauses 2.6-2.7), and treat the merchant as data controller and JCC as data processor of transaction personal data, with JCC acting as controller for risk management, anti-money-laundering screening and legal compliance (clause 14.1). Where the merchant rents the POS from JCC, only JCC-authorised agents may program it (clause 9.3).

m-9c5b44c4.t: Adyen settles by 'sales day': under its Sales Day Payout Terms of Service (last update 17 June 2024, read 4 October 2026) the day's captured volume, net of refunds, fees and chargebacks, is paid on 'the agreed business day after the Transaction Day (e.g. T+2)', whether or not Adyen has yet received the funds; the default day depends on currency, volume and country and is listed in Adyen's documentation, not in the terms. Adyen may delay the payout day if more than 25% of captured volume comes from payment methods that settle later, and claws back any payout for which it has not received funds within thirty days. Merchants may instead choose pass-through payout as funds arrive.

m-9ac55ae8.t: Stripe publishes no standard reserve percentage or holding period (checked 2026-10-04 in its terms, Cyprus pricing page and reserves FAQ). Under the Stripe Payments Terms (last modified 28 September 2026, §5.3–5.5) Stripe may establish a reserve on listed risk triggers, on terms sent in a 'Reserve Notice'; its FAQ names two types, fixed and rolling. For EEA users the reserve sits in accounts of Stripe Technology Europe, Limited, the user has no legal, beneficial or equitable interest in it, and safeguarded funds moved into a reserve stop being safeguarded (Financial Services Terms §3.3, §5.6, §5.9). Stripe may also add a holding period before the first settlement (Payments Terms §4.3(a)).

m-92d09da4.t: SumUp's Cyprus terms (effective 07/02/2022 as printed, read 4 October 2026) run indefinitely. Payment Terms, section 20: SumUp may end them on two months' notice, or at once for breach of the terms or card-network rules, suspected illegality, fraud or money laundering, unacceptable risk, or a compromised account; changes apply within two months of notice, or at once for security or legal reasons. General Terms, section 13, also let SumUp end all terms and close the account 'at its discretion' on 'appropriate notice' of no stated length. The merchant may close the account at any time free of charge; after two years' inactivity it is closed if a notice goes unanswered for thirty days.

m-83220ce6.t: Under Adyen's terms (updated 1 November 2023, read 4 October 2026) a merchant loses its right to a transaction amount once the shopper charges it back and 'must immediately return it'; Adyen deducts chargebacks from settlements or the reserve, charges a non-refundable fee per chargeback, and may recover chargebacks after the agreement ends. Chargeback levels above 0.5% are 'in general' unacceptable and may bring corrective action or fines passed to the merchant. Either party may terminate on two months' written notice; Adyen may suspend services at once on listed grounds (suspected illegality, changed business, missing KYC data, scheme request) and terminate if not cured in 15 business days.

m-81912b27.t: Adyen's terms (last update 1 November 2023, read 4 October 2026) hold security as an 'MPL Reserve', also called a 'Deposit'. Its level is Adyen's estimate of exposure - captured sales not yet delivered or still open to return, refund and chargeback rates, possible fines - and Adyen may adjust it at its sole discretion, disclosing its parameters on request. Adyen may require the initial amount before live processing starts and keeps the level by deducting from each settlement. After termination the reserve is released gradually and 'generally' in full about six months later. No percentage is published; the earlier terms (effective 7 March 2023) gave the same six-month release.

m-714397b5.t: A merchant's contract with Apple depends on the channel. Apple's Apple Pay page (read 4 October 2026) tells a business only: 'If your business already accepts credit and debit cards, simply contact your payment provider to start accepting Apple Pay' - no Apple contract is named, and none was found for a shop terminal. A website enabled through an e-commerce or payment platform is bound by Apple's 'Apple Pay Platform Web Merchant Terms and Conditions' (updated 10 March 2023), accepted by using the web APIs: they end when the merchant's agreement with that platform ends, require the Apple Pay button on parity with comparable wallets, bar end-user fees and set no fee payable to Apple.

m-6ff2a7fe.t: SumUp's published terms for Cyprus changed contracting entity from a UK company to a Lithuanian one between 13 May and 22 June 2020. Archive snapshots of sumup.com.cy/oroi from 15 November 2017 to 13 May 2020 show terms 'last updated 30 March 2017' with SumUp Payments Limited, an FCA-authorised UK payment institution (company no. 07836562), under English law and English courts. The snapshot of 22 June 2020 shows SumUp EU Payments UAB (company no. 305074395, e-money licence no. 56 of 27 August 2019), Lithuanian law and the courts of the Republic of Lithuania; the business card was still issued by the UK sister company. No notice of a transfer of existing merchants was seen.

m-6dec72b7.t: Adyen has no Cyprus version of its merchant terms. Its general 'Adyen Terms and Conditions' (last update 1 November 2023, read 4 October 2026; the only country variant in its legal index is Brazil's) supplement a separate 'Merchant Agreement' with the merchant. The contracting party is Adyen N.V. (Dutch Chamber of Commerce no. 34259528) 'and/or where relevant, one or more of its local affiliates'. The agreement is governed solely by Dutch law; disputes not settled amicably within thirty days go to ICC arbitration seated in Amsterdam, in English. A Cyprus merchant taken on directly would therefore contract under Dutch law with arbitration in Amsterdam, unless its own agreement says otherwise.

m-504b0b5f.t: Under SumUp's Payment Terms for Cyprus (effective 07/02/2022, read 4 October 2026) the merchant bears chargebacks: a payment may be charged back to the account if it is disputed or reversed by the card network, a partner institution or the cardholder, was not authorised, or SumUp has reason to believe it unauthorised, illegal or suspicious. The merchant must help investigate at its own expense and supply documents within ten business days; if the dispute is not resolved in its favour SumUp collects the original amount plus fees (section 16). Refunds through the account are accepted up to thirty days after the payment (section 17).

m-2be02f6c.t: PayPal's user agreement for Cyprus (last updated 7 September 2026) lets it place a reserve on an account 'at any time' if it sees high risk. It names two kinds: a rolling reserve, a percentage of each day's receipts held and released on a schedule, and a minimum reserve, a fixed amount kept in the balance, taken upfront or built from sales. The only figures are an example: 'your reserve could be set at 10% and held for a 90-day rolling period'. The actual terms come by notice. Separately PayPal may hold individual payments, and after restricted activity may hold funds 'for more than 180 days if so required'. The same example is in the versions effective 16 June 2020 and 1 August 2022.

m-1bcf1163.t: A merchant that integrates Google Pay online accepts Google's terms directly, but they are interface terms, not acquiring terms. The Google Pay API Terms of Service (effective 1 March 2021, read 4 October 2026) form 'a binding agreement between Google LLC' and the merchant, say that Google 'only enables transactions through the sharing of payment credentials' and 'is not a party to these transactions', and leave acquiring to the merchant: 'You are solely responsible for the establishment of a payment card acquiring agreement with a card acquiring bank (and all fees, charges and expenses arising from that relationship)'. No surcharge or purchase limit specific to Google Pay users is allowed.

m-1738e1fa.t: Viva's terms (effective 30 September 2026, read 4 October 2026) give no reserve percentage or period: a 'Rolling Reserve' is 'calculated as a percentage of the transactions value' and released at the end of a holding period, and Viva may withhold from the available balance or accrue a reserve to secure the user's obligations. The payout schedule may be extended in writing for breach under investigation, blocked amounts, or high-risk transactions such as card payments for services delivered later or a high rate of chargebacks and refunds. The terms cover sole traders: they speak of 'any freelancer or legal entity' and of 'any natural person or legal entity' holding a business account.

m-0af5017f.t: A Cyprus merchant's contract with SumUp is with SumUp EU Payments UAB (Lithuania). The General Terms on sumup.com/el-cy (Greek only, 'effective from 07/02/2022', read 4 October 2026) are accepted by ticking a box; the Payment Terms, API licence terms, e-commerce terms and Bookings terms are 'additional terms' forming part of the same agreement. The user confirms being 'an entrepreneur, freelancer or business owner' using the services only professionally, must be at least 18, and may hold one account unless SumUp approves more - so a sole trader is eligible under the terms.

m-fbfdc077.t: The European Commission opened an infringement against Cyprus over investor citizenship on 20 October 2020, holding that granting nationality, and so EU citizenship, for a pre-determined payment without a 'genuine link' breaches sincere cooperation (Art. 4(3) TEU) and undermines EU citizenship. It closed the case on 11 March 2026, per Cyprus's Law Office, after Cyprus amended its law at the Commission's request; Law 224(I)/2025 (Gazette 12 December 2025) deleted s. 111A(2) of the Civil Registry Law, the basis for naturalising investors, keeping the old rules only for applications filed by 30 October 2020.

m-e3ab9d20.t: Per Ant1's report of the plenary of 6 April 2026, rapporteur Kyriakos Hadjiyiannis, proposer of Cyprus's leisure-premises bill, said the Government bill had been withdrawn and the House was asked to vote on a member's bill that regulates many other aspects of these premises, and that once it passed the House could carry on and come back with other provisions if convergences were found. The plenary also passed amendments by Hadjiyiannis and by DIKO leader Nikolas Papadopoulos on the obligations of hotels that operate leisure premises, and rejected an oral DIPA amendment for the Commerce Minister to consult local authorities on opening hours.

m-e26c599b.t: Why Cyprus's 2025 catering and leisure premises bill was withdrawn on 19 March 2026, hours before the plenary vote, by the Deputy Minister of Tourism: Politis wrote that the step 'is attributed' to strong reactions from business people in the sector 'and not only', and to concerns about noise from longer opening hours; no Government statement of the reason was found. The committee version would have let restaurants, taverns, beer houses, music-and-dance venues and discos open until 3:30 a.m. all year, entertainment venues to 5 a.m. by ministerial decree; the committee had examined the bill in ten sessions from 14 October 2025 to 10 March 2026.

m-e1ffa6ad.t: The Government reshaped the 2024 bill cutting Cyprus's beneficial-owner penalties. Per the House Commerce Committee's supplementary report of 19 November 2024, the Ministries of Finance and Commerce asked to raise the proposed cap for companies from €2,000 to €5,000, to let the Registrar strike off non-filers as under s. 327 of the Companies Law and to collect charges as court fines, and said the Registrar would revoke charges already imposed and extend the deadline. The law published 6 December 2024 has the €5,000 cap and strike-off. In the first report (8 November 2024) the Ministry of Finance said the Tax Commissioner had lifted his objection to striking off 20,000 dormant companies.

m-dd7e73fd.t: Why the House would not wait for the Registrar's new IT system before capping Cyprus's annual-return late charge at €150 (Law 18(I)/2024): per the House Commerce Committee's report of 13 February 2024, members said the charge applies flatly to all businesses regardless of size, which may discriminate against small businesses, and that the rules need revision 'immediately and not at a later time', when the new system (due 'around the end of 2025') comes in. The same report records the Ministry of Commerce's representative acknowledging that late filing is linked to the difficulty of filing audited accounts together with the return. The committee reserved its position for the plenary.

m-d3818ecd.t: The Central Bank of Cyprus circular of 2 November 2018 on shell companies (ref. BS 6020), sent to all credit, payment and e-money institutions and revising one of 14 June 2018, states no reason: it gives a definition, tells them to avoid such entities in listed cases and to revise their acceptance policies 'with immediate effect'. MONEYVAL's 2019 evaluation gives no reason either; it lists the Bank's guidance on shell companies and tax evasion among initiatives that 'specifically addressed the particular risks faced by Cyprus', and observed that since the circular banks 'have become aggressive' in asking the purpose of legal entities lacking a clear physical presence in Cyprus.

m-bc98a14f.t: The €150 cap on the late charge for a Cyprus company's annual return (Law 18(I)/2024) was a private bill of five MPs, passed on 15 February 2024 over the Government's objection. Per the House Commerce Committee's report of 13 February 2024, the proposers said many small and medium firms file late because the audited accounts due with the return are often not ready in time. The Ministry of Commerce wanted the €500 cap kept because it builds 'a culture of compliance' and keeps the register reliable - late filings had fallen 'significantly' since the charge began - and said a cut was not compatible with the Registrar's IT system; the Ministry of Finance agreed that €150 may not deter.

m-bb409341.t: Law 35(I)/2025 (Gazette of 11 April 2025, a private bill of six MPs, two tabling for the DIKO and DISY groups) exempted payments by casino customers from Cyprus's €10,000 cash cap of 31 December 2024. Its preamble says the immediate cap put the licensed casino at a competitive disadvantage to casinos outside the Republic's jurisdiction and control and hit it disproportionately because its business uses very much cash. Per the committee report of 24 March 2025, the operator said 94% of its transactions were in cash; the Ministry of Finance would accept it only as transitional, until 10 July 2027, but the text sets no end date; the Tax Commissioner opposed it in principle.

m-99bd167d.t: Cyprus's Startup Visa Practical Guide (Deputy Ministry of Research, Innovation and Digital Policy, dated December 2024) states the scheme's goal as 'the creation of new jobs, the promotion of innovation and research, the development of the business ecosystem and consequently the economic development of the country', for talented third-country entrepreneurs setting up high-growth innovative startups, and places it within the National Policy Statement for the Enhancement of the Entrepreneurial Ecosystem. It says the scheme is valid until December 2026 with up to 150 visas; it gives no reason for the 2024 revision and no count of visas issued.

m-95bc18bb.t: Neither of the Cyprus Registrar of Companies' 2026 strike-off announcements gives a reason. That of 4 September 2026 extends to 31 December 2026 the filing of overdue annual returns and accounts, after reminder letters of 9 February 2026, and warns that strike-off under s. 327 will then continue; that of 30 September 2026 starts in December the strike-off of companies with unpaid annual levy for 2012-2023 under s. 327(2A)(b). Both cite only the Companies Law. The 9 February letters were not published, and the Ministry's Annual Action Plan 2026 has no strike-off item.

m-9257fe40.t: Cyprus's Registrar of Companies told a House committee on 3 July 2025, per a Cyprus News Agency report carried by Nomoplatform, that she asks other services for views on companies with Turkish nationals or Turkish Cypriots among their officers, and gave figures for 2023 to mid-2025: with Turkish nationals 30 registered, 7 rejected, 21 withdrawn 'mainly because of the delay' in the reply and 13 pending; with Turkish Cypriot participation 41 registered, 10 rejected and 16 pending; 20 more with other third-country persons rejected. The Legal Service said a bill to regulate this was under legal vetting; no document read ties it to the bill tabled in September 2026.

m-8e85e2fe.t: The House Finance Committee's report on the 2025 tax bills records reservations, not saying by whom, on the 15% corporate rate and the Tax Commissioner's new powers (closing a company and sealing its premises, refusing for tax purposes a change of directors while tax is owed, collecting disputed tax), and on constitutionality, proportionality and legal certainty. Revised texts of 9 and 12 December 2025, among other changes, lowered proposed penalties, gave a company 60 days from incorporation to register for tax, dropped a monthly employer return and dropped a director's criminal liability where his company is officer of another company that offends.

m-8ab822e3.t: Why Cyprus re-legislated rules on payments to blacklisted and low-tax jurisdictions (Laws 47(I)-49(I)/2025, Gazette 16 April 2025). Per the House Finance Committee's report of 8 April 2025, checking recovery-plan milestone 209 (legislated Q4 2021), the Commission found exceptions for certain payments, so aggressive tax planning was not effectively tackled; per the Ministry, the Commission said that the withheld sum would be paid only if the bills were in force before 14 May 2025. The Finance Minister's memo to the House, per the Cyprus Mail, put the sum at €43 million of €150 million. On 13 July 2026 the Commission found milestone 210 fulfilled on them and Law 245(I)/2025 (preliminary).

m-8a9019bc.t: Law 2(I)/2026 (Gazette 6 February 2026), letting small Cyprus companies report under a national small-entity standard instead of IFRS, began as a private bill of MPs Kyriakos Hadjiyiannis and Nikos Sykas tabled 23 October 2025, passed 22 January 2026. Its memorandum cites the 'disproportionate administrative burden' of meeting IFRS for audited statements, 'difficult and costly' for small firms, and the small-business-first principle of Directive 2013/34/EU; it gives no reason for the review limit. The standard part starts on 1 January of the year after the standard is published in the Gazette; only art. 5 (review limit raised from €200,000 to €300,000 turnover) applied on publication.

m-866b4aed.t: A second account of why Cyprus's catering and leisure premises bill was withdrawn on 19 March 2026: on Alpha TV (reported 20 March 2026) MP Alekos Tryfonides said a letter from the Deputy Minister of Tourism to the House leaders' conference asked to send the bill back to committee because the Deputy Ministry wanted corrections, having brought 'bill A' that 'ended up Z'; as House rules do not allow that, the Speaker offered debate or withdrawal, and withdrawal followed. Fanos Leventis, secretary-general of the leisure-centre owners' association, backed the committee text and called the withdrawal unacceptable.

m-7e05c938.t: Cyprus ended its investment citizenship programme by Council of Ministers decision 90.177 of 13 October 2020, effective 1 November 2020, 'taking into account the long-standing weaknesses, but also the abusive exploitation' of its provisions; applications filed by 30 October 2020 were still to be examined under it. The decision adds that, once the Attorney General's inquiry committee reported, the Government would review its whole policy for attracting foreign investment.

m-7071c987.t: The reasons in the preamble of Cyprus's casino exemption from the €10,000 cash cap (Law 35(I)/2025) were written in at the Legal Service's request. Per the House Institutions Committee's report of 24 March 2025, the Legal Service said that, since Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 applies from 10 July 2027, exempting casino customers until then must be 'adequately justified' by a preamble showing that proportionality is respected and that the aim will not harm the fight against money laundering; the committee by majority adopted the preamble wording proposed by MP Marinos Mousiouttas; AKEL and one independent member opposed the bill.

m-6cecc201.t: Cyprus's legal basis for forming a company online, Law 151(I)/2023 (Gazette 19 December 2023), was adopted to transpose Directive (EU) 2019/1151 on digital tools in company law, per the House Commerce Committee's report of 6 December 2023. It provides online formation and online registration of a foreign company's branch, free model documents, the Registrar's power to refuse a director disqualified in another member state, and electronic identification of EU citizens using the Registrar's online services. The committee was concerned that some mandatory provisions were left out; the Registrar's department and the Legal Service said the Registrar already complies in practice.

m-5d65862b.t: The only stated reason in Cyprus's 2026 member's bill on catering and leisure premises is one sentence of its explanatory memorandum, signed by MP Kyriakos Hadjiyiannis (Famagusta): the bill's purpose is new legislation on setting up and running leisure premises and the repeal of the Catering Establishments Law, and the provisions 'are deemed necessary so that the existing legislative framework governing leisure premises is modernised'. The memorandum gives no figure, names no study and does not mention the Government bill withdrawn on 19 March 2026.

m-5d04a559.t: The cut in Cyprus's penalties for not filing beneficial owners (Law 141(I)/2024) began as a private bill of four MPs tabled on 14 March 2024, after the House Commerce Committee's own-initiative debate on companies' problems with the Registrar's beneficial-owner filing method; the memorandum calls the €100 daily charge 'disproportionately high'. Per the committee's report of 8 November 2024, the Registrar of Companies opposed it: the charges had produced 'high rates of compliance', filing costs nothing if done on time, and any reduction 'may harm the credibility of the Republic as regards transparency'; the Ministry of Commerce, CySEC, the Central Bank and the banks' association agreed.

m-4f54f151.t: The two main laws of Cyprus's 2026 tax reform carry their own statement of reasons. Law 244(I)/2025 (income tax) and Law 245(I)/2025 (special defence contribution), both in Gazette No. 5070 of 31 December 2025, open with the same preamble: traditional tax mechanisms 'often prove inadequate'; the reform aims at a fairer system that burdens economic strata proportionally and reduces inequalities; it strengthens competitiveness so that businesses benefit and investment is attracted, and secures effective collection of taxes due. The preamble ends 'For all the above reasons' the House enacts. It names no figure and no external body.

m-48d0c171.t: Why Cyprus merged its local authorities (Municipalities Law 52(I)/2022 and related laws): the Interior Ministry's reform page, written while the bills were before the House (archived 2 July 2022), says the structure of 30 municipalities and 349 communities was 'basically dysfunctional and unusual even internationally', many too small to meet expectations and dependent on the state grant; 121 communities employed no staff and 122 one. It gave as aims administrative and financial autonomy and viability through mergers and savings (it proposed 17 municipalities), five district bodies issuing planning and building permits at one point, and called it a prerequisite for recovery-plan funds.

m-41d31f7e.t: A Cyprus Government bill tabled 17 September 2026 (Companies (Amendment) (No. 2) Law of 2026, pending on 6 October 2026) would let the Registrar strike off a company, or refuse any filing or request under the Companies Law, where its purpose or operation tends to undermine the Republic, national security or public order, 'without any reasoning required', possibly on undisclosable information. The Commerce Ministry's report (21 August 2026) says this rests on classified information from the national-security authority, gives as reason 'the continuing occupation of part of its territory' (the preamble names the Turkish invasion), and exempts the bill from impact assessment.

m-3f772347.t: The findings of the inquiry into Cyprus's investment citizenship programme, appointed by the Attorney General in 2020 and chaired by former Supreme Court President Myron Nicolatos, came out through the press. Presenting its interim report on 16 April 2021, he said naturalisations issued 'by exceeding the boundaries of the law' were 51.81% of the total, per Al Jazeera, which says the inquiry examined 2,478 passports issued in 2007-2016 plus 417 high-risk ones to 2020; the report was not made public then. Al Jazeera adds that more than 3,000 investors paying at least €2 million received passports in 2013-2019.

m-3df1845f.t: The President of Cyprus referred the €10,000 cash-limit law, passed on 5 December 2024, back to the House on 19 December 2024 (date per Nomoplatform's bill record). Per the Cyprus News Agency report carried by Nomoplatform on 20 December 2024, the referral said that because Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 applies only from 10 July 2027, a limit set 'in application of' the Regulation would not apply at once, so that phrase had to be deleted. The House passed the law again at an extraordinary plenary on 23 December 2024 (bill record); the published Law 172(I)/2024 (31 December 2024) does not mention the Regulation, which shows the referral was accepted.

m-391df36b.t: Cyprus's stamp duty was repealed in full on the House's initiative. The Government's tax-reform bill only proposed to end compulsory stamping except for financial-services contracts, insurance policies and property transfers and leases 'whose value exceeds €50,000'. Per the Finance Committee's report of 18 December 2025, business and professional associations proposed full repeal because it 'is a complicated system that does not reflect modern practices'; the committee did not forward the Government bill and its members tabled a repeal bill, tabled and passed on 22 December 2025 (Law 239(I)/2025, Gazette 31 December 2025, in force 1 January 2026), whose memorandum states only its purpose.

m-37b09664.t: Why Cyprus introduced a national minimum wage from 1 January 2023 (Decree K.D.P. 350/2022): the decree itself states no reason. Announcing the Council of Ministers decision of 31 August 2022, Labour Minister Kyriakos Kousios called it a historic day for the welfare state, said a national minimum wage was being set 'for the first time' and that about 40,000 low-paid workers would benefit, per the public broadcaster RIK.

m-317e6893.t: Why Cyprus closed its beneficial-owner register to the general public (Law 25(I)/2026, Gazette 20 March 2026): the Finance Minister's letter tabling the bill (19 December 2025) says it transposes Article 74 of Directive (EU) 2024/1640, which aims at compliance with the CJEU's WM and Sovim judgment that unrestricted public access breaches the rights to private life and data protection. An earlier Ministry bill to comply with the judgment went to consultation in the second half of 2024; diverging views and legal complexity led to a bill limited to Article 74. On 24 September 2025 the Commission had sent a letter of formal notice for non-notification after the 10 July 2025 deadline.

m-311305ec.t: Why Cyprus proposed to replace the 1985 law on catering and leisure premises: the Ministry of Energy, Commerce and Industry's introductory report to the House (2 October 2025), on a Deputy Ministry of Tourism bill approved by the Council of Ministers on 3 September 2025, says it addresses 'the gaps and weaknesses' of the framework to modernise and improve the competitiveness of the tourism product in catering, and removes 'burdensome and anachronistic provisions'. It would have ended unnecessary strict building and equipment criteria, classes and price-list approval, and set hours by category 'with the further aim of tackling noise pollution'. Withdrawn 19 March 2026; never enacted.

m-25057be2.t: Cyprus's House rejected an attempt to bring back an annual company levy on 22 December 2025 (17 for, 32 against, per Nomoplatform). AKEL's bill (tabled 4 December 2025) would have charged every registered company with total assets of €1-2 million €350 a year, rising to €1,250 above €20 million. Its memorandum gives as reasons a 'fair, proportional and graduated' levy, significant public revenue for fiscal stability and support for vulnerable groups, and says SMEs are exempt - though the text spares only companies with under €1 million in assets. The flat €350 levy had been abolished from 1 January 2024 (Law 25(I)/2024).

m-236795c7.t: Why the Cyprus Government opposed bringing back an annual company levy: at the House Finance Committee on 18 December 2025 the Ministry of Finance said the levy had been among the University of Cyprus economics research centre's recommendations and was not adopted because, after the recent abolition of annual fees, reintroducing them so soon 'would be inappropriate and would create an image of uncertainty, instability and unreliability' in the business environment. The Registrar of Companies agreed, adding that with corporate tax rising to 15% a non-targeted fee offers no added return; the Cyprus Bar Association's representative also disagreed.

m-2130d204.t: Cyprus's €10,000 cap on cash payments for goods and services (Law 172(I)/2024, in force 31 December 2024) was a private member's bill of DISY MP Dimitris Dimitriou, not a Government bill; its memorandum presents it as applying Regulation (EU) 2024/1624.
