Per the House Institutions Committee's report of 3 December 2024, he argued that although the Regulation applies only in 2027 its limit should apply 'as soon as possible' to curb suspicious transactions and money laundering; the Tax Commissioner asked for a phased reduction to €10,000 and for imprisonment, and the Financial Intelligence Unit said it could not receive reports of over-limit bank payments before 2027.

m-0b2933ca.t: At the House Finance Committee (ten sessions, 7 November - 18 December 2025) the Finance Minister said the 2026 tax reform rests on the University of Cyprus Economics Research Centre study and an independent expert's study under the recovery-plan milestone on aggressive tax planning, and aims mainly at a fairer distribution and reduction of the tax burden, support for families, a broader base, competitiveness, compliance, less evasion and shadow economy, maintaining and strengthening the foreign-investment regime and sustainable public finances under the EU's new governance framework, among others. The Tax Commissioner said it would broaden the base, raise collection and fight evasion.

m-007ba950.t: The first cut of Cyprus's annual-return late charge, Law 87(I)/2022 (Gazette 24 June 2022), came from a private bill of three MPs tabled on 27 January 2022, whose memorandum cited small and medium companies' inability to pay the charges in the COVID-19 downturn. Per the House Commerce Committee's report of 6 June 2022, the Ministry of Finance expressed reservations, saying the charge was meant to deter money laundering by companies operating in Cyprus, and the Registrar produced data that it improved compliance; after officials met business bodies, the cap was cut to €150 only for returns made up in 2021-2022, until 31 December 2024, with refunds of any excess.

m-f88dc152.t: Cyprus's Fiscal Council, an independent body, described the rise of the corporate tax rate from 12.5% to 15% in other terms than the Government. Its note of August 2025 says the rise, like the green taxes, 'should be regarded as exogenously given' and 'largely abolishes Cyprus's tax competition with other destinations', yet 'cannot be judged undesirable': it answers 'pressures and risks' against the economy and threats 'related also to the country's reputation', and the 'adverse selection' that has become inherent in foreign direct investment in Cyprus. It calls the whole exercise limited to an 'accounting' approach. It gives no figure on the rate.

m-eda408f7.t: Part of Cyprus's 2026 tax reform answers a recovery-plan milestone. The Ministry of Finance's introductory report on the income tax bill (30 October 2025) says the bill includes provisions resulting from an independent study under milestone 211 of reform 10 (combating aggressive tax planning) of the Recovery and Resilience Plan, and that provisions found to lead to aggressive tax planning must be amended or repealed in the first half of 2026; it put the milestone in the 10th instalment of €190 million. The Council annexes amended on 3 July and 20 August 2026 set milestone 211 for Q2 2026 and place it in the ninth and last non-repayable instalment, of €265,772,568.

m-98bc7785.t: Cyprus's 2025 catering-premises bill (withdrawn 19 March 2026) provided for unlicensed premises. Article 14 as tabled gave premises that 'demonstrably operated' as a leisure centre without a licence under the 1985 laws 18 months from the law's start to obtain one, and premises opening later without a licence 18 months from opening, if a planning-permit application and a designer's declaration were filed. On the 2023 draft, which allowed three years, the Police called three years excessive, asked for one year and for deleting the clause on premises opening later unlicensed; the Ministry of Interior also found the period too long. The pack shows no legible count of unlicensed premises.

m-7e42c5a7.t: The Government's stated reason for abolishing Cyprus's €350 annual company levy (Law 25(I)/2024, published 15 March 2024, deemed in force from 1 January 2024) is in the Ministry of Energy, Commerce and Industry's introductory report to the House of 27 February 2024: within 'targeted measures' decided by the Government to strengthen businesses' competitiveness and to meet the challenges they face, it was decided to give them 'additional relief and support' by abolishing the levy. The attached impact-assessment questionnaire adds that the levy had been imposed to deal with the fiscal and economic crisis, as a fiscal-consolidation measure. The pack states no revenue figure.

m-78039fdd.t: Cyprus's incorporation test for corporate tax residence and its withholding tax and non-deductibility rules on payments to blacklisted and low-tax jurisdictions are recovery-plan commitments. The July 2021 annex to the Council Implementing Decision sets milestone 209 for Q4 2022 (withholding tax on payments to EU-listed non-cooperative jurisdictions and 'a further corporate tax residency test based on the incorporation of each entity') and milestone 210 for Q4 2024 (low-tax jurisdictions). Its stated objective: a more effective, efficient and fair tax system 'by combatting tax evasion and aggressive tax planning by Multinational Enterprises'.

m-6330ae5f.t: Why Cyprus cut the special defence contribution on bank interest from 30% to 17% (Law 157(I)/2023, from 1 January 2024): the Ministry of Finance's impact-assessment questionnaire on the bill says the need arises 'because of the low deposit rates offered by credit institutions (despite the rise in lending rates)'. Its introductory report of 18 September 2023 says the cut will raise households' disposable income, strengthen investment, encourage saving and indirectly help consolidate confidence in the banking system. The questionnaire puts the yearly fiscal effect at €16 million. The Council of Ministers approved the bill on 13 September 2023.

m-274bf722.t: The Ministry of Finance's reasons for Cyprus's 2026 tax reform, in its introductory report (30 October 2025) and impact questionnaire on the income tax bill: the aim is 'a fairer tax system' that burdens economic strata proportionally and reduces inequalities; the last broad reform was in 2002, for EU harmonisation, and since then the environment 'has changed radically', so 'an integrated tax transformation' is required; economic and social bodies had called for reform as more than 23 years had passed; it was in the President's election programme. The framework draws on a University of Cyprus Economics Research Centre study. It expects a neutral effect on businesses on average.

m-0feb025e.t: Cyprus's Finance Minister gave separate reasons for the two company-side changes of the 2026 tax reform in his budget speech to the House, published 4 December 2025. Deemed dividend distribution is abolished and the contribution on actual dividends cut from 17% to 5% to 'correct distortions of the tax system' and encourage reinvestment of profits in productive investment. The corporate tax rate is 'readjusted to 15%' as part of the Government's 'political will to strengthen the international credibility and reputation of our country', 'in alignment with international standards', without harm to competitiveness 'as the results of the economic analysis also show'. He cited no figure.

m-f3de8413.t: Amendment No. 1 to the Fourth Issue of the Central Bank of Cyprus AML directive (circular letter SD 6020) took effect on 7 April 2016, on publication on the Bank's website. It added para 76A (audited accounts, or management accounts, from customers); paras 85A-86E on customers introduced by third parties (reliance only at the outset; a meeting with the beneficial owners within three months, in person or online with recording; termination if it cannot be held; a scorecard and register of introducers); and paras 128A-128B (a face-to-face meeting within three months for non-face-to-face customers with account debits or credits above EUR 100,000 a year). It was revoked in February 2019.

m-8e4e41e2.t: The Fourth Issue of the Central Bank of Cyprus AML directive to credit institutions (December 2013, issued under art. 59(4) of Law 188(I)/2007) is still on the Bank's server (118 pages, file last modified 28 May 2015). Its para 228 repealed the Directive of April 2008 (Third Issue) and its amendments. It has no shell-company rule: 'shell' occurs for shell banks and once in a typology appendix. It was amended by Amendment No. 1 of 7 April 2016, also on the Bank's server. The Fifth Edition of February 2019 revoked it 'and its subsequent amendments' (para 322) without listing them; whether a further amendment followed in 2016-2018 was not established.

m-ff1dc5b4.t: The EU list of high-risk third countries in force on 4 October 2026 (Delegated Regulation (EU) 2016/1675, consolidated version of 29 January 2026) names 26 jurisdictions. Part I (action plan with FATF): Afghanistan, Algeria, Angola, Bolivia, British Virgin Islands, Cameroon, Cote d'Ivoire, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Haiti, Kenya, Laos, Lebanon, Monaco, Myanmar, Namibia, Nepal, South Sudan, Syria, Trinidad and Tobago, Vanuatu, Venezuela, Vietnam, Yemen. Part II: Iran. Part III: North Korea. Part IV: Russian Federation. CELLAR lists 13 amending acts, the last two being Delegated Regulations (EU) 2026/46 and 2026/83, both published on 9 January 2026.

m-feac3e63.t: The Central Bank of Cyprus built its account register before the law that names it. Its Annual Report 2019 lists, among systems developed during 2019, 'the centralised bank accounts and payments register to enhance anti-money laundering' (section 4.10.1); the statutory basis, art. 61Δ of Law 188(I)/2007, came with Law 13(I)/2021 on 23 February 2021. MOKAS's Annual Report 2022 says its staff 'have access to databases, central registries (such as, Bank account Registry and Ultimate Beneficial Owner Registry)'. No Central Bank announcement of a go-live date and no gazetted directive on reporting to the register were found (4 October 2026); art. 61Δ(1) rests reporting on art. 59(9).

m-f2251c88.t: 'Cyprus Confidential': ICIJ and partner media published the investigation on 14 November 2023. On Thursday 16 November 2023 the Central Bank of Cyprus issued an 'Announcement … regarding recent reports in the Media': it 'took note' of the reports, said it 'is currently also examining the alleged wrongdoings included in the recent reports, to the extent they relate to credit institutions', and set out its record (42,728 shell-company relationships terminated and 125,782 accounts closed since end-2018; AML/CFT headcount up 50% by 2022). The text does not name the investigation. Press reported on 1 December 2023 that 24 FBI and FinCEN specialists would assist Cypriot authorities.

m-ef256771.t: Shell companies: on 2 November 2018 the Central Bank of Cyprus sent a circular (ref. BS 6020), effective at once, to all credit, payment and e-money institutions, after a first one of 14 June 2018. A shell company has no physical presence and no established economic activity in its country of incorporation (holding shares or assets may count as activity). Relationships 'shall be avoided' if it also is registered where audited accounts are not required and prepares none voluntarily, and/or is tax resident in an EU- or OECD-blacklisted jurisdiction or nowhere; otherwise the institution decides on a documented risk basis. The CBC's February 2019 AML directive revoked it and absorbed its rules.

m-e774503c.t: Cyprus Law 188(I)/2007 art. 64 requires enhanced due diligence for business with high-risk third countries, for cross-border correspondent relationships and for politically exposed persons. For a PEP - and for close relatives and known close associates - the obliged entity must obtain senior-management approval to establish or continue the relationship, take adequate measures to establish the source of wealth and source of funds, and conduct enhanced ongoing monitoring (art. 64(1)(c)). Art. 63 allows simplified measures only after the entity has satisfied itself that the relationship is lower-risk and there is no suspicion. In force on 4 October 2026.

m-da23a4af.t: On 4 October 2026 the narrative text of the Central Bank of Cyprus' English AML page still presents 'the 5th Edition' as 'the CBC AML/CFT Directive', although the same page links the 2025 Directive and K.D.P. 120/2025 para 73 repealed the February 2019 text with effect from 2 June 2025; the law linked there is a 2007-2021 consolidation. A reader of the page text alone would take the repealed edition as current. Method trap: the URL of the 2025 translation contains a non-breaking space before '.pdf'; the same URL without it returns HTTP 200 with an HTML page instead of the PDF, so a status code does not prove the document was fetched.

m-d2e0588a.t: MONEYVAL follow-up of Cyprus: follow-up reports were adopted in December 2021, November 2022 and December 2023; the 4th (MONEYVAL(2025)2) was adopted by written procedure on 12 May 2025, not at a plenary. It re-rated R.13 (correspondent banking) to LC, leaving 38 recommendations at C or LC and two (R.8, R.31) at PC. The report exists in two editions at one address: the PDF archived on 19 June 2025 says Cyprus 'will remain in enhanced follow-up' and report back in two years; the PDF created on 27 June 2025 (archived 8 December 2025) says the sixth-round on-site visit 'will take place in October 2028' and Cyprus 'will no longer be subject to the fifth-round follow-up process'.

m-d1b2500c.t: No official count of the shell-company closures of 2018-2020 was found beyond the Central Bank of Cyprus total of 16 November 2023 (42,728 companies and 125,782 accounts from end-2018 to that date, no yearly breakdown, no counting method), as of 4 October 2026: the Bank's annual reports for 2018, 2019 and 2020 do not contain the word 'shell', and MONEYVAL's report adopted in December 2019 says only that understanding of risk 'has been increased by the closure by banks of a significant number of business relationships, including relationships with shell companies' (para 471). The 2023 statement answers 'recent reports in international and local Media' and names no investigation.

m-c9e32f21.t: Law 13(I)/2021 (5AMLD transposition, 23 February 2021) inserted art. 61Δ into Cyprus Law 188(I)/2007, creating a Central Register of Bank Accounts, Payment Accounts and Safe Deposit Boxes kept electronically by the Central Bank of Cyprus. Institutions supervised by the CBC supply, for every IBAN-identified bank or payment account and every safe-deposit box, the identification data of the holder, of any person acting for the holder and of the beneficial owner, the IBAN and the dates of opening and closing. MOKAS, the Police, the Tax Department and the Customs Department may search it directly. In force on 4 October 2026; the date the register became operational was not established.

m-c4d46fea.t: The Central Bank of Cyprus' AML directive in force on 4 October 2026 is the Prevention of Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Directive of 2025, issued under art. 59(4) of Law 188(I)/2007 and published as K.D.P. 120/2025 in Official Gazette no. 5943 of 2 May 2025; under its para 75 it entered into force one month after publication, i.e. on 2 June 2025. It binds credit institutions, electronic money institutions, payment institutions, bureaux de change, financial leasing companies, credit servicers and other CBC-supervised persons (para 3). It repealed the February 2019 'Directive to credit institutions' (Fifth Edition) and the 2009 Money Transfer Business directive (para 73).

m-c49b5660.t: Cash limit, legislative dates: Law 172(I)/2024 (AML (Amendment) (No. 3) Law of 2024), which caps cash payments for goods and services in Cyprus at €10,000, was published in the Official Gazette No. 5022 on 31 December 2024 and took effect on publication. The House first passed it on 5 December 2024 and, after a presidential referral, re-adopted it on 23 December 2024 (the two vote dates are from press).

m-b73db9d1.t: Two reshuffles of the EU high-risk third-country list changed whose residents, as customer or beneficial owner, trigger enhanced due diligence at a Cyprus bank. Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/1184 of 10 June 2025 (OJ 16 July 2025, in force 5 August 2025) added Algeria, Angola, Cote d'Ivoire, Kenya, Laos, Lebanon, Monaco, Namibia, Nepal and Venezuela and removed Barbados, Gibraltar, Jamaica, Panama, the Philippines, Senegal, Uganda and the United Arab Emirates. Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/83 of 4 December 2025 (OJ 9 January 2026, in force 29 January 2026) added Bolivia and the British Virgin Islands and removed Burkina Faso, Mali, Mozambique, Nigeria, South Africa and Tanzania.

m-b3ccbc5f.t: The Central Bank of Cyprus' press release of 2 May 2025 on the AML Directive of 2025 (K.D.P. 120/2025) lists what changed for customers: review frequency follows each customer's risk, with no minimum frequency set for low-risk customers; a copy of the identity document suffices at an update; information gathered during the relationship may be reused; alternative evidence is allowed for people unable to respond for health reasons; the address may be proved with government documents or electronic utility bills; and documents may be certified by third parties such as state services. The CBC adds that the strictness of the Directive 'remains unchanged' and that it takes effect on 2 June 2025.

m-a7d70314.t: MONEYVAL fifth-round mutual evaluation of Cyprus: on-site visit 13-24 May 2019; report (MONEYVAL(2019)27) adopted at the 59th Plenary (Strasbourg, 2-6 December 2019), Cyprus placed in enhanced follow-up and asked to report back at the first Plenary of 2021; published 12 February 2020. Ratings at adoption: effectiveness 'substantial' on 3 of 11 immediate outcomes (IO.1, IO.2, IO.9) and 'moderate' on the other 8; technical compliance 16 C, 21 LC, 3 PC (R.8, R.13, R.31), none NC. December 2019 is the adoption date and February 2020 the publication date.

m-a5b0db20.t: Cyprus transposed the EU anti-money-laundering directives by amending Law 188(I)/2007, each time after the EU deadline: Directive (EU) 2015/849 (4AMLD, deadline 26 June 2017) by Law 13(I)/2018 (Gazette 3 April 2018), completed by Law 81(I)/2019 (31 May 2019) 'for more correct harmonisation' with listed articles; Directive (EU) 2018/843 (5AMLD, deadline 10 January 2020) by Law 13(I)/2021 (23 February 2021); Directive (EU) 2018/1673 on combating money laundering by criminal law (deadline 3 December 2020; informally '6AMLD', a label now also used for Directive (EU) 2024/1640) by Law 22(I)/2021 (17 March 2021). Each preamble names the directive it harmonises with.

m-a23331dc.t: Russia has been on the EU list of high-risk third countries since 29 January 2026. Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/46 of 3 December 2025 (OJ L, 9 January 2026; in force on the twentieth day after publication) added a point IV to the Annex of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2016/1675 for countries not listed by the FATF 'but whose membership in that international standard-setter is suspended', with the Russian Federation as its only entry. For a Cyprus bank this brings the enhanced due diligence of art. 64(1)(a) of Law 188(I)/2007 for customers resident or established in Russia (CBC Directive of 2025, para 50) and bars reliance on introducers established there (art. 67(2)(b)(i)).

m-9f3db968.t: Cyprus Law 188(I)/2007 art. 62(1) requires the identity of the customer and the beneficial owner to be verified before a business relationship is established or a transaction is carried out. Derogations: verification may be completed during the establishment of the relationship if needed not to interrupt normal business and the risk is low (art. 62(2)); an account may be opened provided no transactions take place until due diligence is complete (art. 62(3)). If due diligence cannot be completed the entity must not transact or open, must terminate, and considers a report to MOKAS (art. 62(4)). Records are kept five years after the relationship ends (art. 68(1)). In force on 4 October 2026.

m-9a9ab4bf.t: Under Cyprus Law 188(I)/2007 a 'high-risk third country' is not only a country on the EU list: art. 2 defines it as a third country identified by the Commission in delegated acts under art. 9(2) of Directive (EU) 2015/849 'and a third country which obliged entities classify as high-risk' under the risk assessment of art. 58A. A bank's own country rating therefore carries the same enhanced measures of art. 64(1)(a) and the same ban on relying on introducers established there (art. 67(2)(b)(i)). Para 50(1) of the Central Bank's Directive of 2025 (K.D.P. 120/2025) adds countries under a FATF call for action. Read in the CyLaw consolidation (amendments to Law 25(I)/2026) on 4 October 2026.

m-8e4abcf2.t: Law 172(I)/2024 (published 31 December 2024; in force on publication) inserted Article 2B into the Cyprus AML Law 188(I)/2007: persons trading in goods or providing services, including the purchase and sale of real estate, may receive or pay cash only up to EUR 10,000, in one or more linked operations; 'cash' includes bearer negotiable instruments, highly liquid commodities and prepaid cards. Exempt: payments between natural persons not acting professionally; payments, deposits and loan repayments at credit institutions, e-money issuers and payment service providers; since Law 35(I)/2025, casino customers. Breach is a crime: fine up to 10% of the cash received and/or up to 5 years in prison.

m-8bab552f.t: The Council of the Cyprus Bar Association is the AML supervisory authority for the professional activities of lawyers and law firms within the meaning of the Advocates Law, and of partnerships whose general partners are lawyers or law firms and their subsidiaries, expressly including the trust and company services to third parties defined in the AML Law (art. 59(1)(ε) of Law 188(I)/2007). A company-formation or nominee service run by a law firm is therefore supervised for AML by the Bar, one run by an accounting firm by ICPAC, and one licensed under Law 196(I)/2012 by CySEC. The second sentence is a reading of art. 59(1)(β)(iii), (δ), (ε) together; consolidated text read on 4 October 2026.

m-8b3726b3.t: FBME Bank, US side: FinCEN found on 15 July 2014 that FBME Bank Ltd was a financial institution of primary money laundering concern under Section 311 of the USA PATRIOT Act; the notice and a proposed rule were published in the Federal Register on 22 July 2014. A first final rule (published 29 July 2015, effective 28 August 2015) was enjoined by the US District Court for the District of Columbia on 27 August 2015 before it took effect. FinCEN replaced it with a final rule published on 31 March 2016 (stated effective date 29 July 2016) barring US financial institutions from opening or maintaining correspondent accounts for FBME; a supplement followed on 1 December 2016 after a court remand.

m-89f7c8ab.t: Under the CBC Directive of 2025 a bank applies specific controls to cash transactions of EUR 10,000 or more - the source and origin of the cash, its purpose and destination, and consistency with the customer's activities and economic profile (para 53) - and is prohibited from accepting cash of EUR 10,000 or more brought in from abroad unless it is accompanied by the customs cash declaration under Regulation (EU) 2018/1672 and Cyprus Law 63(I)/2022; it keeps the original declaration and reports refusals to the Customs and Excise Department (para 54). In force since 2 June 2025.

m-809da571.t: AMLA, the EU Authority for Anti-Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism (Regulation (EU) 2024/1620, applicable in general from 1 July 2025), has had legal existence since 26 June 2024 and started operations in summer 2025. On 4 October 2026 it directly supervises no entity: under art. 13(4) the first selection must begin by 1 July 2027 and direct supervision starts six months after the list is published — AMLA's own timeline says 40 entities are selected during 2027 and direct supervision starts during 2028. Until then, and afterwards for every non-selected firm, a Cyprus bank, payment or e-money institution stays under the Central Bank of Cyprus for AML supervision.

m-7f659199.t: No Cyprus measure transposing arts. 11, 12, 13 and 15 of Directive (EU) 2024/1640 (deadline 10 July 2026) was found on 4 October 2026. The EU's register of national transposition measures holds two Cyprus entries for the Directive: the Protection of Persons Reporting Breaches of Union and National Law (Amendment) (No. 2) Law of 2025 (dated 12 December 2025) and the Prevention and Suppression of Money Laundering Activities (Amendment) Law of 2026 (20 March 2026, i.e. Law 25(I)/2026, whose preamble cites art. 74 only). The CyLaw index of Law 188(I)/2007 ends with Law 25(I)/2026, and the CyLaw list of 2026 laws, which runs to Law 125(I)/2026, contains no other amendment of it.

m-7e51e657.t: Before 2 June 2025 Cyprus banks followed the CBC 'Directive to credit institutions' of February 2019 (Fifth Edition), with its later amendments, issued under art. 59(4) of Law 188(I)/2007 after the 4AMLD transposition. Its para 322 revoked the Fourth Edition of December 2013 with its amendments and the CBC circular letter of 2 November 2018 entitled 'Shell companies/entities'; its paras 151-154 carry a shell-company definition and prohibition (that they reproduce the circular is an inference: the circular text was not obtained). The 2019 text was addressed to credit institutions only; the 2025 directive that replaced it is addressed to all CBC-supervised obliged entities.

m-7cfb5ab0.t: Cyprus's anti-money-laundering statute is the Prevention and Suppression of Money Laundering Activities Law 188(I)/2007, in force since 1 January 2008 (art. 79). As of 4 October 2026 the CyLaw index lists 20 amending laws, all incorporated in the consolidated text, the latest being Law 25(I)/2026 (Official Gazette, 20 March 2026). Customer due diligence is in arts. 60-68, the beneficial-owner definition in art. 2, and the Central Bank of Cyprus issues its binding directive under art. 59(4).

m-70a7824e.t: FBME Bank: the Central Bank of Cyprus announced on 22 December 2015 that the licence granted on 8 September 2003 to FBME Bank Ltd (Tanzania) to operate a branch in Cyprus was revoked as of 21 December 2015 - the revocation date and the announcement date differ by one day. Earlier steps, per CBC announcements: on 21 July 2014 the Resolution Authority placed the Cyprus branch under resolution by decree, with the stated aim of selling its operations, and appointed a special administrator; the branch's obligations were suspended for two working days from 12 noon on 23 July 2014, extended on 25 July 2014. The CBC texts do not mention the US FinCEN finding of 15 July 2014 that preceded them.

m-6b716c6f.t: Under art. 60 of Cyprus Law 188(I)/2007 an obliged entity applies customer due diligence when it establishes a business relationship, carries out an occasional transaction of EUR 15,000 or more (single or linked operations) or a transfer of funds above EUR 1,000, suspects money laundering regardless of amount, or doubts earlier identification data. Art. 61(1) lists the measures: identify and verify the customer; identify the beneficial owner and understand the ownership and control structure; assess the purpose and intended nature of the relationship; and monitor it continuously, including the source of funds where needed. In force on 4 October 2026.

m-596222b9.t: 5AMLD transposition: Law 13(I)/2021 amending the Prevention and Suppression of Money Laundering Activities Laws was published in the Official Gazette No. 4809 on 23 February 2021, to harmonise with Directive (EU) 2018/843, whose deadline was 10 January 2020 - about 13 months late; having no commencement clause, it took effect on publication. Its section 21 replaced section 61A (first inserted by Law 13(I)/2018, which left the register to Regulations): the central register of beneficial owners is kept by the Registrar of Companies, who sets its details by binding Directives, and, as enacted, the public may see an owner's name, birth month and year, nationality, residence country and interest.

m-47fc665e.t: MONEYVAL's fifth-round report on Cyprus (MONEYVAL(2019)27, adopted December 2019) on the banking clean-up: total assets of Cypriot banks fell from EUR 122.9 billion in 2012 to EUR 60.5 billion in 2018; banks' reliance on introducers fell from 1,880 business relationships in 2014 to 1,015 in 2018 (-46%), and 13 of 34 banks still relied on them for due diligence; authorities estimated that 20 to 30% of Cyprus-registered legal persons were owned or controlled by non-residents - an estimate built on Central Bank data on non-resident beneficial owners' share of deposits, which leaves out companies banking abroad and is, the report says, 'likely to be higher'. It gives no count of closed accounts.

m-465324c9.t: Cyprus Law 188(I)/2007 art. 2(1) defines 'politically exposed persons' as a natural person who is or has been entrusted with a prominent public function 'in the Republic or in another country', an immediate close relative, and a person known as a close associate - so domestic office-holders are covered. The listed functions include heads of state and government, ministers, members of parliament, governing bodies of political parties, senior judges, central-bank boards, boards of state enterprises and mayors; middle and junior officials are excluded. After the person leaves office the risk is considered for at least 12 months (art. 64(1)(c) proviso). In force on 4 October 2026.

m-39bf01cd.t: Art. 2(1) of Cyprus Law 188(I)/2007 defines the beneficial owner of a legal person as the natural person who ultimately owns or controls it through a sufficient percentage of shares, voting rights or ownership interest, or by other means; companies listed on a regulated market are excepted. A holding of 25% plus one share, or an ownership interest above 25%, held directly or indirectly, is an 'indication' of ownership. Only if all possible means are exhausted, there are no grounds for suspicion and nobody is identified - or the person identified is in doubt - is the senior managing official treated as beneficial owner. In force on 4 October 2026; the 2024-2026 amendments did not touch it.

m-38face7d.t: MOKAS, the Cyprus financial intelligence unit, is the 'Unit for Combating Money Laundering and Financial Intelligence Unit' established by art. 54 of the AML Law 188(I)/2007. It is composed of representatives of the Attorney General, the Chief of Police and the Director of Customs, is headed by the Attorney General's representative, and under art. 55 is operationally independent. It receives suspicious transaction reports from obliged entities; it does not license or supervise firms — supervision belongs to the authorities listed in art. 59. Consolidated text read on 4 October 2026 (amended up to Law 25(I)/2026).

m-373dcd67.t: Art. 61Δ of Cyprus Law 188(I)/2007 (in force 4 October 2026) is silent on telling an account holder that the Central Register of Bank Accounts was searched: no duty to notify and, unlike arts. 61A(7) and 61B(7) on the beneficial-owner registers, no 'without notification' clause. Its safeguard is a log: the Central Bank records every access (date and time, data used, authority, user), has it checked by its data protection officer, gives it to the data protection Commissioner on request and deletes entries after five years unless an audit is under way (61Δ(5), added by Law 40(I)/2022). For the National Sanctions Implementation Unit, Law 150(I)/2025 s. 18(d) rules out notifying the holder.

m-35d9e111.t: 4AMLD transposition, first step: Law 13(I)/2018 amending the Prevention and Suppression of Money Laundering Activities Laws was published in the Official Gazette No. 4645 on Tuesday 3 April 2018, to harmonise with Directive (EU) 2015/849, whose deadline was 26 June 2017 - about nine months late. Having no commencement clause, it took effect on publication (Constitution, Art. 82). It renamed the regulated persons 'obliged entities' and inserted sections 61A and 61B on beneficial-owner information, leaving the central register's details to Regulations. The Central Bank of Cyprus states that the Directive was transposed by this law together with Law 81(I)/2019, enacted 31 May 2019.

m-32aa6806.t: Pattern in the Cyprus timeline 2021–2026 (checked 2026-10-04): the date in circulation is often not the date the rule or deal took effect. Cases: UBO filing deadline (cited 31 March 2024; extended to 31 January 2025, penalties from 1 February 2025); cash limit (first vote 5 December 2024; re-adopted 23 December after a presidential referral; published and in force 31 December 2024); instant payments (9 January 2025 was the duty to receive, sending 9 October 2025); Hellenic–Eurobank Cyprus (announced 29 August 2025; transfer 1 September; renamed 2 September); Alpha–AstroBank (announced 3 November 2025; effective 31 October); PSD3/PSR (provisional agreement 27 November 2025 is not adoption).

m-2ad7d98f.t: The terms of search of Cyprus's Central Register of Bank Accounts, Payment Accounts and Safe Deposit Boxes changed in 2022, the list of authorities in 2025. As enacted by Law 13(I)/2021 (23 February 2021), art. 61Δ(3) of Law 188(I)/2007 gave direct access to MOKAS and the Police for their tasks under the AML Law and to the Tax and Customs Departments to investigate and prosecute art. 3 offences. Law 40(I)/2022 (30 March 2022) kept the same four but lets them search to prevent, detect, investigate or prosecute a prescribed offence or trace assets, by specially authorised staff only (61Δ(6)). Law 150(I)/2025 s. 18(d) gave the National Sanctions Implementation Unit access from 25 July 2025.

m-278e9920.t: Vendor evidence puts the planned go-live of Cyprus's bank account register in mid-December 2019; that it happened then is not shown. Prognosys, a Nicosia reporting-software vendor, wrote on 5 November 2019 that testing of the 'Bank Accounts Register (BAR)' was planned for the last week of November 2019 'in line with the deadline provided by the CBC', and on 2 December 2019 that over a dozen FULL and a number of DAILY files had been submitted and that go-live was 'planned for the next two weeks'. Its product page (snapshot of 27 February 2021) describes a full file at first submission and a daily file of changes, for accounts and safe-deposit boxes of up to five years. Unconfirmed by the CBC.

m-0b3d58ba.t: Law 98(I)/2023 (Official Gazette no. 4960, 20 October 2023) amended Cyprus Law 188(I)/2007 with one stated purpose: compliance with the FATF standards referred to in MONEYVAL's second follow-up technical-compliance report on Cyprus, 'published in November 2022' (preamble). It redefined which crypto-asset service providers are obliged entities and must register (arts. 2A, 61E), extended enhanced due diligence to all cross-border correspondent relationships, not only third-country ones (art. 64(1)(b)), and rewrote the new-technologies risk duty (art. 66(2A)). It is not the only amendment citing MONEYVAL: Law 96(I)/2025 (18 June 2025) names the third report (December 2023) among five purposes.

m-93f00de0.t: Bank of Cyprus's list for a 'Limited Company Account', linked under 'Limited Companies registered in Cyprus' on its onboarding page (PDF created 22 June 2026, read 6 October 2026), asks for the Registrar's receipt of beneficial-owner registration, nominee trust deeds where applicable, audited or management accounts for up to two years where available or 12 months of VAT payments, a business-address utility bill, a board resolution, and ID and permanent-address proof of directors, secretary, shareholders and signatories; nothing specific for a corporate shareholder. Registrar certificates and the memorandum 'may be requested'. Its only age limit: utility bills within the last 6 months.

m-0cdc68ab.t: What a Cyprus advocate asks of a corporate client, Cypriot or foreign, per the Cyprus Bar Association's AML Directive (Greek edition, August 2023, replacing December 2019's; still its latest general AML directive on 6 October 2026), Annex III, a 'suggested (non-exhaustive)' list: certified true copies showing registration, registered office, directors, shareholders and constitution; evidence of good standing (for Cyprus companies, a certificate if the company is over six months old); where applicable, a group chart and latest financial information. Certification: a notary, a Hague apostille, a regulated professional in the EU or an equivalent or FATF state, or a Cyprus embassy or consulate.

m-fcc1a657.t: Remote account opening in Cyprus predates the 2025 directive and eIDAS. The Central Bank of Cyprus Guidance Note of November 1999 had non-residents 'who wish to open bank accounts by post' verified through a credit or financial institution in their country. Its directives of April 2008 and December 2013 let a customer 'request the opening of an account through mail, telephone, or the internet without presenting himself for a personal interview', with enhanced checks (2013: bank confirmation, or a verified phone call plus a registered letter). From 7 April 2016 (Amendment No. 1) such customers with account debits or credits over EUR 100,000 a year had to be met in person within three months.

m-c6892d4a.t: Sole-trader eligibility as the providers' own texts stood on 5 October 2026 (synthesis; no sign-up tested). SumUp: yes - its terms address freelancers and its Cyprus help centre has a separate sole-trader document list. PayPal: business accounts are for 'people and organizations (whether incorporated or not)'. Viva: yes by the terms' wording ('any freelancer or legal entity'). Adyen: its merchant terms define the Merchant as 'the company' entering into the agreement; only its documentation for platforms covers sole proprietorships, with a Cyprus row. Revolut: its terms admit sole traders, its Cyprus FAQ excludes them. Stripe and JCC accept individuals (records). myPOS: not checked.

m-ac457b90.t: Adyen publishes what a merchant it contracts directly must upload ('Requirements for your live account application', docs.adyen.com, last modified 2 January 2025, read 5 October 2026); its country tables have no Cyprus row except a VAT format. Cyprus rows are in its platform pages, as examples: registration document 'Πιστοποιητικό Σύστασης' (Certificate of Incorporation) from the Registrar of Companies, under 12 months old or signed by a representative; for a sole proprietorship a 'Certificate of Registered Details'; registration number 'C', 'O' or 'P' plus 1-8 digits. Owners of 25% or more, controllers and signatories are verified; directors only in six named countries, not Cyprus.

m-95e65d4b.t: Video entered the Central Bank of Cyprus AML directive on 7 April 2016. Amendment No. 1 to the Fourth Issue (new para 86A) obliged a bank to meet face to face a customer introduced by a third party - for a legal person, its beneficial owners or controllers - within three months of account opening, adding: 'The meeting may be held over the internet on condition that adequate safeguards are in place such as sound / video recording of the meeting.' The Fifth Edition of February 2019 (para 119) kept the sentence and moved the meeting to 'before executing any transaction'; it has no section on non-face-to-face customers. MONEYVAL's 2019 report dates the two requirements to 2016 and 2019.

m-0d01a204.t: PayPal publishes no Cyprus document checklist; its Cyprus-locale pages (read 5 October 2026) are generic. Business accounts are 'for people and organizations (whether incorporated or not)'; a business must be registered in one of 13 listed countries including Cyprus. The sign-up page asks for legal name, email, password, business registration number, business description and bank details. For identity PayPal first tries national databases, else asks for a proof of identity, reviewed within 2 business days. Its article on lifting an account limitation lists ID card, driving licence, passport or other photo ID and proofs of address (no pay slips in the EU), reviewed in about 3 business days.

m-039c9a16.t: Adyen's checklist for a merchant applying to it directly ('Requirements for your live account application', docs.adyen.com, last modified 2 January 2025, read 5 October 2026) asks for digital copies of: a company registration document from a public authority, issued or signed by an authorised signatory within 12 months; proof of tax or VAT information; a payout-account bank statement (marked optional); photo ID and proof of residency of the person who signs the contract and of shareholders with 25% or more. 'In some cases' it also asks for a signed ownership and control chart not older than six months. Online sellers must show a site with terms, privacy, delivery, refund and contact pages.

m-f2a80059.t: Stripe's 'Acceptable verification documents' page for Cyprus (read 2026-10-04) states that the cross-border scenario does not apply to Individual/Sole-Prop accounts: the user must reside in the account country, and an overseas address can be entered only for non-individual accounts (registered businesses, corporations, companies), where 'an owner/rep may be overseas'. For a person linked to an account who lives outside the account country, a valid passport is the only identity document accepted. A sole trader not resident in Cyprus therefore cannot, on Stripe's published rule, hold a Cyprus individual account.

m-ea05d55a.t: Central Bank of Cyprus AML Directive of 2025 (K.D.P. 120/2025, in force since 2 June 2025), para 59(3): identification documents in a language other than Greek or English must be accompanied by a Greek or English document stating that it is a faithful translation of the original, dated and signed by the 'duly authorised person' who made it - for example a certified translator, or a member of the institution's staff with suitable training, the language as mother tongue or a university degree in it. No sworn or state translator is required by the text. At a later update of the file the institution decides by risk whether plain copies of originals suffice (para 59(2)).

m-e4550c3b.t: JCC's Merchant Application Form ('v2.3' and August 2026 come from the file name and path, not from the form) lists 13 documents for a company, 'as applicable': certificates of (1) incorporation, (2) registered office, (3) shareholders, (4) directors and secretary; (5) memorandum and articles certified by the Registrar; (6) board resolution naming signatories; (7) ID or passport and proof of address of directors, direct shareholders, signatories and UBOs; (8) CY/EU permits of third-country nationals; (9) Beneficial Owners Register extract signed by a director; (10) certificates of companies holding 25% or more; (11) nominee trust deeds; (12) proof of outlet address; (13) IBAN certificate.

m-e1585ad8.t: JCC's merchant application form changed its document list for companies over 2021–2026 (versions and dates from file names and upload paths; earlier files read from web-archive snapshots). v1.3 (2021/11): 10 items, no beneficial-owner register extract. v1.8 (2025/01): 11, adding an 'Extract from the register of Ultimate Beneficial Owners (UBO)… signed by a director'. v1.9 (2026/02): 12, adding a board resolution and a Cyprus/EU permit for third-country nationals. v2.2 (2026/04): the present 13 — Registrar-certified memorandum, certificates of companies holding 25% or more, nominee trust deeds — unchanged in v2.3 (2026/08). The €17 once-off registration fee is in all five versions.

m-d1f11340.t: Stripe's 'Acceptable verification documents' page for Cyprus, as of 2026-10-04, accepts as identity documents a driver's licence, identity card, passport or residence permit; as legal-entity documents the articles of association, certificate of incorporation, commercial register extract, financial statements or VAT registration; as address documents a bank statement, mortgage statement, registration certificate, tax bill or utility bill; and as proof of ownership documents including the certificate of corporate status and the Ultimate Beneficial Owner Register. A person residing outside the account country must use a passport.

m-cb95c5d5.t: For a natural person (sole trader) JCC's Merchant Application Form v2.3 requires five items: a valid identity card or passport; proof of permanent residential address; a CY/EU permit if the merchant is a third-country national; proof of business/outlet address; and an IBAN certificate of the merchant's bank account. Proof of residential address must be at most 6 months old and may be a utility bill, municipal tax bill or income tax document; mobile phone bills are not accepted. JCC reserves the right to ask for further documents.

m-acef83e6.t: A Cyprus bank that starts a new relationship with a company, other legal entity or trust obliged to register its beneficial owners must collect proof of that registration or an extract from the register (Law 188(I)/2007, art. 62(1) proviso), and must use the central beneficial-ownership registers as an additional means of verifying the owner's identity (CBC Directive of 2025, para 26(5)). It may not rely exclusively on the register to satisfy its due-diligence duties (art. 61A(6)(a)(ii) proviso). In force on 4 October 2026.

m-aa529169.t: The Commissioner for Personal Data Protection is Cyprus's supervisory authority under art. 51 of the GDPR: Law 125(I)/2018 defines 'supervisory authority' as the Commissioner appointed under its art. 19, in application of art. 51 of the Regulation (consolidated text read 4 October 2026; amended once, by Law 26(I)/2022). For merchants and providers established in Cyprus it is therefore the authority for personal data in KYC files and payment records; a provider established in another Member State answers primarily to that state's authority under the GDPR's lead-authority rule. This application is a reading, not text of the Law.

m-a3684301.t: Stripe publishes no field list for accounts opened directly; the only per-country list is its 'Required verification information' tool for Connect connected accounts. For a Cyprus private company with full Dashboard and Stripe's own service agreement (card payments, transfers) it returned 44 fields on 2026-10-04: company name, address, tax ID (TIC), phone; category code, website, product description, support phone; a representative's name, address, birth date, phone, email, job title; owners' and directors' names, addresses, emails, birth dates; an owners-provided attestation; terms acceptance; a bank account. If automatic checks fail, ID, address, entity or ownership documents follow.

m-9ceef93e.t: Central Bank of Cyprus AML Directive of 2025 (in force since 2 June 2025), para 50(3): a relationship or transaction 'relates to' a high-risk third country if the funds were generated in, are received from or are destined for one, if the customer is a natural person or legal entity resident or established there, or if a trustee is established there or the trust is governed by its law. The enhanced measures of art. 64(1)(a) of Law 188(I)/2007 then apply, as they do where the transaction passes through such a country or the customer's beneficial owner resides there (50(4)). Mere close personal or professional links leave the choice of measures to the bank's risk assessment (50(5)).

m-957db2df.t: Who may certify a customer's documents for a Cyprus bank is wider under the Central Bank's Directive of 2025 (K.D.P. 120/2025, in force 2 June 2025) than in its Fifth Edition as issued in February 2019. The 2019 text (paras 254-255) accepted copies certified by the bank's employee or by a third party the bank relied on and, for non-Cypriot persons and foreign entities, apostilled originals. Para 59(1) of the 2025 text adds copies certified by a competent government department or independent authority, copies retrieved from the website of the Registrar of Companies or its equivalent in an EEA or low-risk third country, and, for remote customers, the EBA remote-onboarding route.

m-93a14de1.t: CBC Directive of 2025 para 59(1), in force since 2 June 2025, lists seven alternative formats for identification documents at onboarding: originals; a true copy certified by the institution's officer who saw the original; a true copy certified by a relied-on third party; for non-Cypriot citizens and entities incorporated outside Cyprus, originals bearing the Hague 'Apostille'; a copy certified by a government department or independent authority; copies retrieved from the website of the Cyprus Registrar of Companies or the equivalent authority of an EEA state or of a third country the institution rates low-risk; or, for remote customers, compliance with the EBA remote-onboarding guidelines.

m-925c9228.t: Under the Central Bank of Cyprus AML Directive of 2025 (K.D.P. 120/2025, in force since 2 June 2025) identity is verified on a valid identity card or passport (para 30(2)); the Cyprus 'Residence Permit of a foreign person (plastic identity card)' is accepted only where a payment service provider offers money remittance (30(3)). Exceptions: a person who reasonably cannot produce those documents may, absent increased risk, be identified on other evidence the institution finds reliable (para 31); and the basic payment account under Law 64(I)/2017 (para 32: special residence permit, refugee travel document). A verified permanent address is required (26(6), 30(6)); no country is prescribed.

m-8ef285e5.t: Before a business relationship starts and before any transaction, a Cyprus bank must build the customer's 'economic and risk profile' (CBC Directive of 2025, in force since 2 June 2025, para 26(11)): purpose of the relationship; anticipated use of products and estimated account volume; nature of transactions; expected source (countries, main partners) and amount of incoming transfers; expected destination and amount of outgoing payments; a detailed description of the main business or professional activities; ownership structure and group information; other relationships with the bank's group. It is recorded on a separate form in the customer file (para 26(12)).

m-8dfe278d.t: CBC Directive of 2025 para 37(2) defines a 'shell company/entity' as one with no physical presence or activity in its country of incorporation other than, usually, a postal address and/or no established business activity and little or no independent economic value; holding shares or assets or acting as group treasurer 'may indicate' business activity. The relationship must be refused or ended if such an entity is registered where audited accounts need not be filed and prepares none voluntarily, and/or is tax resident in a jurisdiction on the EU, Global Forum or another reputable non-cooperative list, or nowhere (para 37(6)). Others: case by case (para 37(7)). In force since 2 June 2025.

m-8c0190e9.t: SumUp's Cyprus help centre (el-CY, undated, read 4 October 2026) lists what it may ask for beyond the ID scan and selfie taken at sign-up. A sole trader ('ατομική επιχείρηση'): photo ID and selfie; proof of home address from the last six months; proof of business activity; other business documents. An organisation: proof of business activity; official documents showing name, birth date and home address of everyone holding 25% or more directly, and their IDs; other corporate documents. Unverified profiles have a €5,000 limit. The payout bank account must be in a eurozone country and in the same name; an organisation's must also be registered in the country where it operates.

m-7ff0ef1c.t: CBC Directive of 2025 (in force since 2 June 2025) para 25 obliges institutions to review customers' identity data and economic profile at intervals set in their own policy by risk category, and on triggers: an unusual or significant transaction; a change of directors, shareholders or beneficial owners, registered office, name, main partners or activities; a change of account operators; a request for new products; reactivation of a dormant account; a change of risk level; adverse information. One interval is fixed: high-risk relationships are updated at least once a year (para 42(7)); for low risk the CBC's FAQ leaves the frequency to the institution.

m-7558431d.t: For business type 'individual' — which Stripe's documents pair with sole proprietors; the tool offers Cyprus no separate sole-proprietorship structure — Stripe's 'Required verification information' tool for Connect connected accounts (a proxy for a direct account) returned on 2026-10-04, for Cyprus (full Dashboard, Stripe's own agreement, card payments, transfers), 17 API fields: first and last name, address (line, postal code, city), date of birth (three fields), phone, email; category code, website, product description, support phone; terms acceptance (IP, date); a bank account. No company, owner or director fields. An ID or address document follows if automatic verification fails.

m-64ac49a8.t: Central Bank of Cyprus AML Directive of 2025 (K.D.P. 120/2025, in force since 2 June 2025), para 42(8)(b)(ii): an enhanced measure institutions 'may' apply (not all in every case, 42(6)) is ensuring that the customer's funds are not proceeds of crime and that source of wealth and of funds match what it knows; where risk is 'particularly high', verifying both 'may be the only appropriate means'. Evidence named, 'inter alia': VAT and income-tax returns, audited accounts, payslips, public documents, independent media. Cases the Directive itself classes as high-risk (paras 43-51) need at least senior-management approval, steps to establish the source of assets and close monitoring (42(12)).

m-63ea8dc0.t: For a natural person the CBC Directive of 2025 (K.D.P. 120/2025, in force since 2 June 2025) requires: name as on the valid identity card or passport; full permanent residential address; telephone; e-mail; date and place of birth; occupation with employer and position; and any other information deemed necessary for the assessed risk (para 30(1)(a)-(g)). Identity is verified on a valid identity card (physical or electronic) or passport (para 30(2)). The address is verified separately - by an officer's visit, a document up to 6 months old (utility bill, home insurance, municipal or income tax document, other government document, bank statement) or double-registered letter (para 30(6)).

m-600234db.t: The Central Bank of Cyprus AML Directive of 2025 (K.D.P. 120/2025, in force since 2 June 2025) has no separate regime for non-resident customers: the same data and documents apply to every natural person (para 30) and foreign companies supply 'corresponding' documents (para 37(11)). Residence appears as a categorisation factor ('country of origin and/or residence', para 12(6)), as a trigger for enhanced measures where the customer or its beneficial owner resides in a high-risk third country (para 50(3)-(4)) and in para 59(1)(d): non-Cypriot citizens and foreign entities may supply apostilled originals. The 2019 Fifth Edition (para 122) said 'natural persons residing in Cyprus or abroad'.

m-58806b77.t: New in the CBC Directive of 2025 (in force since 2 June 2025): para 37(3) allows legal persons that trade remotely to be excluded from the 'shell company' definition - selling products or services to customers, content production 'e.g. digital marketing, affiliate marketing', professional or technological services - provided the bank verifies the activity on a risk basis (para 37(4)), indicatively through financial statements, active bank accounts reflecting commercial transactions, tax returns, a business website or online shop, details of customers and partners, and contracts and sales documents (para 37(5)). The February 2019 Fifth Edition (paras 151-154) had no such carve-out.

m-46398997.t: For a company the CBC Directive of 2025 requires data on its registration, offices, directors, signatories, beneficial owners and nominee shareholders (para 37(9)), verified by: certificates of incorporation, registered office, directors and secretary and (private companies) shareholders; memorandum and articles; a board resolution; nominee trust deeds; an ownership structure certified by the beneficial owner; identity documents of signatories, shareholders and beneficial owners; shareholder certificates up the ownership chain; and recent audited financial statements or, failing those, management accounts (para 37(10)). Foreign companies supply equivalent documents (para 37(11)).

m-41896434.t: Remote onboarding in Cyprus rests on two layers. Law 188(I)/2007 art. 61(1)(a) accepts identification by electronic identification means and trust services under Regulation (EU) No 910/2014 or by any other secure remote or electronic identification process regulated, recognised, approved or accepted by a competent authority of the Republic. The CBC Directive of 2025 (paras 27-28 and 59(1)(g), in force since 2 June 2025) obliges institutions to comply with EBA Guidelines EBA/GL/2022/15 on remote customer onboarding and defines 'non-face to face customers' as including those whose identity is verified 'via a video link or similar technological means'.

m-2d1e3ec7.t: Under para 27 of the Central Bank of Cyprus AML Directive of 2025 (K.D.P. 120/2025, in force since 2 June 2025) a relationship started 'remotely (without the physical presence of the parties)' is not high-risk by default: the institution must assess whether it creates an increased risk and adapt its measures if so (27(1)(b)); enhanced due diligence under para 42 applies only where that risk is high (27(2)); and electronic identification means do not create an increased risk, in particular where they give a high level of assurance under Regulation (EU) No 910/2014 (27(4)). Remote customers are not among the four categories for which para 42(2) makes enhanced due diligence mandatory.

m-2c98daa6.t: myPOS's help centre (UK-English; no Cyprus version found) says the merchant receives an email listing documents required for Merchant Verification, which vary by local legislation, legal form and activity, and uploads them in the myPOS account. Its examples: proof of the company's registered address, proof of operating address, proof of the nature of the business (invoices, website links), proof of director structure (IDs or passports, incorporation document, articles), and documents on owners controlling more than 25% (IDs and proof of address). It says verification usually completes within 72 business hours. Under the Legal Agreement (§3.1) sole traders with an EEA address are eligible.

m-29170055.t: Under art. 67(2) of Law 188(I)/2007 a Cyprus bank may rely only on a 'third person' that is an obliged entity of art. 2A(a)-(d) or another supervised institution in the EEA or a third country applying equivalent due diligence, not on one established in a high-risk third country (branches and subsidiaries of EU obliged entities may be exempted). The Central Bank's Directive of 2025 (in force since 2 June 2025) allows reliance only when the relationship is established (para 29(1)); later profile updates come from the customer (29(2)). The agreement names the introducer's certifying persons, with specimen signatures; the compliance officer assesses the quality of introduced customers (29(6)).

m-25bd40ac.t: Stripe's Connect documentation for European accounts (read 2026-10-04) says European regulations require it to verify the relationship to the legal entity of ultimate beneficial owners — individuals who own or control, directly or indirectly, more than 25% — and, if there are none, of directors (information on at most five is needed). Stripe first tries third-party sources; if that fails, the account uploads an official document or signs a digital attestation, for which Stripe publishes UBO and director templates. Identity is first checked from name, date of birth and address; an ID document, an address document or a liveness check is asked for only if that fails or sanctions concerns arise.

m-25b25a66.t: 'Client accounts' in a third person's name are a mandatory enhanced-due-diligence category in the Central Bank of Cyprus AML Directive of 2025 (paras 42(2)(b), 45; in force 2 June 2025). A pooled account needs sub-accounts or connected accounts and identified beneficial owners of credits of EUR 15,000 or more where the holder is an auditor, accountant, tax adviser, lawyer, trust and company service provider or estate agent from the EEA or a low-risk third country (45(9)-(10)), and of EUR 10,000 or more for other holders managing clients' money (45(12)-(13)). Simplified measures are possible for a low-risk, supervised financial institution from the EEA or a low-risk third country (45(6)-(7)).

m-1ef3dc01.t: CBC Directive of 2025 para 12(7), in force since 2 June 2025, requires obliged entities to ensure that their policies do 'not result in the general refusal or termination of business relationships with entire categories of customers' they regard as higher risk: each relationship is to be assessed individually, the decision documented, alternative risk-mitigation considered before a refusal or termination, and the decision kept available to supervisors. Para 12(8) makes EBA Guidelines EBA/GL/2023/04 on access to financial services the standard. The English text of the February 2019 Fifth Edition contains no such provision.

m-19996731.t: When a customer reaches a Cyprus bank through a third party that performed the identification (Law 188(I)/2007 art. 67), the CBC Directive of 2025 (para 29(4)) requires the bank itself to meet the customer before any transaction takes place - for a company, the natural persons who are beneficial owners, exercise effective control or direct its operations. The meeting may be held online with safeguards such as recording, and evidence of it is kept in the file. Meetings with the introducer, persons linked to it, or registered shareholders acting as nominees do not satisfy the requirement (para 29(5)). In force since 2 June 2025.

m-149f6a45.t: Viva.com's help centre states that in most cases a merchant does not need to upload business documents because Viva retrieves the business details from the national Business Registry; the person must complete identity verification with a valid ID, and more may be requested depending on company structure. Viva's terms (effective 30 September 2026) allow a 'Rolling Reserve' — a percentage of acquired volume held for a period — and list unacceptable categories including weapons, pornography, escort or dating services, gambling that is not legitimately licensed, e-money products, and crowdfunding or bitcoin trading.

m-122f57ef.t: Viva.com's help centre has a Cyprus-specific article, dated 30 January 2025 and read on 2026-10-04, on the 'Beneficial Ownership Declaration': the form must be signed by the company's legal representative (director) and declares the natural persons who own or control the company; holding at least 25% of the shares or ownership is treated as an indication of direct control, and 25% held through another company as indirect control. The article presents the declaration as something a Cyprus company submits but does not say in which cases, so Viva's general 'no business documents in most cases' statement does not rule out a signed beneficial-owner form in Cyprus.

m-f934570a.t: Per the Cyprus Registrar of Companies' page 'After the establishment of place of business' (read 6 October 2026), every overseas company must, within sixty days from its registration, file a notice for registration with the Tax Department and obtain a tax number; register with Social Insurance Services if it employs staff; file its financial statements with the Registrar once every calendar year; and at the end of each tax year prepare audited financial statements and submit them with its tax return to the Tax Department. The page cites no law for these duties; the Tax Department's own rule was not read.

m-ebf62913.t: The Cyprus Companies Law names the electronic identities usable in the Registrar's online procedures by EU-citizen applicants (s. 366A, inserted by Law 151(I)/2023): a means issued under a scheme approved by their own Member State, or one issued in another Member State and recognised for cross-border authentication under art. 6 of Regulation (EU) No 910/2014. The Registrar may refuse a means below the assurance level of art. 6(1) and must publish the recognised means on his website. On 6 October 2026 his 'Obtain access to e-filing' page named only registration with the government gateway; no list of recognised means was found on the pages read. Third-country nationals are not mentioned.

m-e8364099.t: The Business Facilitation Unit's published time for registering a company of foreign interests lengthened between 2022 and 2026. Its page as archived on 20 May 2022 took applications by e-mail and promised that 'all the necessary registrations for the establishment of the company' would be completed 'within seven (7) working days' from submission of all documents. Its gov.cy page (modified 23 September 2026) says registration in the Register of Companies with Foreign Interests is completed 'in no more than ten (10) business days from the date of duly submitting the e-form'. The Valiotti founder's 2022 'another week' fits the 2022 figure.

m-e823c375.t: A company incorporated outside Cyprus that establishes a place of business in the Republic must, within one month of establishing it, deliver to the Registrar of Companies for registration (Companies Law, Cap. 113, s. 347(1)): a written report (name, legal form, seat, objects, home register and number, issued capital and, for a non-EU company, its governing law); a certified copy of its constitutional documents, with a certified translation if they are not in English; a list of its directors, secretary and persons authorised to represent it; and the names and addresses of one or more persons resident in Cyprus authorised to accept service for it. CyLaw consolidated text read 6 October 2026.

m-d3da6ebe.t: Cyprus's foreign-investment screening act is the Establishment of a Framework for the Screening of Foreign Direct Investments Law of 2025, Law 194(I)/2025, published in the Official Gazette (No. 5061) on 14 November 2025 and in force since 2 April 2026 (s. 20). Its preamble says it applies arts 3, 4, 6, 7, 9, 10, 11 and 14 of Regulation (EU) 2019/452. The competent authority is the Ministry of Finance, advised by a seven-member committee of directors-general chaired by its own (ss. 2, 9). Per the Ministry's guidance of 28 July 2026 the Law does not reach investments completed before 2 April 2026, but one agreed or planned earlier and not yet completed may still have to be notified.

m-cc8488f7.t: When a company, Cypriot or foreign, is a founder or officer of a new Cyprus company, the Registrar of Companies' published review criteria (read 6 October 2026) ask only for identifying data on the forms: in the memorandum 'the registration number for legal persons' beside each shareholder; on form HE3 the name of a legal person appointed director or secretary and its registration number, with the note 'In case of a foreign organisation, the registration number is not written'; an officer that is a company signs with its seal. Neither the criteria nor the Registrar's list of incorporation documents names a good-standing certificate, apostille or translation of a foreign shareholder's papers.

m-ca9c0142.t: Cyprus restricts land acquisition by 'aliens' under the Immovable Property Acquisition (Aliens) Law, Cap. 109: an alien may not acquire immovable property, otherwise than on death, without the Council of Ministers' prior permission (s. 3(1)); a registration in breach is void (s. 3(5)). 'Alien' means a non-citizen and includes an alien-controlled company, a foreign company and a trust for an alien; it excludes an 'alien Cypriot' (non-citizen of Cypriot birth or descent as defined), a non-citizen wife of a citizen not separated by court decision, EU and EEA citizens, and legal persons formed under another EU state's law and seated in the EEA (s. 2). Last amended by Law 161(I)/2011.

m-c9f19df9.t: The Central Bank of Cyprus AML Directive of 2025 (K.D.P. 120/2025, Gazette 2 May 2025, in force a month later), binding banks, payment and e-money institutions among others, sets no maximum age for company certificates, Cypriot or foreign. For a company incorporated abroad it asks documents 'corresponding to' the Cypriot set (para 37(11)) and lets the institution, by assessed risk, search the foreign register to confirm the company is not dissolved, in liquidation or struck off (37(12)). For company and address documents its only age rules are a utility bill up to six months old for a person's address (30(6)(b)) and 'recent' audited accounts, else recent management accounts (37(10)(k)).

m-c7f2c90f.t: As of 6 October 2026 CyLaw lists no amendment of Cap. 109 after Law 161(I)/2011, and four members' bills to tighten it are before the House Interior Committee (texts not read). Per Cyprus Property News (2 September 2026) they 'were due to go before the full House for a vote in April' but 'were deferred at the last minute'; two AKEL bills would treat as foreign-controlled any body whose beneficial owner is a foreign national and drop Cabinet approval for a foreign individual buying one shop up to 200 sq m or one office up to 300 sq m; a cross-party bill would require 51% of a buying company's capital, votes or control to be held by citizens of Cyprus, the EU or the EEA.

m-b3aed493.t: Cyprus's Companies Law (Cap. 113) lets a legal person be a director or secretary and sets no nationality, residence or seat condition for it: the register records a corporate director's name and registered or principal office, a corporate secretary's name and registered office (s. 192(2)(β), (3)(β)). Two bars on single officers, both lifted for a single-member private company: a sole director may not also be secretary (s. 171(1)); a company may not have as secretary a body whose sole director is its sole director, nor as sole director a body whose sole director is its secretary (s. 172). One on whose instructions the directors must act is deemed a director for s. 192 (s. 192(9)(α)).

m-a8f60511.t: An overseas company with a place of business in Cyprus files with the Registrar every financial year the accounts, management report and audit or review report it presented to its last general meeting and published at home (Cap. 113, s. 350(1)(α)), unless an EU company exempt at home under Directives 2013/34/EU and 2006/43/EC (s. 350(1)(β)). It must also prepare, have audited or reviewed and file branch accounts as if the branch were a company, subject to prescribed exemptions (s. 350(2)(α)), unless it prepares, audits and publishes accounts at home under those Directives and has filed them (s. 350(2)(β)). Changes of constitution, officers, representatives or address: 15 days (s. 349(1)).

m-a4a0433c.t: Under Law 45(I)/2019 on sworn translators (unamended on CyLaw, 6 October 2026), a 'certified translation' is a valid and accurate translation between a foreign language and Greek or Turkish, bearing the Republic's official seal and duly stamped, made by a sworn translator on the Council's Register (s. 2). Foreign-language official documents are entered in public registers after translation by a sworn translator into an official language (s. 18). An advocate not on the Register may translate only for his own cases, accepted exceptionally with a sworn statement of the reason (s. 14(2)); the Registrar's pages accept a Greek translation 'by an affidavit in court' or by a sworn translator.

m-a3d637c9.t: Per Tothemaonline (9 October 2025), presenting its special report on property acquisition by foreigners to the House Audit Committee, the Audit Office said the practice built on Ministry of Interior circulars in effect widens 'owner-occupation' and 'professional premises', allowing more units to be bought without the Cap. 109 regulations being amended, which raises doubts about its legality; the law provides no check on the source of funds, and no check is made on use after purchase. Its count: sales to non-EU foreigners were 4,321 of 15,797 in 2024 (27%), excluding Cyprus companies with foreign shareholders.

m-9eb64325.t: A foreign investment in Cyprus must be notified to the Ministry of Finance and approved before completion only if three conditions all hold (Law 194(I)/2025, s. 3(1)-(3), in force 2 April 2026): the investor acquires, directly or indirectly, alone or in concert, at least 25% of the share capital and/or votes, or equivalent decisive influence; the investment, alone or with other deals between the same parties within 12 months, is worth €2,000,000 or more; and the target is an 'undertaking of strategic importance' in the Annex's sensitive sectors. An increase crossing 25% or 50% must be notified whatever its value, if the target is of strategic importance (s. 3(4); Ministry guidance Q3.8).

m-9956fa47.t: Directive (EU) 2025/25 of 19 December 2024, amending Directives 2009/102/EC and (EU) 2017/1132 on digital tools and processes in company law, was published on 10 January 2025 and entered into force on the twentieth day after publication, 30 January 2025. Member States must adopt and publish transposing measures by 31 July 2027 and apply them from 31 July 2028; the provisions for Article 19(2)(i) and Article 19b of Directive (EU) 2017/1132 are due by 1 August 2028 and apply from 1 August 2029 (art. 4). On 6 October 2026 the Directive is in force and none of its new instruments is yet applicable.

m-97900142.t: At the House Interior Committee on 3 September 2026, per the Cyprus News Agency report republished by Nomoplatform on 4 September, Interior Minister Konstantinos Ioannou said the consolidated text under discussion includes a ban on acquiring land outside the set development limit, to protect farmland, and on land next to the ceasefire line or vital infrastructure, plus limits on the plot and on the size of a home bought to live in, the exact area still to be discussed; four members' bills from DISY, AKEL and DIKO were before the committee. The chair said it would return in October, including rules for legal persons; no session date or report of one was found by 6 October 2026.

m-92bfd3b6.t: The Cyprus Ministry of Finance's guidance on Law 194(I)/2025 (28 July 2026) draws two lines for small firms. A greenfield investment, 'establishing a new undertaking rather than acquiring an existing one', is within the Law's scope but does 'not satisfy the statutory conditions for mandatory notification'; the Ministry may still examine it within 15 months of completion where it may affect security or public order (s. 3(8)). The Annex sectors, judged by the target's actual activities: critical infrastructure (incl. tourism, health, media, data), critical technologies, critical inputs, sensitive information incl. personal data, and media pluralism. Filing: e-service only, in English, free.

m-826a432f.t: The EU act behind Cyprus's screening law is being replaced. Regulation (EU) 2026/1386 of 17 June 2026 on the screening of foreign investments, published on 26 June 2026, entered into force on 16 July 2026 and applies from 17 January 2028 (art. 31); some provisions apply from 16 July 2026, among them art. 3(2), the duty to notify national screening measures to the Commission by 17 January 2028. It repeals Regulation (EU) 2019/452 from 17 January 2028 (art. 30(1)); investments under screening or completed by then stay under the 2019 Regulation (art. 30(2)-(3)). Cyprus's Law 194(I)/2025 defines 'Regulation (EU) 2019/452' as that act 'as amended or replaced from time to time' (s. 2).

m-816f5cd8.t: Cap. 109 itself sets an area threshold for non-EU buyers: where an acquisition exceeds the land strictly needed for a home or professional premises 'and in any case' two σκάλες, the permission is also subject to conditions that Council of Ministers regulations approved by the House may set (s. 3(1A)). The Department of Lands and Surveys' page (read 6 October 2026) gives the cap as 2,676 m² and above it allows only an own home on up to 4,014 m², professional or commercial premises, or industry the Council deems beneficial; the Ministry of Interior's page gives 4,000 m² for an own-home plot.

m-80af8d8c.t: From 31 July 2028 (application date of national measures), Directive (EU) 2025/25 gives limited companies and listed partnerships of one Member State three tools in another: an EU Company Certificate, 'accepted in all Member States as sufficient evidence' of incorporation and listed data (art. 16b); a digital EU power of attorney, evidence of authority only in procedures within its scope, e.g. forming a company or registering a branch (art. 16c); and exemption of register-certified copies 'from all forms of legalisation and any similar formality', apostille included (recital 29; art. 16d). Home-register documents may not be asked for to form a subsidiary or a branch (arts 13g(2a), 28a(5a)).

m-79e93adc.t: How Cyprus applies Cap. 109 in practice, per the Ministry of Interior's page 'Purchasing Property' (updated 2 October 2024, read 6 October 2026): a non-EU national, a foreign company or a company controlled by foreign nationals must first get permission from the District Administration where the property lies, on form COMM 145; no fee is payable and applications take 2-3 weeks. A foreign national or couple may be allowed a plot of up to 4,000 m² for an own home, or up to two units: two dwellings, or a dwelling and a shop of up to 100 m², or a dwelling and an office of up to 250 m². A company adds its Registrar certificates, memorandum and articles, and staff details.

m-6ef33fad.t: Per the Cyprus Mail (3 September 2026) and Cyprus Property News (2 September 2026), the Audit Office's special report on property acquisition by foreigners found that a company incorporated in Cyprus or another EU state and controlled by non-EU beneficiaries is counted in official sales statistics as a Cypriot or EU buyer (Cyprus Mail: it 'is classified as a domestic entity'), so the foreign share of sales, over a quarter in 2024, was likely understated. This is the statistics' classification: Cap. 109's text treats a Cyprus company under alien control as an alien, but not a company of another EU state seated in the EEA.

m-6392a258.t: For a shop or cafe the reach of Cyprus's Cap. 109 depends on the right taken. 'Acquisition of immovable property' covers a lease for over thirty-three years, or one that can exceed it through unilateral options to renew (s. 3(6)(α)); acquiring a share in a Cyprus company holding immovable property where that makes it alien-controlled (s. 3(6)(β)); and a trust for an alien over such property, lease or share (s. 3(6)(γ)). For land beyond what a home or business premises needs, and in any case over two donums, a lease over ten years already counts (proviso to s. 3(6)(α), s. 3(1A)). On the text, an ordinary commercial tenancy taken by a third-country national or his company needs no permission.

m-47523634.t: If an Estonian company is resident in both states under their domestic laws, the Estonia-Cyprus double tax convention (signed 15 October 2012, in force 8 October 2013) has no automatic tie-breaker: under art. 4(3) the competent authorities 'shall settle the question by mutual agreement due regard being had to the place of effective management of such person or any other relevant criterion'. Estonia reserved MLI Article 4 in full, so the MLI leaves this rule in place.
