The House's weekly committee programme could not be read (parliament.cy answers with a security check; the only 2026 web-archive copy is of 6 August 2026), and no report of a committee session on it was found.

m-f4c20d8d.t: Cyprus's 2018 rules on lawyers' out-of-court fees (K.D.P. 171/2018, adopted by the Bar's extraordinary general meeting on 19 June 2018) let the client fix the price in writing: an advocate must otherwise claim a fee set by the regulations' criteria for a reasonable fee (regs 4, 10), but is released from that if the client signs an 'Advocate Appointment Form' or agreement containing the provisions of Annex I (reg 5(1)(a)). Annex I names the client and the advocate or law office, describes the matter, states the fee the client agrees to pay and how it will be paid, and is signed by the client. Documents an advocate drafts in such matters carry his name, office, signature and stamp (reg 17).

m-dc13ec2c.t: On 6 October 2026 anyone could check a Cyprus firm, without logging in, in CySEC's list of licensed administrative service providers (126 licences); the Cyprus Bar Association's grids of lawyers' limited companies (689, each with HE number, compliance officer and advocates) and of administrative service providers (1,442, each with HE number, connected lawyer or law firm and services); and ICPAC's registers, which load the whole list on opening: 1,391 individuals and 984 firms with a general practising certificate, 1,119 statutory auditors, 785 audit firms, and 472 persons and 316 firms with ICPAC's administrative-services certificate.

m-d4d1954f.t: Part III of the Advocates' Pension Fund (Fees) Regulations (Table set by K.D.P. 605/2007 from 1 January 2008; items 1, 8 and 9 not changed by the 2017-2023 amendments) sets the advocates' stamps on filings at the Registrar of Companies: €9 on an application to register a business name (item 1), €26 on the founding document of a general or limited partnership whatever its capital (item 8), and €40 for a limited company with capital up to €2,000, €50 up to €30,000 (item 9). The Regulations are made under s. 27 of the Advocates Law (Cap. 2), whose fees fall on practising advocates.

m-cc9a7d82.t: What a hired lawyer or provider cannot close in Cyprus, read from the sources as of 6 October 2026. The bank decides whether to open an account: the right to a basic payment account covers consumers, not businesses, and provider schedules read sell only an 'application' with no guaranteed success. Beneficial-owner details are filed by the company's own officer, so a provider files only if it is itself an officer. A company's CY Login profile is verified in person at a centre by an officer, or by a provider with his signed authorisation. Planning applications are made in the owner's name or by his authorised representative, through a designer he authorises. Biometrics need the person.

m-c8dce863.t: Cyprus's Advocates Law (Cap. 2, cylaw text to Law 17(I)/2024, read 6 October 2026) defines 'practising law' (s. 2(1)) as including appearing in court for anyone; preparing pleadings for a client; registering trade marks or patents; drafting, revising or amending a company's founding documents or any application, report, statement, sworn statement, resolution or other document on the formation, registration, organisation, reorganisation or dissolution of any legal person; ship registration; legal opinions; estate-administration filings. Only a registered advocate holding the annual licence, with no Pension Fund arrears, may practise (s. 11(1)); unlicensed practice is an offence (s. 11(3)).

m-b07bba0a.t: Ioannou & Co Ltd (HE489547), a Paphos accounting business, was in none of four public registers on 6 October 2026: not on CySEC's provider list, not in the Bar's provider or law-company registers, not in any ICPAC list by name or number. Its site says its founder obtained the US CPA title and AICPA membership, and that 'Our partners provide audit, legal and incorporation services'. It offers incorporation (€1,000) and a registered address (€250 a year) without naming who supplies them. Law 196(I)/2012 lets only eligible persons, save its exemptions, provide a registered office (ss. 4(1)(b)(iv), 5(1)); Cap. 2 s. 11(5) reserves drafting the memorandum and articles to advocates.

m-ae083335.t: Under s. 4(3) of Law 196(I)/2012 (cylaw, read 6 October 2026) a natural person needs no licence to act as director of a company at least 25% owned by him or his family, or, without controlling its board, of fewer than ten companies; and, if resident in Cyprus, as its secretary where he or his family own at least 50% (25% if all shareholders are Cyprus-resident individuals) or the company is his sole employer - provided the service is not advertised or offered to others. Sections 4(3)-(5) give no like exemption for providing a registered office address (s. 4(1)(b)(iv)); whether a founder giving his own address to his own company 'provides' that service, the Act does not say.

m-abd314c4.t: Florin Piciorlung, whose law office's undated price page first-wave facts cite, appears in the Cyprus Bar Association's public list of Cypriot advocate members (Limassol district) on 6 October 2026, but in neither the Bar's register of lawyers' companies nor its register of administrative service providers, nor on CySEC's list. The office's page says it is registered 'under license number 3993/2009'; the Bar's grid shows no licence number and keeps its licence-print button disabled for visitors, so the current licence could not be confirmed.

m-a75398e5.t: ICPAC's registers, read 6 October 2026, list Asterisk Corporate Services Ltd (HE427805) as an accounting firm with general practising certificate E1379/G/2022 and administrative-services certificate E1379/F/2023, which bears out its claim to be licensed by ICPAC; and CYAUSE Audit Services Ltd (HE287397) with certificates E321/G/2013 and audit certificate E321/A/2013 but no administrative-services certificate. Philippou Accounting & Tax Ltd and Ioannou & Co Ltd (HE489547) appear in none of ICPAC's six lists, by name or by HE number; neither is on CySEC's list or the Bar's provider register.

m-9d3b343e.t: The advocates' Pension Fund stamps reached filings at the Registrar of Companies only in 1988. As published on 15 September 1966 (K.D.P. 643/1966, under s. 27 of the Advocates Law), regulation 3 of the Fees Regulations charged an advocate's appearances before a court and the filing of listed documents with a court or court officer; the 1968 and 1976 amendments added no Registrar filings. K.D.P. 103/1988 (Gazette of 26 March 1988) inserted regulation 3(3) and replaced the Table with one whose new Part III covered filings with the Official Receiver and Registrar of Companies and the Ship Registrar; its first item was the application to register a business name, then £1.

m-95d81a43.t: Although appearing before a court for another person is practising law reserved to licensed advocates in Cyprus (Advocates Law, Cap. 2, s. 2(1) and s. 11), s. 30 of the same Law lets every party to civil or criminal proceedings appear in person and conduct his own case; where several parties to civil proceedings share an interest, one may be authorised in writing by the others to appear for them, and the court may on a party's personal application let a close relative appear for him. Read in the cylaw consolidated text on 6 October 2026.

m-8889c7f3.t: Regulation 3(3) of the Advocates' Pension Fund (Fees) Regulations charges the Part III stamps 'for the filing by an advocate' of a listed document with the Registrar of Companies or the Ship Registrar, and bars registering such a filing unless 'the said fees' are duly paid (K.D.P. 103/1988). The amendments read on cylaw, 1996, 1997, 2005, 2007, 2017 (no. 409), 2022 and 2023, replace the Table, repeal or change other regulations, or allow electronic payment, and leave 3(3) as it was. Its wording reaches filings made by an advocate; it names no fee on a business-name application, HE32, HE2 or HE4 filed by the founder or a company officer himself.

m-8578de6a.t: Chambers & Co, a Limassol law firm that publishes formation fees at chambersandco.com, names no company or HE number on its site (read 6 October 2026); it says it is regulated by the Cyprus Bar Association and a member 'since 1996', and its profile page names Richard Chambers, admitted in 1998, as managing partner and founder. The Bar's member list has an advocate Richard Chambers with the telephone number the site prints, and its register of lawyers' companies lists him among the advocates of Michael Chambers & Co. LLC (HE296062), which runs chambers.law. Which legal entity contracts through chambersandco.com was not established.

m-7f9517d3.t: In the Cyprus Bar Association's registers on 6 October 2026: Christophi & Associates LLC is a lawyers' company (HE240652) with three connected administrative service providers, Businessmatters Shareholders Ltd, Businessmatters Secretarial Ltd and Businessmatters Directors Ltd; Polycarpos Philippou & Associates LLC (HE320422) has Kindlus Trustees Ltd and Kindlus Secretaries Ltd; Harris Koufettas & Associates LLC (HE366364) has Topstone Nominees Ltd; Georgios K. Konstantinou LLC (HE321623), which trades as George K. Konstantinou Law Firm, is listed as a lawyers' company with no provider found under its name or number. None of the four is on CySEC's provider list.

m-788e17d9.t: Zeno and Expanship, formation providers whose prices existing records cite, say they are not law firms. Zeno's page (updated July 2026): 'Zeno is a Cyprus-based digital business services brand, not a Cyprus Bar-registered law firm', working through independent advocates and ICPAC accountants, at Lesvou 11B, Paphos, the address Nexora Cyprus gives as 'Operated by Ebrovia Ltd'. Expanship: 'We are a corporate services company, not a law firm...', though it sells office, secretary and nominee services. On 6 October 2026 none of the four names was in CySEC's, the Bar's or ICPAC's registers; the Bar's member list has an advocate Sergios Chr. Charalambous (Paphos), the name of Zeno's founder.

m-72d2b2a3.t: No general Cyprus statute on how a power of attorney is executed was found on 6 October 2026: cylaw's index of Chapters has none, and the Contract Law (Cap. 149, Part XIII 'Agency') says only that authority may be express or implied, express when given orally or in writing (ss. 146-147). Specific acts set formalities: for a land transfer or mortgage through an agent, Law 9/1965 s. 10 requires a written authority certified by a certifying officer (or mukhtar) if signed in Cyprus, or by a Cyprus consular officer if signed abroad. Under K.D.P. 48/2024, private documents for use abroad, such as powers of attorney, go on to the Justice Ministry or citizen service centres.

m-72611b32.t: A Cyprus advocate's annual practising licence is issued or renewed only if he holds professional-negligence insurance with a licensed insurer (Advocates Law, Cap. 2, s. 6E(1)); the Bar Council fixes the minimum cover (s. 6E(2)). The Council's decision on basic specifications, the document the Bar links on 6 October 2026 (file created 25 March 2013), sets minimum limits of €170,860 per claim and €341,720 per insurance period, plus at least €25,630 for defence costs, a deductible of at most 1% of the limit per claim, and cover for practice in the EEA on the basis of Cyprus law; the insured include the lawyer's LLC, employees and his own service, management or trustee companies.

m-6e7fb745.t: Cyprus's Advocates Law (Cap. 2, s. 11(5), cylaw text through Law 17(I)/2024, read 6 October 2026) does more than reserve the drafting of a company's memorandum and articles to a practising advocate: a practising advocate must not sign such documents that he did not draft (s. 11(5)(γ)), and any person who undertakes, holds himself out as accepting or advertises as accepting the drafting of a memorandum or articles commits an offence punishable by up to three months' imprisonment or a fine of up to £500, or both; for a legal person the same criminal liability falls on the officers who approved or voted for such acts (s. 11(5)(ε)).

m-5c81fcac.t: K.D.P. 220/2017 (Gazette of 30 June 2017), made by the Cyprus Bar Council with Cabinet approval, amended the Advocates' Pension Fund (Fees) Table without touching regulation 3. It replaced the payment column of Part III items 3-7 (trade-mark filings at the Registrar) so that, where filing is electronic, the equal fee is paid after filing to the Pension Fund through its website, re-priced ship-registry items 15-18 and added items 19-23. Part III items 1 (business name, €9) and 12-14 (HE32, HE2, HE4, €9 each) were not amended.

m-450283a3.t: CySEC's list of approved administrative service providers, read 6 October 2026, carries Fidesta Ltd (ex Nestorel Ltd), licence 197/196 of 23 April 2018, company number 351992, and C. Savva & Associates Ltd, licence 29/196 of 10 March 2014, company number 261578, whose contact e-mail is at savvacyprus.com; the 'Savva Cyprus' site whose prices existing records cite names C. Savva & Associates Ltd in its footer. Both are licensed for trust management (s. 4(1)(a) of Law 196(I)/2012) and company management (s. 4(1)(b)(i)-(viii)). Neither appears in the Bar's provider register; C. Savva & Associates is a different firm from the ICPAC audit firm Savva Frangous & Associates Ltd.

m-3f41dafe.t: A client unhappy with a Cyprus lawyer has two routes on the Bar's pages (read 6 October 2026). Conduct: a written complaint to the Advocates' Disciplinary Board, a statutory body chaired by the Attorney General, with a €68 fee, for fraudulent, disgraceful or unprofessional conduct or breach of the conduct rules; mishandling a case is not itself an offence. A private complaint proceeds only with the Board's leave, and if the advocate is acquitted the complainant may be ordered to pay costs (Cap. 2, s. 17(2), (3)(δ)). Fees in a non-court matter: a Bar committee of three advocates under K.D.P. 171/2018, whose decisions have the status of arbitral awards enforceable through a District Court.

m-2c3c761b.t: Under Cyprus's Advocates Law (Cap. 2, s. 17, cylaw text through Law 17(I)/2024, read 6 October 2026) the Disciplinary Board may warn or reprimand an advocate, fine him up to €20,000, suspend his licence or strike him off. A person complaining of an advocate's conduct starts proceedings only with the Board's leave (s. 17(3)(δ)), and if the advocate is acquitted the Board may order the complainant to pay the costs, assessed on the €10,000-€50,000 scale of civil actions (s. 17(2)). The Bar's public page 'Inadequate Professional Services', read the same day, still gives the fine limit as one thousand pounds.

m-22bc80c8.t: Anyone can look up a Cyprus lawyer or law firm on the Cyprus Bar Association's e-services site without logging in. On 6 October 2026 its grids, by their own counters, held 4,414 'Cypriot Advocate Members' (searchable by name or phone; columns: name in Latin and Greek, phone, fax, court box, district), 93 registered European lawyers, 689 lawyers' limited companies (with HE number, compliance officer, email, the firm's advocates and an 'ASP' button on each row), 22 partnerships and 152 insolvency practitioners. The members grid does not show whether an entry holds the current annual licence; its per-row 'Details' button, internally a licence print, is disabled for visitors.

m-1c5b219e.t: Cyprus lawyers have had no minimum fees for out-of-court work since 29 June 2018, when K.D.P. 172/2018 repealed the minimum-fee regulations of 1985-2017 and K.D.P. 171/2018 took effect. Under the latter an advocate must tell the client in advance how the fee will be set, 'especially' when it is hourly, and must deliver a fee account within a reasonable time and at the latest one month after the client asks; breach is a disciplinary offence (regs 7-9). The conduct rules (K.D.P. 237/2002, reg 19 as replaced by K.D.P. 142/2013) let an advocate inform the public about his services in any medium if the information is accurate and not misleading; they say nothing specific on publishing prices.

m-1a05a4b4.t: The Cyprus Bar Association's register of administrative service providers, read 6 October 2026, lists Meridian Trust Limited (HE454766), connected with Saveriadou & Petrou LLC, with the same Larnaca telephone number as the cypruscompany.net price page, alongside other Meridian-named nominee, director, secretary and trustee companies of that firm; and A.N. Easy Corporate Ltd (HE456719), connected with an individual advocate in Larnaca, services 'ALL', which fits EasyCorporate's claim to be 'Licensed and Supervised by the Cyprus Bar Association'. Neither company is on CySEC's provider list or in ICPAC's registers.

m-196fcc75.t: The Advocates' Pension Fund (Fees) Regulations, whose Table K.D.P. 605/2007 replaced from 1 January 2008, were amended four times since: K.D.P. 220/2017, 409/2017, 227/2022 and 280/2023 (cylaw KDP indexes 2008-2026 and Gazette texts read 6 October 2026; none found for 2024-2026). None changes item 9 of Part III, the stamp on the founding document of a limited company (€40 for capital up to €2,000); they touch court fees, trade-mark and ship-registry items and add a Part IV. K.D.P. 227/2022 adds that where a filing is made electronically the fees are paid by electronic means, online or as the Bar Council sets.

m-13671b50.t: Chambers & Co, whose site chambersandco.com publishes hourly and formation fees, names no legal entity, registration or Bar number (read 6 October 2026), though every page says it is 'Regulated by the Cyprus Bar Association'; it gives Kosta Partasidi 11, Limassol 3030. The Registrar's open data (29 September 2026) has no matching entity: C & H CHAMBERS & CO is a Nicosia partnership (no. 11585), and a Greek-named Limassol law partnership of 1996 (no. 9639) differs by partners and address; the 24 companies registered at Kosta Partasidi 11 date from 2025-2026 and none bears a lawyer's name. Michael Chambers & Co. LLC (HE296062; Bar no. 363) is at 25 Voukourestiou, Limassol 3045.

m-0f9a82ec.t: Per cylaw's yearly indexes of regulatory administrative acts for 1988-2026 (read 6 October 2026), the Advocates' Pension Fund (Fees) Regulations of 1966 were amended after regulation 3(3) was inserted only by K.D.P. 122/1996, 222/1997, 129/2005, 605/2007, 220/2017, 409/2017, 227/2022 and 280/2023, with K.D.P. 306/2008 fixing the stamp's form; none rewrites regulation 3(3). The 2020-2021 dates in the recitals of K.D.P. 227/2022 and 280/2023 (31.1.2020 to 5.11.2021) are the Gazette dates of the laws amending the Advocates Law, Cap. 2 (Law 6(I)/2020 to Law 145(I)/2021), not amendments of the Regulations.

m-041f38b2.t: ICPAC handles complaints only about accountants and firms on its registers, which its guidance of June 2025 (linked on 6 October 2026) tells complainants to check first; complaints are filed only on its website with a €200 fee paid via JCC Smart, and a complainant who settles and withdraws before the Disciplinary Committee concludes may bear part of the costs. Complaints about an auditor or audit work go to the Cyprus Public Audit Oversight Board (ΑΔΕΕλΕπ). ICPAC says it examines complaints against members, does not mediate or arbitrate client disputes, imposes only disciplinary penalties (reprimand, fine, removal, licence withdrawal) and leaves compensation to the courts.

m-d5a2cc4d.t: The Research and Innovation Foundation's PRE-SEED/0526 start-up call (announced 20 May 2026; budget €1,000,000, at most €119,999 per project) closed on 11 September 2026 with 284 proposals, a record for the programme, per RIF's press release of that day, which says selection follows 'in accordance with the RESTART Programmes' Call for Proposals' - a preliminary eligibility check, then scientific evaluation. RIF's announcements list, read 6 October 2026 (latest item 5 October 2026), showed no results for the call.

m-cfbbb1fc.t: For its PRE-SEED start-up grants the Research and Innovation Foundation expected a registered company by contract signature, on the FAQ of its 2023 call (PRE-SEED/0823, PDF of 11 September 2023, still on its site on 6 October 2026): a group of natural persons may submit a proposal, 'however the registration of the company should be completed until the signing of the Contract with the RIF'. The startup it funds is, per the RESTART 2016-2020 Work Programme the FAQ cites, a small unlisted enterprise up to five years after its registration that has not yet distributed profits, among other conditions. Whether the 2026 call, PRE-SEED/0526 (closed 11 September 2026), keeps this rule was not seen.

m-c68227dc.t: The Cyprus Registrar's review criteria for a business-name application on form EE1 (page published 25 April 2019, read 6 October 2026) check that the owner is 'a single person either natural or legal', that a home or registered-office address in Cyprus is given, that the owner signs, and, under nationality, that 'in case of non-EU, permission is required by the Immigration Officer'. The page does not say what that permission is or how it is shown; it names no advocate's stamp or signature.

m-be3e2c0f.t: On the Registrar's texts read 6 October 2026 (the form page, the form, the business-name guidance and the EE1 review criteria), registering a Cyprus business name online asks for no certification of the owner's signature by an officer: the 'solemn declaration of witness of signatures' attached to the e-filing (no fee) is a one-page Greek form in which a witness declares that the owner's handwritten signature on the business-name application (form EE1) was placed before him, with the witness's name, signature and date. The form, a file of December 2015, states no qualification for the witness.

m-bd487277.t: New registrations at the Cyprus Registrar of Companies by legal form, per the Registrar's own year-end charts: in 2024 - 14,444 companies, 96 partnerships, 1,824 business names, 43 overseas companies and 2 European companies or EEIGs; in 2025 - 16,781 companies, 108 partnerships, 1,914 business names, 55 overseas companies and none of the last kind. The charts (posted 10 January 2025 and 7 January 2026) count entities newly registered from 1 January to 31 December. They give no split by activity, and a business name is counted whether its owner is a person or a company.

m-add9e419.t: Which form new Cyprus businesses take, by activity, per Eurostat's business demography table (updated 1 October 2026; enterprise births in 2022, 2023, 2024). Food and beverage service (NACE division 56): 432, 487 and 439 births, of which sole proprietorships 282, 267 and 232 and limited liability enterprises 149, 219 and 199. Retail not in stores, stalls or markets (NACE group 47.9, which holds internet retail): 97, 105 and 78 births, sole proprietorships 55, 68 and 28. Computer programming and consultancy (division 62): 711, 438 and 433 births, of which limited liability enterprises 606, 364 and 353 and sole proprietorships 104, 74 and 80.

m-a7ae2318.t: For a company, limited liability in Cyprus comes from incorporation under the Companies Law, Cap. 113: under s. 3(1) seven or more persons, or for a private company 'one or more persons', associated for any lawful purpose may form a company with limited liability by subscribing the memorandum and registering; under s. 3(2)(α) each member of a company limited by shares is liable only for any amount unpaid on his shares. A one-person private company is therefore possible. A limited partner is not liable beyond his contribution, but a limited partnership needs at least one general partner liable for all its debts (Cap. 116, s. 47(2)). Read 6 October 2026.

m-a6127347.t: Public tenders in Cyprus are not reserved to companies. The Public Procurement Law 73(I)/2016 defines an 'economic operator' as any natural or legal person, public body or group of them that offers works, products or services on the market (s. 2), and s. 45(1) forbids rejecting operators entitled to provide a service in their home member state 'solely on the ground' that Cyprus law would require them to be natural or legal persons; groups may bid without a particular legal form, which may be required only after award (s. 45(3)-(4)). Read 6 October 2026, consolidated text with amendments through Law 113(I)/2025.

m-9e2cee69.t: A self-employed person in Cyprus who declares a trade name in his Tax Register request must attach the Registrar's certificate of registration of that business name: the Tax Department's page on registering individuals (updated 28 September 2026, read 6 October 2026) and its list of required documents (PDF of 7 October 2025) say 'In the case of entering a Business Name, the Certificate of Registration of the Business Name is to be attached'. So where a trade name is declared, business-name registration at the Registrar comes before the tax request; a person trading in his own name has no such step.

m-9b183f7e.t: The Ministry of Energy, Commerce and Industry's New Business Activity Support Scheme (THALIA 2021-2027, 2024 call) does not require a company but excludes shops. Beneficiaries 'will register as self-employed or may, if they wish, register a company or co-operative' holding at least 75% and sole management, and must remain its employees for three years after the grant is paid (7.3-7.4). Applicants must have lived lawfully in the government-controlled areas for 6 months, 'have the right of free access to employment' and be unemployed or employees (7.1). Annex I excludes wholesale and retail trade 'including e-commerce'. The call closed 31 July 2024; none later is listed (6 Oct 2026).

m-89b448ed.t: Form EE1 for registering a Cyprus business name (Registrar's PDF of 30 March 2015, served 6 October 2026; it cites 'Article 52 of the Law', Cap. 116) asks for the owner's names, a registration number of an unnamed register, identity card and passport numbers, date of birth, country of nationality, occupation and address; no field is labelled residence permit or immigration permission. The Registrar's attachment lists (page of 15 April 2019, read 6 October 2026) name a witness's solemn declaration (online) or EE1 (by hand), any permission the name's words or the business need, and €80 - no immigration document; the page points to the review criteria, which carry the non-EU permission.

m-785a0849.t: The Cyprus Registrar of Companies published year-end charts of new registrations for 2022 and 2023 too: 2022 (posted 3 January 2023) - 12,583 companies, 108 partnerships, 1,890 business names, 75 overseas companies; 2023 (posted 4 January 2024, on a page mistitled 'Total registered business entities as at 31/12/2023' whose text describes newly registered entities) - 12,674 companies, 107 partnerships, 1,863 business names, 56 overseas companies and 1 European company or EEIG. With the 2024 and 2025 charts this gives four years of the Registrar's own counts.

m-6ac57117.t: What a Cyprus partnership owes each year. It keeps books (Cap. 116, s. 64). Only where the sole or all general partners are limited companies (Cypriot, EU or comparable) or partnerships do the Companies Law's annual-return and accounts rules apply: the return within six months of the year-end, a late one charged €50, €1 a day for six months and €2 a day after, up to €500 (s. 64A). For tax, every partnership with business income has its accounts audited or reviewed by a licensed auditor unless the Commissioner exempts it (Law 4/1978, s. 30(1)(b): 'person' includes a partnership, which lacks the individual's turnover exemption). It is not a 'company' for income tax (Law 118(I)/2002, s. 2).

m-65600282.t: Cyprus consumer law reaches the officers of a company: under s. 65 of the Consumer Protection Law 112(I)/2021 (consolidated to Law 122(I)/2026, read 6 October 2026), where an infringement of the Law by a legal person is shown to have been committed with the consent, connivance or approval of, or facilitated by the neglect of, a director, manager, secretary or other officer, or a person acting as such, that natural person 'is also guilty' of the infringement.

m-62220f17.t: A sole trader can register a business name in Cyprus without a lawyer, on the Registrar's guidance read 6 October 2026: after name approval, and within one month of starting business, he files either form EE1 by hand or post, or the online form through e-filing as a registered user with a witness's solemn declaration of signatures, plus any authority's consent that the name's words or the business require; fee €80, plus €40 accelerated. Unlike company incorporation, the guidance asks for no statutory declaration sworn by an advocate and no memorandum, so no step of the self-employed path found in this round is reserved to an advocate.

m-5eaa3bd4.t: A partnership carrying on business in Cyprus, general or limited, must register with the Registrar of Companies within one month of its formation (Cap. 116, ss. 50(α), 51(1)). The statement, signed by all partners, gives the firm name, the nature and principal place of business, each partner's name, nationality and usual residence (for a legal person its name and office), the term and start date, whether it is a limited partnership, each limited partner's contribution, and the general partners authorised to manage and sign. Per the Registrar (read 5 October 2026): name approval first, then e-filing or form Σ1; fee €120, plus €40 accelerated; 'up to 100 partners'.

m-5c928444.t: Liability in a Cyprus partnership (Cap. 116, read 5 October 2026): every partner in a firm is liable jointly with the other partners for all debts and obligations of the firm incurred while he is a partner (s. 12). A limited partnership has one or more general partners liable for all debts and one or more limited partners liable only up to the amount contributed (s. 47(2)); a legal person may be a limited partner (s. 47(4)); limited partnerships 'are not considered legal persons with separate legal personality' (s. 47(6)); and one that is not registered as such is deemed a general partnership, every limited partner a general partner (s. 48).

m-55bc1575.t: A Cyprus business name carries no annual return and no yearly fee at the Registrar; Cap. 116 leaves four standing duties. Any change of the registered particulars is notified within seven days (s. 54(1)); cessation of business within one month (s. 57(1)); catalogues, circulars and business letters show the owner's name and, if he is not Cypriot, his nationality (s. 65(1)(β)); the Registrar may ask for the data to be confirmed (s. 58A(3)). A late notice of a new place of business or changed owner's particulars is charged up to €50 plus €1 a day, at most €250 (s. 61A(1)); while in default the owner cannot enforce the business's contracts by action unless a court grants relief (s. 62).

m-5307248d.t: As of 6 October 2026 the Cyprus Registrar of Companies' 'Business Name - e-Services' page links: name reservation at https://eforms.eservices.cyprus.gov.cy/MCIT/RCOR/NameApproval (opening it redirects to the CY Login sign-in), 'Business Name Incorporation' at https://efiling.drcor.mcit.gov.cy/drcorprivate/organizationselection.aspx (the e-filing system), and the register search at https://efiling.drcor.mcit.gov.cy/DrcorPublic/SearchForm.aspx?sc=0. Name-approval results are published through e-services. Online, the €80 registration fee is 'payable by credit card'; the page header sends unregistered users to CY Login sign-up.

m-380642e7.t: Stock of entities on the Cyprus Registrar of Companies' register as at 31 December 2025, per the Registrar's chart posted on 7 January 2026: 205,258 companies, 50,306 business names, 4,852 partnerships, 1,209 overseas companies, 16 European companies and 12 European economic interest groupings. The chart does not define 'registered'; the company figure evidently includes companies in the strike-off procedure or in liquidation, since the Registrar's open-data file of 29 September 2026 shows only 127,746 companies registered by end-2025 with the status 'registered' and 57,751 with 'reminder letter sent'.

m-37c64048.t: For an online business-name registration the Registrar's witness form (Greek, 'Annex A', file of December 2015, served 6 October 2026) has the witness declare only that the owner of the business name signed the application form EE1 by his own hand before him, and asks his name, signature and date; it sets no qualification and no oath before an official. On the Registrar's forms page the English link to this form points to a file named only '.pdf', which nonetheless serves the Greek form.

m-30ddcaaa.t: A Cyprus business-name statement (Cap. 116, s. 52(1)) gives the name, nature and principal place of the business, its start date and, for an individual owner, names, nationality and usual residence. Cap. 116 sets no nationality or residence condition; the duty to register falls on a person with 'a place of business in Cyprus' trading under a name other than his surname with his forenames or initials (s. 50(β)). Per the Registrar (read 6 October 2026) the name is approved first (€10 per name, €20 more accelerated; reserved six months), then filed within a month of starting business, by e-filing with a solemn declaration of the signatures' witness or on form EE1: €80, €40 more accelerated.

m-30d7aa27.t: The Cyprus Registrar of Companies names one place for filing by hand: its cashiers' office on the ground floor of the 'Xenios' Building, corner of Makariou III Avenue and Karpenisiou Street, 1427 Nicosia; post goes to the same address (page 'Submission by hand / post', read 6 October 2026). Both the name-approval application and form EE1 may go in this way; by hand the €80 EE1 fee is paid in cash, by cheque, from an account with the Department or by bank transfer. The page names no counter in Limassol, Larnaca or Paphos; the contact page gives telephone hours Monday-Friday 7:30-15:00 and no appointment rule.

m-2a503185.t: Among businesses that actually start trading in Cyprus, sole proprietors outnumber companies. Eurostat's business demography table by legal form (updated 1 October 2026) counts, for industry, construction and market services, 8,619 enterprise births in 2022 (4,878 sole proprietorships, 3,727 limited liability enterprises, 14 partnerships and the like), 8,797 in 2023 (5,301; 3,490; 6) and 9,152 in 2024 (5,666; 3,456; 30). An enterprise birth is a unit that becomes active, so the series is not comparable with the 12,600-14,400 companies entered in the Registrar's register in the same years.

m-27ab2fb0.t: Limited liability in a Cyprus company has a statutory exception applied by the court in a winding up. Under s. 311(1) of the Companies Law, Cap. 113, if in a winding up it appears that any business of the company was carried on with intent to defraud creditors of the company or of any other person, or for any fraudulent purpose, the Court, on application of the Official Receiver, the liquidator or any creditor or contributory, may, if it thinks proper, declare persons knowingly party to it personally responsible, 'without any limitation of liability', for all or any of the company's debts or liabilities as it directs; s. 311(3) also makes this an offence. Read 6 October 2026.

m-25e09dfb.t: Cyprus's state business development organisation (ΚΟΑΕ) defines beneficiaries without regard to legal form. The Cyprus Business Development Organisation Law 124(I)/2026 (Gazette No. 5094, 24 July 2026; in force from 6 August 2026 by Council of Ministers decision No. 984) lets it give loans, guarantees, grants and advisory programmes, only through its schemes, to micro, small and medium-sized enterprises as defined in Annex I to Regulation (EU) No 651/2014 'registered and active in the Republic' (ss. 2, 6(1)); 'enterprise' comes from s. 2 of Law 30(I)/2001: a natural or legal person, or a group or association of persons with or without legal personality, carrying on an economic activity.

m-0f84e7ef.t: Registrations at the Cyprus Registrar of Companies in 2022 and 2023 split by sub-type, counted from the Registrar's open-data register (file last modified 29 September 2026) by registration date: 2022 - 12,583 companies (12,452 of them private), 1,890 business names, 108 partnerships (70 general, 38 limited), 75 overseas companies; 2023 - 12,674 companies (12,561 private), 1,863 business names, 107 partnerships (78 general, 29 limited), 56 overseas companies. The totals equal the Registrar's own year-end charts for 2022 to 2025; the file holds no European companies or EEIGs (the 2023 chart shows one).

m-010cf27e.t: What became of the Cyprus companies registered in 2022, per the Registrar's open-data register of 29 September 2026: of 12,583, 7,459 (59.3%) are 'registered', 3,532 (28.1%) 'reminder letter sent', 375 (3.0%) 'three-month notice published', 1,010 (8.0%) struck off and 207 dissolved, merged or in liquidation. 3,518 of the reminder statuses are dated February 2026, the month of the Registrar's reminder letters of 9 February 2026 on overdue annual returns and financial statements (filing extended to 31 December 2026, then the s. 327 strike-off procedure). Of 1,890 business names registered in 2022, 196 are struck off; of 108 partnerships, 28.

m-e188b7c9.t: Mastercard chargeback time frames (Chargeback Guide, 19 May 2026, newest archived edition; 'all other transactions' rows): authorisation-related (4808) within 90 calendar days of the settlement or Central Site Business Date, 120 for ATM and Maestro transactions with both customers in Europe; no cardholder authorisation (4837) within 120 days; cardholder dispute (4853) over goods or services not as described between 15 and 120 days from that date or from delivery or cancellation, over goods or services not provided within 120 days of that date or of the delivery date the merchant named; interrupted services up to 540 days. The acquirer's second presentment is due within 45 days.

m-a7a46a6f.t: The thresholds Mastercard still prints are MATCH Pro listing reasons (Security Rules and Procedures - Merchant Edition, 4 August 2026). Code 04 'Excessive Chargebacks': the merchant's Mastercard chargebacks over the previous three months exceeded 1.5% of its sales transactions and reached USD 5,000 in total. Code 05 'Excessive Fraud': a fraud-to-sales dollar ratio of 8% or greater and 10 or more fraudulent transactions 'equal to or greater than USD 5,000' in the previous three months. Up to the edition of 6 August 2024 both were measured in one month: code 04 at 1%, code 05 with fraud 'totaling USD 5,000 or more'. The three-month wording first appears in the 11 February 2025 edition.

m-96a7accb.t: The PCI Security Standards Council is closing its two older phone-acceptance standards. A bulletin of 1 May 2026 opened a formal sunset period for PCI SPoC (Software-based PIN Entry on COTS) and PCI CPoC (Contactless Payments on COTS) running from 1 May to 31 October 2026: new submissions are accepted during the period and none after it. Existing SPoC and CPoC listings stay valid through their normal lifecycle and expire on their existing re-evaluation or expiry dates. The Council gives the continued expansion and maturity of MPoC as the reason and points vendors to MPoC 'where appropriate'. As of 4 October 2026 the sunset period is still running.

m-804999bd.t: Visa's public VAMP fact sheet (unchanged since at least 15 July 2025; read 5 October 2026) defines the VAMP ratio, for card-not-present transactions, as the count of fraud reports (TC40) plus disputes (TC15) divided by the count of settled transactions (TC05). An acquirer is 'Above Standard' at 50 basis points or more and 'Excessive' at 70 or more; a merchant of an acquirer that is neither is 'Excessive' at 220 or more, which the sheet says is cut to 150 on 1 April 2026 (AP, Canada, EU, US). Each level also requires at least 1,500 fraud-plus-dispute items a month there. Two enumeration thresholds are listed: a ratio of 2,000 basis points or more and 300,000 or more enumerated authorisations.

m-71e62ad5.t: Visa's Merchant Data Standards Manual of April 2026, marked 'VISA PUBLIC', prints the 'current high integrity risk MCCs'. For all card-absent transactions: 5122 (drugs), 5966 (outbound telemarketing), 5967 (adult content), 7273 (dating, escort), 7995 (betting) and - outside the US Region only if the merchant conducts non-domestic transactions - 5912 (pharmacies) and 5993 (cigar stores). For certain card-absent transactions: 4816 (cyberlockers), 6211 (trading platforms), 5968 (negative-option subscriptions), 5816 (skilled game wagering), 6051/6012 (crypto, with Special Condition Code 7). Under Visa rule 10.4.5.1 the non-public Visa Integrity Risk Program Guide remains the governing source.

m-708d775b.t: No PCI DSS self-assessment questionnaire is written for reader-less tap-on-phone acceptance: on 2 October 2026 the Council's Document Library listed nine merchant questionnaires, none for CPoC or MPoC solutions. SAQ SPoC, new with PCI DSS v4.0 (September 2023), is only for attended card-present merchants that enter all card data through a PCI-listed secure card reader (SCRP) paired with a phone or tablet in a listed solution. The SAQ Instructions and Guidelines (v4.0.1 r1, April 2025, read in a copy) do not mention CPoC or MPoC; by their residual row a merchant outside the listed descriptions falls to SAQ D - an inference: the Council leaves validation requirements to brands and acquirers.

m-4378677a.t: Mastercard printed its merchant chargeback thresholds in older public editions of the Security Rules and Procedures - Merchant Edition. The edition of 10 September 2019 (section 8.3.1) defines a Chargeback-Monitored Merchant as one with a chargeback-to-transaction ratio above 100 basis points and at least 100 chargebacks in a calendar month, and an Excessive Chargeback Merchant as one with at least 150 basis points and at least 100 chargebacks in each of two consecutive months. By the edition of 9 February 2021 the definitions refer to the Data Integrity Monitoring Program manual, though assessments are still computed above '150 basis points'; the edition of 26 October 2021 prints no figure.

m-42b16e3b.t: Visa Core Rules section 1.9.5.1 (ID# 0026383, edition 18 April 2026, last updated October 2024) adds two details to the High-Integrity Risk registration duty: the acquirer registers each High-Integrity Risk merchant 'using the Program Request Management application', and the merchant-registration duty does not apply to merchants under MCC 5122 or 5912 accredited by the National Association of Boards of Pharmacy or another regulatory body recognised by Visa. Section 10.4.5.2 (ID# 0026340) makes the acquirer keep daily data on such a merchant's gross sales, average transaction amount, receipts and disputes, and compare it daily with a baseline from the 31st day after the first deposit.

m-387d8f80.t: PCI DSS v4.0 added 64 new requirements (the Council's total): 13 applied at once to all v4.0 assessments, 51 were best practice until 31 March 2025, then mandatory. Of the 51, 41 are marked for all entities and 10 for service providers only (our count). The all-entity ones include 6.4.3 and 11.6.1 (payment-page scripts, tamper detection), 6.4.2 (automated protection of public web applications), 8.3.6 (passwords of 12 characters, or 8 where the system cannot support 12), 8.4.2 (multi-factor authentication for all access into the cardholder data environment), 5.4.1, 11.3.1.2 and 12.3.1. A merchant's questionnaire decides which apply: SAQ A dropped 6.4.3, 11.6.1 and 12.3.1 in January 2025.

m-341fe70f.t: The PCI standard for card acceptance on a phone is Mobile Payments on COTS (MPoC): published on 16 November 2022, revised as v1.0.1 in February 2023 and v1.1 in November 2024, still current in the Council's Document Library on 2 October 2026. MPoC builds on the two older standards - Software-based PIN Entry on COTS (SPoC) and Contactless Payments on COTS (CPoC) - allowing PIN and contactless entry on the same off-the-shelf device, with three product types: MPoC Software, an Attestation and Monitoring Service, an MPoC Solution. They are evaluated by PCI-recognised laboratories; the Council 'encourages' merchants and acquirers to choose a listed one and leaves any mandate to the brands.

m-3083db2c.t: Visa's revised Acquirer Monitoring Program (VAMP) took effect on 1 April 2025, merging its earlier fraud and dispute monitoring programmes into one acquirer programme, with an advisory period that Visa extended on 24 March 2025 to six months, 1 April to 30 September 2025. The public fact sheet dates the current thresholds from 1 June 2025 and the cut of the merchant threshold from 220 to 150 basis points (AP, Canada, EU, US) from 1 April 2026. Visa's page of 9 October 2025 says enforcement after the advisory period starts with the 'Excessive' level only. Brazil, Chile and India were to be announced separately.

m-2c59eb82.t: PCI DSS v4.0.1 has nine merchant self-assessment questionnaires (SAQ Instructions and Guidelines, v4.0.1 r1, April 2025): A - card-not-present merchants outsourcing all account data functions; A-EP - e-commerce sites that do not receive card data but affect the payment page's security; B - imprint or dial-out terminals; B-IP - standalone PCI-approved terminals with an IP connection; C-VT - manual entry into a third-party virtual terminal; C - payment applications connected to the internet; P2PE - terminals in a PCI-listed point-to-point encryption solution; SPoC - a phone or tablet with a listed secure card reader; D - all other merchants. All but D assume no electronic card-data storage.

m-2af92a25.t: No Visa Core Rules edition later than 18 April 2026 was published as of 5 October 2026: usa.visa.com, visa.co.uk and visa.com.cy serve the same 7,591,762-byte file (identical sha256), whose summary of changes runs 'since the 18 October 2025' edition. Of the 25 Visa rule IDs cited in the first-round records, three are stamped 'Last Updated: Apr 2026': sections 5.8.4.1 (ID# 0008635) and 5.2.1.6 (ID# 0028044) - a restructure effective 25 July 2026 that Visa says introduces 'no new requirements or change to existing intent' - and 1.9.8.6 (ID# 0025893), which gains a disclosure duty for the Canada and US Regions only, effective 24 October 2026.

m-2905d68b.t: Visa dispute time limits (Visa Core Rules, edition 18 April 2026): an issuer may dispute fraud in a card-absent transaction (condition 10.4) within 120 calendar days of the transaction processing date, and a declined-authorisation case (11.2) within 75. For merchandise or services not received (13.1) the limit is 120 days from the processing date or from the last date the cardholder expected delivery, not beyond 540 days from the processing date, after a 15-day wait in listed cases. The acquirer then has 30 calendar days from the dispute processing date: a pre-arbitration attempt for fraud and authorisation disputes, a dispute response for processing-error and consumer disputes.

m-2470f7bc.t: The number of PCI DSS requirements the PCI SSC assigns to an e-commerce SAQ A merchant changed between versions. The Council's slides of September 2023, for PCI DSS v4.0, give 11 requirements where the merchant has no access to its own website, 27 for a redirect to a compliant third party and 29 for that party's embedded payment form (iframe); SAQ A-EP stands at 139. The SAQ Instructions and Guidelines v4.0.1 r1 of April 2025 (read in a copy) give 14, 27 and 27, SAQ A-EP still 139; their change table says the October 2024 edition updated the SAQ A numbers and r1 corrected them. In between the Council added a requirement to SAQ A (October 2024) and removed three (announced 30 January 2025).

m-226d342e.t: Mastercard's current public manuals do not print its merchant chargeback thresholds. The Security Rules and Procedures - Merchant Edition of 4 August 2026 (s. 8.3) defines basis points as a merchant's chargebacks in a calendar month divided by its Mastercard transactions in the preceding month, times 10,000, but an Excessive or High Excessive Chargeback Merchant only as one 'identified as noncompliant' under Edit 2 in Chapter 8 of the Data Integrity Monitoring Program manual, a manual for Mastercard customers. This has been so since the edition of 9 February 2021 at the latest; the edition of 10 September 2019 printed the thresholds. Excessive Fraud Merchant thresholds are not printed.

m-1a6ada34.t: For e-commerce the PCI SSC's SAQ Instructions and Guidelines (v4.0.1 r1, April 2025, read in a copy) show which questionnaire 'may apply' to eligible merchants: a fully outsourced shop where the merchant has no access to its own webpage - SAQ A with 14 PCI DSS requirements; a redirect to a compliant third-party payment page, or that provider's embedded payment form (iframe) - SAQ A with 27; a payment form created by the merchant site and posted directly to the processor ('Direct Post'), or a merchant site that loads scripts into the consumer's browser - SAQ A-EP with 139; all other e-commerce implementations - SAQ D for Merchants with all PCI DSS requirements.

m-125fe3d6.t: Visa's public Acceptance Risk Standards (VARS, October 2024, control AHIR.C1.1) describe High Integrity Risk acquirer registration in three risk tiers. To apply, an acquirer submits the High Integrity Risk Acquiring Registration Application with documents for the chosen tier(s), attests in writing that no transaction in a VIRP category has entered or will enter the Visa system before approval, and pays a one-time non-refundable fee. Tier 1: an initial control assessment per merchant category and an annual self-assessment; Tier 2: an initial assessment and an annual self-assessment; Tier 3: registration, with a self-assessment on request. Which category sits in which tier is not stated there.

m-09cbae31.t: On 30 January 2025 the PCI SSC changed SAQ A for e-commerce merchants: it removed PCI DSS requirements 6.4.3 and 11.6.1 on payment-page scripts and tamper detection, and requirement 12.3.1 (the targeted risk analysis supporting 11.6.1), and added an eligibility criterion that the merchant 'confirm their site is not susceptible to attacks from scripts that could affect the merchant's e-commerce system(s)'. The October 2024 version of SAQ A was retired on 31 March 2025 and the January 2025 version took effect that day. The Council stressed that the change affects reporting in SAQ A and does not remove the underlying requirements from PCI DSS.

m-069812a3.t: Visa's Core Rules of 18 April 2026 extend an address-check liability shift to the Europe Region from 24 October 2026: under dispute condition 10.4 (card-absent fraud) an issuer's dispute is invalid for an authorised domestic transaction where the acquirer attempted the Address Verification Service and received result code U - unless the issuer could not answer because the card was a Visa Commercial Card or a non-reloadable prepaid card. Until 23 October 2026 the row covers Canada, the US and the UK. Section 10.11.1.2, with a printed effective date of 1 October 2025, requires Europe Region issuers to take part and verify the postal code. On 5 October 2026 the change is not yet in effect.

m-af4e7d43.t: Visa's public rules (edition 18 April 2026) put wallets that hand the card credential to the merchant - the model of Apple Pay and Google Pay - in their own class, 'Pass-Through Digital Wallet', outside the 'Digital Wallet Operator' class. The glossary defines it as functionality of a non-issuer that is usable at more than one merchant, stores a payment credential and transfers it directly to the merchant, after which the merchant 'finalizes the Transaction with its Acquirer, and the Pass-Through Digital Wallet is not involved in the Authorization, Clearing, or Settlement payment flow'. A Digital Wallet Operator is one operating a staged or stored-value wallet. Visa names no wallet brand.

m-3e1f1393.t: Mastercard's Rules (edition 2 June 2026) treat the wallet as Mastercard's customer, not the merchant's contractor. A 'Pass-through Digital Wallet' is functionality by which the operator stores account data provided by the cardholder and, at a transaction, 'transfers the Account data to the Merchant or Sponsored Merchant or to its Acquirer or the Acquirer's Service Provider'; its operator is 'a Digital Activity Customer or other Customer, approved by the Corporation'. Rule 9.2.2 forbids a pass-through operator to charge a merchant 'any fee or other charge for the acceptance of Mastercard Account credentials' (other fees only by agreement) or to restrict which interfaces a merchant supports.

m-fe80566b.t: B-READY 2025 counts an intermediary's fee in the Cyprus cost: the World Bank's reproducibility package (file BReady_Aggregate.xlsx) gives the Cyprus experts' median answer that 'Services of Third-Party Intermediaries' (the question names notaries, lawyers, accountants) are required by law to start a company, at 4 days and 1,450 (euro) - the largest per-step cost, against 575 for registry registration and 30 for name verification. This matches their answer that a limited company cannot be registered without a mandatory intermediary. The 1,450 is the experts' estimate, not an official fee; the handbook counts such a cost only where mandatory, as its own step.

m-fcd10ddb.t: Pending annual returns are common on the Registrar's free search, not a mark of the case companies: of eight unrelated companies taken by arbitrary registration numbers that had any HE32 in their file on 6 October 2026, seven list HE32 applications under 'pending services' - the oldest of 17 January 2018 (Psillides Painters Ltd, ΗΕ 56521), four since 19 June 2023 at Α.Χ.Π. Καλούπια Λτδ (ΗΕ 400000) - each also in the file's HE32 archive. All five of them registered in 2022-2024 leave 'date of last HE32 registration' empty, including Ermogenides, Yiallouros & Georgiou LLC (ΗΕ 452000), which has nothing pending. The search does not say what 'pending' means.

m-e14b2f5e.t: The World Bank's B-READY 2025 data (the first to cover Cyprus; workbook of 23 December 2025, report of 29 December 2025) give 11.5 calendar days for 'the entire company entry process' in Cyprus for domestic and foreign-owned companies alike, and a total cost of 1,920 (domestic) and 1,750 (foreign) in local currency (euro). These are expert answers with 1 September 2024 as reference point, not register measurements: average time in practice for the most common limited company in the largest city, with employees and turnover above the VAT threshold; cost is official fees plus the experts' estimate for steps without one (e.g. a bank account), excluding VAT, a lawyer counted only if mandatory.

m-e08d769d.t: The B-READY Methodology Handbook, Third Edition (January 2026, for the B-READY 2026 report), drops the per-step questions on business entry: experts give only total time and cost, from name verification to tax and employee registration, 'official fees only (exclude VAT)', third-party costs 'only if mandatory', overlapping steps timed by the longest. It adds five unscored questions for a foreign company: whether FDI screening is mandatory, its time, its cost including legal fees, whether a business bank account can be opened fully remotely, and how long that takes. The foreign case: USD 500,000 capital, 5 shareholders, 12 employees. So B-READY 2026 data can carry no per-step time for Cyprus.

m-dd1c4107.t: On 6 October 2026 the Registrar's free search shows the annual returns (HE32) lodged by three of the case companies still under 'pending services', with no date of a registered HE32: KFB Hospitality Concepts Ltd, application of 24 July 2025 (439 days earlier; return made up to 24 May 2025); Levasco Concept Ltd, applications of 14 October 2025 (357 days earlier) and 16 July 2026; Kuns Studio Ltd, application of 20 April 2026. The search does not say why; an HE32 listed there is a lodged return, not a registered one.

m-da95c0f7.t: As of 6 October 2026 no Cyprus authority publishes how long name approval or company incorporation takes. The Ministry of Energy, Commerce and Industry's latest posted annual report (for 2023, posted 2 October 2025; none for 2024 or 2025 on its page) says the Registrar's companies branch processes applications 'within the timeframes the Department sets per sub-branch' but prints none. The Registrar's monthly charts (latest posted 23 September 2026, to 31 August 2026) count applications submitted - searches, annual returns, register updates, certificates, name approvals, e-filings, s. 327 strike-offs - not durations. The Ministry's 2026 action plan sets no service time.

m-d2eb8645.t: The Cyprus Tax Department's guides to online registration of a legal or non-natural person and of a self-employed person (both last updated 28 May 2026, still linked on 6 October 2026) say that after submission, with reference REGxxx, 'processing of your request may take up to ten (10) days'; calendar or working days are not said, and the registration pages and FAQ state no time. The legal-person guide describes the Tax For All account route, closed to HE and AE companies and registered partnerships since 1 July 2026 (CY Login only); no text says the ten days apply to the CY Login route.

m-c977ad87.t: A registration date in the Cyprus register is not always a working day, so elapsed times read from it should be counted in calendar days. In the Registrar's open-data file of organisations (published monthly; version of 29 September 2026), among companies (type 'Εταιρεία', current name) with a registration date in 2025, 1,557 carry a Saturday and 1,090 a Sunday date - 2,647 of 16,780, or 15.8%; for 2023 the share is 819 of 12,674 (6.5%), for 2024 1,333 of 14,444 (9.2%). Two of the cases here are dated on Sundays: Kuns Studio Ltd on 31 December 2023 and Etxetera Ltd on 25 January 2026.

m-c40f2c9a.t: Cyprus Post runs Citizens Centers (KE.PO.) at its district post offices, per its page read 6 October 2026: Nicosia, 100 Prodromou Street, 2063 Strovolos; Limassol, 3 16th June 1943 Street, 3022; Larnaca, Vasileos Pavlou Square, 6023; Paphos, 23 Aristoteli Savva Street, 8025; and at Agros, Kakopetria, Pano Lefkara and Xylofagou post offices. They are open Monday to Friday 8:00-14:30, appointments 'can be booked online', and they serve, among others, the Deputy Ministry of Research, Innovation and Digital Policy, to which CY Login belongs; CY Login's help page lists KE.PO. as identification centres.

m-bad8af34.t: The B-READY 2025 Cyprus answers leave the bank account out of company entry: to 'Is opening a bank account required by law or commonly done in practice to start a domestic company?' the experts' median answer is No, so no time or cost for it is counted in the 11.5 days and 1,920. The questionnaire counts the step only where needed for entry, such as depositing paid-in minimum capital, and says to answer No where an account is opened only for operational reasons.

m-b510872a.t: Free to read about a Cyprus business on the Registrar's search, as of 6 October 2026: number, type, status and status date, registration date, directors and secretary (or a business name's owner), registered office or owner's address, 'pending services' with application dates, the date the last annual return (HE32) was registered, and lodged HE32 forms and accounts with the dates they are made up to - listed even while pending. No shareholders; at most 200 results per search; no details page opens outside a search. The register is also published monthly on data.gov.cy in three files (organisations, officials, registered offices), last modified 29 September 2026.

m-a90e1a15.t: Cyprus's Citizen Service Centres (KEP) are open Monday to Friday 8:00-17:00 and serve the public only by appointment, booked on 22309100 or at https://kep-kepo.gov.cy/appointments, per the Public Administration and Personnel Department's KEP page (update of December 2025, read 6 October 2026). Its address list (1 December 2025) gives: Nicosia, Georgiou Seferi (former State Fair), 2415 Engomi; Limassol, 21 Spyrou Araouzou, 3036; Larnaca, 42 Spyrou Kyprianou Avenue, 6051; Paphos, 62 Eleftheriou Venizelou Avenue, 8021; plus Famagusta (Deryneia), Kolossi, Polis Chrysochous and Pelendri. The page says the KEP offer about 100 services of several ministries.

m-a72bed26.t: In the World Bank's B-READY 2025 (101 economies; scores file of 10 December 2025; expert answers as of 1 September 2024) Cyprus scores 82.29 of 100 on Business Entry: 86.67 regulatory pillar, 73.33 digital public services and transparency, 86.86 operational efficiency. Sorting the 101 topic scores puts Cyprus 35th (Greece 3rd, Estonia 7th); the rank is our count. Behind the middle pillar the experts answered that incorporation service standards are not online, that there is no electronic, fully automated identity check of entrepreneurs at registration or of beneficial owners at their registration, and that key authorities do not exchange company information automatically and electronically.

m-8d6f9d41.t: The latest published measured times for premises steps in Cyprus found are World Bank B-READY 2025 aggregates (workbook of 23 December 2025). Expert consultations, reference date 1 September 2024: a building permit for a commercial office building takes 90 calendar days in total and costs 4,045 (currency unstated; presumably euro). Enterprise Survey medians (surveys run December 2021-March 2025): 120 days for a construction-related permit, 120 days for an electrical connection, 7 days for internet. These are aggregates for an office scenario, not a café's change of use. The discontinued Doing Business 2020 (data as of 1 May 2019) gave 507 days for a warehouse permit and 137 for electricity.

m-70cb1471.t: In B-READY 2025 each Cyprus figure is a separate median of the experts' answers (handbook Annex B), so the parts do not add up: the per-step medians sum to 20.5 days and 2,055, the questionnaire's own sum-of-steps field gives 21.5 days and 1,885, and the published total is 11.5 days and 1,920. For a foreign-owned company the median answers report no additional step and no step differing in time or cost, yet the published foreign total is 11.5 days and 1,750.

m-45dbdd23.t: Per the B-READY Methodology Handbook (Second Edition, final, December 2025), each expert reports for the Cyprus case: time as the average practical time from first to last step, waiting included, not the legal deadline, at least one day per step, simultaneous steps taken into account; cost as official fees, or a best estimate where a step has none (third-party services, company seal, bank account), VAT excluded, the total 'the exact sum of the costs per step'; a lawyer or notary only where mandatory, as its own step. The published figure is the median of the experts' answers (Annex B). The case: the most common limited company in the largest city, with employees and VAT-level turnover.

m-2d2aaf14.t: As of 6 October 2026 CY Login's help page names two kinds of 'Identification Centers' for in-person identification - the Citizen Service Centres (KEP) and Cyprus Post's Citizens Centers (KE.PO.) - and asks the visitor to check that the centre handles his type of profile, to have 'arranged an appointment in advance' and to bring the evidence. The KEP list of services (1 December 2025) carries 'Confirmation and approval of a natural person's profile in CY-Login' (7.01) and of a legal person's (7.02); identification by video call (7.03) is for Cypriot citizens only. Sign-up itself is online at https://cge.cyprus.gov.cy/cyloginregistration/register.

m-0789c2ea.t: The World Bank's B-READY 2025 reproducibility package (catalogued 29 December 2025, files of 14 April 2026) gives Cyprus per-step medians of expert answers, which its answer workbook omits: name verification 3 days and 30; beneficial-owner registration 1 day, 0; third-party intermediaries 4 days, 1,450; registration at the registry 6 days, 575; tax registration 2.5 days, 0; employer or employee registration 4 days, 0 (cost in euro). No bank account, general licence or other step is counted, and some steps are marked as done at the same time; the published totals are 11.5 days and 1,920.

m-72127d2b.t: The Cyprus Registrar of Companies' own annual-return date calculator (queried 5 Oct 2026) gives, for the first annual return of a company registered on 1 October 2026, the reference date 2 April 2028 and submission deadline 30 April 2028; registered 15 October 2026 - 16 April and 14 May 2028; registered 31 October 2026 - 1 May and 29 May 2028. It applies s. 120(1A)(α) of the Companies Law (first reference date: the day after 18 months from incorporation) and s. 120(1) (delivery within 28 days). Under the proviso to s. 125(1) the first annual general meeting need not be held in 2026 or 2027 if held within those 18 months, i.e. by 1-30 April 2028.

m-624c7e16.t: Cyprus statutory periods counted in days exclude the starting day: s. 31(α) of the Interpretation Law, Cap. 1 (cylaw consolidated text read 5 Oct 2026) says that, in computing time for the purposes of a Law or public instrument and unless the contrary appears, a period of days from an event is deemed to exclude the day on which the event happens; under s. 31(β), if the last day is a Sunday or public holiday the period includes the next day that is neither. Saturdays are not named. By its terms this governs the 60 days for a company's Tax Register notice and the 90 days for its first beneficial-owner filing, both counted from incorporation.

m-ddf591d5.t: The Central Bank of Cyprus register of e-money institutions held 29 licensed institutions at end-2025: its files dated 29 September 2025 and 27 February 2026 (web-archive copies) each list 29 EMIs and 7 withdrawn licences, and no licence or withdrawal is dated between 29 September 2025 and 24 June 2026. The Annual Report 2025 gives 28 EMIs that 'were operating' at year-end, though its own flows (26 at end-2024, 4 licensed and 1 withdrawn in 2025) give 29. Two of the 29 carry register notes that the e-money licence is not yet in use: Nec Pay Limited (licensed 12 August 2025) and Payabl. Cy Limited (still also a payment institution). The report does not say which institution it leaves out.

m-c49d20d7.t: ECB payments statistics, 'Electronic money institutions, Number of institutions', reference area Cyprus (series SSP.A.CY.122L.N50.1.U6.Z0Z.Z, annual, end of period): 2013 - 4; 2014 - 5; 2015 - 7; 2016 - 5; 2017 - 7; 2018 - 11; 2019 - 13; 2020 - 13; 2021 - 16; 2022 - 15; 2023 - 23; 2024 - 16; 2025 - 13. Payment institutions are published only from 2022: 14, 13, 18, 25. The two series sum to 36, 34 and 38 for 2023-2025 - the totals of the Central Bank of Cyprus Payment Statistics releases, not the 37 (26 EMIs + 11 PIs) and 40 (28 + 12) of its annual reports for 2024 and 2025; the EMI/PI split is the reverse of the annual reports'. No note says who is counted. Read 5 October 2026.

m-c3962a8d.t: Revolut in Cyprus, dated from registers and its own documents. The Central Bank of Cyprus register of e-money institutions passported into Cyprus (file updated 11 October 2018) lists the UK firm Revolut Limited with date of notification 2 June 2016; the file of 4 September 2019 adds Revolut Payments UAB (Lithuania), notified 7 December 2018. Revolut's post of 28 April 2022 announced that on 1 July 2022 Revolut Payments UAB would merge into Revolut Bank UAB and all its customers 'will be migrated to Revolut Bank UAB and become our bank’s customers from 1 July onwards'; the bank's audited 2022 statements confirm completion on 1 July 2022. Neither names Cyprus: both cover all EEA customers.

m-98bf2022.t: Dated stocks of e-money institutions licensed by the Central Bank of Cyprus, counted in its register files (web-archive copies and the live file): 18 on 28 February 2023; 23 on 23 November 2023; 29 on 14 July 2025, 29 September 2025 and 27 February 2026; 32 on 28 September 2026. Withdrawn licences listed: 2, 5, 6, 7, 7 and 8. The 23 of November 2023 equals the ECB figure for end-2023. End-2024 is not fixed by these files: the July 2025 list less its three 2025 licences gives 26, but Saamipay Ltd, withdrawn 9 July 2025, has no grant date. A file of 14 January 2020 is archived but encrypted; files named for 6 January 2021 and 18 May 2022 are indexed without content.

m-83b975bc.t: Authorisation dates in the Central Bank of Cyprus register of e-money institutions (file of 28 September 2026): of the 32 institutions listed, the original EMI licence dates from 2007 (1), 2014 (1), 2015 (1), 2016 (2), 2017 (4), 2018 (3), 2021 (3), 2022 (2), 2023 (5), 2024 (2), 2025 (4) and 2026 (4); none from 2019 or 2020. The nine granted before mid-2018 carry a 'current licence date' of 18 June-19 July 2018. Eight withdrawn licences are listed, six with dates (13 Feb 2019, 5 Aug 2020, 26 Jun 2023, 9 Jul 2025, 29 Sep 2025, 3 Aug 2026). Three withdrawn firms (FBME Card Services, Atlas Pay, Saamipay) have no grant date in any file read, so year-end stocks cannot be rebuilt exactly.

m-02a8f8d0.t: The Central Bank of Cyprus publishes different totals of payment and e-money institutions 'licensed in Cyprus'. Payment Statistics releases: 36 at end-2023 and 38 at end-2024 (release for the second half of 2024); 38 at mid-2024 and 41 at mid-2025 (first half of 2025); 34 at end-2024 and 38 at end-2025 (second half of 2025). Annual reports: 37 at end-2024 (26 EMIs + 11 PIs) and 40 at end-2025 (28 + 12). The releases draw on the ECB payments-statistics collection (Regulation ECB/2013/43): their totals equal the sums of the ECB's two 'number of institutions' series for Cyprus, revised between releases (end-2024: 38, then 34); the annual reports count licences. Neither says who is counted.

m-00ca6cb1.t: Two firms appear in both Central Bank of Cyprus registers (files of 17 and 28 September 2026): Payabl. Cy Limited and Paycomcy Limited are listed as payment institutions and, licensed 4 January 2024 and 24 June 2026, as e-money institutions, each with a note that it keeps its payment-institution licence until the e-money licence 'gets activated'. The 32 e-money and 10 payment-institution rows are therefore 40 legal entities. The register also separates the licence date from a 'Start of operations permit' - Sliq Payments: licensed 14 July 2023, permit 17 January 2025 - and marks four institutions licensed in 2025-2026 'the operations shall commence upon approval granted by the CBC'.

m-feab2f65.t: Central Bank of Cyprus registers, read on 2026-10-04: the register of electronic money institutions (file dated 28.09.2026) lists 32 institutions authorised by the CBC — four of them with licence dates in 2026 (Paycomcy 24 June, Iconglobal 15 July, Quickpay Tech and Mustpa 4 August) — and eight withdrawn licences, the latest La Orange CY Limited on 3 August 2026; the register files of 29 September 2025 and 27 February 2026 each list 29. The register of payment institutions (file dated 17.09.2026) lists 10 payment institutions and 1 account-information service provider; Masari Payment Services' licence was withdrawn on 28 January 2026. Passported EU firms are kept in separate registers and are not in these counts.

m-e711c122.t: The Central Bank of Cyprus' public register of electronic money institutions (file dated 28 September 2026) carries 32 institutions with a licence number on its 'EMIs' sheet. One is marked as terminating, four may commence only upon CBC approval, and two (Payabl. Cy Limited, Paycomcy Limited) hold an EMI licence not yet activated and still operate under payment-institution licences; 25 rows carry no such note. The register of payment institutions (file dated 17 September 2026) carries 10 licensed payment institutions, including those two, plus one account-information service provider: 41 distinct licensed entities. Withdrawn licences (8 EMI, 6 PI) sit on separate sheets and are not counted.

m-dc54effb.t: Wise's help article 'How can I verify my business?' (updated 7 September 2026) says a Wise Business sign-up needs the business registration number, registered and trading addresses, industry, details of directors and owners and, if the applicant is not a director, proof of authority; on further review it asks for proof of business registration, proof of trading address, ownership documents and personal ID. A one-time setup fee is mandatory in some regions, and additional review 'usually takes up to 10 working days'. For EEA customers the provider is Wise Europe SA, a payment institution authorised by the National Bank of Belgium - not a Cyprus licensee and not a credit institution.

m-c3f16213.t: The Central Bank of Cyprus EMI register (file dated 28/09/2026) lists the Cyprus-licensed EMIs behind three online-payment brands: Unlimit EU Ltd (formerly CardPay Limited; licence 115.1.3.7/2018, HE328641, services 3(c), 5, 7), Nuvei Limited (formerly Safecharge Limited; 115.1.3.9/2018, HE129880, services 3 and 5) and TFI Ecommpay Ltd (formerly TFI Markets Ltd; 115.1.3.52, HE253524, EMI licence 14/07/2023, services 3(c), 4(c), 5, service 5 added 14/07/2026). Service 5 is 'issuing of payment instruments and/or acquiring of payment transactions'; the register does not say which a firm does. Unlimit and Nuvei passport their services EEA-wide; TFI Ecommpay's passport rows cover only 3(c), 4(c).

m-a87e5412.t: Licensed institutions, Central Bank of Cyprus counts at end-2025 (Annual Report 2025, Table 5.2): 17 entries under 'credit institutions' — 5 local authorised, 3 subsidiaries of EU banks, 1 of a non-EU bank, 3 EU branches, 4 non-EU branches and 1 representative office — plus 28 electronic money institutions and 12 payment institutions authorised by the CBC (passported firms are not counted). End-2024: 26 EMIs and 11 PIs. The numbers do not reconcile: Table 5.3 shows 4 EMI licences granted and 1 withdrawn in 2025 (26 + 4 − 1 = 29), the CBC's EMI register shows two withdrawals in 2025 (9 July and 29 September), and its files of 29 September 2025 and 27 February 2026 each list 29 EMIs against the 28 of Table 5.2. The CBC register read on 2026-10-04 lists 4 local authorised credit institutions.

m-9e0dc764.t: The Central Bank of Ireland register (page last updated 1 October 2026) lists myPOS Limited, reference C475122, as an e-money institution authorised on 16 September 2022 for payment services 3(a), 3(b), 3(c) and 5 (issuing/acquiring of payment transactions), with Cyprus among the states where it operates on a freedom-of-services basis. GLEIF records MYPOS LIMITED under LEI 984500FR5373B5043A92, Irish company number 700880, entity status ACTIVE - the company number given in myPOS's Legal Agreement.

m-8f6f881a.t: Money held with a Cyprus electronic money or payment institution is safeguarded, not deposit-guaranteed. By statute it is not a deposit (Electronic Money Law 81(I)/2012 art. 15(3)-(4); Payment Services Law 31(I)/2018 art. 18(3)), and recital 29 of Directive 2014/49/EU keeps e-money outside deposit guarantee. Law 31(I)/2018 art. 10(1), replaced by Law 100(I)/2025 (June 2025) and now covering EMIs, gives two methods: no commingling and, by the end of the next day, a separate account at a credit institution or central bank, or secure low-risk assets; or insurance or a comparable guarantee from an insurer or credit institution outside the group. Scheme members are credit institutions only.

m-818a205e.t: myPOS serves Cyprus merchants through myPOS Limited, an Irish company (no. 700880) authorised by the Central Bank of Ireland as an electronic money institution (ref. C475122) on 16 September 2022, with acquiring among its services and Cyprus covered under freedom of services; the Central Bank of Cyprus lists it among incoming EMIs. The merchant's contract is the 'Legal Agreement for the myPOS Service' (last updated 3 April 2026), accepted electronically by clicking 'Accept', governed by Irish law, with the Acceptance Policy, tariff and application form as inseparable parts.

m-64209949.t: SumUp serves Cyprus through SumUp EU Payments UAB (Lithuania, company code 305074395). Its Greek-language Cyprus site (sumup.com/el-cy, read 2026-10-04) says the company is authorised by the Bank of Lithuania as an electronic money institution, 'licence number 56, 27 August 2019' - the number is SumUp's own. The Bank of Lithuania register shows an EMI licence valid from 2019-08-27 (authorisation code LB001900) and lists Cyprus among the countries served without a branch, with issuing of payment instruments and/or acquiring from 2019-10-30. The Central Bank of Cyprus register of incoming EMIs (file dated 23/09/2026) lists it with notification date 06/11/2019 and services 2, 3, 5.

m-603a1f78.t: RCB's successor held an e-money licence briefly: the Central Bank of Cyprus register of electronic money institutions (file dated 28.09.2026), sheet of withdrawn licences, lists 'Finstella Ltd', licence no. 115.1.3.60, 'licence withdrawn on 26/06/2023'. Finstella Ltd is the present name of the entity with LEI 253400EBCBBVB9TUHN50, formerly RCB Bank Ltd, whose banking licence the ECB withdrew in December 2022.

m-56863d59.t: Non-bank access to central-bank payment rails in Cyprus: the TARGET-CY System (Amending) Directive of 2025, K.D.P. 293/2025 (Official Gazette Annex III(I) No. 5972, 3 October 2025), in force from 6 October 2025, adds 'non-bank payment service providers' as defined in ECB Decision (EU) 2025/222 — payment institutions and e-money institutions — to the entities the Central Bank of Cyprus 'may at its discretion' admit as TARGET-CY participants. Admission is conditional (compliance with the national rules transposing Art. 35a(1) of PSD2) and the accounts carry a maximum holding amount. Whether any non-bank PSP has been admitted was not established as of 2026-10-04.

m-1cb28bad.t: Entry into the Cyprus EMI/PI licence changed on 3 August 2026: by announcement of 31 July 2026 the Central Bank of Cyprus introduced a 'pre-application exploratory stage' before a licensing application for a payment or electronic money institution can be submitted, with a non-refundable €5,000 fee and a preliminary assessment within 30 working days (50 if an enhanced due-diligence report is requested), followed by 'Application Submission and Assessment'. The application fee rose from €5,000 to €10,000; inactive applications are deemed withdrawn. Stated aims: transparency about CBC requirements and early identification of issues, 'particularly with regard to the criterion of good repute'.

m-f3753573.t: From 10 July 2027 Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 (AMLR; in force, applies then) adds two foreign-element duties. Nominee shareholders and directors must disclose their status, nominator and its beneficial owners to the legal entity, which reports them to the central register and to obliged entities (art. 66). A legal entity created outside the Union must first file its beneficial owners with the register of the Member State where it buys real estate or costly vehicles, vessels or aircraft, wins a public contract, or opens a business relationship with an obliged entity - the last only if that obliged entity, or the foreign entity's type or sector, is rated medium-high or high risk (art. 67).

m-9cafc834.t: Unlike the companies register, Cyprus's register of beneficial owners of trusts (kept by CySEC under s. 61Γ of the AML Law) has a published legitimate-interest route. Under CySEC Directive K.D.P. 257/2021 as amended by K.D.P. 77/2025 (in force 18 March 2025), a person files a duly substantiated request to CySEC through the register's system (para. 13) and pays €75 per express trust or similar arrangement for a written report (para. 10(4)); obliged entities pay €4 per trust (para. 10(3)).
