K.D.P. 243/2026 (Gazette No. 6026, 29.5.2026, in force on publication) deleted only para. 14 and fee para. 10(5) - the route of s. 61Γ(12)(δ), which Law 25(I)/2026 art. 4(γ) had removed. Read 5 Oct 2026.

m-9b075a65.t: For the beneficial-owner register the Cyprus Registrar of Companies offers access through CY Login by the legal entity's own profile or by that of its official (a natural or legal person). Its guidance page (served 5 October 2026) marks the official route: 'Currently this procedure applies only to Cypriot citizens holding a Cypriot identity card'; its Guidance to the register, version 2.1 of February 2025, repeats this and adds that identification 'via passport number is not accepted'. On these texts a non-Cypriot director files through the company's own profile. CY Login's help page, the same day, accepts residence permits and EU registration certificates for natural-person profiles.

m-4381ba61.t: For a company incorporated in October 2026 the Registrar's notice of 16 September 2026 on the yearly confirmation of beneficial-owner details (window 1 October - 31 December 2026) says: where the deadline for the initial submission (90 days from incorporation) falls within the window, or the initial registration is made within it, the details must also be confirmed by 31 December 2026, once. By our arithmetic (incorporation day excluded, per s. 31(α) of the Interpretation Law, Cap. 1) the 90 days end between 30 December 2026 (incorporated 1 October) and 29 January 2027 (31 October). The notice is silent on a company first filing in January 2027; first confirmation in late 2027 is inferred.

m-210284d3.t: A director without a Cypriot identity card - EU citizen or third-country national - cannot, on the Registrar's guidance, file a company's beneficial-owner details through his personal CY Login profile: the 'Guidance for the Beneficial Ownership Register' (Version 2.1, February 2025, the edition linked on 5 Oct 2026) and the Registrar's page on access say identifying a natural person's profile for this purpose is 'at present' possible 'only for Cypriot citizens holding a Cypriot identity card'; a passport number is not accepted. Two routes remain: the company's own CY Login profile, verified in person, or the profile of an officer that is a legal person. Filing at ubo.meci.gov.cy is free.

m-fb27075d.t: Law 25(I)/2026 (Official Gazette No. 5079, 20.3.2026; harmonising with Art. 74 of Directive (EU) 2024/1640; no commencement clause) replaced s. 61A(6)(α)(iii) of the AML Law: instead of 'a member of the general public', the beneficial-owner register is open to a person or association proving a legitimate interest in access for the purpose of preventing and combating money laundering and terrorist financing, limited to the owner's name, month and year of birth, country of residence, nationality and the nature and extent of the interest. As of 4 Oct 2026 no implementing directive or procedure was found; the Registrar's FAQ still offers search to authorities and obliged entities only.

m-cde7500d.t: As of 4 Oct 2026 a newly incorporated Cyprus company must file its beneficial-owner details in the Registrar's electronic register within 90 days of incorporation (para. 9(1) of Directive K.D.P. 112/2021), record any change within 45 days of learning of it (para. 10(2)) and confirm the details between 1 October and 31 December each year (para. 10(3)). All three periods were set by amending Directive K.D.P. 34/2024 (Official Gazette No. 5851, 29.1.2024), replacing 30 days, 14 days and a 1-31 December window; K.D.P. 423/2024 (No. 5913, 16.12.2024) restated para. 9 and placed the duty on the company alone instead of the company and each officer.

m-cab1df21.t: The central register of beneficial owners of companies and other legal entities in Cyprus is drawn up, kept and published by the Registrar of Companies under s. 61A(4)(β) of the AML Law (Law 188(I)/2007). Its rules are in the Registrar's Directive K.D.P. 112/2021 (Official Gazette No. 5479, 12.3.2021), amended by K.D.P. 317/2021, 101/2022, 116/2022, 401/2023, 34/2024, 120/2024 and 423/2024; no later amendment appears in the cylaw index of regulatory acts to 25 Sep 2026. Filing through an interim system opened on 16 March 2021 and the final system went live on 14 November 2023. The register is electronic only; no documents or fees are submitted when filing.

m-c1be706a.t: Until 20 March 2026 the text of art. 61A(6)(a)(iii) of Cyprus Law 188(I)/2007, as enacted by Law 13(I)/2021 (Official Gazette no. 4809, 23 February 2021), gave 'a member of the general public' access to the name, month and year of birth, nationality and country of residence of a company's beneficial owner and the nature and extent of the interest held. Law 141(I)/2024 left that sub-paragraph untouched; Law 25(I)/2026 (Official Gazette no. 5079, 20 March 2026) replaced it with access for persons who prove a legitimate interest, eight months after the 10 July 2025 deadline of art. 74 of Directive (EU) 2024/1640.

m-903bcf56.t: As of 4 Oct 2026 the Cyprus Registrar of Companies publishes two routes to beneficial-owner data, both for obliged entities only: an e-request in the register system, approved by Registrar officials, €3.50 per legal entity (FAQ 'E-search'), and the 'Application for Beneficial Ownership report of a Legal Entity' by hand or post (since 1 August 2022): €3.50 per entity, €7.00 for Greek and English, with a solemn declaration whose single wording (file dated 2 January 2023) is that of an obliged entity under art. 2A of the AML Law asking for customer due diligence. No form, fee or procedure exists for a person claiming a legitimate interest under s. 61A(6)(α)(iii) as replaced by Law 25(I)/2026.

m-87ec15f0.t: Law 141(I)/2024 (Official Gazette no. 5017, 6 December 2024) cut the administrative penalty for a Cyprus company that fails to file its beneficial-owner details under art. 61A(10) of Law 188(I)/2007 from EUR 200 plus EUR 100 per day up to EUR 20,000 (as enacted by Law 13(I)/2021) to EUR 100 plus EUR 50 per day up to EUR 5,000, and obliged the Registrar of Companies to notify each entity by letter or e-mail at least 30 days before a filing or confirmation deadline. According to the Registrar (read 4 October 2026) non-compliance is penalised from 1 February 2025.

m-7bba6788.t: UBO register, chain of deadlines (Registrar of Companies): notice of 1 September 2023 — file by 30 September 2023; final system live 14 November 2023; period to 31 December 2023 without charges; charges paid between 1 and 16 January 2024 were refunded after the deadline moved to 31 March 2024 (announcement 17 January 2024; K.D.P. 34/2024 of 29 January 2024); penalties announced from 1 April 2024; K.D.P. 120/2024 of 29 March 2024; Law 141(I)/2024 of 6 December 2024; K.D.P. 423/2024 of 16 December 2024 — deadline 31 January 2025, confirmation for 2024 extended to 31 March 2025, charges imposed since 1 April 2024 revoked; penalties from 1 February 2025.

m-7487996b.t: UBO register, interim solution: the Registrar of Companies' directive K.D.P. 112/2021 on the register of beneficial owners of companies and other legal entities was published in the Official Gazette No. 5479 on 12 March 2021 and is in force from publication; existing entities got six months to file, new ones 30 days from incorporation. The Registrar's announcement of 12 March 2021 said the e-filing service 'will be available on 16.03.2021': 12 March is the legal start, 16 March the announced opening of e-filing. Its February 2024 guidance says the register holds no beneficial-owner data from before 12 March 2021 and that the final system replaced the interim one on 14 November 2023.

m-6785b008.t: Law 141(I)/2024 (Official Gazette No. 5017, 6.12.2024) replaced s. 61A(10)(ε) of the AML Law: a company that fails to file its beneficial-owner details is charged €100 plus €50 for each day the breach continues, capped at €5,000, and its director or managing director is jointly and/or severally liable for the charge; the Registrar may also strike the company off under s. 327 of the Companies Law. Under s. 61B (other legal entities) the cap is €2,000. The earlier amounts, €200 plus €100 per day up to €20,000, had been fixed by the same provision as enacted by Law 13(I)/2021 and repeated in Directive K.D.P. 112/2021. The Registrar stated that charges would be imposed from 1 February 2025.

m-52c8cf51.t: The Registrar of Companies states in guidance (served 4 Oct 2026) that beneficial-owner details may be submitted only by the entity's own officer or partner, 'and not by a person acting on its behalf (e.g. a service provider), unless he/she is an official/partner in that entity'; the Directive itself (K.D.P. 112/2021, para. 17) only requires electronic filing with access codes obtained by the entity. Cyprus companies, European companies and partnerships must file; overseas companies, business names and companies listed on a regulated market are exempt. The indicator of ownership is 25% plus one share or an ownership interest above 25%; failing that, the senior managing official is recorded.

m-42e0d689.t: As of 4 Oct 2026 the Registrar's Directive on the beneficial-owner register has not been aligned with either change to public access: para. 12(1)(γ) of K.D.P. 112/2021, never amended, still gives 'any member of the wider public' electronic access to the owner's name, month and year of birth, nationality, country of residence and interest for a fee of €3.50 per entity, although the Registrar suspended that access by announcement from 23 November 2022 and Law 25(I)/2026 replaced public access in s. 61A(6)(α)(iii) of the AML Law with a legitimate-interest test on 20 March 2026. Only K.D.P. 116/2022 amended para. 12, adding access for audit bodies of EU funds.

m-41373bc4.t: Access to Cyprus's beneficial-owner register passed through three regimes in 2021-2022: at first only competent and law-enforcement authorities could consult it; from 1 June 2022 the general public and obliged entities could obtain a report for a fixed fee of €3.50 per company; and from 23 November 2022 the Registrar suspended access for the general public by announcement, following the CJEU judgment of 22 November 2022 in joined cases C-37/20 and C-601/20 (ECLI:EU:C:2022:912), while keeping access for authorities and for obliged entities that add a solemn declaration that the request serves customer due diligence. The statute itself kept its public-access wording until March 2026.

m-38f84cde.t: The Registrar of Companies heads the Department of Registrar of Companies and Intellectual Property under the Ministry of Energy, Commerce and Industry — the name since Law 133(I)/2021 (Gazette of 12 October 2021), after official-receiver functions moved to the Department of Insolvency. Art. 61A(4) of AML Law 188(I)/2007 still says the Central Register of Beneficial Owners of Companies and Other Legal Entities is compiled, kept and published by the 'Registrar of Companies and Official Receiver'; art. 7(1)(γ)(iii) of Law 133(I)/2021 reads that as the Registrar of Companies. The Registrar is a registry authority, not one of the AML supervisory authorities listed in art. 59 of that Law.

m-36c6d21e.t: Cyprus banks must report beneficial-ownership discrepancies. Art. 61A(5)(b) of Law 188(I)/2007 obliges obliged entities to report to the Registrar of Companies any difference they find between the beneficial-owner information in the register and the information available to them, and CBC Directive of 2025 para 37(13) requires the bank to investigate such a difference and, where necessary, file a suspicion report with MOKAS. According to the Registrar, discrepancy reports can be submitted electronically since 1 April 2024, and the company is given 30 days to answer the Registrar's notice with a reasoned statement and evidence. In force on 4 October 2026.

m-d1577f69.t: Law 36(I)/2023 (Official Gazette No. 4947, 2 June 2023) amended Article 60(1) of the Cyprus Payment Services Law 31(I)/2018 by replacing its opening word 'Where' with 'Subject to paragraph (5) of Article 62, where'. Since then the duty to tell the payer in advance about a charge or discount for a given payment instrument is expressly subordinate to the rule that a payee may not request charges for using a specific payment instrument. The preamble says the Law re-harmonises with Article 60(1) of Directive (EU) 2015/2366; PSD2 Article 62(5) lets Member States 'prohibit or limit the right of the payee to request charges'. CyLaw's consolidated text, read 4 October 2026, shows the new wording.

m-9f552687.t: The Cyprus Government reads Article 62(5) of Law 31(I)/2018 as a ban with no exceptions. The report of the House Finance and Budget Committee of 23 May 2023 records the Ministry of Finance explaining that the Consumer Protection Service, investigating complaints about payees charging for card use, had found an 'interpretative conflict' between Articles 60(1) and 62(5), and that 'the legislator's intention was the universal prohibition, without exceptions' of such charges. The Committee reserved its position for the plenary; the House then passed the Bill as Law 36(I)/2023. That commercial and three-party cards are covered is an inference from 'without exceptions', not the report's words.

m-97c81247.t: The Consumer Protection Service polices the Cyprus surcharge ban under powers written into the Payment Services Law by Law 16(I)/2022 (Official Gazette No. 4876, 4 March 2022). Article 99(1A) makes it the competent authority for payees' compliance with Articles 60 and 62; Article 99A lets it demand information from a payee, inspect its premises and order it to stop an infringement at once; Article 99B allows, after hearing the payee, an administrative fine of up to EUR 2,000 and, if the infringement continues, up to EUR 100 a day, recoverable as a civil debt. Giving the Service false information is a criminal offence (up to six months in prison, a fine up to EUR 10,000, or both).

m-2c1686ce.t: No published decision or judgment applying the Cyprus surcharge ban was found on 5 October 2026. The Consumer Protection Service's 2022-2026 decision lists hold 94 entries. Titles name only sanction and trader, but each entry has a code for the law applied and Article 99B caps a surcharge fine at EUR 2,000: of the 15 fines at or under that amount nine were opened and six share the price-monitoring code - all under other laws. CyLaw's search of all Cypriot judgments returns five naming Law 31(I)/2018 and one with the wording of Article 62(5) - Trustdon Investments Ltd v Eurobank Ltd (Nicosia District Court, action 3380/2017, 9 September 2026), on unauthorised payments; none is on a surcharge.

m-10096c1a.t: No Commission or EBA answer on surcharging commercial or three-party cards was found on 5 October 2026 in the two places looked. The Commission's PSD2 FAQ (MEMO/15/5793, dated 12 January 2018) says surcharging is banned wherever card charges are capped under the Interchange Fee Regulation and that the ban covers 'some 95% of all card payments in the EU' (its own estimate, unexplained); it names neither card type. For the rest, PSD2 Article 62(5) lets Member States 'prohibit or limit' the payee's right to charge. The EBA Q&A tool has no final answer under 'surcharge' or 'surcharging'; its only payments question so titled (2019_4576, on currency conversion) was rejected on 11 February 2022.

m-fef169a8.t: Before a user is bound by a framework contract, Cyprus Law 31(I)/2018 art. 51(1) requires the provider to give, in good time and on paper or another durable medium, the terms listed in art. 52, in clear wording and in an official language of the Member State of the service or another agreed one; a draft contract suffices (art. 51(3)). Art. 52 lists seven groups: the provider, use of the service, charges and rates, communication, safeguards and liability, changes and termination, and redress including any choice of law or court. Art. 53 lets the user obtain the terms on request at any time; art. 40(1) bars charging for it; art. 41 makes the provider prove it met these information duties.

m-d8dbd345.t: Unauthorised payments under Cyprus Law 31(I)/2018 (read 4 Oct 2026): the user notifies without undue delay and within 13 months of the debit date (art. 71(1)); the provider must prove authentication and accurate recording, and recorded use of an instrument is not necessarily sufficient proof of authorisation (art. 72); the provider refunds by the end of the next business day unless it has reasonable grounds to suspect fraud and reports them to the Central Bank in writing (art. 73(1)); the payer may bear up to EUR 50 for a lost, stolen or misappropriated instrument - nothing if it was undetectable to him beforehand - and all losses if he acted fraudulently or with gross negligence (art. 74).

m-b1fa6f04.t: Cyprus Payment Services Law 31(I)/2018 (in force since 18 April 2018; consolidated text read 4 October 2026), art. 38: Part III - transparency of conditions and information requirements - applies to single payment transactions and to framework contracts, and the parties may agree that it does not apply in whole or in part where the payment service user is not a consumer (art. 38(1)). Art. 38(2) applies Part III to micro-enterprises in the same way as to consumers, so a micro-enterprise cannot contract out. Art. 2 defines a micro-enterprise by arts 1 and 2(1) and (3) of the Annex to Recommendation 2003/361/EC, tested at the time the contract is concluded.

m-aafe6be4.t: A Cyprus merchant may not surcharge card payments. Article 62(4) of Law 31(I)/2018 repeats PSD2 Article 62(4): no charge for instruments with interchange regulated by Regulation (EU) 2015/751 or for payments under Regulation (EU) No 260/2012. Article 62(5), unchanged since 18 April 2018, adds, unqualified, that the payee is not permitted to request charges for the use of a specific payment instrument - on its wording also commercial and three-party cards. Paragraph (3) reproduces PSD2's cost-based allowance, and no court or Central Bank reading was found (4 October 2026). Visa section 1.5.5.2 (ID# 0006948, 18 April 2026) bans surcharges unless law expressly requires that they be permitted.

m-9748ee8f.t: The European Banking Authority does not license or supervise individual Cyprus payment firms. Under art. 15 of Directive (EU) 2015/2366 (PSD2; in force and not repealed per its CELLAR notice on 4 October 2026) it develops, operates and maintains the electronic central register of the information notified by national competent authorities (for Cyprus, the Central Bank), is responsible for presenting it accurately and makes it public free of charge; the national authorities remain responsible for the accuracy of what they notify and for keeping it up to date (art. 15(3)). EBA drafts the technical standards for the register, which the Commission adopts (art. 15(4)–(5)).

m-8d484d43.t: What a business may waive under Cyprus Law 31(I)/2018 art. 61(1), as amended by Law 32(I)/2019 art. 5 (Official Gazette No. 4690, 15 March 2019): where the user is not a consumer, the parties may agree that art. 62(1) (charges), art. 64(3)-(4) (withdrawal of consent), art. 72 (provider's burden of proving authentication), art. 74 (payer's liability capped at EUR 50), arts 76-77 (refunds of payee-initiated payments), art. 80 (irrevocability), and arts 89-90 (liability for non-execution or defective execution) do not apply in whole or in part, and may agree time limits other than the 13 months of art. 71. Art. 61(2) applies Part IV to micro-enterprises in the same way as to consumers.

m-79b58202.t: PSD3 and the Payment Services Regulation, dated steps: Commission proposals COM(2023) 366 (directive) and COM(2023) 367 (regulation) 28 June 2023; Parliament first-reading position 23 April 2024; Council negotiating mandate 18 June 2025; provisional agreement between Council and Parliament 27 November 2025; COREPER confirmation 22 April 2026; ECON approval of the agreed text 5 May 2026. Status on 2026-10-04 for both files: 'Awaiting Council's 1st reading position' (EP Legislative Observatory), indicative plenary date 14 December 2026; the Council's state-of-play note of 2 October 2026 lists no later step. Neither act is adopted or published; PSD2 and Cyprus Law 31(I)/2018 remain in force.

m-4d7cf8ee.t: Changes to a framework contract under Cyprus Law 31(I)/2018 art. 54: the provider must propose any change to the contract or to the art. 52 information at least two months before its proposed date of application, on paper or another durable medium (art. 54(1)); if the contract so provides, silence counts as acceptance, and the user may terminate free of charge before that date (art. 54(2)). Changes in interest or exchange rates may apply immediately and without notice if the contract says so and they follow agreed reference rates (art. 54(3)); rate changes in the user's favour need no notice (proviso to art. 54(4)). Charges are art. 52 information, so a fee change falls under art. 54(1).

m-18b2e9c7.t: Ending a framework contract under Cyprus Law 31(I)/2018 art. 55: the user may terminate at any time unless a notice period of not more than one month is agreed (art. 55(1)); termination is free of charge unless the contract has been in force for less than six months, and any charge must be reasonable and in line with costs (art. 55(2)); the provider may terminate a contract of indefinite duration only if the contract so provides and with at least two months' notice on paper or another durable medium (art. 55(3)); regular charges are due only pro rata and prepaid charges are refunded pro rata (art. 55(4)). Art. 55(5) leaves national rules on rescission and nullity untouched.

m-1265a1c6.t: What the PSD2 transposition changed in the statutory terms of a framework contract in Cyprus: the repealed Payment Services Law 128(I)/2009 let a user terminate free of charge only after 12 months from conclusion (art. 43(2)) and capped the payer's liability for a lost or stolen instrument at EUR 150 (art. 57(2)); Law 31(I)/2018, in force from 18 April 2018, cut these to 6 months (art. 55(2)) and EUR 50 (art. 74(1)). Unchanged: two months' notice of contract changes (art. 42(1) of 2009; art. 54(1) of 2018), two months' notice of termination by the provider (art. 43(3); art. 55(3)), and a user notice period of not more than one month. Both laws treat micro-enterprises like consumers.

m-06443526.t: PSD2 does not apply to 'services provided by technical service providers, which support the provision of payment services, without them entering at any time into possession of the funds to be transferred' (IT, network, terminals), payment initiation and account information services excepted (Directive (EU) 2015/2366, Article 3(j), as replaced by Directive (EU) 2022/2556 from 17 January 2025; in force on 4 October 2026). Article 4(44) defines acquiring as contracting with a payee to accept and process payment transactions 'which results in a transfer of funds to the payee'. Inference: a gateway-only or terminal-only contract is outside licensing only while the provider never holds funds.

m-05224147.t: Cyprus transposed PSD2 by the Provision and Use of Payment Services and Access to Payment Systems Law of 2018, Law 31(I)/2018, published in Official Gazette No. 4649 on 18 April 2018 and in force from publication (Article 112) - 95 days after the transposition date of 13 January 2018 - except the security measures of Articles 65, 66, 67 and 97, in force within 18 months of the regulatory technical standards entering into force. It repealed the Payment Services Laws of 2009 and 2010 (Article 111) and, per CyLaw's consolidated text read 4 October 2026, was amended by Laws 32(I)/2019, 16(I)/2022, 36(I)/2023, 16(I)/2025 and 100(I)/2025; CyLaw's 2026 index (to No. 125(I)/2026) shows no later one.

m-d9b53118.t: Since 27 March 2023 EU law forbids allowing Russian nationals or natural persons residing in Russia 'to hold any posts in the governing bodies of the owners or operators of critical infrastructures, European critical infrastructures and critical entities' (art. 5o(1) of Regulation (EU) No 833/2014, inserted by Regulation (EU) 2023/427; consolidated text of 24 July 2026). The exemption is narrower than in the Regulation's deposit and trust provisions: it covers nationals of an EU or EEA state or of Switzerland, not holders of a residence permit there (art. 5o(2)). It is a rule on board seats in a defined class of undertakings, not a general bar on Russian nationals directing EU companies.

m-562c12fc.t: Art. 2 of Regulation (EU) No 269/2014 freezes funds 'belonging to, owned, held or controlled by' listed persons and bars making funds available to them 'directly or indirectly'. In its non-binding Opinion of 19 June 2020, C(2020) 4117 final, the Commission takes the view that once a listed person is determined to control an unlisted entity, control 'can be presumed' to extend to all its assets, which 'must be frozen' unless the entity shows, under national procedure, that given assets are not controlled; funds made available to such an entity are 'in principle' made indirectly available to the listed person unless it is reasonably determined they will not reach him.

m-c75247c6.t: In Cyprus the reports required by art. 5r(1) and (2) of Regulation (EU) No 833/2014 go to the National Sanctions Implementation Unit of the Ministry of Finance. Its document 'Reporting/Disclosure Obligations to the NSIU' (posted 24 April 2026, read 5 October 2026) says notifications 'shall be submitted electronically by all persons, using prescribed templates', to sanctions.compliance@mof.gov.cy, and attaches separate templates for art. 5r(1) (EU companies more than 40% Russian-owned) and art. 5r(2) (credit and financial institutions), plus templates for art. 5a and for arts. 8-9 of Regulation (EU) No 269/2014. It adds that the templates 'are due to be revised shortly'.

m-f02400d7.t: Art. 5m of Regulation (EU) No 833/2014, in force on 4 October 2026 (inserted by Regulation (EU) 2022/576 from 9 April 2022; wording of 2022/879, para 4 of 2022/1904), prohibits registering, or providing a registered office, business or administrative address or management services to, a trust or similar legal arrangement whose trustor or beneficiary is a Russian national, a resident of Russia, an entity established in Russia, an entity they own above 50% or control, or anyone acting for them; and, since 5 July 2022, acting as trustee, nominee shareholder, director or secretary for such a trust. Exempt: nationals of, or residence-permit holders in, an EU or EEA state or Switzerland.

m-affb7af0.t: Art. 5r of Regulation (EU) No 833/2014 (inserted by Regulation (EU) 2023/2878 of 18 December 2023; in force on 4 October 2026) puts a reporting duty on EU-established companies more than 40% owned, directly or indirectly, by a Russian national, a natural person residing in Russia or an entity established in Russia: since 1 May 2024 they report to their Member State's competent authority, within two weeks of the end of each quarter, any transfer of funds exceeding EUR 100,000 out of the Union. Since 1 July 2024 credit and financial institutions report each semester the outbound transfers above EUR 100,000 in total that they initiated for such companies.

m-a1b049f5.t: The Central Bank of Cyprus's sanctions rulebook on 4 October 2026 is still its Directive for compliance with UN Security Council resolutions and EU Council decisions and regulations (First Edition, March 2020), issued under Law 58(I)/2016. That Law was repealed in July 2025, but s. 37(3) of Law 150(I)/2025 keeps supervisory directives issued under it in force until replaced; no replacement was found. It requires screening of new customers and related parties (directors, beneficial owners, signatories, nominees, trustees) before any service or transaction (para 26(a)), reporting of true matches to the Central Bank (paras 33-35) and a yearly report of frozen balances by 31 January (para 37).

m-a1843c93.t: Since 25 August 2026 Russian nationals and natural persons residing in Russia may not directly or indirectly own or control, or sit on the governing bodies of, any legal person incorporated under the law of an EU Member State that provides crypto-asset services as defined in Regulation (EU) 2023/1114; from 18 January 2024 the ban covered only providers of crypto-asset wallet, account or custody services. The extension was made by Council Regulation (EU) 2026/1848 of 23 July 2026 (the 21st package, in force the day after publication), which replaced art. 5b(2a) of Regulation (EU) No 833/2014. Nationals and residence-permit holders of an EU or EEA state or Switzerland are exempt (art. 5b(3)).

m-89697bc1.t: Art. 5n(1) of Regulation (EU) No 833/2014 (in force 4 October 2026, wording of Regulation (EU) 2025/2033) bans legal advisory services and 'accounting, auditing, including statutory audit, bookkeeping, tax consulting and business and management consulting, or public relations services' 'to the Government of Russia or to legal persons, entities or bodies established in Russia'. The accounting-to-consulting ban dates from Regulation (EU) 2022/879 (4 June 2022), legal advice from 2022/1904 (7 October 2022). The text names neither Russian nationals nor EU companies they own. Services strictly necessary for court, administrative or arbitral proceedings in a Member State are exempt (5n(5)-(6)).

m-7df1b1cb.t: On 4 October 2026 the 'Circulars' page of Cyprus's National Sanctions Implementation Unit (gov.cy/nsiu) carries no circular, in English or Greek; 'Guidance' holds only a link to the Commission's FAQs on Russia and Belarus sanctions. The Unit publishes the three laws of 25 July 2025 (150(I), 149(I), 148(I)/2025, in Greek only), a FAQ posted 8 September 2025, an online licence-application service, news items (e.g. 24 July 2026 on the 21st package) and a note 'Reporting/Disclosure Obligations to the NSIU' (posted 24 April 2026): information on funds of designated persons is due within two weeks. The FAQ says licence decisions can be challenged by hierarchical recourse (s. 12, Law 150(I)/2025).

m-6d10ea31.t: EU sanctions limit deposit-taking by Cyprus banks from Russian clients. Art. 5b(1) of Regulation (EU) No 833/2014 (inserted by Regulation (EU) 2022/328, in force 26 February 2022; consolidated text of 24 July 2026) prohibits accepting deposits from Russian nationals, residents of Russia, entities established in Russia, or non-EU entities more than 50% owned by such persons, if total deposits per credit institution exceed EUR 100,000. Exempt: nationals of, or residence-permit holders in, an EU or EEA state or Switzerland (art. 5b(3)). Deposits for non-prohibited EU-Russia trade are no longer exempt: since Regulation (EU) 2022/1269 (21 July 2022) they need an authorisation (art. 5c(1)(f)).

m-43e4268d.t: Belarus's counterpart of Russia's deposit and payment-services bans is art. 1u of Regulation (EC) No 765/2006 (consolidated text of 24 July 2026). The ban on deposits above EUR 100,000 per bank from Belarusian nationals, residents and entities dates from Regulation (EU) 2022/398 (in force 10 March 2022); Regulation (EU) 2025/392 added non-EU entities >50% Belarusian-owned and a crypto-wallet ban; Regulation (EU) 2025/2041 widened that to all crypto-asset, payment, acquiring and e-money services. EU, EEA and Swiss nationals and permit holders are exempt. Art. 1jc is narrower than Russia's: accounting, audit, tax and legal advice are barred only to the Belarusian state and its agents.

m-3f049716.t: Art. 5b of Regulation (EU) No 833/2014 as in force on 4 October 2026 (consolidated text of 24 July 2026) is a patchwork of four amending acts. Para 1 (no deposits above EUR 100,000 per credit institution from Russian nationals, residents of Russia, entities established there or non-EU entities more than 50% owned by them) has the wording of Regulation (EU) 2022/1269; para 2 (no crypto-asset services, payment instruments, acquiring, payment initiation or e-money) that of Regulation (EU) 2025/2033; para 2a that of Regulation (EU) 2026/1848; para 3 (exemption for EU, EEA and Swiss nationals and holders of a residence permit there) that of Regulation (EU) 2023/2878.

m-3bfa0692.t: Sanctions enforcement unit: Law 150(I)/2025, published in the Official Gazette No. 5050 on 25 July 2025 and in force from publication, establishes within the Ministry of Finance a directorate called the National Sanctions Implementation Unit (ΕΜΕΚ; internationally NSIU) to apply and supervise EU restrictive measures and UN Security Council sanctions as regards financial sanctions and to coordinate all authorities; it took over the pending requests of ΜΕΚ and ΣΕΟΚ. Law 149(I)/2025, same issue, criminalises violations of EU restrictive measures (Directive (EU) 2024/1226). The Unit is operating as of 2026-10-04: its website (gov.cy/nsiu), launched 14 May 2026, takes licensing requests online.

m-2587c2e6.t: Sanctions pressure, 12 April 2023: OFAC, in coordination with the United Kingdom, designated 25 individuals and 29 entities with touchpoints in 20 jurisdictions; its release has a section 'Usmanov's Cyprus Network' and names Cyprus national Demetrios Serghides. OFAC's SDN notice of that day, which also carries State Department designations, lists 34 individuals and 91 entities; 16 and 18 of them respectively have a Cyprus address, nationality or passport (verifier's count on 2026-10-04), including the Nicosia law firm Christodoulos G. Vassiliades & Co. LLC. The UK the same day sanctioned two 'Cypriot professional enablers', Demetris Ioannides and Christodoulos Vassiliades.

m-1810818c.t: Cyprus Law 149(I)/2025 criminalising violations of Union restrictive measures (Official Gazette no. 5050, 25 July 2025; transposes Directive (EU) 2024/1226) has no commencement section, so it applies from publication (Constitution art. 82). S. 15(1) repealed Law 58(I)/2016, the earlier sanctions statute. A natural person faces at most five years' imprisonment and/or a fine of up to EUR 100,000; for most offences that tier requires funds worth at least EUR 100,000 (s. 7). A legal person faces a fine of up to 1% or 5%, by offence, of worldwide turnover in the financial year before the offence or, if neither that nor the latest approved accounts can be used, up to EUR 8 or 40 million (s. 8).

m-11e45204.t: Since 24 October 2025 EU sanctions bar payment services for Russian clients. Regulation (EU) 2025/2033 replaced art. 5b(2) of Regulation (EU) No 833/2014, prohibiting the provision of crypto-asset services, issuing of payment instruments, acquiring of payment transactions, payment initiation services and issuing of electronic money to Russian nationals, natural persons residing in Russia and entities established in Russia. Nationals of, and residence-permit holders in, an EU or EEA state or Switzerland are exempt (art. 5b(3)); authorities may authorise exceptions (arts. 5c, 5d). The rule binds acquirers, payment and e-money institutions in Cyprus directly (consolidated text of 24 July 2026).

m-02566155.t: Cyprus Law 150(I)/2025 (Official Gazette no. 5050, 25 July 2025) makes sanctions compliance a supervised duty of every AML obliged entity: it must have policies, controls and systems to identify, assess, mitigate and manage the risk of breaching sanctions (s. 25(1)) and must pass to the National Sanctions Implementation Unit any information on a possible breach (s. 26(1)). Its supervisory authority may issue binding directives (s. 25(3)) and fine a non-compliant entity up to EUR 500,000 plus up to EUR 500 a day (s. 27(1)(b)). The Unit itself may fine up to EUR 100,000 plus EUR 100 a day for breach of the reporting duty of s. 19, which gives two weeks to report frozen funds (s. 29(1)).

m-ee9808dc.t: Whether a newly formed Cyprus company may have a review instead of an audit in its first or second financial year is not answered by any public official text found as of 4 Oct 2026. Section 152A(1)(d) of the Companies Law requires the limits to be met for at least two consecutive financial years; ICPAC's TC 2/2026 (19 February 2026) repeats this, has no first-period example and refers to TC 5/2022 'Guide to Review Engagements' (10 August 2022), whose link leads to the members' login. The Registrar's news list has six items for 2026 to 30 September, none on it. Tax Department guidance was not searched. The one explicit statement found is a provider's: the first two periods need an audit.

m-d82dccd2.t: ICPAC's Technical Circular 2/2026 (19 February 2026, Audit and Assurance Committee) reads the commencement of art. 5 of Law 2(I)/2026 as follows: because art. 5 entered into force on publication, the €300,000 net-turnover limit for choosing a review instead of an audit applies to reporting periods beginning on or after 6 February 2026; periods beginning earlier are tested against €200,000. For a calendar-year company the first financial year under the new limit is therefore 2027, not 2026. The Law itself has no transitional clause: art. 7(2) only says art. 5 enters into force on publication. This is the professional body's reading, not a ruling of the Registrar or a court.

m-d665bcde.t: Cyprus tax law does not narrow the review option for companies: s. 30(1)(b) of Law 4/1978 requires accounts that are 'audited or reviewed ... as provided in the Companies Law' by a person licensed to be appointed company auditor, and s. 5(1A) ties the later return deadline to accounts that are 'audited or reviewed'. Section 29, as replaced by Law 243(I)/2025 (in force 1 January 2026), lets the tax authority disregard accounts not prepared and certified by a statutory auditor or audit firm, and tax computations not prepared and certified by a holder of a practising certificate from ICPAC or another recognised body of auditors. Read on cylaw 4 Oct 2026.

m-d0ef51ac.t: The Institute of Certified Public Accountants of Cyprus (ICPAC, ΣΕΛΚ) is the AML supervisory authority for the professional activities of its members and of firms controlled by its members, expressly including trust and company services to third parties (art. 59(1)(δ) of Law 188(I)/2007). In tax procedure, from 1 January 2026 the Tax Commissioner may disregard accounts not prepared and certified by a statutory auditor or audit firm under the Auditors Law 53(I)/2017, and tax computations not certified by a holder of an ICPAC practising certificate or of another recognised body of auditors (art. 29 of Law 4/1978 as replaced by Law 243(I)/2025).

m-cf36c4c7.t: The Determination of Financial Reporting Standards Law of 2026, Law 1(I)/2026 (Gazette No. 5071, 6.2.2026), makes ICPAC the competent authority for setting Cyprus financial reporting standards: ICPAC develops a standard and submits it to the Minister of Finance, who approves it, notifies the European Commission for its approval and publishes the standard so approved in the Official Gazette (ss. 2-5). Publication of the 'Financial Reporting Standard for small-sized entities' starts the clock for most of Law 2(I)/2026 (in force on 1 January of the following year). On 4 Oct 2026 neither ICPAC's website nor cylaw's 2026 index of regulatory acts (to 25.9.2026) showed a published standard.

m-c15c6b76.t: Law 2(I)/2026 also lets a small-sized company prepare its financial statements under a national 'Financial Reporting Standard for small-sized entities' instead of IFRS; those provisions enter into force on 1 January of the year after the standard is published in the Official Gazette. A press report of 26 May 2026 carried ICPAC's announcement that it had appointed the standard-setting committee and that the implementation timeline would be determined later. On 4 Oct 2026 ICPAC's 'FRS for SEs Standard' web section listed only the committee, its terms of reference and a due-process handbook - no standard.

m-c14101ac.t: Since the Companies (Amendment) (No. 2) Law 2022, Law 88(I)/2022 (Official Gazette No. 4897, 24.6.2022; in force 1 January 2023 and applying to financial statements for periods ending on 31 December 2022 or later), a private limited company may have its financial statements reviewed under ISRE 2400 by a statutory auditor or audit firm instead of audited, provided its net turnover and total assets stay within set limits for at least two consecutive financial years. The limits enacted in 2022 were €200,000 of net turnover and €500,000 of total assets; turnover for this test includes rents, interest, dividends and royalties.

m-bbb040e6.t: Size of the pool of licensed professionals a Cyprus company can hire, by ICPAC's own count as at 31 August 2026: 1,122 statutory auditors and 786 statutory audit firms; 1,392 individuals and 985 firms holding general practising certificates; 469 individuals and 316 firms licensed as administrative services providers; 86 insolvency practitioners; 6,291 members in total. ICPAC's public registers (statutory auditors, audit firms, accountants, accounting firms, ASP licensed persons, ASP firms) are search pages 'as at the current date' that load names on request and print no total.

m-aad85c7f.t: In Cyprus a statutory audit may be carried out only by statutory auditors or audit firms licensed under the Auditors Law (Law 53(I)/2017, s. 33(1)); a review in place of an audit must likewise be done by a statutory auditor or audit firm (Companies Law s. 152A(1)(d)). The Auditors Law makes the Cyprus Public Audit Oversight Board (ΑΔΕΕλΕπ) the competent authority for licensing, oversight and discipline (ss. 4, 5(1), 33(2)); as of 4 Oct 2026 ICPAC states that it licenses statutory auditors under a Delegation Agreement with the Board and publishes their lists. A company obliged to have an audit or review appoints its auditor at each annual general meeting (s. 153(1)).

m-7e7fdee6.t: Market prices for the yearly accounts of a small Cyprus company, as published by one service provider on 14 July 2026 (Savva Cyprus) - not an official or professional-body tariff: full statutory audit €1,200-€3,500+, review engagement under ISRE 2400 €600-€1,500, statutory accounting €1,000-€2,500+. Another provider (Zeno, 3 July 2026) puts the all-in yearly cost of a dormant company at roughly €1,250-€2,150 and of a small trading company with VAT and two employees at €3,500-€5,500. No ICPAC fee guide was found on ICPAC's website on 4 Oct 2026.

m-780bc6bd.t: ICPAC Technical Circular 2/2026 (19 February 2026) applies the two-consecutive-years test of s. 152A(1)(d) of the Cyprus Companies Law year by year, each year against the turnover limit in force for that year. Its example 3: a company with net turnover of €150,000 in the year ended 31 December 2026 (old €200,000 limit) and €250,000 in the year ended 31 December 2027 (new €300,000 limit), total assets €400,000 in both, is eligible for a review for 2027. Its example 1: €250,000 in each of the years ended 28 February 2025, 2026 and 2027 - not eligible for the year to February 2027, because the earlier year exceeded the €200,000 then applicable.

m-72847054.t: Section 152A(1)(a) of the Cyprus Companies Law (Cap. 113) requires every private limited liability company - like public companies, public-interest entities and companies that must consolidate - to submit its financial statements to audit by statutory auditors or audit firms. Private limited companies have been listed there since Law 97(I)/2016 (Gazette No. 4576, 23.9.2016), applied to statements ending on 31 December 2016 or later. As of 4 Oct 2026 the Law has no size-based exemption from external examination; the only relief is the review option of s. 152A(1)(d), whose limits (€300,000 turnover, €500,000 assets) lie far below the statutory 'small-sized company' category.

m-40c42453.t: A reading of the two-year condition for the Cyprus review option that no official source confirms: Savva Cyprus (14 July 2026) states that, because both limits must be met for two consecutive financial years, every new company undergoes a full audit for its first two financial periods and can switch to a review only from year 3. The statute (Companies Law s. 152A(1)(d), first proviso) allows a review 'only in cases where, at the balance-sheet date, [the companies] do not exceed or cease to exceed the limits of the two criteria ... for at least two consecutive financial years'. No ICPAC or Registrar guidance on newly formed companies was found on 4 Oct 2026.

m-1d69b3e1.t: Under s. 142(2)(a) of the Cyprus Companies Law (Cap. 113) a company's financial statements are filed with the Registrar no later than 18 months after incorporation, then at least once every calendar year, and within 12 months of the balance-sheet date (the 12-month limit was added by Law 191(I)/2020, Gazette No. 4794, 17.12.2020). The Registrar's guidance, read 4 Oct 2026, adds that none are filed in the year of incorporation, nor in the next year if a general meeting was held in the year of incorporation. Under s. 151(1)(η)-(θ) unlisted small-sized companies are exempt from the management report; medium-sized ones only from its non-financial information; the guidance wrongly exempts both.

m-150c1d27.t: Article 5 of the Companies (Amendment) Law 2026, Law 2(I)/2026 (Official Gazette No. 5071, 6.2.2026), raised the net-turnover limit for choosing a review instead of an audit under section 152A(1)(d) of the Companies Law from €200,000 to €300,000; the total-assets limit stays at €500,000. Article 5 entered into force on publication, 6 February 2026. The relief is closed to parent companies that must prepare consolidated statements and their subsidiaries, to groups exceeding the limits, and to companies supervised by the Central Bank of Cyprus, the Superintendent of Insurance or CySEC and holders of qualifying holdings in them.

m-0e985f67.t: As of 4 Oct 2026 the Cyprus 'Financial Reporting Standard for small-sized entities' is not published, so the bulk of Law 2(I)/2026 has not started: under art. 7(1) it enters into force on 1 January of the year after the Standard is published in the Official Gazette. ICPAC's General Circular 6/2026 (25 May 2026) reports only that its Council appointed the Financial Reporting Standards Setting Committee, that the Standard will be based on the IFRS for SMEs Accounting Standard and be voluntary for eligible small-sized entities, and that 'the implementation timeline will therefore be announced at a later stage'. ICPAC's web pages 'The Standard' and 'Consultation' are empty.

m-ed4dd02b.t: The Central Bank of Cyprus publishes its own English texts of the deposit-guarantee rules: an unofficial consolidation of the Scheme Regulations of 2016 to (No. 2) of 2020 (latest update 16 November 2020) and of the Scheme Laws of 2016 to 2021 (latest update 30 July 2021). Its 'Legal Framework DGS' page, as served on 5 October 2026, lists the basic Regulations and four amendments (2016, 2018, 2020 and No. 2 of 2020) and the basic Law and four amendments (2018, two of 2020, 2021), and nothing later. The consolidation gives the look-through rule as reg. 10(e), the client-account holder's information duty as reg. 10(g) and the e-money exclusion as s. 3(2) of the Law.

m-e853b626.t: Cyprus raised the extra deposit-guarantee cover for temporary high balances in 2020. Reg. 8(2) of K.D.P. 27/2016 covered such deposits - for example proceeds of transactions in private residential property - up to EUR 50,000 above the EUR 100,000 limit for up to six months; K.D.P. 84/2020 (6 March 2020), reg. 7(b), replaced 'fifty thousand euro (EUR 50,000)' with 'three hundred thousand euro (EUR 300,000)' and 'six (6)' with 'twelve (12)'. The Central Bank's FAQ (file dated 8 October 2025) states the cover as up to EUR 300,000 for no longer than 12 months.

m-deec706c.t: EBA Opinion EBA/Op/2021/11 of 27 October 2021 found that deposit guarantee schemes treated client funds differently as Member States read arts. 5(1) and 7(3) of Directive 2014/49/EU differently: among the 27 of 30 EEA states that answered its survey, client funds placed with banks by payment institutions were covered in 16 and not in 10 (one unsure), those placed by e-money institutions in 13 and not in 13 (one unsure). It recommended clarifying the Directive so that client funds deposited by credit, payment and e-money institutions and investment firms are covered where the clients are not excluded, the deposit segregates their funds as the law requires and the clients are identifiable.

m-b6b2b3bf.t: The term 'client account' entered Cyprus's deposit-guarantee regulations with K.D.P. 84/2020 (6 March 2020): an account whose absolute beneficiaries are persons other than those in whose name it is held and which is held on their behalf. The same instrument added reg. 10(g): every holder of a client account must obtain and keep accurate and up-to-date information on the persons absolutely entitled to the money, including their identity, and give it to the credit institution and/or the scheme's Management Committee within seven working days of a request. The definition does not depend on who the holder is and mentions neither payment or e-money institutions nor safeguarding.

m-a2bbadb8.t: Deposits with credit institutions established in Cyprus are covered by the Deposit Guarantee and Resolution of Credit and Other Institutions Scheme up to EUR 100,000 per depositor per credit institution, including accrued interest (CBC page and FAQ, read 4 October 2026). Company deposits are eligible, but 'deposits by financial institutions' are excluded; it is the CBC's FAQ, not the regulation text read, that counts as such companies whose main activity is acquiring participations (holding companies), lending, leasing, payment services or portfolio management. The EU definition behind the exclusion (CRR art. 4(1)(26), as amended in 2024) carves out a 'pure industrial holding company'.

m-45664163.t: Directive (EU) 2026/804 of 30 March 2026 (OJ 20 April 2026, in force 10 May 2026) amends the Deposit Guarantee Schemes Directive to cover safeguarding accounts expressly. A new art. 8b obliges Member States to guarantee 'client funds deposits' that financial institutions place with a bank for the account of their clients, where the clients are themselves eligible, the deposits sit in segregated accounts under EU safeguarding rules, and the clients are identified or identifiable. The EUR 100,000 limit applies to each client and, by derogation from art. 7(1), the client's own deposits at the same bank are not added. Member States must adopt the measures by, and apply them from, 11 May 2028.

m-2922adac.t: Does Cyprus's deposit guarantee cover customers of a payment or e-money institution whose safeguarding account is at a Cyprus bank? On 4 October 2026 the texts pull two ways. The regulations define a 'client account' regardless of who holds it and cover the persons absolutely entitled (K.D.P. 27/2016 reg. 10(e), K.D.P. 84/2020); 'irrespective of the account holder' is FAQ wording only. That fits a payment institution's segregated account. But art. 3(2) of Law 5(I)/2016 puts 'amounts defined as electronic money' outside the scheme, which tells against cover for e-money holders. No Cyprus text names safeguarding accounts; the express EU rule (Directive (EU) 2026/804) applies from 11 May 2028.

m-237bb07f.t: The Central Bank of Cyprus' deposit-guarantee FAQ (file dated 8 October 2025, q.24) states that, irrespective of the account holder, the scheme covers the absolute beneficiaries of 'client accounts', provided they are not themselves in an excluded category, and that the holder must keep up-to-date information on them. Deposits held by payment service providers in their own right fall under the excluded 'deposits by financial institutions' (FAQ q.15(d)). The FAQ does not say whether the safeguarding account of an e-money or payment institution at a Cyprus bank counts as a client account, so look-through cover for its customers is not established (read 4 October 2026).

m-129c886b.t: The look-through rule of Cyprus's deposit guarantee scheme is reg. 10(e) of the Deposit Guarantee and Resolution of Credit and Other Institutions Scheme Regulations (K.D.P. 27/2016, 11 February 2016): where the depositor is not absolutely entitled to the sums in an account, the guarantee covers the person who is, provided that person's identity is or can be established before the deposit becomes unavailable; where several are entitled, each one's share under the arrangements governing the money counts towards the EUR 100,000 limit. The Regulations were amended by K.D.P. 73/2016, 136/2018, 84/2020 and 267/2020; the CyLaw lists for 2021-2026 show no later amendment (checked 4 October 2026).

m-0db15524.t: Cyprus's deposit-guarantee statute excludes electronic money in terms. Art. 3(2) of the Deposit Guarantee and Resolution of Credit and Other Institutions Scheme Law 5(I)/2016 (CyLaw consolidated text with amendments up to Law 119(I)/2021, read 4 October 2026) provides that amounts defined as electronic money under the Electronic Money Law do not fall within the scope of the Law; art. 3(1) applies the Law to credit institutions. The Law itself contains no rule on client or beneficiary accounts - the words for 'client account', 'absolutely entitled' and 'beneficiary' do not occur in it; those rules sit in the Regulations made under its art. 32 (K.D.P. 27/2016 as amended).

m-0425d04a.t: The Central Bank of Cyprus's deposit-guarantee FAQ (file dated 8 October 2025, read 4 October 2026) says in q.24 that 'irrespective of the account holder' the scheme covers the absolute beneficiaries 'of all client accounts' unless they fall into an excluded category, up to EUR 100,000 per person per credit institution, and that a beneficiary's share in a client account and his or her personal deposit at the same bank 'are summed up', the total being capped at EUR 100,000. So money a customer holds through a client account at a bank where the customer also has an account does not add a second EUR 100,000. The FAQ does not name safeguarding accounts of payment or e-money institutions.

m-8d81078d.t: A natural person - a sole trader - may register in Cyprus as an employer. The Social Insurance Services' form YKA 1-001 (edition 9/2021, linked on their employer-registration page updated 30 September 2026; read 6 October 2026) has a block 'to be completed only if the employer is a natural person' (date he became an employer, kind of business, activity, NACE code) beside one for a legal person, partnership or other entity, and asks for the employer's surname, nationality, social insurance number and identity card, EU registration, alien registration or passport number. Its document list names items only for companies and partnerships, not for a natural person.

m-f6a3162a.t: Cyprus's minimum wage is reviewed on a fixed cycle. Para 7 of the Minimum Wage Decree 2022 (K.D.P. 350/2022) sets an adjustment mechanism: a nine-member committee reports to the Minister of Labour at least two months before each revision and the Minister proposes an adjustment - which may be zero - to the Council of Ministers; it applied first on 1 January 2024 and 'thereafter every two years'. The 2024 and 2026 rates followed that cycle (K.D.P. 402/2023, K.D.P. 427/2025), so the next revision falls on 1 January 2028. Paras 10-11 allow reductions: by agreement up to 15% where the employer provides food and up to 10% for accommodation; 25% for casual work of under-18s up to two months.

m-e4c67e73.t: How an employer identifies the person in a hire notice in Cyprus's Ergani system depends on nationality, per the system's user manual (PDF of 7 September 2021, linked from the Ergani login page on 5 Oct 2026), s. 4.2.1. Cypriot: identity-card number or social insurance number. Citizen of an EU state: an EU identity number with the country, an alien registration number and/or a social insurance number; if the match fails, the notice can go on once an identification file is uploaded. Non-EU national: an alien registration number or a social insurance number; a failed match stops the notice, and submission cannot be completed without uploading documents legitimising the person's access to work.

m-b323e21d.t: A Cyprus company owes a director a written statement of terms if he is its employee. Law 25(I)/2023 on Transparent and Predictable Working Conditions (transposing Directive (EU) 2019/1152) applies to 'all employees' except those working on average up to three hours a week; seafarers and fishermen are covered with carve-outs (art. 4). 'Employee' (art. 3) turns on an employment relationship, 'taking into account the case law of the Court of Justice'. The employer gives the basic terms (parties, place, job, start date, pay, working time and others) on paper or electronically within seven calendar days of the start, the rest within one month (arts 11-12). No exception for directors is named.

m-b0fd609d.t: Not every step of a Cyprus founder's path runs through CY Login. As of 5 October 2026 the Ministry of Labour's Ergani system (hiring notifications, terms of employment) has its own user name and password, and its registration form begins with the employer's registration number from the Social Insurance Services, in the format 123456/1/1234 - so an Ergani account cannot exist before the company is registered as an employer. The Services' Employer Guide (PDF of 2 June 2025) says contributions are paid electronically through SISnet. CY Login is required by the Tax Department for a company's tax registration and is the gateway to the beneficial-owner register.

m-973808ae.t: Cyprus's national minimum wage in force on 5 October 2026 is €1,088 a month for full-time employment, and €979 for an employee who has not completed six months of continuous employment with the same employer. It is set by the Minimum Wage Decree of 2022 (K.D.P. 350/2022, made under s. 3(1) of the Minimum Wage Law, Cap. 183, in force 1 January 2023), para 5 as replaced by the amending Decree K.D.P. 427/2025 (Gazette No. 5989, 31 December 2025) with effect from 1 January 2026. Earlier steps: €940 and €885 from 1 January 2023; €1,000 and €900 from 1 January 2024 (K.D.P. 402/2023, repealed by the 2025 decree). Part-time pay is adjusted in proportion to hours.

m-74a20520.t: Cyprus's Minimum Wage Decree has no exception and no rule for directors or shareholders. K.D.P. 350/2022 applies to 'all employees in the Republic' (para 3(1)); an employee is a person working for another under a contract or relationship of employment or apprenticeship, or in circumstances from which an employer-employee relationship can be inferred (para 2). Outside it (3(2)-(5)): domestic, farm and livestock workers, seafarers; workers under more favourable arrangements; hotel staff under their own decree; trainees for a diploma or profession. 'Minimum monthly wage' means total gross monthly insurable earnings in money. Whether a sole shareholder-director is an 'employee' is not addressed.

m-7217f510.t: Where a new employer registers in Cyprus, per the Social Insurance Services' Employer Guide (PDF created 2 June 2025, on a page of the Services last updated 30 September 2026): the application (form YKA 1-001) is handed in at any District Social Insurance Office or at a Citizen Service Centre, no later than one day before the applicant expects to become an employer; an employer with branches in several districts or more than one economic activity registers separately for each; after registration the employer is told its register number, used for paying contributions and in all dealings with the Services; contributions are paid through SISnet. The Guide states no time for issuing the number.

m-43ec2fef.t: The Cyprus employer registration form YKA 1-001 (9/2021; linked on 5 Oct 2026 from the Social Insurance Services' employers page, updated 30 September 2026, and from the business portal) lists seven 'certificates/supporting documents' without saying which are alternatives: copies of the certificate of incorporation and of directors; 'certificate of registration with the VAT Service and first VAT return'; the lease of the place of work; a contract for works; and proof of the real start date if it differs from the incorporation date. It also asks for details of one intended employee, and for each director an identity-card number or, 'for aliens', an alien registration or passport number.

m-0f44a559.t: A new employer in Cyprus can enter the Ergani hiring system only once the Social Insurance Services have registered it. The gov.cy page 'Recruitment of new employees' (read 5 Oct 2026) says registering at Ergani needs the employer registration number plus a contributions receipt number, a SISNET payment order number of the last three years, 'or the date of commencement of employment of the employer'. Form YKA 1-001 (9/2021) names in that place the date of the employer's registration with the Services, 'stated in the letter approving the employer's registration' - by inference the same date; number and date also open the contributions payment system. Ergani has its own login, not CY Login.

m-ca23a3e8.t: ECB payments statistics, card payments made with cards issued by payment service providers resident in Cyprus ('card payments, sent'): 2012 - 41.5 million, EUR 3.51 billion; 2013 - 41.1m, 3.20bn; 2014 - 38.7m, 2.85bn; 2015 - 44.3m, 3.22bn; 2016 - 50.4m, 3.46bn; 2017 - 58.7m, 3.87bn; 2018 - number suppressed, 5.00bn; 2019 and 2020 - suppressed; 2021 - 123.8m, 7.37bn; 2022 - 174.3m, 11.43bn; 2023 - 211.2m, 13.37bn; 2024 - 230.5m, 14.60bn; 2025 - 250.8m, 16.36bn. From reference year 2022 the data are collected under Regulation ECB/2020/59 (Regulation (EU) 2020/2011), so the step from 2021 to 2022 includes a change of method.

m-be721aa4.t: Eurobank reaches 100% of Hellenic Bank: Eurobank S.A. announced on 11 June 2025 the completion of the squeeze-out (CySEC's approval of the squeeze-out application had been announced on 8 May 2025) at €4.843 per share in cash; the consideration was paid on 10 June 2025 and the remaining 8,279,967 shares (2.006% of the share capital) were transferred to Eurobank. From then Hellenic Bank was a wholly owned subsidiary of a Greek banking group.

m-ba6b753b.t: Cyprus Cooperative Bank (CCB): the European Commission approved liquidation aid for CCB's orderly market exit by decision of 19 June 2018; CCB and Hellenic Bank signed the final business transfer agreement on 25 June 2018, with closing set for 3 September 2018; the Commission approved the amended aid on 28 August 2018 (C(2018) 5674 final, SA.35334 (2018/N-3)). The Commission's post-programme surveillance report of November 2018 states that CCB surrendered its banking licence on 3 September 2018, when the sale to Hellenic Bank was effectively completed. The deal was an acquisition of certain assets and liabilities, not a purchase of the bank; the remainder stayed in a residual entity.

m-8a4b416b.t: Bank of Cyprus listing, step 1: Bank of Cyprus Holdings Public Limited Company (the Irish-incorporated holding company placed on top of the group) was admitted to listing and trading on the London Stock Exchange and the Cyprus Stock Exchange on 19 January 2017.

m-587772d8.t: RCB Bank: on 24 March 2022 the ECB announced decisions on RCB Bank Ltd's voluntary phase-out of banking operations (no new deposits, loans or investments; sale of part of its performing loans to Hellenic Bank approved; a temporary administrator; full repayment of depositors). On 22 December 2022 the ECB announced that it had withdrawn the bank's licence following the 'orderly completion' of that phase-out. The legal entity was not dissolved: LEI 253400EBCBBVB9TUHN50, which the ECB's list of February 2022 carried for 'RCB Bank LTD', is registered on 2026-10-04 to FINSTELLA LTD (HE 72376, Limassol), status active.

m-49f79240.t: Bank of Cyprus, how the Athens listing ended in 2017: Bank of Cyprus Public Company Ltd announced on 4 January 2017 that its existing shares would be suspended from trading on the Cyprus Stock Exchange and the Athens Exchange 'with effect from and including 10 January 2017'; the court-sanctioned scheme of arrangement that put Bank of Cyprus Holdings plc on top of the group became effective on 18 January 2017; the holding company's shares were admitted on 19 January 2017 to the London Stock Exchange (standard listing) and the Cyprus Stock Exchange only. The group returned to Athens in September 2024.

m-44e355e2.t: Bank of Cyprus listing, step 2: Bank of Cyprus Holdings' shareholders approved a listing on the Athens Stock Exchange on 13 September 2024 and the ATHEX listing committee approved it on 17 September 2024. The company confirmed on 23 September 2024 that delisting from the London Stock Exchange took effect at 8:00 a.m. (London time) on 19 September 2024 (last LSE trading day announced in advance as 18 September) and that trading on ATHEX began on 23 September 2024 under the symbol BOCHGR. The shares continue to trade on the Cyprus Stock Exchange, and Ireland remains the home member state.

m-3ca23e34.t: AstroBank after the transfer: GLEIF record 549300VB6UM9TUOCYW67 (ASTROBANK PUBLIC COMPANY LIMITED, HE 189515) carries a mergers-and-acquisitions event effective 31 October 2025 with Alpha Bank Cyprus Ltd (LEI 529900VS0F7BA91P4I60) as successor, and shows the entity as inactive, registration retired (last update 28 July 2026). The Central Bank of Cyprus counted 5 local authorised credit institutions at end-2025 but lists 4 in its LEI list (file dated 28.05.2026) and in its register read on 2026-10-04 (Ancoria Bank, Bank of Cyprus, Cyprus Development Bank, Housing Finance Corporation), so AstroBank's banking licence ended between 31 December 2025 and 28 May 2026; the exact date was not found.

m-2815444c.t: Eurobank takes control of Hellenic Bank: on 3 June 2024, after regulatory approvals, Eurobank S.A. bought a further 26.1% of Hellenic Bank Public Company Limited (107,694,301 shares at €2.56, €275.7 million in total), lifting its direct holding from 29.20% to 55.3%, and on 4 June 2024 announced a mandatory takeover bid for up to 100% at €2.56 per share. 3 June 2024 is the date control passed; the earlier share-purchase agreements were announcements, not completion.

m-269c1cae.t: Pattern in the Cyprus timeline 2013-2021 (checked 2026-10-04): the date in circulation is often not the date the rule took effect. Cases: capital controls (the last day of restrictions was Sunday 5 April 2015, by expiry of the 35th decree; the first free day was 6 April); IP box (in force 1 July 2016 only by retroactive commencement of Law 110(I)/2016, published 27 October 2016); beneficial-owner register (directive in force 12 March 2021; e-filing announced to open 16 March 2021); card acceptance (art. 30A in force 20 August 2020, decree published 18 June 2021 - the cylaw index dates it 28 June - and the duty operative three months later); strong customer authentication (legal date 14 September 2019; 31 December 2020 is the date the EBA recommended for ending supervisory flexibility).

m-d6f6284c.t: K.D.P. 267/2026, the TARGET-CY System (Amending) Directive of 2026 (Official Gazette Annex III(I) No. 6029, 12 June 2026), was issued by the Central Bank of Cyprus to comply with ECB Guideline ECB/2026/11 of 4 May 2026. It adds the EPC 'One-Leg Out' instant credit transfer scheme (OCT Inst) to the TIPS conditions and restates para 4(1) of the participation rules (credit institutions and central banks); parts apply from 15 June 2026, the rest from 14 November 2026. It does not mention non-bank payment service providers: in the Bank's unofficial consolidation for 2023-2026 they remain among the entities it may admit at its discretion (para 4(2)(da), inserted by K.D.P. 293/2025).

m-c893ebfc.t: Three dated versions of the EPC SCT Inst register show how the Cyprus rows changed. The export archived on 21 October 2025 has 20 Cyprus rows, among them 'AstroBank Limited' (PIRBCY2NXXX, readiness 2 December 2024), Hellenic Bank (HEBACY2NXXX) and Housing Finance Corporation with readiness 9 January 2025. In the version of 9 January 2026 (22 rows) AstroBank is still listed, with no leaving date, and Housing Finance Corporation already carries 8 December 2025. The export of 11 September 2026 has 25 rows: AstroBank is gone, HEBACY2NXXX is named Eurobank Limited, and six non-banks are new. The register rewrites names and readiness dates and drops leavers: it is not a history.

m-fa15111f.t: The ECB's 'List of TIPS participants and reachable parties' (euro; last update 1 October 2026) contains 38 BICs with the Cyprus country code, held under 23 institution codes: 14 of banks or bank branches (among them the Central Bank of Cyprus, the Cyprus branches of Central Cooperative Bank and First Investment Bank, and PIRBCY2N, shown as 'Alpha Bank Cyprus Ltd (formerly AstroBank ...)') and 9 of non-banks - Unlimit, Xryma, Intraclear, Onevault, Oro Pay, Payabl. CY, Solid Processing, Sureswipe and TFI Ecommpay. The list gives only BIC and name: it does not say who is a direct participant, who is reachable behind another participant, or at which central bank the account is held.

m-f213fbf9.t: EPC register of SEPA Instant Credit Transfer (SCT Inst) participants, export of 11 September 2026: 25 rows (BICs) with country Cyprus. Bank readiness dates: Bank of Cyprus 1 July 2024; Ancoria, Banque SBA and Eurobank Limited (HEBACY2N, ex-Hellenic) 2 December 2024; Alpha Bank Cyprus and National Bank of Greece (Cyprus) 6 January 2025; Central Bank of Cyprus, Societe Generale Cyprus, Cyprus Development Bank and 'Eurobank Cyprus Ltd' (ERBKCY2N, now part of Eurobank Limited) 9 January 2025; Housing Finance Corporation 8 December 2025 (9 January 2025 in the export archived 21 October 2025). AstroBank, in that earlier export, is gone. 'Readiness Date' is not the date of the first customer offer.

m-f172adee.t: As of 4 October 2026 the Central Bank of Cyprus lists the participants of T2-CY, the Cyprus component of T2, as 'credit institutions operating in Cyprus, the Cyprus Stock Exchange, the Cyprus SEPA Direct Debit Payment System (CY-SDD), the Cyprus Clearing House for cheques (CCH), JCC Cards and the Central Bank of Cyprus'. No payment or e-money institution is named, a year after K.D.P. 293/2025 made their admission possible; on TIPS-CY the page says only that the Bank 'stands ready' to support credit institutions 'and other potential participants'. The page is undated and lists no TARGET-CY or TIPS-CY account holders, so it does not show whether any non-bank has been admitted.

m-e4d64d16.t: In the EPC SCT Inst register the earliest Cyprus readiness dates belong to non-banks: Xryma Plc (ex-ISX Financial EU, an e-money institution) 6 May 2019, Unlimit EU 7 March 2022, Intraclear 12 September 2022 and Payabl.CY 31 October 2022 - the only four Cyprus rows in the register version of 12 January 2024, before the first bank (Bank of Cyprus, 1 July 2024). Later non-banks (export of 11 September 2026): Solid Processing 2 December 2024, Ecommbx 3 March 2025, TFI Ecommpay 31 March 2025, Sureswipe 6 October 2025, Onevault 2 February 2026, Moneygate 1 April 2026, Oro Pay 8 April 2026, AEON and Altery EU 31 August 2026, Sepaga 7 December 2026 (a future date): 14 of 25 Cyprus rows.

m-dbd6ae75.t: Instant payments at Cyprus banks: Bank of Cyprus offered outgoing instant euro transfers by July 2024, calling itself 'the only Bank in Cyprus at the moment' to do so (reported 22 July 2024) — before the regulatory deadline. 9 January 2025 was the deadline to receive; the Governor of the Central Bank of Cyprus said on 16 January 2025 that 'as of the 9th of January of this year, instant payments have become a reality for all banking participants'. Sending became mandatory on 9 October 2025; the CBC's Annual Report 2025 records a significant rise in instant-payment settlement in the second half of 2025 'as a result of the gradual expansion of instant payment services by credit institutions'.

m-521d8e65.t: Instant Payments Regulation (EU) 2024/886 (done 13 March 2024, OJ 19 March 2024): PSPs in euro-area member states that offer ordinary euro credit transfers must offer receiving of instant credit transfers in euro by 9 January 2025 and sending by 9 October 2025; charges may not exceed those for ordinary credit transfers from 9 January 2025; the verification-of-payee service is due by 9 October 2025; payment institutions and e-money institutions in the euro area have until 9 April 2027 for both sending and receiving. The Central Bank of Cyprus reminded the market of these dates on 10 December 2024 ('banks to receive' by 9 January 2025, 'banks to send' by 9 October 2025).

m-f9af2ebb.t: Visa's published domestic interchange table for Cyprus, dated April 2025 and still the one linked from Visa's European interchange page on 4 October 2026, sets consumer debit and prepaid cards at 0.20% and consumer credit and deferred debit at 0.30% (government payments capped at EUR 10.00 and EUR 15.00 a transaction). Commercial cards are far higher: Visa Business, Corporate and Purchasing 1.75%, Platinum and Infinite Business 2.00%, with 0.90% for government payments (minimum EUR 0.45, cap EUR 45.00) and utility bills (minimum EUR 0.24, cap EUR 61.20); only the 'Small Market Expense' and 'Large Market Enterprise' products are at 0.30%. No domestic V PAY cards are in issue.

m-908f9e98.t: The 2019 antitrust commitments capping interchange on non-EEA consumer cards used at EEA merchants have expired; the same caps continue voluntarily until November 2029. The Commission's Daily News of 5 July 2024 'takes note of the voluntary continuation by Visa and Mastercard of the caps' beyond November 2024, for 'another 5 years': 0.2% debit and 0.3% credit when the card is present, 1.15% debit and 1.5% credit when it is not. Mastercard Europe's undertaking, signed 1 July 2024, says its commitments 'will expire on 1 November 2024' and takes effect that day for five years. Visa's live table (5 October 2026) and Mastercard's table as archived on 11 December 2025 still show those four rates.

m-81479ea2.t: For a card issued in one EEA country and used at a merchant in another, Visa's intra-EEA interchange table (April 2025, live on 4 October 2026) gives 0.20% for consumer debit and prepaid and 0.30% for consumer credit. Commercial cards are outside the caps: Visa Business debit and credit 1.30% for chip or contactless and 1.65% for e-commerce; Platinum Business and Corporate 1.55% and 1.90%; Infinite Business 1.65% and 2.00%; Purchasing 1.55% and 1.90%; prepaid business cards carry a EUR 0.35 minimum. A footnote lets a cross-border acquirer of an in-country consumer transaction choose between the intra-EEA rate and the equivalent domestic rate.

m-497e8165.t: Mastercard's domestic interchange table for Cyprus (archive capture of 11 December 2025) sets consumer credit at 0.30% and consumer debit, prepaid and Maestro at 0.20% in every fee tier (valid from 1 April 2020; government payments capped at EUR 15.00 and EUR 10.00). Commercial cards, valid from 1 February 2023: 1.75% for Mastercard Business, corporate debit, fleet and purchasing cards, 1.80% for Corporate Prepaid, 1.90% for Corporate Credit, Business Preferred Credit and Business Premium Debit; lower sector rates - 1.45% at supermarkets and insurers, 1.00% at petrol stations, education and charities, 0.90% for utilities (EUR 0.24 to 61.20) and government (EUR 0.45 to 45.00).

m-43a01b68.t: Neither card scheme's European fee page publishes the scheme fees billed to a Cyprus merchant's acquirer. Visa's page (5 October 2026) links interchange tables only - inter-EEA, intra-EEA and one per country; Mastercard's page (captured 13 September 2026) likewise lists interchange files, an undertaking to the Commission and fallback interchange. A Cyprus merchant can therefore see its acquirer's pass-through schedule - JCC's is public - plus interchange: 0.20% and 0.30% on EEA consumer cards; mostly 1.3% to 2.0% on commercial cards, lower (0.30% to 1.45%) for some products and sectors; and 0.2%/0.3% card-present or 1.15%/1.5% card-not-present on consumer cards from outside the EEA.

m-ced0c98c.t: Regulation (EU) 2015/751 caps the per-transaction interchange fee at 0.2% of the transaction value for consumer debit card transactions and 0.3% for consumer credit card transactions (Articles 3(1) and 4), only where both the payer's and the payee's payment service providers are located in the Union (Article 1(1)); commercial cards, cash withdrawals and three-party schemes are outside the caps (Article 1(3)). It entered into force on 8 June 2015; the caps apply from 9 December 2015, and the rules on separation of scheme and processing, co-badging, unblending and 'honour all cards' (Articles 7 to 10) apply from 9 June 2016 (Article 18).

m-95217c55.t: Article 10 of Regulation (EU) 2015/751, applicable from 9 June 2016, forbids schemes and payment service providers to oblige a merchant that accepts one issuer's card to accept all other cards of the same scheme; the exception is consumer cards of the same brand and same category (prepaid, debit or credit) subject to the interchange caps, and a merchant that does not accept all cards must say so at the shop entrance and at the till, or on its website. Scheme rules follow: a Visa 'Limited Acceptance Merchant' in the EEA that accepts credit cards must accept all EEA-issued credit cards but need not accept EEA-issued commercial cards (Visa section 1.5.4.6, ID# 0008680, edition 18 April 2026).

m-314458ac.t: Since 9 June 2016 Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2015/751 requires each acquirer to offer and charge merchant service charges individually specified for different categories and brands of cards, and to state in the merchant agreement the merchant service charge, interchange fee and scheme fees per category and brand, unless the merchant asks in writing for blended pricing. Visa mirrors this for Europe: the Merchant Agreement must tell the merchant that pricing on a 'MIF Plus Plus' basis is available and must not blend charges between Visa and other schemes unless the merchant specifically requests it (Visa section 5.2.1.6, Table 5-1, ID# 0028044, edition 18 April 2026).

m-d109dd0a.t: With 3-D Secure, fraud liability moves to the issuer under both schemes. Visa's condition 10.4 (card-absent fraud; edition 18 April 2026) makes a dispute invalid for a transaction sent with Electronic Commerce Indicator 5 where the issuer confirmed authentication using Visa Secure with EMV 3DS and the CAVV was in the authorisation request, and for ECI 6 with an attempt response and a CAVV, unless the card is a non-reloadable prepaid card. Mastercard's Chargeback Guide (19 May 2026) lists as ineligible for the fraud chargeback 4837 'properly authenticated transactions' with security level indicators 211, 212, 217 or 242, naming Identity Check as an example. Other grounds stay available.

m-c2c774c9.t: SCA in Cyprus, the missing step: on 24 December 2019 the Central Bank of Cyprus announced that, in view of the EBA Opinion of 16 October 2019, it 'does not intend to take supervisory enforcement action against licensed institutions which have not implemented SCA in remote electronic card transactions by 31 December 2020, provided that these institutions have submitted a migration plan' to it; the same was sent directly to licensed institutions. It stressed that 14 September 2019 'remains as the legal deadline' and that the risk of not using compliant SCA after that date is borne fully by payment service providers under Article 74 of the Payment Services Laws of 2018 and 2019.

m-c20e22bb.t: The EBA's report on the SCA migration (EBA/REP/2021/16, 11 June 2021) shows Cyprus only in bar charts by Member State, without printed values.
