EU-wide, as of 30 April 2021: 94% of payment cards were SCA-enabled (88% at end-2020), 82% of payment service users enrolled (75%) and 99% of e-merchants able to support SCA (98%). Read off Figure 1, Cyprus stood at roughly 94% of cards and about 80% of users. The report warns that jurisdictions with large shares of cross-border transactions may show lower compliance rates, and that some authorities surveyed all providers and others a subset. It is a data report: it does not list which authorities adopted the 31 December 2020 date.

m-36c35071.t: No public Mastercard network document read gives the end date of 3-D Secure 1.0 (SecureCode). What is public: Europe Region rule 5.8.1 of the Transaction Processing Rules of 14 June 2022 still said a merchant supporting SecureCode 'must continue to support the current 3DS 1.0.2 format'; the edition of 20 December 2022 drops the sentence and notes 'References to SecureCode changed to Identity Check'. Mastercard's gateway business wrote that it was 'aligning with the Schemes mandates and discontinuing our support of 3DS 1.0 in October 2022'. The vendor Netcetera announced on 10 August 2022 that Mastercard would decommission it on 18 October 2022, and on 3 October 2023 in India and Bangladesh.

m-b86a14bb.t: SCA, EU step: EBA Opinion EBA-Op-2019-11 of 16 October 2019, addressed to national competent authorities, states that migration plans of payment service providers for e-commerce card payments, 'including the implementation and testing by merchants, should be completed by 31 December 2020'. It is a recommendation on when supervisory flexibility should end, not a new legal date: the Opinion itself says the SCA requirements apply as of 14 September 2019 and that flexibility only means authorities would not take enforcement action against providers that keep to the plan. The Central Bank of Cyprus adopted that date, conditionally on a migration plan, in its announcement of 24 December 2019.

m-97691380.t: SCA, Cyprus step: on Monday 2 September 2019 the Central Bank of Cyprus told the payments industry that, in line with the EBA Opinion published on 21 June 2019, it intended to grant card issuers and acquirers that already supported a non-reusable, non-replicable element (e.g. OTP) for online card transactions 'a limited migration period' for SCA in remote card transactions. Its length had 'not yet been determined by the EBA'; once the duration was communicated, affected issuers and acquirers would have to draw up a detailed migration plan and submit it to the CBC. The application date of the SCA rules, 14 September 2019 (Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/389, Art. 38(2)), was not changed.

m-1ecb19c8.t: Visa announced on 4 February 2021 (article AI10745) that it would discontinue support for 3-D Secure 1.0.2 effective 15 October 2022, and repeated the date in a final reminder of 29 September 2022 (AI12378) scoped global except Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Maldives, Nepal and Sri Lanka; EMV 3DS, first published in October 2016, is the successor. Mastercard's Transaction Processing Rules for the Europe Region (edition 9 December 2025) state that for a Remote Electronic Transaction 'authentication using EMV 3DS and Identity Check is required and may be omitted only if an Acquirer exemption to SCA applies' or another SCA-compliant method or an Article 17 exemption is used.

m-eb07b1f1.t: Under Visa section 5.3.1.4 (ID# 0030891, edition 18 April 2026, last updated Oct 2025) an acquirer must sign a direct Merchant Agreement with a Sponsored Merchant that 'exceeds USD 1 million in annual Transaction volume' - before processing for a merchant new to the facilitator, or within 2 years after an existing one crosses it. 'Transaction' is a glossary term tied to Visa-branded Cards, so the base is the merchant's own Visa volume. Exempt: relationships held 2 years with the same acquirer, with reporting and continued acquirer oversight, and listed MCCs (utilities, healthcare, schools, tax and others). Brazil and Chile are carved out; there is no Europe variation.

m-c31043ee.t: Mastercard Rule 7.8 (edition 2 June 2026, archive snapshot of 28.09.2026) requires any Sponsored Merchant exceeding USD 10,000,000 in combined annual Mastercard and Maestro transaction volume to sign a Merchant Agreement directly with a Customer (a Mastercard licensee) unless either all of these hold - facilitator registered as a Network Enablement Partner, Franchise Management Program review of the acquirer, acquirer read-only access to the facilitator's systems, e-commerce merchant monitoring, monthly acquirer review of 5% of new sponsored merchants - or its primary MCC is on an exception list (utilities, rent, healthcare, schools, tax, MCC 6012). No Europe Region variation exists.

m-a2d8ff73.t: Per brand, from the Central Bank of Cyprus incoming EMI register (file of 23.09.2026) and each firm's own pages read 04.10.2026: Stripe Technology Europe Limited (notified 25.03.2019) is named in Stripe's Acquirer Disclosure as the EEA 'Payment Method Acquirer' - an acquirer, not a payment facilitator; myPOS Limited (20.09.2022) calls itself a member of Mastercard, Visa and Amex; SumUp EU Payments UAB (06.11.2019) is the entity on SumUp's Cyprus site, and its Payment Terms say it accepts cards through partner acquirers (Worldpay, First Data, Adyen, American Express) without saying which one serves Cyprus; Squareup International Limited (29.11.2021) is a notification only - Square offers no card acceptance in Cyprus. All four rows list service 5. Inference: facilitator thresholds do not reach a merchant acquired directly (Stripe, myPOS); SumUp's terms provide for a separate agreement above a payment volume.

m-9617d11f.t: For Mastercard a Payment Facilitator is a Service Provider registered by an acquirer, and its Sponsored Merchant Agreement 'must clearly and conspicuously reflect that the Payment Facilitator is entering into the Sponsored Merchant Agreement on behalf of and as an agent of the Acquirer' (Rule 7.8.1, edition 2 June 2026). Rule 7.6.5 makes the acquirer responsible for all acts and omissions of the facilitator and its sponsored merchants. Rule 7.6.5.1 requires the sponsored merchant, not the facilitator, to be within the acquirer's Area of Use; in the Europe Region chapter an EEA licence covers the whole EEA (Rule 1.7) and central acquiring authorisation replaces a licence extension.

m-2ef59dbb.t: Visa defines a Payment Facilitator as 'an entity that contracts with an Acquirer to deposit Transactions, receive settlement from, or contract with an Acquirer on behalf of a Sponsored Merchant' (glossary ID# 0028921, edition 18 April 2026). Under section 5.3.1.2 (ID# 0006574) a Sponsored Merchant is treated as a merchant of the facilitator's acquirer, and the acquirer is liable for all acts, omissions and other adverse conditions caused by the facilitator and its sponsored merchants.

m-07fbb831.t: Mastercard raised its payment-facilitator sub-merchant threshold tenfold in December 2022. Rule 7.8 of the Mastercard Rules dated 7 June 2022 required a direct Merchant Agreement for 'any Submerchant that exceeds USD 1,000,000' in combined annual Mastercard and Maestro volume; the 6 December 2022 edition kept USD 1,000,000 and added the 'Submerchant Threshold Conditions'; the 13 December 2022 edition's summary of changes reads 'Updated value 1,000,000 to 10,000,000'; the 6 June 2023 edition only renamed Submerchant to Sponsored Merchant. Visa's threshold was USD 1 million in both its 23 April 2022 and 18 April 2026 editions. Mastercard editions were read from Internet Archive snapshots.

m-e105fbbd.t: Law 41(I)/2026 (Official Gazette no. 5082, 2 April 2026), adopted 'for re-harmonisation with article 16 of Directive 2014/92/EU', replaced art. 17(9) of Cyprus Law 64(I)/2017: a bank may no longer refuse a payment account with basic features on the ground that the consumer already holds a payment account with another credit institution in Cyprus. It also deleted art. 17(10) (the bank's check for an existing account) and art. 20(2)(e) (termination because the consumer later opened a second account). Before the amendment the law allowed such a refusal. On 4 October 2026 CyLaw's consolidated text does not yet incorporate the change.

m-b8e0b8bf.t: Bank of Cyprus' 'Payment Account with basic features' (read 4 October 2026) is addressed to physical persons legally residing in the European Union, is opened at a branch, is limited to one per customer, carries no overdraft or chequebook and can be linked only to a Classic Visa debit card; the page states 'The customer cannot be a legal entity'. The maximum charge is EUR 36 per calendar year provided the number of transactions does not exceed 100. For such applicants the CBC Directive of 2025 (para 32) accepts identification on official documents issued by the Cypriot authorities, such as the special residence permit or refugee travel document, and address verification by sworn affidavit.

m-678a5dd3.t: Cyprus transposed Directive 2014/92/EU by Law 64(I)/2017 (Gazette no. 4604, 16 June 2017; amended 2020, 2021, 2026). All credit institutions must offer basic payment accounts to consumers (art. 17(1)) unless the Central Bank exempts one on a reasoned application (art. 17(2)); consumers legally resident in the EU, including asylum seekers, have the right to open one (art. 17(4)); the bank must decide within ten business days of a complete application (art. 17(7)) and must refuse if opening would breach Law 188(I)/2007 (art. 17(8)); services are free or reasonably priced (art. 19(1)). 'Consumer' is a natural person acting outside trade or profession (art. 2); legal entities have no such right.

m-66b403ad.t: Directive 2014/92/EU (in force, unamended on 4 October 2026) gives the right to a basic payment account to 'consumers legally resident in the Union', including asylum seekers and persons with no fixed address (art. 16(2)). A consumer is a natural person acting outside trade, business, craft or profession (art. 2(1)), so companies and individuals acting in business have no such right. The account covers deposits, cash withdrawals, direct debits, card payments and credit transfers (art. 17(1)). The bank must open or refuse within 10 business days of a complete application and must refuse if opening would breach AML rules (art. 16(3)-(4)). Chapter IV applies from 18 September 2016.

m-ab638aa1.t: ECB direct supervision of Cyprus banks, per the ECB list of supervised entities with cut-off date 1 July 2026 (110 significant entities): Bank of Cyprus Public Company Ltd (LEI PQ0RAP85KK9Z75ONZW93), under Bank of Cyprus Holdings PLC (Ireland), significant for national economic importance; Eurobank Limited (LEI CXUHEGU3MADZ2CEV7C11 — per GLEIF the former Hellenic Bank) and Alpha Bank Cyprus Ltd (LEI 529900VS0F7BA91P4I60), among the three largest credit institutions in Cyprus, listed under their Greek parents; National Bank of Greece (Cyprus) Ltd (LEI 5493008QZPPHVJ8Q4F45) under the NBG group. Four other Cyprus credit institutions are listed as less significant (Central Bank of Cyprus).

m-64d1235e.t: The Central Bank of Cyprus registers of institutions passported into Cyprus (files dated 23/09/2026) list 244 EMIs and 344 payment institutions, against 32 EMIs (file 28/09/2026) and 10 payment institutions (17/09/2026) licensed in Cyprus. Incoming EMIs include Stripe Technology Europe Limited, myPOS Limited and Squareup International Limited (IE), SumUp EU Payments UAB (LT), Paynetics AD and iCard AD (BG); incoming PIs include Worldline Greece Payment Institution S.A. (acquiring only), Worldline SA (BE), Wise Europe SA (BE) and eMerchantPay Netherlands B.V. A listing proves a passport notification, not active selling in Cyprus. Adyen, Revolut, PayPal and Viva are banks and are not listed.

m-3a6d983e.t: Two source traps met on 2026-10-04. (1) https://www.centralbank.cy/en/announcements/<slug> answers HTTP 200 with the site frame and an empty body for slugs that do not exist (seen for 18072014-1, 19072014, 20072014, 24072014), and a mis-encoded file URL on the same site returns the home page with status 200; a 200 does not show that a Central Bank of Cyprus announcement or file exists - the body must carry a title and a date line, or the PDF signature. (2) The cylaw.org index of regulatory acts dates K.D.P. 259/2021 '28/6/2021', while the Gazette page itself reads Friday 18 June 2021: index dates must be checked against the PDF header.

m-33460116.t: Central Bank of Cyprus — what it supervises (statutes read on cylaw.org, 4 October 2026). Credit institutions under the Business of Credit Institutions Law 66(I)/1997, with significant banks supervised prudentially by the ECB; payment institutions under the Payment Services Law 31(I)/2018 (art. 22(1): licensing and prudential supervision; art. 99(1): compliance with the Law, except merchants' surcharge rules); electronic money institutions under the Electronic Money Law 81(I)/2012 ('Competent Authority' means the Central Bank). Under art. 59(1)(α) of AML Law 188(I)/2007 it is the AML supervisor of all three, including branches and agents of institutions licensed in other Member States.

m-d559f313.t: Direct supervision by the EU Anti-Money Laundering Authority (AMLA) had not started on 4 October 2026. Under art. 13(4) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1620 (consolidated text of 10 November 2025) AMLA must commence the first selection of 'selected obliged entities' by 1 July 2027, conclude it within six months, publish the list without undue delay and begin direct supervision six months after publication, which puts the start in 2028; selection is repeated every three years. Selected entities are credit and financial institutions or groups whose residual risk profile is high (art. 13(1)); where none qualifies in a Member State, an additional selection is run there (art. 13(3)).

m-944aacef.t: The other two acts of the 2024 EU AML package run on their own clocks. Directive (EU) 2024/1640 must be transposed by 10 July 2027, except art. 74 (access to beneficial-ownership information for persons with a legitimate interest) by 10 July 2025, arts. 11, 12, 13 and 15 (access to beneficial-ownership registers) by 10 July 2026, and art. 18 (single access point to real-estate information) by 10 July 2029 (art. 78(1)). Regulation (EU) 2024/1620 establishing the Anti-Money Laundering Authority (AMLA) has applied since 1 July 2025, with some articles applying from 26 June 2024 and art. 103 from 31 December 2025 (art. 108). Cyprus implemented art. 74 by Law 25(I)/2026 of 20 March 2026.

m-5c67bb3d.t: Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 (the AML Regulation, OJ 19 June 2024) applies from 10 July 2027, and from 10 July 2029 for football agents and professional football clubs (art. 90); on 4 October 2026 it is in force, unamended and not yet applicable. Art. 52(1) sets the ownership test for a beneficial owner at direct or indirect ownership of '25 % or more' of shares, voting rights or other ownership interest, against '25% plus one share' or 'more than 25%' in art. 2 of Cyprus Law 188(I)/2007. For higher-risk categories of entities the Commission may set a lower threshold by delegated act: at most 15%, unless it finds a higher one more proportionate, in any case below 25% (art. 52(2)).

m-39513d57.t: From 10 July 2027 Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 fixes the minimum identification data EU-wide, except in lower-risk cases (art. 22(1)). Natural person: all names and surnames, place and full date of birth, nationalities, national identification number where applicable, usual place of residence and, where available, tax identification number. Legal entity: legal form and name, registered office and principal place of business, country of creation, legal representatives and, where available, registration number, tax identification number and LEI, plus nominee shareholders and directors. Updates: at least yearly for higher-risk customers, every five years for others (art. 26(2)).

m-b934a7c3.t: Cyprus Securities and Exchange Commission (CySEC), continued under Law 73(I)/2009 (set up by a 2001 law that it repealed) — what it supervises: investment firms under Law 87(I)/2017; administrative (trust and company) service providers under Law 196(I)/2012; collective investment schemes and their managers; crypto-asset service providers — for all of which it is the AML supervisor under art. 59(1)(β) of Law 188(I)/2007. Under MiCA, national-regime providers had to apply by 27 February 2026 and their transitional period ended on 1 July 2026. ESMA's table of 7 July 2026 lists CySEC and the Central Bank of Cyprus as Cyprus's MiCA competent authorities; the designating act is the ministerial notification K.D.P. 310/2024 of 13 September 2024 under art. 56A of Law 73(I)/2009.

m-17060244.t: MiCA in Cyprus: Regulation (EU) 2023/1114 applies from 30 December 2024 (Titles III and IV from 30 June 2024). Cyprus kept the full 18-month transitional period of Art. 143(3) (ESMA list); CySEC's announcements rest on that article directly. On 17 October 2024 CySEC stopped accepting CASP registrations under national rules; providers registered before 30 December 2024 could continue until 1 July 2026 or until authorisation was granted or refused, and CySEC set 27 February 2026 as the deadline to apply. As of 2026-10-04 the period has ended: crypto-asset services in Cyprus need a MiCA authorisation (Art. 63) or, for already-licensed financial entities, an Art. 60 notification.

m-76e660fd.t: The Central Bank of Cyprus sent credit institutions a circular letter on shell companies on 14 June 2018; its text was not found (CBC site, web archive, 4 October 2026), though the CBC's circular of 2 November 2018 cites it and revises its definition. A law-firm alert of 20 June 2018 describes the June letter as notice of an intention, 'not yet officially adopted', to make banks avoid starting or renewing relationships with non-listed entities that have no physical presence beyond a mailing address, no established economic activity, registration where audited accounts need not be filed, or tax residence in a 'tax haven' or nowhere, and as a request to review the client base and report.

m-4a5ebf89.t: The Central Bank of Cyprus stated on 16 November 2023 that, as a result of its targeted supervisory actions, credit institutions had from the end of 2018 until then terminated relationships with 42,728 shell companies and closed 125,782 bank accounts; that it had imposed fines relating to AML/CFT inspections in 13 cases since 2015; and that a recruitment drive begun in 2019 had raised the headcount of its AML/CFT department by 50% by 2022. The statement gives no method, period breakdown or definition for the two counts.
